articles_hidden.title: The NF Data Portal: A Community-Driven Resource to Accelerate Neurofibromatosis and Schwannomatosis Research and Drug Development
articles_hidden.authors: Kara Quaid; Belinda B. Garana; Chang In Moon; Aditya Nath; Christina Parry; Efren Munoz; Jineta Banerjee; Alexandra J. Scott; Milen Nikolov; Sang Y. Lee
articles_hidden.abstract:
The NF Data Portal (nf.synapse.org) is a free, open-science platform that centralizes data and resources related to neurofibromatosis (NF) and schwannomatosis (SWN), a group of rare genetic tumor predisposition syndromes. The portal hosts a growing collection of NF and SWN multimodal datasets including genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics and imaging with links to resources such as patient-derived tumor tissue collections, cell lines and preclinical models. The goal of the portal is to provide the broader academic and commercial research community with well-annotated, trusted datasets that can be used in a variety of ways, including asking new scientific questions, benchmarking new methods or tools, and combining datasets across studies. Ultimately, our mission is to accelerate the discovery of treatments and cures for NF and SWN through maximizing the global usability of high-quality data. . 
The NF Data Portal has a cross-institutional backbone of supporters composed of funding organizations, a data coordination center, and a community of clinicians and scientists. Together, this community has developed reusable building blocks for open science, including shared infrastructure, governance frameworks, metadata standards, and a structured data contribution lifecycle. In this publication, we reflect on over a decade of effort to support the data contributor and data user journeys. We share recent platform features and integrations and highlight newly available datasets. 
Whether longtime NF scientists or those encountering this resource for the first time, the NF Data Portal provides access to one of the largest NF datasets available to advance academic research, industry-driven discovery and therapeutic development. For industry users, the portal serves as a strategic translational research asset that supports target validation, biomarker discovery, patient stratification and data-driven decision making, helping to de-risk development programs and inform clinical strategy. As AI-driven analytical methods transform biomedical research, richly annotated, disease-specific datasets like those housed in the NF Data Portal, will be essential raw material for developing and validating new tools and novel treatments.

articles_hidden.title: How Much Replication Is Enough? Balancing Novelty and Replication in a Truth-Driven Evolutionary Simulation
articles_hidden.authors: Kaitlyn Harper; Felix D. Schönbrodt
articles_hidden.abstract: Scientific progress relies on a balance of original research, which furthers the boundaries of knowledge, and replication, which assures the quality of existing knowledge. In recent years, calls for increased replication have gained momentum, but replication requires resources that could otherwise support novel research. Here, we take a cultural-evolutionary approach to answer the question: what share of limited scientific resources should be allocated to original versus replication studies? We simulated a scientific ecosystem with a “utopian” selection criterion: whether research moves beliefs closer to the truth. Within this ecosystem, researchers differ in their tendency to pursue original or replication work, and more successful strategies (i.e., those which contribute most to truthful Bayesian information gain) are selected for over time. Under broadly realistic parameter assumptions, the model suggests an optimal replicator share of 5-32%, with 7-21% of published studies being replications, and replication success rates of 20-30% (all replications) and 72-88% (only published replications). Stronger publication bias, greater base null rates, and smaller original study sample sizes all increase the optimal replicator share. Our model may underestimate the optimal replicator share, because the model omits biases such as p-hacking that additional replication could help correct, or overestimate, because our model’s simplistic choice of replication targets may be less efficient than more strategic ones. Ultimately, our simulations suggest that replication primarily evolves as a compensatory mechanism in response to distorted research environments, and that overall scientific progress is maximised when underlying issues such as publication bias are resolved, which would largely eliminate the need for replications.

articles_hidden.title: Time for Journals to Claim a Sustainable Future in Scientific Publishing
articles_hidden.authors: yong sik ok
articles_hidden.abstract: Scientific publishing depends on trust, fairness, and transparency. This article argues that publishers should take greater responsibility for how research integrity concerns, investigations, and retractions are handled. It calls for clearer procedures, fair opportunities for authors to respond, stronger editorial involvement, and proportionate decisions based on scientific judgment. Greater accountability and cooperation among publishers, editors, researchers, and institutions are essential for building a more trustworthy and sustainable scientific publishing system.

articles_hidden.title: Including the Tool Statcheck in Peer Review to Increase Analytical Reproducibility: A Randomized Experiment in Two Psychology Journals - STAGE 1 REPORT
articles_hidden.authors: Michele B. Nuijten; Don van Ravenzwaaij; John Edlund
articles_hidden.abstract: Many published papers in psychology and other fields are not reproducible: running the same analysis on the same data leads to different results. This undermines the credibility of reported findings. Some reproducibility problems, such as reported statistics that are internally inconsistent, can be spotted without access to raw data. In this study, we will test if using the tool statcheck in peer review could reduce such inconsistencies, by automatically flagging p-values that do not match their test statistic and degrees of freedom. We propose an experiment in two psychology journals in which, for the duration of one calendar year, a statcheck report will be included as an independent review in the editorial decision for half of the submissions that go out for peer review. We hypothesize that resulting published papers from the statcheck condition will contain fewer inconsistent p-values than papers from the control condition. We also hypothesize that there is a positive “spill-over” effect of the statcheck report and assess if overall reproducibility has improved more in the experimental condition than in the control condition. To test this, we will reanalyze the raw data of a subset of 20 papers per condition to verify all numbers in the Results section. Finally, we will keep track of rejection rates throughout the trial to assess if any reduction of statistical inconsistencies in published papers is due to corrections on the authors’ side or to a change in editorial rejection rates.

articles.title: Shared research materials in psychology are widely downloaded but often difficult to reuse
articles.authors: Daniel S Quintana
articles.abstract: Open science reforms have made posting data and code common, but are shared materials actually used, and easily reused? Treating download counts of Open Science Framework (OSF) supplements as a usage index, I analysed 1,660 articles from four psychology journals (Cognition, Psychological Science, Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, Journal of Memory and Language) across three years (2015, 2020, 2025). OSF sharing rose from 9% in 2015 to 52% in 2025. Among 392 papers with download data, materials were downloaded a median of 152 times; only 1% went undownloaded. Download volume was associated with citation count and altmetric attention. Availability did not ensure easy reuse: only 40% of repositories provided documentation, 34% were flagged for a hard-coded file path, and 42% referenced a missing file — shortcomings that did not improve as sharing grew. Altogether, shared materials are being used, but often not easily reusable.

articles.title: Partisans are more likely to entrench their beliefs in misinformation when political outgroup members correct claims
articles.authors: Diego A. Reinero; Elizabeth Ann Harris; Steve Rathje; Annie Duke; Jay Joseph Van Bavel
articles.abstract:
Misinformation has become a global issue with potentially dire consequences (e.g., election
results, COVID-19 vaccines, international conflicts). The most common strategy to reduce
beliefs in misinformation is to issue corrections or fact-checks. However, fact-checks are often
ineffective for polarized issues and there has been debate over whether misinformation
corrections sometimes "backfire," causing people to become more entrenched in misinformation.
Across three experiments (N = 1,217) we identify a key feature – the partisan identity of the
source – that explains when corrections will be effective and when they will be most likely to
backfire. We found that while corrections work on average, backfires still occurred 23% of the
time and were 52% more likely to occur when the correction came from a political outgroup vs.
ingroup member – leaving people with more entrenched beliefs in misinformation. Indeed, the
effect of partisan bias on initial belief in misinformation was 5x larger than the effect of
corrections. Partisan bias was most prominent and corrections were least effective when famous
politicians were involved. In sum, corrections have small effects compared to partisan identity
congruence, and sometimes backfire–especially if they come from a political outgroup member.

articles.title: Does Person-First Language Reduce Stigma? Evidence Across Health Condition Labels From Two Experimental Studies
articles.authors: Elizabeth Kruse; Paige Amormino; David Dodell-Feder
articles.abstract: The stigmatization of mental health conditions remains a widespread problem. One proposed intervention involves reforming the language used to describe people with mental health conditions by using terminology that separates the individual from the label (i.e., person-first language) rather than language that defines the individual by the label (i.e., identity-first or identity-only language). Across two studies, we tested whether manipulating the language used to describe an individual alters multiple dimensions of stigma, including attitudinal stigma, trait-based stereotype judgments, and dehumanization, across a broad and intentionally heterogeneous set of labels spanning mental health and related conditions. In Study 1, language framing did not consistently influence attitudinal stigma across labels, with the exception of responses to psychopathy. In Study 2, language framing did not significantly influence perceived stereotype judgments or dehumanization for any label examined. Instead, the specific label used and, to a lesser extent, personal familiarity with mental health conditions showed the most consistent associations with stigma across both studies. These findings suggest that individual labels are embedded in distinct social schemas that shape perceptions independent of language framing, and that social or personal contact may be a more reliable pathway to reducing stigma than terminology reform.

articles.title: Media Selectivity Research in Light of Self-Defeating Tendencies: Towards a Novel Understanding of Media Effects on Well-Being
articles.authors: Nicole Bizzotto; Tobias Dienlin; Silvia Knobloch-Westerwick
articles.abstract: A critical gap persists in media uses and effects research: while existing work has predominantly focused on self-serving motivations for media selection, an expanding body of evidence suggests that individuals—including those with psychological vulnerabilities—may seek out online content that aggravates, rather than alleviates, distress. Drawing on scholarship on self-defeating tendencies in offline contexts, we argue that the same process may unfold in mediated environments, especially on social media: when negative self-concepts are salient, users may gravitate toward content that validates these self-views, even at the expense of their well-being. We focus on mental health content as an illustrative case in which these dynamics become particularly visible and harmful, while arguing that similar processes apply to other domains. To guide this line of inquiry and offer a more comprehensive account of media selection processes and their implications for well-being, we extend the established Selective Exposure Self- and Affect-Management (SESAM) model by incorporating self-defeating motivations and outline a research agenda.

articles.title: Socialization in the Spotlight: Early Parent-Infant Synchrony, Mind-Mindedness, and Children’s Later Expressions of Shyness
articles.authors: Christopher Riddell; Milica Nikolic; Agneta Fischer; Itir Onal Ertugrul; Moniek Zeegers; Susan Bögels; Cristina Colonnesi
articles.abstract: Owing to their burgeoning understanding of the social world, the early childhood years represent a critical developmental period in which children's first expressions of shyness take shape. Nonverbal expressions of shyness have been argued to take two forms: positive shyness, characterized by smiling with a gaze and/or head aversion, and negative shyness, characterized by negative affect with a gaze and/or head aversion. Although early parental socialization practices are known to shape children’s emotions, few studies have examined how these influence shyness expressions beyond infancy. In a sample of 120 Dutch children and their parents, we examined two potential socialization mechanisms of preschool children’s expressions of shyness: positive affective synchrony (measured at 4-months) and mind-mindedness (measured at 12- and 30-months). We assessed these facets separately with both mothers and fathers during free-play tasks, and children’s expressions shyness during a public performance. Mothers’, but not fathers’, positive affective synchrony was associated with lower levels of negative shyness in childhood, consistent with a potentially protective role of early synchrony. Fathers' appropriate mind-mindedness, however, was unexpectedly associated with less positive and more negative shyness, while mothers' non-attuned mind-mindedness was associated with more positive shyness. Together, our results highlight the importance of early parent-child socialization practices in infancy for later expressions of shyness in childhood but suggest that these operate in context dependent ways.

articles.title: ChirPing: A Social Media Simulation Platform Developed for Scientific Research
articles.authors: Nadia Said; Lena Plötz; Nicole Antes
articles.abstract: Experimental research on behavior on social media platforms typically relies on two methodological approaches, each with advantages but also limitations. Experimental studies, while having the advantage of giving researchers full control over the content presented and allowing for direct assessment of other variables of interest, often lack ecological validity, as behavioral intentions are only weakly predictive of actual sharing behavior. Studies conducted directly on live platforms, by contrast, offer ecological validity. However, the lack of control over the experimental environment makes it difficult to draw causal inferences. To address those issues, social media simulation platforms have gained increasing popularity in research. However, these platforms vary widely in usability and flexibility: some require more advanced programming skills, while others are fairly easy to use but may be limited in their use cases. Here we present our social media simulation platform, ChirPing, a new tool embedded within the widely used experimental research platform SoSci Survey. The main advantage of our platform is that it is part of an established platform; thus, researchers can easily integrate it into their surveys and adjust it within a familiar tool environment. Furthermore, our platform is highly customizable, allowing researchers to systematically manipulate experimental parameters (e.g., content presentation and post order). Allowing researchers to examine, for example, causal effects on behavioral outcomes such as sharing, engagement, and decision-making.

articles.title: Dyadic JITAIs in Health Behavior Change: Key Components and Design Principles
articles.authors: Inbal Nahum-Shani; Lex Hurley; Ziping Xu; Carolyn Yoon; Jean-Philippe Laurenceau; Susan A Murphy
articles.abstract:
Purpose: The widespread adoption of digital technologies offers unprecedented opportunities for delivering accessible and affordable health behavior interventions. Advances in mobile and wireless technologies have the capacity to collect rich and granular data about people’s states and contexts and utilize this information to intervene in (near) real-time in everyday life. Just-in-time adaptive interventions (JITAIs) can realize these opportunities by guiding how rapidly changing information about the person should be used in practice to decide whether, when and how to intervene. However, promoting health behavior change often requires interventions that harness and/or modify existing dyadic relationships, such as those involving parents, partners, care partners, or peers. To date, most JITAIs have been designed around a single individual rather than the coordinated delivery of support across two interdependent individuals. 
Methods: This manuscript establishes a common terminology to guide the development of dyadic JITAIs and advance innovation in the field of dyadic health behavior change. By synthesizing literature on JITAIs and dyadic interventions, we define dyadic JITAIs, clarify their scientific rationale, and describe their key components. We also offer guidelines for designing effective, resource-efficient dyadic JITAIs and identify directions for future research. 
Conclusion: Dyadic JITAIs have substantial potential to support health behavior change through shaping and harnessing close relationships. Realizing this potential will require new theories, experimental designs, and data analytic approaches to empirically inform their development.

articles.title: Do trait and state empathy facilitate interpersonal synchrony in musical interactions?
articles.authors: Persefoni Tzanaki; Lieke Perik; Cagri Erdem; Jonna Katariina Vuoskoski
articles.abstract: Recent research suggests that cognitive empathy facilitates interpersonal synchrony, yet the role of affective empathy and its impact when experimentally induced remain less explored. We investigated how empathy, both as a trait characteristic and the result of induction, influences synchrony in a musical context. Thirty-three dyads completed two synchrony tasks, one before and one after an empathy induction session. In Task 1, participants tapped in time with a metronome before synchronising with their partner’s tapping, whereas in Task 2, they synchronised melodic sequences. To induce empathy, participants shared personal events while their partners were instructed either to empathise (empathy induction) or memorise factual details (control condition). Trait empathy was measured using the Interpersonal Reactivity Index (IRI). Emotional engagement and behavioural mirroring during empathy induction were assessed using self-report and motion-capture measures. Results showed that both cognitive and affective trait empathy contributed to synchrony: higher Empathic Concern (an affective IRI subscale) predicted better alignment with a metronome in Task 1, while higher Fantasy (cognitive IRI) predicted greater synchrony in Task 2, suggesting that empathy’s role may rely on the type of coordination required by the task. Induced empathy showed no main effects; however, high-Fantasy participants who reported greater emotional engagement with partners’ stories synchronised better in Task 2 than those who engaged less. Moreover, high-Fantasy dyads showed greater mirroring of narrators’ head movements in the control condition, whereas this association became weakly negative when empathy was induced. The findings indicate a multifaceted role of empathy in joint action, and future directions to fully understand this role are discussed.

articles.title: Developmental Trajectories of Pro-Environmental Behavior in Adolescence:  A Cross-National Longitudinal Study
articles.authors: Stathis Grapsas; Andrik Becht; Lukas Baumann; Sander Thomaes
articles.abstract: Adolescence is a critical period for the formation of sustainable lifestyles. However, evidence on the development of pro-environmental behavior in adolescence is limited and inconsistent, suggesting either an inverted U-shaped developmental dip or a developmental increase. In the present longitudinal study, we pitted against each other the dip and increase hypotheses in early to mid-adolescent samples across three countries (four annual measurements in the Netherlands, three in China and Colombia) and two behavior types (private and public sphere). We also examined the potential presence of youth subgroups with different trajectories of pro-environmental behavior and how these youth subgroups differed in levels of baseline sustainability motive-alignment (perceptions of pro-environmental behavior as granting autonomy and peer status). Findings provide a more nuanced picture than either hypothesis alone predicts. Latent growth models mostly revealed developmental stability, except for a linear increase in private behavior in Colombia. Latent class growth models revealed no subgroups in China and Colombia. In the Netherlands, these analyses revealed, for both behaviors, a subgroup of engaged youth with higher, stable levels, and a subgroup of temporarily disengaged youth showing a dip towards mid-adolescence. Baseline motive-alignment positively predicted pro-environmental behavior across waves and characterized the pro-environmentally engaged subgroups of youth. Together, these findings show relative developmental heterogeneity across youth subgroups and call for tailored interventions that align pro-environmental behavior with adolescents’ developmentally salient motives.

articles.title: Alpha Oscillations Reflect Curiosity During Information-Seeking
articles.authors: Hanna Julku; Sebastian Österman; Caitlin Dawson; Kaisa Elovaara; Jaana Simola
articles.abstract: Curiosity is a fundamental driver of information-seeking, but its electrophysiological correlates are poorly understood. To investigate how curiosity and information quality affected neural activity during information-seeking, we recorded electroencephalography (EEG) while participants collected information in a multi-armed bandit task. Participants (N=60) read statements of varying scientific quality to decide their stance on health-related topics. After reading each statement, participants rated their state curiosity level, the usefulness and clarity of the statements, and their confidence of the usefulness rating. We also measured participants’ trait curiosity (N=53) with a questionnaire and asked whether they had searched for more information about the topics after the experiment. The EEG analyses included a cluster-based permutation analysis (N=60), which indicated two clusters where alpha power differed between information quality categories: frontal and parietal. Then, by using generalized linear mixed effects modeling (N=53), we tested whether information quality, trait and state curiosity, other statement related ratings, and thinking about or searching for more information about the topics after the laboratory experiment predicted alpha power in these clusters. A decrease in frontal alpha power was associated with an increase in state curiosity and deprivation sensitivity dimension of trait curiosity. A decrease in parietal alpha was related to an increase in deprivation sensitivity and searching for more information about the topics. These results show that lower alpha power reflects higher curiosity and the strength of cognitive engagement during information-seeking.

articles.title: The Missing Quadrant: Population Health in the Conversation About AI and Mental Health
articles.authors: Emily E Haroz; Peter P. Zandi; Roy Adams
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence now occupies two roles in mental health that call for different sciences. As an intervention it is deliberately deployed to improve care or to improve understanding. As an exposure it is not deployed for those purposes at all but encountered, largely through consumer products outside any clinical setting. Crossing these two roles with a clinical lens focused on individual patients and a population lens focused on whole communities yields four domains of work, three of which have active research, while the fourth, the population view of AI as an exposure, has comparatively little attention. Public health's tools are the natural starting point for that fourth domain: measurement, surveillance, epidemiologic design, and the study of social, structural, and commercial determinants. But this exposure has features that mean those methods cannot simply be imported, and adapting them is the work now in front of the field. The exposure is already at population scale, but the science that would study it as one is not.

articles.title: No convincing evidence of longitudinal effects linking neuroticism, gaming disorder, and future time perspective: A reanalysis of Guo et al. (2026)
articles.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen; Bo Melin; Marika Melin
articles.abstract: Guo et al. investigated longitudinal associations among neuroticism, internet gaming disorder, and future time perspective, concluding that the findings supported reciprocal influences over time. However, statistically significant cross-lagged parameters do not necessarily indicate genuine prospective effects because such estimates can emerge from alternative statistical mechanisms. Using simulated data that reproduced the sample size and correlation structure reported by Guo et al., we evaluated the consistency of the reported findings across several plausible analytic approaches. The conclusions varied considerably across model specifications. Some approaches yielded positive longitudinal associations, whereas others produced negative or non-significant estimates. When all results were integrated using meta-analytic methods, none of the overall effects reached statistical significance. These findings suggest that the evidence presented by Guo et al. does not provide a robust basis for claims of prospective influence. In line with recommendations from the multiverse-analysis framework, investigators should examine multiple defensible analytic specifications and base conclusions on the aggregated evidence rather than on a single model.

articles.title: Making Room for Autistic Identity: An Experimental Investigation of Self-as-Context with Autistic Adults
articles.authors: Lauren Lawson; Olivia Corda; Miranda Mirabile; Laura Therese Broadbent; Simon Bury
articles.abstract:
Background: Autistic adults experience higher rates of mental health difficulties than non-autistic adults, driven in part by marginalisation, minority stress and internalised stigma. Self-as-context, a core process of Acceptance and Commitment Therapy, may offer a way to loosen the grip of identity-related distress, but it has not previously been tested experimentally in an autistic sample.
Method: In a preregistered online randomised experiment, 101 UK-based autistic adults recruited via Prolific were allocated to an 8-minute self-as-context skills video or a time-matched neutral video control (final N = 93). Participants completed baseline measures, wrote about a time they felt out of place due to being autistic, viewed the intervention or control video, re-read their account, and then viewed a calming video, completing momentary state measures after each of five phases. Data were analysed using 2 (condition) × 5 (phase) mixed ANOVAs.
Results: After re-reading their account, the self-as-context condition reported significantly lower state shame than controls (Mdiff = −1.52, p = .036, ηp² = .048). The between-condition difference in state self-compassion at that point was non-significant (Mdiff = 0.34, p = .062), although the self-as-context condition scored higher immediately after the intervention (p = .046) and at the end of the study (p = .030). Significant condition × phase interactions emerged for state self-compassion, F(3.04, 276.84) = 6.14, p < .001, ηp² = .063, and state experiential avoidance, F(3.40, 309.14) = 5.22, p = .001, ηp² = .054, with the self-as-context condition reporting lower experiential avoidance from the intervention onwards (ps ≤ .010). No effects were found for state self-as-context.
Conclusions: A single brief, self-paced self-as-context exercise reduced state shame and showed promise for improving self-compassion and reducing experiential avoidance in autistic adults reflecting on identity-related distress. These first experimental data support self-as-context as a therapeutic target for this population and brief online delivery as feasible; replication with larger samples and validated self-as-context measures is needed.

articles.title: Allocation bias in past and future words
articles.authors: Noa Uchikawa; Kayo Miura; Kyoshiro Sasaki
articles.abstract: The mental timeline (MTL) refers to the conceptual association between time and horizontal space, such that past and future are linked to left and right, respectively. The present study investigated whether the MTL metaphor-congruency effect would be observed using a word allocation task (WAT), in which participants freely positioned past- and future-related words within a rectangular frame. The results showed that future words were placed significantly further to the right than past words, supporting the presence of the MTL metaphor-congruency effect in a voluntary, unconstrained task. Additionally, handedness did not significantly modulate this effect; it is possible that the MTL operates through a mechanism distinct from the body-specificity hypothesis. These findings suggest that the WAT is a viable paradigm for investigating spatial metaphors and that the MTL may be more readily involved with voluntary and controlled processing than automatic processing.

articles.title: Loneliness and Perceived Cognitive Function: Evidence from a Large-Scale Daily Study
articles.authors: Martina Luchetti; Antonio Terracciano; Selin Karakose; Justin Brown; Hannah Lovett; Samia C. Akhter-Khan; Damaris Aschwanden; André Hajek; STEPHAN; Angelina Sutin
articles.abstract:
Background and Objectives: Loneliness is linked to poor cognition and dementia risk. Yet, little is known about how loneliness relates to perceptions of cognitive functioning in daily life, particularly among individuals at-risk for dementia. We examined within-person and between-person associations between daily loneliness and subjective cognition and tested moderation by cognitive status, dispositional loneliness, and sociodemographic characteristics.
Research Design and Methods: Data were from 2,540 adults aged 40 years and older (Mage= 63; 59.6% female; 32.7% with subjective cognitive decline [SCD]; 7.3% with cognitive impairment, no dementia [CIND]), who completed 8 daily assessments of loneliness, subjective cognitive functioning, forgetting, and forgetting-related irritation and interference.
Results: Participants with higher mean daily loneliness reported worse cognitive functioning and greater odds of forgetting over the study period. On days when participants felt lonelier than their average, they reported poorer cognition. Daily loneliness was not associated with forgetting on a given day but was associated with greater forgetting-related irritation and interference. While participants with SCD or CIND reported higher daily loneliness, associations did not differ by cognitive status, dispositional loneliness, or socio-demographic factors. There was limited evidence of lagged associations.
Discussion and Implications: Loneliness was negatively associated with subjective cognition between persons and within persons. Associations were consistent across normal cognition, SCD, and CIND, suggesting loneliness may be relevant to subjective cognition regardless of clinical stage. The higher daily loneliness among SCD and CIND participants underscores the need to address psychosocial well-being in efforts to promote cognitive health and support dementia prevention strategies.

articles.title: The Australian under-16 social media ban: Early influences on access and its relationship with reading
articles.authors: Signy Wegener; Jasmine Spencer; Andrea Salins; Serje Robidoux; Robert Savage; Anne Castles
articles.abstract: Concerns abound that time spent on social media might displace more developmentally adaptive activities, such as reading. In December 2025, the Australian government introduced a world-first social media ban for young people under the age of 16, providing an opportunity to explore whether social media use and the efficacy of the ban are associated with current reading behaviours. In this study, Australians aged 12 to 15 years completed a cross-sectional self-report online survey between March and June 2026. Prior to the ban, 81.55% of the sample used social media. Users of social media reported reading less frequently, for shorter periods and had lower reading motivation than non-users of social media. For users, the initial effect of the ban was often incomplete or transient, with many users subsequently able to regain access to lost accounts. Post-ban, time spent on social media reduced for those who lost access to some or all of their accounts. Although there were differences in reading times by the effect of the ban in the predicted direction, they were not significant. Further, there were no differences in the strength of the association between reading motivation and reading duration by the effect of the ban. These findings suggest that social media use is associated with lower levels of reading engagement than non-use. The early implementation of the social media ban has only been partially effective and there is presently insufficient evidence that the effect of the ban is associated with differences in current reading engagement.

articles.title: Five questions to ask when studying cultural change
articles.authors: Igor Grossmann; Michael E. W. Varnum
articles.abstract: In 2016 we reported that infectious-disease prevalence and gender inequality shifted together across six decades in the US, and argued from parasite-stress theory that declining pathogen load contributed to declining gender inequality. In their Matters Arising, Koplenig and Wolfer (K&W) reanalyzed data from our 2016 report, finding that both series show strong trends that our models left unaccounted for, and that the positive association does not survive several standard time-series corrections.  K&W identified an important statistical problem, and we are grateful for their work. But addressing that problem does not by itself determine the appropriate test of the substantive hypothesis. Most of K&W’s specifications ask whether annual changes in pathogen prevalence covary with changes in gender inequality. However, at least some of the mechanisms that parasite-stress theory invokes, such as norm transmission or cohort replacement, operate over longer time horizons. As reported below, specifications built on annual changes detect delayed effects a tenth to a fifth as often as they detect contemporaneous effects of identical size. Focusing on the theory-method alignment, here we organize our response around five questions about studying societal change, using our own data and errors as examples.

articles.title: To Be a Mental Disorder: Revisiting Behavioral Addictions
articles.authors: Joshua B. Grubbs; Nicholas Borgogna; Beáta Bőthe; Hyoun Soo Kim; Rory A Pfund; Shane Winfield Kraus
articles.abstract: Behavioral addictions have been recognized in various forms for centuries, yet only three—Gambling Disorder, Gaming Disorder, and Compulsive Sexual Behavior Disorder—are currently included in formal diagnostic systems. In the past decade, research on these conditions has expanded dramatically in both volume and methodological rigor, drawing on longitudinal, neurobiological, and cross-cultural designs and evolving into a truly global science. Even so, the field remains beset by unresolved controversies. Chief among these is a persistent tendency to import substance use disorder concepts—tolerance, withdrawal, and dependence—that lack conceptual and empirical support when applied to behavior. Related challenges concern the over-pathologizing of normal engagement and a reliance on confirmatory, self-report measurement of uncertain validity. We argue that advancing the field requires sustained funding, theory grounded in the disorders themselves, objective and intensive-longitudinal methods, greater diversity, and public health and regulatory attention to increasingly technological environments.

articles.title: Predicting memory distortions in hundreds of verbal recalls
articles.authors: Phoebe Chen; Omri Raccah; Vy Vo; David Poeppel; Todd Matthew Gureckis
articles.abstract: Memory distortions emerge from a complex interplay between prior knowledge and ongoing experience—dynamics which are not readily provoked in controlled laboratory experiments. Here we investigate naturally occurring memory distortions using the largest known dataset of narrative recall, comprising hundreds of spoken recollections. Using large language models (LLMs), we developed an automated pipeline to detect and classify spontaneous false memories. Across several validation experiments, we demonstrate that human-AI agreement matches inter-human reliability in detecting memory distortions. We found that similarity to prototypical narrative segments — how closely narrative events in our dataset resembled text from thousands of other narratives – predicted overall false memory rates. Furthermore, we provide initial evidence that these false memories may separate into two distinct phenomena with distinct drivers: similarity to prototypical narrative segments drives factual conflicts (distortions of actual content), whereas contextual surprise drives confabulations (entirely fabricated details). Through this combination of large-scale naturalistic data and AI-powered automation tools, we reveal memory processes that controlled laboratory paradigms cannot easily capture and illuminate the complex dynamics of human (mis)remembering in real-world contexts.

articles.title: Adversity sum scores: A causal perspective on studying adverse life events
articles.authors: Milan Zarchev; Natalie Slopen; Charlotte Cecil; Henning Tiemeier
articles.abstract: In adversity research, a widely adopted approach to studying poor health outcomes is to create sum scores of adversities, rather than examine individual adverse experiences. Using simplified causal scenarios, we argue that sum scores often oversimplify the complex causal structure among co-occurring adversities. Summing adversities can increase rather than decrease bias due to omitted common causes and among adversities causing each other. We also consider well-defined hypothetical interventions to better inform intervention and prevention efforts. We demonstrate these points by revisiting the original Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACE) study from a causal perspective. We also discuss sum scores in relation to multicollinearity concerns, the development of prediction models, and improving measurement models of adversity. We provide concrete recommendations about using directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) to visually map out common causes of adversities and their temporal sequence, to inform decisions about when adversity sum scores can be used without introducing bias. Furthermore, we advocate for well-defined adversity exposures that can be connected to real-world interventions to guide decision-making.

articles.title: Wise Empathy Improves Well-being on Instagram
articles.authors: Gregory John Depow; Christopher Oveis; Emily Zohar; Michael Inzlicht
articles.abstract: Most of the global population spends significant time browsing social media making it critical to understand how to improve experiences online to support well-being. Here, we test whether a brief intervention training individuals to use wise empathy on Instagram can improve users’ well-being. In an ecological momentary intervention, we trained half our sample (N = 260) to wisely regulate empathy for positive and negative posts. Using experience sampling (Nobs. = 5,902), we tracked empathy and well-being in daily life. The intervention increased wise empathy online—boosting appreciative joy, positive emotion sharing, and compassion for negative emotions—while reducing negative emotion sharing, upward social comparisons, and personal distress. When participants had recently browsed Instagram, those in the wise empathy condition reported higher well-being than controls, an effect mediated by changes in wise empathy. These findings position wise empathy as a scalable, trainable skill that can enhance well-being on social media.

articles.title: A Matter of Time? The Impact of Time Frames on the Self-Report Assessment of Personality Pathology
articles.authors: Kristin Jankowsky; Maybrit Filiz Fuhrmann; Ulrich Schroeders; Johannes Zimmermann
articles.abstract: Diagnosing a personality disorder requires that impairments in personality functioning have persisted over an extended period—at least 2 years according to the ICD-11, with an onset traceable to adolescence or early adulthood according to the Alternative DSM-5 Model for Personality Disorders. Common self-report measures of personality pathology, however, specify no time frame in their instructions, leaving unclear which reference periods respondents adopt and whether instructed time frames alter their responses. In a preregistered experiment, N = 1,447 U.S. adults currently receiving or awaiting treatment for a mental health condition completed the Level of Personality Functioning Scale-Brief Form 2.0 (LPFS-BF 2.0), the modified Personality Inventory for DSM-5-Brief Form (PID5BF+M), and the Personality Disorder Severity ICD-11 scale (PDS-ICD-11) after random assignment to one of three instruction conditions: the original instructions (no specific time frame), a short time frame (“in the last 2 weeks”), or a time frame matching diagnostic criteria (“in the last 2 years”/“since early adulthood”). Multigroup confirmatory factor analyses supported strict measurement invariance across conditions for all three instruments. Correlations with depressive symptoms (Patient Health Questionnaire-9) and factor means did not differ systematically between conditions, a pattern that replicated in two sensitivity analyses (one of them including only participants correctly recalling the time frame). Notably, only 45% of participants recalled the instructed time frame correctly. Time frame instructions thus appear to have little impact on self-reported personality pathology, possibly because respondents disregard them or because trait-like item content elicits semanticized self-knowledge irrespective of the instructed reference period.

articles.title: Dynamic attribute activation explains gaze biases in choice.
articles.authors: Xiaozhi Taro Yang; Sudeep Bhatia
articles.abstract:
People tend to choose the options they look at more. Prior work explains this effect by assuming that visual attention increases preference for the attended option. However, it remains unclear why looking at an option increases its preference and when this relationship is
weakened. Using an experimental paradigm that combines eye-tracking and a think-aloud protocol, we provide evidence that visual attention shapes preference by activating attributes associated with the attended option. Critically, the content of these activated attributes
depends on contextual factors such as stimulus desirability and behavioral goals. In standard choice settings, where the goal is to choose the preferred option, visual attention primarily activates positive attributes. In contrast, when these contextual factors are incongruent, activated attributes become less positive, reducing the influence of visual attention on choice. To account for these patterns, we propose a new computational model of gaze-driven attribute activation. Our model subsumes existing theories as special cases, and uniquely predicts which attributes are brought to mind by gaze and how they shape downstream decisions. Together, our work offers a mechanistic explanation of a fundamental driver of choice as well as its boundary conditions.

articles.title: Phonological changes facilitate pragmatic inference during lexical access in Bengali verbs
articles.authors: Pijush Kanti Gayen; Monsija Mitra; Samar Husain
articles.abstract: How do listeners map fine-grained phonological variation onto a speaker’s communicative intention during lexical access? We address this question using a restricted set of Bengali imperative verb forms in which stem-vowel height alternation is associated with different directive speech acts. Native speakers of Bengali (N=176) completed (i) an intention-scaling task to assess perceived illocutionary force and (ii) a cross-modal lexical decision task with auditory verb primes and visual speech-act targets. The lexical decision experiment manipulated prime--target stimulus onset asynchrony (SOA: 30 ms, 60 ms, 240 ms) to test the time course of phonological-to-pragmatic activation. Intention-scaling results showed that participants reliably distinguished the two intended speech acts. In the lexical decision task, congruent speech-act targets were recognised substantially faster than controls at the 60ms SOA (approximately 100ms facilitation for both order and request), whereas effects were small and not reliable at 30ms and 240ms. Request trials also showed slightly longer latencies than order trials, consistent with a higher inferential load for requests. Together, the results provide behavioural evidence that phonological cues can rapidly bias speech-act interpretation, with a temporally constrained window for lexical-pragmatic integration.

articles.title: Voice Can Help and Hurt AI Empathy: How Context Shapes the Effects of Vocal Delivery
articles.authors: Joshua D Wenger; Daryl Cameron; Reza Hadi Mogavi; Michael Inzlicht
articles.abstract: As people increasingly turn to artificial intelligence (AI) for empathy, new modes of human–AI empathic interaction have emerged. While prior research on empathic AI has focused almost exclusively on text-based empathy, we explored how vocal delivery of empathetic messages might enhance or undermine AI versus human empathy. Across five studies (N = 1,584) we examined how the mode of expression (voice vs. text) and the empathy source (human vs. AI) jointly shape perceptions of empathic quality and experiences of feeling heard across different interaction contexts. In interactions involving pre-recorded empathic messages, vocal delivery reduced perceptions of quality and experiences of feeling heard for both human and AI empathizers, though the reduction was stronger for AI. This reduction was eliminated for human empathizers by giving empathy recipients the option to first opt in or consent to receiving empathy from a human empathizer, though the reduction remained for AI voices in this pre-recorded context. The reduction for AI voices also disappeared, and sometimes reversed into a benefit, in more immersive and personally relevant interaction contexts such as extended, live interaction with an AI chatbot. We further explored how the mode of expression impacts feelings of uncanniness, and the mediating role uncanniness plays in shaping feelings of being empathized with and feeling heard. Together, these findings demonstrate that whether voice helps or hurts AI empathy critically depends on the interaction context, and highlight uncanniness as one factor that can undercut spoken empathy in some contexts.

articles.title: Evaluating the Credibility of Human and AI Forecasters: Receivers Discriminate Performance More Finely for Humans
articles.authors: Robert N. Collins; David R. Mandel
articles.abstract: Decision-makers in high-stakes forecasting domains are increasingly asked to weigh probabilistic judgments from human experts alongside those from artificial intelligence (AI) systems. Whether source attribution alters how forecasts are received has been largely unexamined. Three accounts make competing predictions. Algorithm aversion and algorithm appreciation predict a source dependent bias in favor of humans and AI, respectively: both assume that source attribution may affect forecaster evaluation. By contrast, responsibility-attribution research predicts differential discrimination, with credibility ratings distinguishing performance levels more finely for human than AI sources. We tested these accounts in two experiments (N1 = 667; N2 = 1,170). Participants translated verbal probability expressions communicated by either a human expert or an AI system into numeric point estimates and ranges. Separately, participants evaluated source credibility after reviewing a forecaster’s performance record, with accuracy manipulated between subjects. Interpretation was largely unaffected by source: numerical point estimates were similar and ranges equivalent for both human and AI sourced forecasts. In contrast, credibility ratings depended on source: receivers discriminated performance more finely for human than AI forecasters: human forecasters were rated as more credible than equally accurate AI when accuracy was high and less credible when accuracy was low. This differential discrimination is inconsistent with algorithm aversion and appreciation accounts, but consistent with the responsibility-attribution research, according to which people hold human advisors more accountable for outcomes than algorithms. We discuss implications for integrating AI-assisted forecasts into decision support roles.

articles.title: Positive Emotion Displays Support Preschoolers’ and Adults’ Word Learning
articles.authors: Mira L Nencheva; Michael C. Frank
articles.abstract: Emotion displays are one of the most salient features of early social interactions - caregivers often smile, change their vocal register to convey positive emotions to their children. Despite the fact that these emotion displays often accompany the moments in which children learn language, prior work on the role of emotion in word learning has been sparse and has resulted in conflicting findings. The present investigation examines how emotion displays that vary in valence (positive vs. negative) and arousal (high vs. low) influence word learning in preschoolers and adults. Across five experiments, participants completed a word learning task in which novel object-label pairs were introduced by a character displaying one of four emotional states: high-arousal positive, low-arousal positive, high-arousal negative, or low-arousal negative. Results consistently showed that positive emotion displays facilitated word learning relative to negative displays in adults and preschoolers alike, with web-based eye tracking indicating that high-arousal negative displays modestly pull attention away from the labeled object. Following the study, preschoolers preferentially chose stickers depicting objects that had been paired with positive displays as a prize, suggesting that emotion signals shape not only which words children learn but also how they value the objects paired with emotion displays. Together, these findings establish that emotional signals are not merely a backdrop to early language input but an active ingredient in word learning. Specifically, positive emotion in caregivers’ communication to young children may serve a functional role in supporting language development.

articles.title: “More research being done is so validating”: Insights from transgender and gender-diverse participants on a psychophysiological study with deception
articles.authors: Nina Micanovic; Camden Trepanier; Maddie Katz; Vera Vine
articles.abstract: Laboratory-based research methods (e.g., psychophysiology, stress induction paradigms) are insightful for understanding the mechanisms underlying health disparities experienced by transgender and gender-diverse (TGD) people. Among this population, fear and mistrust of research remain due to historical mistreatment, and TGD people remain under-represented in experimental research. Researchers sensitive to these issues may hesitate to recruit TGD participants in fear of causing discomfort associated with more invasive laboratory-based research methods. Inclusive study design efforts exist, but it is unclear how they are received by TGD people. We explored TGD participants’ experiences in a study involving social exclusion and psychophysiological measurements (electrocardiogram and impedance cardiography) to understand how inclusive study design efforts were perceived. We conducted interviews with the first 10 TGD participants in a study where participants completed a social exclusion manipulation involving deception (i.e., Cyberball; Williams, 2000) while providing psychophysiological data (larger study N = 105). Informed by interpretive description (Thorne, 2016), we coded interview transcriptions to identify commonalities and patterns of participant experiences across each study phase. Overall, participants appreciated research efforts to increase transparency and encourage participant agency. Despite some discomforts, participants report that inclusive efforts fostered a sense of trust and safety throughout the study. During deception (and debriefing) and psychophysiological measurement, participant experiences in the study were positive or neutral. Participants provided constructive feedback about several study design elements. These findings provide researchers with tangible recommendations for inclusive experimental research for TGD participants that may help build trust and mutual respect between minoritized groups and researchers.

articles.title: The partner as reader: recognition, disclosure risk, and the unit of analysis in dyadic reflexive thematic analysis
articles.authors: Vince Jacques de Blauwe; Alina Gheorghita; Antonio Fidalgo
articles.abstract:
In dyadic qualitative research, an account may have an informed reader before it reaches any public audience: the person who shared the encounter. Conventional de-identification is generally calibrated to an external reader and may therefore leave unresolved recognition through shared memory, relational sequence, or a singular circumstance. This methodological case study examines that condition in a corpus of 150 immediate written micro-accounts from 30 university students following brief structured interactions in 15 stranger dyads. Reflexive thematic analysis generated four interpretive themes: calm-as-distance, vocabulary-as-bridge, masking under instruction, and provisional we-ness. A subsequent dialogue-informed dyad-level configurational reading extended, complicated, and bounded selected individual-level interpretations; it was not treated as independent corroboration.

The study develops the Partner-Recognition Framework for qualitative research in which both members of an encounter provide accounts. The framework specifies four prospective rules: name partner recognition in consent; declare dyadic provenance and the intended relationship between individual- and pair-level analysis; separate paired accounts by default in public reporting; and screen derived artefacts as data. The case also documents the evidential cost of partner-protective reporting and recursive disclosure risk, whereby protective documentation can create new linkage routes requiring further review. The framework is offered as a set of prospective design and reporting principles, not as a validated risk-assessment instrument, a guarantee of anonymity, or a substitute for case-specific ethical and legal review

articles.title: Directional Asymmetry in Reasoning About National and Religious Identity Is Category-Specific: Evidence From Palestine, Israel, and the United States
articles.authors: Mostafa Salari Rad; Jeremy Ginges
articles.abstract: Judgments about whether a person can gain or lose a group identity may depend both on which category is at stake and on the direction of transfer. For national identity, people judge that an outgroup-born child raised by the ingroup becomes one of us more readily than an ingroup-born child raised by the outgroup becomes one of them (Rad & Ginges, 2018). That work varied which outgroup was named but never which category, leaving open whether the asymmetry is a general property of reasoning about ingroups, is specific to nationality, or varies with how membership in a category is represented, which differs across populations. We tested these alternatives in settings where religion and nationality pick out nearly the same adversary, using switched-at-birth tasks with Muslim-Palestinians (N = 1,205), Americans (N = 989), and religious Israeli Jews (N = 280). The asymmetry appeared for national identity in all three samples and did not depend on the outgroup being the adversary. For religious identity it was absent among Palestinians and Americans, but present among Israeli Jews and not reliably different from nationality's. Across conditions and studies, directional asymmetry appeared only where membership was treated as substantially fixed at birth, and where it appeared it was carried almost entirely by judgments of what ingroup upbringing confers rather than of what birth transmits. The asymmetry is therefore neither a general feature of group boundaries nor a property of nationality in particular, but emerges where membership is understood as substantially fixed at birth.

articles.title: Measuring audience experience across 20 showings of the same theatre performance using customer feedback kiosks and a questionnaire
articles.authors: Mikko Sams; Einat Amir-Ahola; Enrico Glerean; Sirpa Kähkönen; Taru Mäkelä; Reetta Ristimäki; Antti Ruotoistenmäki; Veli-Matti Saarinen
articles.abstract:
Audience experiences can vary both between performances and among spectators, but little is
known about how different methods capture this variation across repeated showings of the
same production. We therefore examined audience experience across twenty live performances
of the same music theatre production. We combined two complementary methods: immediate
audience ratings collected through customer feedback kiosks and more detailed postperformance
questionnaires. The kiosks recorded 1,887 responses, corresponding to 67% of
total attendance, and 458 audience members (16%) completed questionnaires. Overall, the
reception was positive, but kiosk ratings varied significantly across performances, indicating
that audience-level enjoyment ratings differed from one showing to another. Kiosk and
questionnaire responses to the same enjoyment question did not differ significantly at the
aggregate level, suggesting that brief kiosk feedback may provide a practical, low-burden
measure of audience-level enjoyment. Cluster analysis of questionnaire data identified three
descriptive response profiles that differed primarily in overall engagement and ratings of
specific artistic elements. These profiles illustrate heterogeneity within the audience of a single
production. Qualitative responses from participants whose quantitative ratings were closest to
each cluster centroid provided illustrative accounts of the experiences associated with these
profiles. These narratives added context to the quantitative findings by showing differences in
emotional tone, interpretive emphasis, and personal connection to the performance.
Supplementary interviews with the director, artistic director, and an external playwright
illustrated both interest in and reservations about incorporating audience data into creative
work. Their comments emphasised the potential of empirical findings to support artistic
reflection, while also underscoring the importance of how and when feedback is communicated
within production teams.

articles.title: A Practical Causal Mediation Workflow for Psychologists: From Concepts to Implementation
articles.authors: Joshua D Wenger; Zoe Baker; Vasant G Honavar
articles.abstract: Mediation analysis is widely used across psychology to support claims about psychological mechanisms. Such claims often carry causal interpretations that depend on assumptions that are frequently left unstated, and may not be justified under traditional mediation approaches. Despite substantial advances in mediation best practices emerging from the field of causal inference, uptake of these approaches has remained low, possibly due to the highly technical literature and lack of practical implementation guidance. This paper addresses that gap by integrating developments in causal mediation into an accessible, fully demonstrated workflow for applied researchers without prior knowledge of causal inference. We identify two major limitations of traditional mediation approaches: vulnerability to mediator–outcome confounding and reliance on a product-of-coefficients approach that cannot account for predictor–mediator interactions and certain nonlinear models more generally. We then present concrete solutions to each that can be applied throughout the research workflow with limited additional work: before data collection (design-based solutions), during mediation effect estimation, and after analysis to assess robustness (sensitivity analysis). In doing so, we introduce key causal inference frameworks (directed acyclic graphs and potential outcomes) to facilitate understanding of these problems, bridge conceptual reasoning and practical solutions, and equip readers to reason about these issues within their own study contexts. Finally, we provide a fully worked example, including R code that readers can adapt for their own use. Overall, the proposed workflow requires only modest extensions to standard practice but can substantially improve the validity of causal claims drawn from mediation analysis.

articles.title: Naming variation across languages is shaped by shared histories, semantics and familiarity
articles.authors: Alzbeta Kucerova; Carlo Y. Meloni; Johann-Mattis List
articles.abstract: Speakers all around the world use words to name the objects around them. While they often agree on a common word, this is not always the case. Certain concepts seem to attract many different words, while others remain fairly stable in their naming patterns. It is still unclear where these naming differences stem from, which factors trigger the variation, and to which degree this variation results from universal linguistic tendencies, contact, inheritance or concept-level properties. Here, we analyze naming variation patterns in an open dataset that elicits naming responses for 500 unique concepts across 34 languages from 8 distinct families. Our results show that cross-linguistic similarities in naming variation are systematically associated with genetic relatedness, geographical proximity between languages, concept basic-ness, semantic categories, and object familiarity. Although the magnitude of semantic category effects varies across languages, several semantic categories display broadly consistent tendencies toward higher or lower naming diversity across most languages in the sample. These findings indicate that naming variation reflects both concept-level properties, as well as cross-linguistic historical and spatial relationships, while also exhibiting meaningful language-specific heterogeneity.

articles.title: Shame- and Fear-based Autobiographical Memories and Their Identity Centrality and Intrusiveness in Young Adults Exposed to Childhood Maltreatment
articles.authors: Ellen Iredale; Xenia Bunk; Jasmine Stringer; louise johns; Carmen Chan; Alex Lau-Zhu
articles.abstract:
Background: Exposure to childhood maltreatment is an established risk factor for adult psychopathology, but the underpinning mechanisms remain unclear. Developmental theory suggests that alterations in cognitive processes, such as autobiographical memory, play an important role.  
Aim: We examined whether autobiographical shame vs fear memories differ in intrusiveness and identity centrality in young adults with high exposure to childhood maltreatment compared to low exposure peers. Furthermore, we investigated whether such memory characteristics could reflect markers of latent vulnerability to psychopathology, with implications for early intervention efforts.  
Methods: In a cross-sectional design, we examined shame- and fear-based autobiographical memories in a UK community sample of young adults aged 18 to 25 (N = 127), with high vs low exposure to childhood maltreatment. Participants completed an online survey including questions on adverse experiences, current psychological symptoms and an autobiographical memory task involving recall of specific childhood events most strongly associated with shame and fear, followed by ratings of memory intrusiveness and centrality.  
Results: Intrusiveness and identity centrality of shame and fear memories were rated as significantly higher in young adults exposed to high levels of maltreatment than their low-maltreatment peers. Centrality (but not intrusiveness) ratings remained significantly associated with maltreatment after accounting for concurrent psychopathology. However, there was no evidence that the association between maltreatment and memory characteristics differed between shame- and fear-based memories. This may indicate that the observed memory alterations may not reflect shame-specific mechanisms and suggest that the conceptual distinction between shame- and fear-related autobiographical memory processes may be less clear-cut. 
Conclusion: The present work suggests that autobiographical memory – irrespective of emotional category (shame vs fear) – may be one mechanism through which childhood maltreatment increases risk for later psychopathology. While memory intrusiveness may reflect ongoing psychopathology, its centrality to identity may reflect a latent vulnerability to future psychopathology. Pending further work with longitudinal designs, autobiographical memory could offer a mechanistic focus for early interventions in maltreatment-exposed youth.

articles.title: People want human and AI social partners to follow different relational norms despite similar roles
articles.authors: Madeline G. Reinecke; Yueying Chu; Ivar Rodríguez Hannikainen; Andreas Kappes; Sebastian Porsdam Mann; Ilina Singh; Julian Savulescu; Brian D. Earp
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly assuming social roles traditionally held by humans—but do people want human-AI relationships to be governed by the same behavioral norms as human-human relationships? In three pre-registered studies using demographically representative samples in the United Kingdom (N = 910) and United States (N = 862), including a US pilot study (N = 432), we assessed public preferences across four cooperative domains—care, hierarchy, transaction, and mating—within seven relationship types (e.g., romantic partners, close friends, coworkers). Participants rated their ideal norms for each domain and relationship type, either in a human-human or human-AI context. Contrary to a common assumption in alignment research, participants reported systematically different ideals for human-AI versus human-human relationships: across all seven types, they distinguished ideal AI from ideal human behavior in at least one cooperative domain, with the direction and size of differences also varying by relationship type. Specifically, these included preferences for AI assistants and sellers to show greater care than humans in identical positions; AI teachers and mental health providers to express lesser authority; and AI romantic partners, friends, and coworkers to behave more platonically. Participants also preferred humans to show lesser care and greater authority toward AIs across several roles. These findings suggest public expectations for social AIs are shaped by relational context rather than a simple human-to-AI transfer rule, with implications for social AI design.

articles.title: Boghossian et al.’s (2026) critique of humanistic scholarship is itself bad scholarship and should be corrected or retracted
articles.authors: Patrick E. Savage
articles.abstract: Boghossian et al.’s (2026) “Report on the State of Scholarship in the Humanities and the Humanistic Social Sciences” argues that humanistic scholarship has experienced “a deterioration in scholarly standards fueled by the substitution of political criteria for properly scholarly criteria”. I argue that their report itself represents low scholarly standards. Specifically: 1) it is primarily based on unpublished, unverifiable data; 2) the limited data that have been published (largely from unvalidated LLM categorisations) do not support the main claims of a “deterioriation in scholary standards”; and 3) the report unjustifiably generalises from a narrow set of examples (e.g., the cancelation of a panel on sex and gender by the American Anthropological Association) to make sweeping conclusions about global humanities scholarship. I describe counter-examples from past and present research in the humanities and the sciences by myself and others to show that biased and low-quality scholarship is not a new or unique problem for progressive humanistic research. While I agree with the authors that critical evaluation of the quality of academic scholarship (both humanistic and scientific) is urgently needed in today’s global political climate, the report’s strongest conclusions are not justified by their data and thus are not of sufficient quality to achieve their intended goal of helping university leaders to make policy decisions. I recommend it be corrected or retracted to resolve these issues.

articles.title: Language supports the emergence of abstract relational reasoning in early childhood
articles.authors: Emilie Serraille; Jean-Rémy Hochmann
articles.abstract: Young children demonstrate sensitivity to abstract relations such as same and different, yet they typically fail analogical reasoning tasks such as the Relational Match-to-Sample (RMTS) until four to five years of age. We investigate whether this developmental discontinuity reflects general task demands or a qualitative change in the representational format of thought. Specifically, we contrast accounts according to which young children have the competence to solve RMTS but fall victim of an induction problem, with accounts proposing that early cognition lacks the discrete representations of relations necessary to solve RMTS. Across three experiments involving 3- to 6-year-old children, we progressively reduced the inductive demands of RMTS tasks by priming relational content and constraining the hypothesis space. Although these manipulations improved performance, success consistently depended on children’s knowledge of the relational terms “same” and “different.” Children lacking evidence of relational vocabulary continued to perform at chance despite succeeding in simpler relational tasks. These findings suggest that early relational cognition does not rely on discrete relational symbols and that lexical acquisition plays a critical role in enabling abstract relational reasoning. More broadly, the results favor the hypothesis that developmental changes in language contribute to transformations in the format, structure and flexibility of human thought.

articles.title: Effects of Anthropomorphic Characteristics of Chat Agents on Perceptions of Bad Advice: An Exploratory Study
articles.authors: Kate Alberga; Michael A. Nees
articles.abstract: Anthropomorphic form is an inherent characteristic of artificial intelligence chatbots driven by large language models and appears to have profound effects on user perceptions of chatbots.  The proliferation of anthropomorphized chatbots has raised concerns about miscalibrated trust and misplaced attributions of responsibility for chatbot mistakes. An exploratory experiment examined the potential effects of anthropomorphic design in both the user interface and the linguistic output of a chatbot that provided bad advice about an everyday medical situation.  In a simulated chatbot interaction, participants experienced either humanlike or machinelike language output.  Additionally, the user interface either simulated typing (i.e., the typewriter effect) or presented a static text response all at once.  Humanlike language increased perceived anthropomorphism and social presence but had no effect on perceived competence and trust.  There were no significant effects of the typewriter effect user interface. More frequent AI usage was associated with higher chatbot trust and perceived social presence. Perceived anthropomorphism, social presence, trust, and competence were all highly intercorrelated. Interestingly, participants who were apparently unaware of the obviously bad advice tended to show considerably higher levels of chatbot perceived anthropomorphism, social presence, trust, and competence.  Finally, we found some evidence that higher perceived anthropomorphism is associated with greater perceived responsibility of the chatbot itself for the advice it gave, whereas higher perceived chatbot trust and competence were associated with lesser perceived responsibility of the developing company for the chatbot’s output. Potential future research directions are discussed.

articles.title: The Flattening Effect: A Comparative Study of Sociopragmatic Erasure and Identity Loss in Translated Vietnamese-English Cyber-Discourse
articles.authors: Ming Ze Tang; Phan Quynh Thu Nguyen; Thi Hong Nhung Nguyen
articles.abstract: This study investigates the "flattening effect" in translated Vietnamese-English code-mixed discourse, a phenomenon where semantic content is preserved while sociopragmatic nuances are erased. Utilizing a subset of the VietMix corpus, an "LLM-as-a-Judge" framework was employed to evaluate four dimensions: Structural Hybridity, Emotional Buffering, Status Signaling, and In-group Identity. While the model demonstrated moderate reliability in binary feature detection (inclusive $\kappa = 0.416$), its alignment with human consensus collapsed when quantifying erasure severity (expressive $\kappa = 0.141$). Qualitative analysis revealed that the model frequently over-interprets functional jargon while failing to recognize localized subcultural markers. These findings highlight a critical capability gap in current models, which prioritize global linguistic patterns over localized sociopragmatic functions. Consequently, future developments should move beyond semantic equivalence to incorporate localized cultural awareness within automated computer-mediated communication (CMC) analysis.

articles.title: Two Paths, Two Fates: The Differential Democratic Outcomes of Disappointment-Based and Hatred-Based Affective Polarization
articles.authors: Mabelle Kretchner; Julia Elad-Strenger; Eran Halperin; Daan Vandermeulen; Sivan hirsch hoefler
articles.abstract: Does affective polarization (AP) threaten democratic life? Findings on democratic erosion and political violence remain mixed. We argue this reflects treating AP as unidimensional, when its democratic implications may differ by which emotions dominate. We propose an emotional dual-path model for AP. The more prevalent disappointment-based path (dominated by disappointment and anger) reflects perceptions of opponents as fellow citizens who have failed to meet shared expectations and associated with continued investment in democratic processes. The less prevalent hatred-based path (dominated by hatred, disgust, and contempt) reflects perceptions of opponents as total enemies and is associated with willingness to undermine democratic norms and support political violence. We tested this model in two surveys of Jewish Israelis (Study 1a: N = 1,120; Study 1b: N = 690) conducted during a period of political instability. Across ideological camps and time, disappointment-path emotions dominated, while hatred-path emotions remained low, extending prior single-emotion findings to the path level.  Latent profile and regression analyses showed that, consistent with the model, AP's democratic implications differed by emotional path: while the disappointment path was linked to greater support for democratic norms, the hatred path was linked to lower support for democratic norms and greater support for political violence.

articles.title: Immediate effects of body talk on body image in daily life: An experience sampling study
articles.authors: Nahori Ito; Akira Hasegawa; Asami Beppu; Yuko Matsuda; Ayano Kichinaka; Tetsuya Yamamoto
articles.abstract: This experience sampling study investigated whether momentary changes in state body talk were associated with concurrent and subsequent changes in state body image variables, including body fat dissatisfaction and body appreciation, providing insight into their short-term temporal dynamics. Overall, 118 female university students younger than 30 years completed baseline trait body talk and body image measures, followed by six assessments per day for seven days. Multilevel analyses showed that trait negative fat talk was significantly but weakly associated with a higher average level of state negative fat talk, whereas no such association was observed for positive body talk. Multilevel path analyses showed that state negative fat talk was concurrently associated with higher state body fat dissatisfaction and lower state body appreciation but not with either outcome at the subsequent assessment. These findings provided no evidence for a causal effect, although it remains possible that state negative fat talk had short-lived effects. The concurrent associations of state positive body talk with both body image variables were nonsignificant but in the same direction as those for state negative fat talk. Both forms of state body talk were concurrently associated with higher state appearance comparison. In contrast, trait negative fat talk was significantly associated with higher state body fat dissatisfaction and lower state body appreciation, and these associations appeared stronger than those observed for state negative fat talk. Future research should employ assessment methods that can adequately capture the occurrence of state body talk and study designs capable of detecting its immediate effects.

articles.title: Combining Psychedelics with Religion or Spirituality: Spiritual Bypassing, Receptivity to Pseudo-Profound Bullshit, Subclinical Psychotic Experiences and Well-Being.
articles.authors: Baptiste Fauvel; Myriam Ichchou; Chérine Elhssaini; Joy Zogheib; Ewen Kervadec; Bruno Roméo; Antoine Bioy; Pascale Piolino
articles.abstract:
Abstract: Psychedelics have been used for spiritual purposes for centuries. However, concerns have been raised regarding spiritual bypassing, maladaptive meaning-making, and increased suggestibility when psychedelics are combined with religious or spiritual beliefs.
