We examined spiritual bypassing, receptivity to pseudo-profound bullshit, subclinical psychotic experiences, well-being, and mystical and challenging intensity of the most significant psychedelic experience in 147 Western psychedelic users with different motives (religious: n = 21; spiritual but not religious: n = 79; neither religious nor spiritual: n = 47). Religious users were predominantly Christians, whereas spiritual and secular users primarily identified themselves as mindfulness-based practitioners and philosophers or existential meaning seekers. Groups did not differ in education level, psychiatric diagnoses, or receptivity to pseudo-profound bullshit. Religious and spiritual users reported more intense mystical experiences and higher well-being compared with secular users. Religious users reported fewer subclinical psychotic experiences. They also scored higher on spiritual bypassing, which was positively associated with well-being. No association were found between pseudo-profound bullshit receptivity and either mystical experience or spiritual bypassing. Overall, these findings do not support concerns that psychedelic use with religious or spiritual intentions is associated with increased cognitive or psychological vulnerabilities. 
Keywords: psychedelics, spirituality, religion, spiritual bypassing, suggestibility, well-being

articles.title: Short-term prior knowledge improves speech-in-noise perception independently of autistic imagination subtrait
articles.authors: Yurika Tsuji; Shu Imaizumi
articles.abstract: Autistic individuals often experience difficulties using prior knowledge and perceiving speech in noisy environments. Imagination difficulties associated with autistic traits have been linked to difficulty perceiving high-familiarity words, suggesting that this association may reflect difficulty using prior lexical knowledge. The present study aimed to directly examine the effects of prior knowledge on speech perception in noise in relation to imagination difficulties. We hypothesized that greater imagination difficulties would be related to poorer performance in perceiving learned words, but not unlearned words. Seventy-three participants from the general population identified unlearned and learned low-familiarity words presented in noise. In the learned conditions, participants learned the target words through written and spoken presentations and then identified them in noise. The results suggested that learning improved subsequent speech-in-noise perception. However, imagination difficulties were not associated with performance, regardless of whether the words had been learned. Therefore, imagination difficulties may not be associated with the ability to use short-term prior knowledge. Exploratory analyses suggested that attention-to-detail traits and communication difficulties may be associated with better perception of learned words, whereas attention-switching difficulties may be associated with poorer perception. Future studies should replicate these exploratory findings and investigate the role of other types of prior knowledge, such as long-term and semantic priors.

articles.title: Do Youth Offending Labels Matter? The Impact of the Label “Young Serious Offender” on Public Attitudes Toward Youth Justice
articles.authors: Julia Yesberg; Clare-Ann Fortune; Hasi Kolongahapitiya
articles.abstract: Research on the impact of crime-first labels on public attitudes has focused almost exclusively on sexual offending. This pre-registered conceptual replication of Harris and Socia (2016) examined the effect of the label 'young serious offender' on support for punitive youth justice policies and beliefs about rehabilitation. Using an experimental design, 393 adult residents of New Zealand and Australia were randomly allocated to receive statements using either 'young serious offender' or the person-first alternative 'young people who have committed serious offences'. Contrary to our hypotheses, we found no evidence the label influenced attitudes relative to the person-first alternative, and no consistent moderation effects were observed. Exploratory analyses identified political orientation, ethnicity, and educational attainment as significant predictors of both punitive attitudes and belief in rehabilitation. These findings suggest crime-first labelling effects may only appear where strong stigma and well-established stereotypes already exist (e.g., sexual offending). However, this null result reflects only a single, one-off exposure in a survey context. The introduction of the Young Serious Offender designation in New Zealand embeds crime-first language into policy, with potentially cumulative effects that a one-off exposure cannot capture. Future research should use longitudinal designs to examine repeated exposure to labels over time.

articles.title: Developing a Neuroimaging Training Framework and Certificate Program
articles.authors: Dianne Karen Patterson; Thomas Hicks; Aneta Kielar
articles.abstract: As neuroimaging workflows grow increasingly reliant on complex computational ecosystems, cloud and cluster computing, and open science standards, academic training programs must evolve to provide relevant instruction and practice. This paper describes the design, implementation, and evolution of a fully asynchronous neuroimaging education framework at the University of Arizona. Designed to support the rapidly expanding computational ecosystems demanded by modern neuroimaging workflows, the curriculum targets a diverse trainee cohort; including graduate and undergraduate students, research staff, and faculty. In addition to teaching experimental design, data processing, and statistical analysis, the program provides practical competencies in modern computational skills, such as the Brain Imaging Data Structure (BIDS) specification, Unix command-line navigation, High-Performance Computing (HPC), notebooks (JupyterLab), basic programming (MATLAB, Bash), and containerization (Docker/Apptainer). A key contribution of the framework is its focus on pedagogical adaptability: we've found that many modern learners seek flexibility, in support of active laboratory research, over certification. To this end, our framework provides online, a la carte lessons and individual course access in addition to a complete neuroimaging certificate path. The granularity of the offerings facilitates expanding and updating materials to accommodate community requirements and feedback. Recognizing the challenges that Artificial Intelligence (AI) presents to traditional testing, we are exploring new assessment techniques that are both more resilient to AI's disruptions and incorporate AI into the evaluation process. Our AI-ready framework replaces easily exploitable multiple-choice questions with interactive matching questions and traditional testing with structured generative AI workflows, while retaining hands-on practicals. Ultimately, this case study provides a template for institutions seeking to deliver targeted, cutting-edge, on-demand training in computational neuroimaging and demonstrates how curricular flexibility can reach a broad audience but still be tailored to individual learners.

articles.title: Cultural Values Shape Acceptance of Electronic Performance Monitoring
articles.authors: Christine M Cairoli; David L Tomczak; Mauren S. Wolff; Tara S. Behrend
articles.abstract: Employee reactions to electronic performance monitoring (EPM) are mixed and depend on both the characteristics of the monitoring and the individual differences of those being monitored. Using information boundary theory as a foundation, our study investigates how horizontal-vertical individualism-collectivism dimensions affect acceptance of EPM practices that vary in invasiveness. Data from 501 participants showed that horizontal and vertical individualism and collectivism are positively associated with EPM acceptance. Furthermore, verticality is a predictor of acceptance for invasive EPM, such that people with strongly positive vertical individualism values are more likely to accept EPM. Our study demonstrates the need for organizations to consider both cultural values and the invasiveness of EPM methods when implementing monitoring policy. Further research is needed to understand how cultural values shape attitudes toward EPM in various geographic and legal settings. An awareness of cultural differences is crucial for policy makers and organizations aiming to implement EPM in ways that align with people’s norms and expectations.

articles.title: The respiratory cycle shapes perceived and self-generated time
articles.authors: Carlotta Lega; Maaike Weevers; Federica Biondi; Luigi Cattaneo
articles.abstract: Bodily rhythms are increasingly recognized as active organizers of brain function. Respiration, in particular, rhythmically modulates cortical excitability, perceptual sensitivity, memory, and action well beyond its homeostatic role. Whether breathing also shapes the brain's representation and generation of time, however, remains poorly understood. Here, we asked whether respiratory phase modulates two complementary domains of human timing, temporal perception and temporal production. Across two experiments in healthy adults (N = 40 each), respiration was continuously recorded and instantaneous respiratory phase reconstructed using Hilbert-transform-based analyses. In Experiment 1, participants performed an auditory temporal bisection task, judging intervals as “short” or “long” relative to previously learned anchors. Stimulus presentation was prospectively triggered at different phases of the respiratory cycle. Temporal judgments varied systematically with respiratory phase, particularly for perceptually ambiguous intervals: identical durations were judged as longer around peak inhalation/early expiration and shorter near peak exhalation. This modulation was specific to respiratory phase during stimulus presentation and was absent when phase was measured at the subsequent manual response, supporting a perceptual rather than response-related locus. In Experiment 2, participants synchronized finger taps to auditory metronomes at three tempi (75, 100, and 125 bpm) and subsequently continued tapping at the same tempo without external pacing. During self-paced continuation, the respiratory phases associated with slowest tapping clustered consistently across participants, particularly at the slowest tempo, with shorter inter-tap intervals occurring around inspiration. No corresponding respiratory modulation emerged during externally paced synchronization. Together, these findings suggest that respiration rhythmically shapes both perceived and self-generated time, consistent with a transient acceleration of internal timing around inspiration. Thus, the brain’s sense of time may fluctuate with each breath, suggesting that temporal processing is dynamically embedded within the ongoing physiological rhythms of the body.

articles.title: Bilateral continuous theta-burst stimulation of the anterior prefrontal cortex impairs emotional change detection and facial mimicry while enhancing metacognition of facial identity: a TMS–EMG study.
articles.authors: Luis Carlo Bulnes; Axel Cleeremans; Chotiga Pattamadilok; carmen De Vos; Marie Vandekerckhove
articles.abstract: The anterior prefrontal cortex (aPFC/BA10) is causally implicated in visual metacognition, including low-level perceptual judgments about faces. Whether it similarly contributes to the perception and metacognition of facial emotion, and also contributes to embodied facial responses, remains unclear. Facial electromyography (EMG) and skin conductance level responses were recorded while participants performed a change detection task of gradually evolving emotional (anger, happiness) facial changes from neutral (ON condition). A non-emotional change (identity) served as control. Subsequently, participants performed the reverse condition on emotional changes only, by reporting the end of an emotional expression (OFF condition). Confidence was assessed on each trial. Inhibitory continuous theta burst transcranial magnetic stimulation (cTB) was delivered bilaterally over the anterior prefrontal cortex (aPFC) using a pre-post treatment design, with Sham and NoTMS (no-stimulation) control groups. cTB did not alter confidence ratings for emotional changes. Instead, it enhanced relative metacognitive accuracy for changes in facial identity. Crucially, Sham and NoTMS groups became faster at detecting facial changes overall, as expected, whereas the cTB group did not, most clearly for happiness in the ON condition. In the OFF condition, cTB increased reaction times for anger offset detection. EMG results converged with behavioral data and showed reduced happiness-related zygomaticus activity, indicating disrupted congruent facial mimicry. These results suggest that aPFC causally contributes to distinct processing of emotional and non-emotional facial changes and exerts a downstream regulatory effect on embodied responses.

articles.title: Gratitude Towards Our Past Self and General Gratitude Enhance Self-Continuity
articles.authors: Zoe Fowler; Kyle Fiore Law; Liane Young; Madeleine Gross; Jonathan Schooler; Stylianos Syropoulos
articles.abstract: Does gratitude for the past strengthen our connection to our past and future selves? Across three pre-registered studies (N=1,779 US participants), we explored the relationship between gratitude and self-continuity–our sense of self-similarity across time. In Study 1, higher general gratitude and past-self gratitude (PSG) were associated with increased self-continuity 10 years into the past and future, with the association between gratitude and future self-continuity (FSC) significant when controlling for demographic variables and the alternative temporal dimension of self-continuity. Study 2 replicated these results in a representative US sample, finding that gratitude is linked to FSC up to 25 years ahead. Study 3 demonstrates that expressing PSG causally increases past and future self-continuity, effects not observed for gratitude towards others. Our findings suggest that individuals with higher general gratitude feel more connected to their intertemporal selves, and that promoting PSG could strengthen self-continuity, with the potential to benefit future-oriented decision-making.

articles.title: Trauma Exposure Changes Substance Use Expectancies and Affects Subsequent Use among Early Adolescents
articles.authors: Herry Patel; Fiona A Ralston; Cheyenne Yochum; Jack Waddell; Emily C. Kemp; Isabel R. Aks; William E. Pelham; Sandra Brown
articles.abstract: We examined changes in substance use (SU) expectancies following potentially traumatic events (PTEs) in a community-based cohort of early adolescents for three common substances used by teens (alcohol, cannabis, and nicotine) how those changes affected SU itself. We leveraged data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study (N=11,868, 48% female, 52% White), containing annual assessments of PTEs, SU expectancies, and SU itself from ages 10 to 14 years old. Using multilevel models to estimate between- and within-person effects, we tested whether PTEs predict negative and positive SU expectancies concurrently and prospectively and whether those expectancies forecast subsequent use. At the between-person level, PTEs were associated with increased negative and positive SU expectancies and subsequently associated with greater SU, directly and indirectly via positive expectancies concurrently and prospectively. At the within-person level, PTEs were associated with increased negative and positive SU expectancies concurrently but not prospectively. PTEs were associated with increases in SU directly and indirectly via positive expectancies and decreases in cannabis and nicotine use only via negative expectancies. But prospectively, PTEs were only associated with greater SU directly and not indirectly via positive or negative expectancies. Closer in time to each other, PTEs heighten the saliency of both positive and negative expectancies; however, over time, the effect of PTEs on expectancies diminishes. Current findings highlight a temporal window for optimal intervention to prevent SU following PTEs by assessing and targeting SU expectancies.

articles.title: Scroll and Snack: Daily Life Exposure to Healthy Food Content on Instagram Boosts Cravings for Healthy Snacks
articles.authors: Monique Caroline Alblas; Matthias Burkard Aulbach; Lena Jeremias; Veronika Pavlovova; Leonardo Pimpini
articles.abstract: Background: Food content pervades social media, yet how everyday exposure shapes momentary craving and snacking in daily life remains unclear. We tested whether experimentally adding unhealthy (H1) vs. healthy (H2) food content on top of participants’ Instagram feeds increased craving for and intake of unhealthy and healthy snacks, relative to adding art content (control). Method: In this preregistered randomized controlled field trial, 116 healthy-weight young adults (Mage = 22.46 years, 79.3% female) completed a 10-day smartphone ecological momentary assessment protocol (five prompts/day; five baseline, five manipulation days). Participants were randomly assigned to follow existing preselected Instagram accounts featuring unhealthy food, healthy food, or art (control); the number of additional accounts was 5% of those already followed. Outcomes (craving, consumption) were modeled using multilevel linear mixed models. Results: Manipulation checks confirmed expected shifts in food-related Instagram content. Against H1, added unhealthy content increased neither craving for (p = .194) nor intake of (p = .867) unhealthy snacks. Supporting H2, healthy food content increased craving for healthy snacks relative to both the control and the unhealthy condition (p < .001), but not healthy snack intake (p = .061). Conclusions: Curating a healthier Instagram feed may increase the desire for healthy snacks, but this effect, possibly due to the short duration of the manipulation, did not extend to intentions and/or intake. In conclusion, food craving may thus be used as early intervention target in future weight loss intervention, whereas changing actual intake likely requires longer or personalized exposure.

articles.title: My better half? Predicting self-esteem using appraisals of oneself, real others, and fictional characters
articles.authors: Eliott K. Doyle; Sara D. Hodges
articles.abstract: In what ways do perceptions of fictional characters supplement and differ from perceptions of real people in the context of self-esteem? The present study investigates differences between appraisals of the self, favorite fictional characters, and close real others, and the relationship between these appraisals and self-esteem. Participants (N = 265) rated themselves and their chosen real and fictional targets on likable and unlikable traits, then completed a measure of self-esteem. Appraisals of self and close real others were more favorable than appraisals of favorite fictional characters. Self-esteem was more strongly associated with self-appraisals than with appraisals of non-self targets. Differences between unlikable self and real other appraisals interacted with unlikable self and character appraisal differences in predicting self-esteem: Less unlikable appraisals of close real others compared to self-appraisals were predictive of lower self-esteem. Results suggest that fictional characters offer opportunities for self-enhancement not always afforded by real others.

articles.title: Which gambling harm prevention messages appear the most effective? Results of an online experiment comparing self-appraisal, positive emotional, loss-based, and counter-industry approaches
articles.authors: Philip Newall; William George Chapman; Simon Thomas van Baal; Jamie Torrance; Maira ANDRADE; Leonardo Weiss-Cohen
articles.abstract: Gambling harm prevention messages are increasingly catching up with best practices from tobacco of utilizing independently-designed warnings. Australia was the first country to impose this policy, using messages from three persuasion strategies: “loss-based” messages warn of the likelihood of losing money, “self-appraisal” messages prompt self-reflection of gambling behaviors, and a “positive emotional” message highlights the benefits of not gambling. In the present online experiment (N=3,486) we compared four well-performing messages from each of these classes against four well-performing “counter-industry” messages, which highlight the industry’s role in gambling harms. Messages were compared across six self-report outcomes (e.g., “this message makes me want to gamble less”), and based on the sentiment of optional free-text comments via a natural language processing analysis. Messages were ranked based on the overall sample and the high-risk sub-sample according to the Problem Gambling Severity Index (PGSI). Overall, one message of each class appeared best, with positive emotional and self-appraisal messages appearing better suited to high-PGSI audiences, and loss-based messages to low-PGSI audiences. Counter-industry messages performed similarly among all audiences, but with longer counter-industry messages performing worse in sentiment-based analysis. These findings inform future theory-informed message development and campaign implementation.

articles.title: Zürich Voice Super-Recognizer Test (ZVSRT): Normative Data from Law Enforcement Personnel on Voice Discrimination and Sorting
articles.authors: Andrea Fröhlich; Volker Dellwo; John Peter French; Meike Ramon
articles.abstract: In 2009, Russell et al. identified four “Super-Recognizers” (SRs) with exceptional face processing abilities. The potential existence of voice Super-Recognizers (VSRs) has been discussed both scientifically and related to high-stakes areas like law enforcement, which they could in principle support. Existing methods to formally assess voice identity processing (VIP) are both limited, and oftentimes lack the sensitivity required to reveal superior performance. Moreover, their de facto applied value, e.g. for forensic speaker comparison remains empirically unaddressed. To fill this gap, and drawing on findings from research on (face) SRs, we propose a preliminary working definition for VSRs and report normative data for a novel test battery designed to assess superior VIP: the Zürich Voice Super-Recognizer Test (ZVSRT). Modelling potential VSR deployment scenarios, the ZVSRT involves three difficult perceptual tasks. Its stimuli – derived from a forensic corpus – were selected using a deep learning–based open-source automatic speaker recognition system to ensure the creation of challenging trials befitting its intended purpose. The reported ZVSRT normative data was obtained from a cohort of Swiss law enforcement personnel (N = 204), who completed its constituent components: a voice discrimination, and two voice sorting tasks. These data demonstrate the ZVSRT sensitivity towards capturing the full range of VIP ability – from very low to high performance levels. We discuss future directions, including the utility of the ZVSRT and VSRs’ potential relevance for forensic applications.

articles.title: Vocabulary depth, vocabulary breadth, and speechreading as predictors of reading comprehension and inference accuracy in deaf adolescents
articles.authors: Fiona Elizabeth Kyle; Roxy Cosma; Kyi Aye
articles.abstract: The current study examined the contributions of vocabulary breadth, vocabulary depth, and speechreading to reading ability in 37 severely and profoundly deaf adolescents aged 14 to 16 years. Participants completed assessments of nonverbal cognitive ability, vocabulary breadth, vocabulary depth, speechreading, word reading, sentence comprehension, and passage comprehension. Vocabulary depth was the most consistent predictor across all reading outcomes, whereas vocabulary breadth was not significantly associated with any reading measure. Nonverbal cognitive ability, vocabulary depth, and speechreading together accounted for 77% of the variance in word reading accuracy and 86% of the variance in sentence-level comprehension. Vocabulary depth and nonverbal cognitive ability were significant predictors of passage comprehension (explaining 67% of variance), as well as performance on both literal and inferential comprehension questions. These findings underscore the importance of rich and precise word knowledge for reading development and suggest that interventions targeting vocabulary depth may enhance reading comprehension in deaf adolescents.

articles.title: Informed Voting Through Incidental News Exposure? –  Reconceptualizing the O-S-R-O-R Model for Social Media
articles.authors: Jana H Dreston; German Neubaum
articles.abstract: The O-S-R-O-R framework posits that news exposure affects political participation by promoting political discussion and increasing political knowledge. However, due to the widespread adoption of social media as news platforms, this model requires revision for three reasons. First, the level of intentionality of news exposure should be considered because intentional versus incidental exposure to news on social media was found to affect learning and discussion differently. Second, subjective knowledge must be considered alongside objective knowledge because accumulating evidence suggests that the actual and perceived learning effects of social media news use differ. Third, prior work has largely neglected qualitative distinctions of different forms of participation. We address this issue by incorporating “aligned voting” as an outcome. To test these model refinements, we conducted a pre-registered, two-wave panel survey surrounding the 2025 German federal election (N = 697). The results showed that the intentionality of social media news exposure is key in shaping subsequent knowledge gains and political actions, such as voting. Consistent with the O-S-R-O-R framework, exposure to news on social media can enhance the subjective sense of political knowledge. When individuals are incidentally exposed to news on social media and recognize its relevance, this can enhance their objective knowledge. This, in turn, helps them vote in line with their personal stances. These findings support a reconceptualization of the  O-S-R-O-R framework to account for learning and participation in algorithmically curated social media news environments.

articles.title: Errors in social network knowledge predict how ties evolve in the future
articles.authors: Alice Xia; Yi Yang Teoh; Apoorva Bhandari; Oriel FeldmanHall
articles.abstract: A striking feature of people’s social knowledge is that it is riddled with errors. These errors—e.g., making mistakes about who are actually friends in a social network—has typically been attributed to cognitive limitations or heuristics that prioritize knowledge of general social patterns over details about specific ties. Here, we demonstrate that such errors instead reflect an adaptive link prediction process that anticipates how the network will evolve far into the future. By longitudinally following a large, real-world social network (N=196) and tracking the formation and dissolution of social ties over the course of a year, we show that judgments that are wrong in the moment accurately forecast which relationships will emerge or dissolve up to six months later. On average, participants’ errors predicted tie formation nearly 3x, and tie loss more than 1.2x above chance levels. Beyond the use of simple heuristics like triadic closure and homophily, computational modeling reveals that successful link prediction relies on mental representations of the social network that integrates information about both direct and indirect, long-range ties between individuals. Having a social network representation that is future-oriented yields distinct social advantages: those who are better able to predict changes in the network become more centrally positioned over time, contingent on their initial position.

articles.title: Instrumentalising gender conspiracy theories: how narratives about gender ideology may both reflect and fuel general institutional distrust
articles.authors: Peter Teličák; Jakub Šrol; Eva Ballova Mikuskova; Magdalena Adamus
articles.abstract: In two cross-sectional and one longitudinal study conducted in Slovakia and Czechia (total N = 2339, 50,7% women; aged between 18 and 89 years), we tested whether gender ideology narratives are linked with conspiratorial thinking - operationalised as either specific conspiracy beliefs or conspiracy mentality - and pinpointed their most pronounced correlates as political ideologies and institutional distrust. The cross-sectional results show that support for gender ideology narratives is associated with conspiratorial thinking and, albeit unrelated to sociodemographic variables, shows systematic associations with institutional distrust and political stances as expressed by either collective narcissism or conservative political orientation. The preregistered Study 3 fine-tunes the findings by revealing some bidirectional temporal patterns at the within-participants level only with institutional distrust. The results point to a mutually reinforcing nexus between the gender ideology narratives and distrust thereby fostering the understanding of the narratives as embedded within a wider context of power challenging conspiracy theories. Finally, the paper offers insights into how–by exploiting and instilling the sense of distrust–gender ideology narratives can be instrumentalised to tilt political preferences towards anti-establishment, non-mainstream parties that present themselves as beacons of traditional values.

articles.title: Subject Preference as a Flexible Interpretive Heuristic in Thematic Role Assignment
articles.authors: Qingwei Xue; Yi Liu; Mingzhu Yuan; Zhurui Zhang; Tilo Kircher; Luyao Chen; Yifei He
articles.abstract: Sentence-initial arguments often receive interpretive priority during thematic role assignment, reflecting a tendency commonly referred to as “subject preference”. However, whether this preference reflects a stable commitment to a subject-first structural analysis in the final interpretation of the sentence remains unclear. To address this question, we manipulated the availability of verb-based semantic cues in a Mandarin NP1–NP2–Verb paradigm, such that they either provided sufficient information to determine the actor in subject–object and object–subject orders (cue-determined conditions) or remained insufficient to uniquely determine the actor (cue-underdetermined, ambiguous condition). One hundred and twenty native Mandarin speakers completed an actor-choice task, with response times and confidence ratings recorded. Our results showed no evidence of an NP1 advantage under cue-determined conditions. When semantic cues are underdetermined, we observed a modest NP1 preference emerged, accompanied by faster but lower-confidence responses. These findings suggest that subject preference is characterized as a flexible, cue-sensitive heuristic rather than a fixed structural default.

articles.title: PTSD risk detection from trauma narratives using natural language processing
articles.authors: Giuliano Groer; Laurin Plank; Armin Zlomuzica
articles.abstract:
Objective: Natural language processing shows promise for detection of trauma-related
disorders through the analysis of trauma-related narratives. We developed a classifier
detecting high or low PTSD symptoms from "PTSD Checklist for DSM-5" (PCL-5) scores
using semantic embeddings derived from autobiographical narratives of participants’ most
traumatic life events.
Methods: Participants (N=150) provided narratives about a traumatic, negative,
and neutral life event, and completing the PCL-5 and the "Depression, Anxiety, and Stress
Scale" (DASS-21). Semantic embedding models were used to represent narrative content
numerically. These semantic representations were used to train classification models via
nested cross-validation procedures, and model performance was evaluated using
permutation testing.
Results: The best performing classifier family trained on trauma narratives
achieved significant PTSD symptom detection performance (pooled AUC = .734, p < .002)
and significantly outperformed a word-frequency baseline (pooled AUC difference = .152,
95% CI [.070, .202]). They significantly outperformed classifiers trained on negative or
neutral narratives, which themselves did not achieve significant detection, highlighting the
unique role of traumatic memories in PTSD symptom detection. Classifiers trained on
trauma narratives showed no significant detection of DASS-21 subscales, despite strong
correlations of PCL-5 and DASS-21 values.
Conclusion: Our findings support the potential of language-based assessment of
trauma narratives for the detection of concurrent PTSD symptomatology.

articles.title: Embodied visitor experience in a festival attraction: A mixed-methods evaluation of Art of Perception in Pune, India
articles.authors: Kohinoor Monish Darda; Hansika Mangwani; Sanjana Edwankar; Sakina Bharmal; Tanvi Raghuram; Siyona Varghese; Samrddhee Pathare; Amisha Keshan; Ritika Deshpande; Sakshi Kharbanda
articles.abstract: This study evaluates Art of Perception, a seven-zone attraction presented at Creative Lab Festival 2026 in Pune, India. A convergent mixed-methods design combined matched pre-post surveys from 200 visitors (166 complete cases) with learning statements, 1,339 face-judgment votes, and 65 post-workshop drawings. Five of six self-report outcomes showed positive paired differences after Holm correction. Bodily relaxation showed the largest difference (22.9 points on a 0-100 scale; standardised difference = 0.69); trust in perception did not differ reliably. Data indicated learning about perception, neuroplasticity, art-brain relations, and nature connection. The observational, immediate, and self-reported design does not establish causation or durability. The paper proposes a public laboratory of perception as a provisional framework for construct-aligned attraction design and evaluation.

articles.title: Factors Influencing Attitudes Towards Help-Seeking Behavior In Individuals Identifying As Affected By Depersonalization/Derealization Disorder
articles.authors: Giovanni Foglia; Wendy Ross
articles.abstract: This mixed method study examined factors influencing attitudes towards help-seeking behavior in individuals identifying as affected by Depersonalization/Derealization disorder (DDD). Participants (N= 140) completed online questionnaires, including the Cambridge Depersonalization Scale, the Attitudes Towards Help-Seeking Professional Psychological Help scale, and the Self-Stigma of Seeking Help scale.58.9% of participants lacked a formal DDD diagnosis. While participants demonstrated positive attitudes towards help-seeking behaviour, this was coupled with high levels of self-stigma. However, there was no significant difference in scores between those with a formal diagnosis and those without, suggesting that structural rather than psychological factors may lie behind the underdiagnosis of DDD. Free text answers indicated that for 45% of participants, the reasons for not having a diagnosis were related to lack of knowledge or belief from medical professionals, indicating that targeted training may be more effective than psychological support.

articles.title: The Australian under-16 social media ban: Early influences on access and its relationship with reading
articles.authors: Signy Wegener; Jasmine Spencer; Andrea Salins; Serje Robidoux; Robert Savage; Anne Castles
articles.abstract: Concerns abound that time spent on social media might displace more developmentally adaptive activities, such as reading. In December 2025, the Australian government introduced a world-first social media ban for young people under the age of 16, providing an opportunity to explore whether social media use and the efficacy of the ban are associated with current reading behaviours. In this study, Australians aged 12 to 15 years completed a cross-sectional self-report online survey between March and June 2026. Prior to the ban, 81.55% of the sample used social media. Users of social media reported reading less frequently, for shorter periods and had lower reading motivation than non-users of social media. For users, the initial effect of the ban was often incomplete or transient, with many users subsequently able to regain access to lost accounts. Post-ban, time spent on social media reduced for those who lost access to some or all of their accounts. Although there were differences in reading times by the effect of the ban in the predicted direction, they were not significant. Further, there were no differences in the strength of the association between reading motivation and reading duration by the effect of the ban. These findings suggest that social media use is associated with lower levels of reading engagement than non-use. The early implementation of the social media ban has only been partially effective and there is presently insufficient evidence that the effect of the ban is associated with differences in current reading engagement.

articles.title: Phonological changes facilitate pragmatic inference during lexical access in Bengali verbs
articles.authors: Pijush Kanti Gayen; Monsija Mitra; Samar Husain
articles.abstract: How do listeners map fine-grained phonological variation onto a speaker’s communicative intention during lexical access? We address this question using a restricted set of Bengali imperative verb forms in which stem-vowel height alternation is associated with different directive speech acts. Native speakers of Bengali (N=176) completed (i) an intention-scaling task to assess perceived illocutionary force and (ii) a cross-modal lexical decision task with auditory verb primes and visual speech-act targets. The lexical decision experiment manipulated prime--target stimulus onset asynchrony (SOA: 30 ms, 60 ms, 240 ms) to test the time course of phonological-to-pragmatic activation. Intention-scaling results showed that participants reliably distinguished the two intended speech acts. In the lexical decision task, congruent speech-act targets were recognised substantially faster than controls at the 60ms SOA (approximately 100ms facilitation for both order and request), whereas effects were small and not reliable at 30ms and 240ms. Request trials also showed slightly longer latencies than order trials, consistent with a higher inferential load for requests. Together, the results provide behavioural evidence that phonological cues can rapidly bias speech-act interpretation, with a temporally constrained window for lexical-pragmatic integration.

articles.title: Before There Is a Tool: Using Early-Stage Co-Design to Examine the Legitimacy of Digital Pathways for Youth Social Prescribing
articles.authors: Simone Minett; Nikki Rickard
articles.abstract: Young people experience high levels of loneliness and social disconnection, yet they often make limited use of formal mental health services. Social prescribing aims to support wellbeing through connection to community-based activities, including arts and cultural participation. In practice, however, prevailing social prescribing models are commonly organised around practitioner-mediated pathways that may be poorly aligned with how many young people seek and negotiate support. This Commentary offers a critical reflection on an early-stage youth social prescribing project that explored the possibility of an AI-enabled digital pathway for young people as a complement to existing models. Rather than assuming the value or necessity of such an approach, the project treated the proposed digital pathway as provisional and used exploratory co-design, informed by participatory action research principles, to support reflection on its purpose, role, and boundaries. Drawing on our experience of this process and relevant published literature, we argue that early-stage co-design should attend not only to technological functionality but also to questions of legitimacy, discovery, identity and social fit, feasibility, readiness, trust, and system positioning. We offer eight practice-oriented recommendations for using early-stage co-design to support informed judgement about whether, how, and under what conditions digital pathways to offline social connection for young people should proceed within health and community systems, before tools are built.

articles.title: Feminized Perceptions of Care Work Create Unique Barriers to Labor Organizing
articles.authors: Grace Flores-Robles; Ana Gantman
articles.abstract: Care work (e.g., nursing) is critical to a functioning society, yet workers in these occupations (predominantly women) often experience low pay, and face opposition when they organize for better wages. In the current research, we examined whether care workers face gendered barriers in labor organizing. Using historical data of work stoppages in the United States, Study 1 established differences in the frequency and duration of work stoppages for care and non-care unions. Study 2 found that jobs higher in perceived care were less likely to receive support for their labor organizing. Study 3 experimentally found differences in the preferred length of strikes for care and non-care workers and separately found that gender ideologies were related to how long participants wanted workers to go on strike. Together, these findings demonstrate that care workers face unique barriers to organizing partly because the work they do is feminized.

articles.title: When showing and telling convey different stories: iterated learning of concepts leads to different outcomes when using demonstrations vs. verbal descriptions
articles.authors: Ariel Levy; Fiery Andrews Cushman
articles.abstract: When trying to convey conceptual knowledge to others, we may either show examples of the concept, or explicitly describe its defining features. Here, we ask whether the dominant mode of knowledge transmission in an experimental micro-society shapes how concepts are ultimately represented by its members.  We develop a computational model that generates novel predictions about how communication methods of a culture shape its conceptual structure. To test these predictions, we used an iterated learning experiment where participants transmit information about an imaginary biological category from one person to another along a chain, using only verbal descriptions ("tell") or only examples ("show"). Even though both conditions began with the same concept, the mode of transmission can lead participants to develop nearly orthogonal representations: “Tell” chains lead participants to overemphasize easily nameable features,  whereas “show” chains lead them to rely more on their inductive biases.

articles.title: Can a Fine-Tuned Language Model Assess Personality Equitably Across Race in Older Adults?
articles.authors: Tu Do; Tong Li; Patrick Hill; Seanna Leath; Mehak Gupta; Joshua R. Oltmanns
articles.abstract:
Artificial intelligence (AI) enables large-scale personality assessment from language. Differential performance across racial groups should be evaluated before applied use. The present study systematically examines bias in language-based personality prediction from life narrative interviews across Black and White American community older adults. Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC), BERTopic, and fine-tuned RoBERTa language model predictions of FFM traits were evaluated in a sample of n = 450 Black and n = 450 White older adults matched on education and income. LIWC and BERTopic associations differed little across race, with the few significant differences near chance levels. Fine-tuned RoBERTa predictive accuracy differed significantly for extraversion: the model performed well for White and near chance for Black participants (r = .41 vs. .17). Calibration likewise differed significantly across race only for extraversion. Openness showed significant directional bias, underpredicting scores for Black participants relative to White participants, without a significant calibration difference. These findings indicate that strong aggregate performance across race can mask differential subgroup performance. 
Keywords: language, natural language processing (NLP), artificial intelligence (AI), personality, five-factor model, big five, racial differences

articles.title: The Nature of Phonological Impairments in Dyslexia and Stuttering: Evidence from Phonemic, Semantic, and Design Fluency Tasks
articles.authors: Mahmoud Medhat Elsherif; James H Smith-Spark; Richard Kirkden
articles.abstract:
Objective: Given that dyslexia and stuttering are defined by phonological processing challenges, we investigated whether these challenges stem from poor, or inefficient access to, phonological representation. This study aimed to dissociate these cognitive mechanisms underlying verbal fluency in adults who stutter (AWS) and dyslexic adults. 
Method: An online, unsupervised sample of 62 AWS, 62 dyslexic adults and 62 neurotypical adults completed a modified, typed version of semantic and phonemic fluency with a mouse-drawn version of design fluency as a nonverbal control. We analyzed switching (shifting between subcategories; proxy for retrieval efficiency) and cluster size (words per subcategory, proxy for representational integrity). 
Results: Controlling for nonverbal IQ and language measures, hierarchical regression showed that dyslexia and stuttering significantly predicted reduced overall phonemic output, whereas semantic and design fluency remained unaffected. Both groups showed reduced switching, though more pronounced in the dyslexia group. Conversely, only stuttering predicted reduced cluster size.
Conclusion: These findings suggest in dyslexia, the access to phonological representations is affected, while it is the representations themselves in stuttering. Given the heterogeneity of these neurodivergent profiles, these challenges are not universal. However, for individuals presenting these specific cognitive signatures, interventions could be tailored toward either retrieval strategies or representational strengthening.

articles.title: COMPREHENSION VALIDATION OF THE REVISED EAWS DANGER SCALE DESCRIPTORS: LESSONS FROM A LARGE-SCALE EUROPEAN END USER SURVEY ON AVALANCHE RISK PERCEPTION
articles.authors: Philip Alexander Ebert; Frank Techel; Matthias Walcher; Benjamin Reuter; Igor Chiambretti; Lorenzo Bertranda; Montse Bacardit Pennaroya; Jaka Ortar; Mark Diggins; Karsten Müller
articles.abstract: The descriptors of the European avalanche danger scale, in use since 1993, are being revised. In June 2025 EAWS forecasters agreed on a new provisional wording and, in doing so, provided its content validation. Because the descriptors are first of all a public communication tool, we ran a comprehension validation: a survey testing whether end users read the wording as forecasters intend. It ran online from 3 February to 8 April 2026 in six languages and retained 17,335 responses after cleaning, of which 15,749 were completed. All wording comparisons were randomised between subjects. We evaluated each proposal against three conditions: correctness (do users recover the order forecasters intend?), simplicity (how easy is the task?), and increase (does the wording convey how much the danger increases from level to level?). For avalanche occurrence the main finding is reassuring: all four wording variants were ranked accurately (83–92% correct), and most differences that reach significance in the pooled data do not survive within individual languages. Only the variant that drops the distribution wording is clearly weaker. On the increase condition the variants do separate. Respondents placed the four statements on a continuous danger scale; wording level 2 as “in some places” rather than “in a few places” moves it closer to level 3 and shrinks the perceived difference between moderate to considerable from 36% to 31% of the distance between levels 1 and 4 (Cohen’s d = 0.39, p < 0.001). For size and impact the wording effect is large: adding size class words (small, medium, large, very large) to the impact wording raised accuracy from 61% to 95% and self-reported ease from 4.7 to 6.1 (Cohen’s d = 1.04). Most of that failure comes from using “bury and kill” at both levels 1 and 2, which makes them hard to tell apart. We also report how users read seven phrases that forecasters already use. For avalanche occurrence, the largest differences are between languages rather than between wordings.

articles.title: Brief Summarization Improves Effectiveness of Fact-Checks, whereas a Mental-Imagery-Based Mnemonic Does Not
articles.authors: Lucy Butler; Constantina I. Gile; Toby Prike; Ralph Hertwig; Briony Swire-Thompson; Ullrich K. H. Ecker
articles.abstract: Fact-checks reliably reduce belief in misinformation, but their effects diminish over time, partially due to forgetting—this is known as belief regression. Across two experiments, we tested whether memory-enhancing techniques could improve the long-term efficacy of fact-checks. In Experiment 1 (N = 555; one-week delay) we examined a mental-imagery-based mnemonic linking false and true claims to a ‘liar’ and ‘truthteller’, respectively, alongside conditions varying the extent to which active encoding of the fact-check was encouraged. The mnemonic did not improve fact-check memory or reduce belief regression. In contrast, briefly summarizing fact-checks improved memory and sustained belief change relative to a control condition. Experiment 2 (N = 269) replicated the enhanced effectiveness of fact-checks in the summarization condition over a longer delay period (two weeks); however, belief regression did not significantly differ from control. These findings suggest that low-barrier interventions implemented at the time of encoding can improve the effectiveness of fact-checks but may not slow the rate of belief regression. To provide theoretical and practical insight into the drivers of belief regression, future research may benefit from examining the impact of retrieval-based interventions.

articles.title: Resilience in Young Children with Social-Relational Risk for Developing Psychopathology: A Literature Review
articles.authors: Suzanne Bast; Mira Janssen; Nienke Bouw; Martine van Dongen-Boomsma; Ron Scholte; Linda Visser
articles.abstract: This literature review aimed to identify which protective factors are associated with positive mental health outcomes in young children (ages 0-6) exposed to social-relational risk factors. A structured literature search was conducted in MEDLINER, Web of Science, PsycINFO and ERIC, resulting in the inclusion of 50 studies. Guided by Bronfenbrenner’s bio-ecological model, protective factors were categorized into child, parent, family, and environmental factors. Child-factors identified were self-regulation, self-concept development, language and physical developmental, and temperament. Examples of protective factors within the parent-domain were positive parent-child interactions and parental psychological well-being. Within the family-domain, parental cohesion, quality of family relationships, and family structure and stability emerged as key protective factors. Within the broader environmental domain, protective factors identified included social support and community involvement, a supportive relationship with teachers and grandparents, and the quality of the neighbourhood. The findings support a transactional, multi-level perspective in which protective processes operate across interconnected systems. This underscores the importance of early, system- and individual-orientated screening and intervention aimed at strengthening protective processes in vulnerable young children and their caregiving environment.

articles.title: Instrumentalising gender conspiracy theories: how narratives about gender ideology may both reflect and fuel general institutional distrust
articles.authors: Peter Teličák; Jakub Šrol; Eva Ballova Mikuskova; Magdalena Adamus
articles.abstract: In two cross-sectional and one longitudinal study conducted in Slovakia and Czechia (total N = 2339, 50,7% women; aged between 18 and 89 years), we tested whether gender ideology narratives are linked with conspiratorial thinking - operationalised as either specific conspiracy beliefs or conspiracy mentality - and pinpointed their most pronounced correlates as political ideologies and institutional distrust. The cross-sectional results show that support for gender ideology narratives is associated with conspiratorial thinking and, albeit unrelated to sociodemographic variables, shows systematic associations with institutional distrust and political stances as expressed by either collective narcissism or conservative political orientation. The preregistered Study 3 fine-tunes the findings by revealing some bidirectional temporal patterns at the within-participants level only with institutional distrust. The results point to a mutually reinforcing nexus between the gender ideology narratives and distrust thereby fostering the understanding of the narratives as embedded within a wider context of power challenging conspiracy theories. Finally, the paper offers insights into how–by exploiting and instilling the sense of distrust–gender ideology narratives can be instrumentalised to tilt political preferences towards anti-establishment, non-mainstream parties that present themselves as beacons of traditional values.

articles.title: The Utilities of Beauty and Money are Largely Additive
articles.authors: Youjing Luo; Anna Bruns; Laurence T. Maloney; Olivia S. Cheung; Denis G. Pelli
articles.abstract: Beauty is typically excluded from quantitative models of economic value. We use BDM-auction and 2AFC tasks to find instead that the feeling of beauty increases willingness to pay, and its utility combines with that of money in a largely additive way. The contribution of beauty to utility is nearly independent of money’s contribution, with only a small interaction effect. These results show that incorporating beauty as a component of utility can greatly enhance prediction of choice and valuation.

articles.title: Fine-grained variation in caregivers’ /s/ predicts their infants’ /s/ category
articles.authors: Alex Eguiluz; Alejandrina Cristia
articles.abstract: Within the debate on the mechanisms underlying infant perceptual acquisition, one hypothesis proposes that infants’ perception is directly affected by the acoustic implementation of sound categories in the speech they hear. In consonance with this view, the present study shows that individual variation in fine-grained, subphonemic aspects of the acoustic realization of /s/ in caregivers’ speech predicts infants’ discrimination of this sound from the highly similar /S/, suggesting that learning based on acoustic cue distributions may indeed drive natural phonological acquisition.

articles.title: Toward a Sequencing Framework for Teaching and Using Self- Enactable Behavior Change Techniques: A Conceptual Review and Proposed Approach
articles.authors: Alexandre Mazéas; Nikos Ntoumanis
articles.abstract:
Objective: Self-enactable behavior change techniques (BCTs) may help individuals initiate and sustain health behavior change. However, existing taxonomies provide limited guidance on how such techniques should be selected, taught, combined, and sequenced over time. This perspective aimed to review previous approaches and to develop a conceptual framework for organizing and sequencing self-enactable BCTs for intervention design and participant learning.
Methods: A critical conceptual review was conducted to identify published approaches to BCT grouping, temporal organization, prerequisites, and stage-specific sequencing. Literature identified through four databases was synthesized alongside the compendium of self-enactable BCTs to inform a five-step framework-development process. 
Results: The review showed that existing taxonomies and sequencing approaches provide useful classifications but limited guidance for progressive teaching and self-enactment. To address this gap, we proposed a framework comprising 108 self-enactable BCTs organized into nine clusters and 27 groups. We mapped prerequisite relations, classified techniques by their predominant prospective or reactive function, and sequenced their groups across the Model of Action Phases. 
Conclusion: Our framework provides a theory-informed structure for teaching and applying self-enactable BCTs. It is intended to guide intervention design and generate testable hypotheses about technique sequencing that need to be empirically explored in future studies.

articles.title: Affect, Social Support and Gratitude among Ukrainian University Students in the Acute Phase of War, November 2022
articles.authors: Volodymyr Evheniiovych Momot
articles.abstract:
Research on the psychological impact of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine has been dominated by distress instruments and by data collected retrospectively or through online snowball recruitment. Comparatively little is known about the resource side of the acute phase: what remained intact, and in what form.

This study reports data collected in a single session on 15 November 2022, three weeks after the first sustained Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure, from second- and fourth-year students at a private university in Dnipro (aged approximately 17-18 and 19-20). Four instruments were administered consecutively in a 20-minute window following a deliberately non-reassuring reflective framing: SoZU-14 (N = 146), PANAS (N = 103), GQ-6 (N = 117) and a 15-item proactive-position scale (N = 114).

The affective profile did not correspond to acute distress. Negative affect was indistinguishable from the published normative mean (18.0 vs. 17.4, d = +0.10, p = .43), whereas positive affect was reduced (30.7 vs 33.3, d = -0.36, p = .001). Within negative affect the elevated items were those of chronic friction, while acute-threat and self-blame items sat at the floor (scared 1.40, ashamed 1.37); within positive affect, engagement was preserved (interested 3.47, active 3.44) while peak states were suppressed (proud 2.83, excited 2.47).

The relational instruments showed a parallel asymmetry along an unexpected line. SoZU-14 items did not separate close from distant ties; they separated the presence of supportive relationships (4.39) from turning to them for help (3.83; dz = 1.00, 82% of respondents). The three items shared with the F-SozU K-3, near-identical in a German representative sample (4.29, 4.30, 4.21; range 0.09), spread across 0.63 here, with the presence item above the German mean and both mobilisation items below it, while the three-item total matched the German norm (12.27 vs 12.33). Support was normal in volume and atypical in structure. Gratitude fell below undergraduate norms (d = -0.52 to -0.62) and attached to life in general (6.27) rather than to a wide range of people (4.80; dz = 0.90). The three comparisons form a gradient ordered by how much outward investment each construct presupposes. No cohort difference appeared on any instrument.

The dissociation was graded by resource state: the presence-mobilisation gap fell to near the German value in the highest quintile of support and followed an inverted-U, peaking not among the most deprived but among those with substantial close ties and limited overall resource (quadratic R2 = .205 vs .055 linear, p < .0001; replicated on gratitude).

We interpret this configuration as resource conservation rather than depletion: the stock of affective and relational resources is intact while its expenditure is restricted. Conservation of Resources theory accounts for rationing of a preserved stock; Socioemotional Selectivity Theory for which states and network layers were retained.

articles.title: Evaluation of replication success: A statistical perspective and extended analysis of the SCORE data
articles.authors: Robbie Cornelis Maria van Aert; Marcel A. L. M. van Assen; Ruben Lopez-Nicolas
articles.abstract: Replications are more and more conducted in multiple research fields. A recent large-scale replication project, Systematizing Confidence in Open Research and Evidence (SCORE) project, replicated 274 effects from research on business, economics, education, political science, psychology, and sociology. An open question remains how replication success can best be assessed. Thirteen methods for assessing replication success were applied in the SCORE project. The first goal of this paper is studying the statistical properties of replication success methods by a numerical study tailored to the characteristics of the SCORE data. The results of the numerical study show that replication success methods are unable to reliably draw a conclusion about replication success for typical sample sizes of the original study and replication. Hence, there is often insufficient information in one original study and one replication for drawing definite conclusions. The second goal of this paper is taking a novel perspective on the SCORE data by estimating the effect size of an original study and replication. Meta-analysis methods that correct for potential bias in the original study yielded close to unbiased estimates when synthesizing the original study and replication. The reanalysis of the SCORE data revealed that meta-analytic estimates were substantially closer to the effect size of the replication compared to the original study. The null hypothesis of no effect was rejected by the meta-analysis methods in 59.2% to 81.3% of the pairs of an original study and replication. We recommend researchers to make sure that methods for analyzing replicability have favorable statistical properties for the data at hand before applying these methods.

articles.title: LLMs reveal how ideology and time shape intuitive vs. deliberative rhetoric across 31 European parliaments
articles.authors: Julian Kauk; Edda Humprecht; Stefan R. Schweinberger; Tobias Rothmund
articles.abstract: Democratic deliberation depends on how political actors balance intuitive, affective appeals with analytically structured argumentation. Yet how ideology and time shape this rhetorical balance across diverse national contexts at large scale remains poorly understood. Informed by dual-process theories, we leverage large language models (LLMs) to analyze 3.3 million speeches from 31 European parliaments (2004–2023), quantifying two fundamental rhetorical styles: intuitive rhetoric, characterized by affective and heuristic expression, and deliberative rhetoric, characterized by analytical and evidence-oriented language. Across parliaments, ideological position is systematically associated with rhetorical style through curvilinear relationships. Intuitive rhetoric increases toward both ideological extremes, whereas deliberative rhetoric peaks near the political center and declines toward the fringes, forming a robust ideological horseshoe across institutional contexts. Temporal dynamics further document a shift toward greater reliance on intuitive rhetoric, accompanied by a modest decline in deliberative rhetoric, while the curvilinear ideological structuring of rhetorical styles persists throughout. These trends are consistent with a gradual adaptation to attention-driven communication environments, which structurally favor intuitive and affective expression over analytical depth. Together, our findings map the ideological and temporal contours of deliberative erosion in European democracies, with implications for institutional design and the resilience of democratic discourse.

articles.title: Thinking With AI, Reasoning Without It: Cognitive Offloading to Generative AI Weakens Effort Regulation
articles.authors: Dawid Ratajczyk; Agata Dymarska; Adam Matłoka; Michał Tomczyk; Małgorzata Wiącek
articles.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (genAI) can make complex cognitive tasks easier, but it remains unclear how relying on such support affects people's ability to reason independently afterwards. We investigated whether using genAI to solve a complex reasoning task influences subsequent reasoning, memory, and effort when the technology is no longer available. In a preregistered laboratory experiment with a final sample of 193 participants, we used a three-stage relational reasoning task developed for the study, in which participants learned and reasoned about a network of fictional entities and their relationships. During the first stage, participants completed the task either with or without access to ChatGPT, while performance incentives were independently manipulated. All participants then completed a more complex reasoning task based on the same relational network without genAI support, followed by a memory test. GenAI support improved accuracy during the initial task and reduced perceived difficulty. In the subsequent unaided reasoning task, prior genAI use was associated with some evidence of poorer independent reasoning. GenAI use was also associated with weaker adjustment of effort to incentives and task difficulty once the tool was removed. No clear effects were observed on later memory. Overall, the findings suggest that genAI can facilitate performance while it is available, but may also alter how users process task-relevant information and regulate effort during subsequent independent performance.

articles.title: Conversing with a disagreeing LLM improves people’s inaccurate predictions
articles.authors: Emir Efendic; Philippe van de Calseyde
articles.abstract: Accurately predicting the outcome of future events improves decisions in domains ranging from health to finance, yet prediction errors are common. One reliable way to improve accuracy is to engage with disagreeing views through dialogue, which can reveal weak assumptions and facilitate belief revision. However, people often avoid disagreeing exchanges because they are socially and emotionally costly or inconvenient to seek out. Here, we examine whether a disagreeing large language model (LLM) can provide the benefits of disagreement while sidestepping these interpersonal barriers. Across two experiments (total N = 807 adults making 4,564 predictions; Experiment 2 was incentivized and preregistered), participants: i) predicted the likelihood of various events, ii) discussed each prediction with an LLM by articulating their reasoning, and iii) submitted final predictions. Crucially, we manipulated the LLM’s stance during these discussions: it responded either supportively (agreeing) or critically (disagreeing) to participants’ reasoning. The results showed that, when initial predictions were erroneous, conversing with a disagreeing LLM produced more accurate final predictions than conversing with a supportive one. This advantage was primarily driven by directionally correct revisions, with participants shifting their final predictions more often toward the realized outcome. However, interacting with an LLM was not uniformly beneficial as it decreased accuracy when initial predictions were already accurate. These findings underscore the value of designing LLMs that challenge rather than affirm users’ views and opinions, while highlighting the importance of tailoring their responses to the expected accuracy of initial predictions.

articles.title: Not All Eye Occlusions Are Equal: Expressive and Mechanical Eye Occlusion Differentially Shape Emotion Recognition and Eye-Tracked Visual Attention
articles.authors: Daniel Granja; Nicolas Burra
articles.abstract: Emotion recognition from facial expressions is commonly assumed to depend on the visibility of diagnostic features, particularly the eyes. Accordingly, eye occlusion is often treated as a unitary manipulation, under the assumption that comparable informational loss yields equivalent perceptual consequences. The present study challenges this assumption by testing whether expressive (closed eyes) and mechanical (sunglasses) forms of eye occlusion differentially affect emotion recognition and visual attention. In a preregistered within-subjects experiment combining multidimensional emotion ratings with eye-tracking, participants judged emotional and neutral faces presented with open eyes, closed eyes, or sunglasses. The results revealed a critical dissociation: closed eyes reduced emotion recognition more strongly than sunglasses, yet elicited longer fixation durations on the eye region. Notably, fearful faces with closed eyes were associated with increased pleasure ratings, indicating a reinterpretation of the expression rather than simple signal loss. This fixation pattern rules out attentional withdrawal as an explanation for reduced recognition, as participants attended more, rather than less, to closed eyes. Together, these findings demonstrate that eye occlusion alters emotion recognition through interacting perceptual and interpretive processes. Distinguishing between expressive and mechanical eye occlusion provides a refined framework for understanding how reduced eye visibility shapes social perception.

articles.title: Belief traps hinder small business climate action
articles.authors: Jeffrey Martin Lees; Dror Etzion; Christoph Ungemach; Sara Madureira Constantino; Frederik Dahlmann; Maria Laura Frigotto
articles.abstract: Climate (in)action by small business owners is not driven solely by policy or economic considerations, but also by sociological and psychological factors, as leaders mimic the behaviours they perceive among their peers. We find that these social inferences about what others believe are often incorrect. In this registered report of 4432 small-to-medium business owners and leaders across seven countries, we observe a persistent gap between perceived and actual beliefs. And this gap matters: SME owners exhibiting a larger gap have fewer sustainability policies in place. These results highlight how peer effects can spur climate action among business leaders.

articles.title: Validating LLMs as Coders of Cultural Constructs: a Large-Scale Test of Minimally Counterintuitiveness using Pokémon
articles.authors: Masaki Suyama; Yo Nakawake
articles.abstract: Minimally counterintuitiveness (MCI) theory predicts that concepts violating a small number of intuitive ontological expectations (1--2 violations) are transmitted more successfully than either fully intuitive concepts or maximally counterintuitive (3+ violations) ones. Testing this inverted-U prediction at scale has been limited by the cost of human content coding. We evaluate whether large language models (LLMs) can serve as valid, scalable coders of MCI violations, and use a validated pipeline to re-test the inverted-U prediction on a substantially larger sample than prior work. In Study 1, zero-shot coding by two LLMs (Claude and Gemini) against a human-coded baseline showed only moderate agreement driven by systematic over-attribution of violations. In Study 2, a leave-one-out few-shot calibration procedure -- coding each item zero-shot while supplying the other human-coded items as in-context examples -- raised agreement to nearly double specificity while preserving sensitivity. In Study 3, we applied the calibrated pipeline to Generation 2+ Pok\'{e}mon and merged the result with an independent popularity ranking to test the inverted-U prediction. The predicted curvature became significant, with the fitted parabola's vertex at MCI score 2.04, overlapping theory's predicted optimum. Together these studies show that a modest human-coded seed set can calibrate an LLM coder well enough to test a classic cultural-transmission theory at a scale far beyond what human coding alone permits.

articles.title: Affective benefits of daily life activity and experiential diversity are associated with catecholamine systems across the adult life span
articles.authors: Jennifer Lee Crawford; Johanna Matulonis; Mariah Lewis; Hsiang-Yu Chen; Jacob M. Hooker; Heidi I. L. Jacobs; Aaron S Heller; Anne S. Berry
articles.abstract: Engaging in varied behaviors promotes well-being in both humans and non-human animals. The current study tested whether the diversity of daily life activities and experiences are associated with affect and cognition across adulthood. Additional analyses explored the role of the catecholamine systems in sustaining the benefits of daily life diversity. Participants (N=184) ages 18-87 completed three weeks of daily life sampling that included repeated measurements of activities, affect, and geolocation. In a subset of these participants, we used MRI (N=72) and PET (N=35) to measure catecholamine systems. Both activity and experiential diversity were independently associated with affect, but not cognition. Interestingly, the coupling between affect and activity diversity was related to the dopaminergic system, whereas the coupling between affect and experiential diversity was associated with the noradrenergic system. These findings suggest that catecholamine systems play complementary roles in supporting the affective benefits of activity and experiential diversity across adulthood.

articles.title: Knowledge in the Post-Truth Era: The Relations of Established Personality Traits, Exclusionary Authoritarian Worldviews, and Planetary Health Knowledge
articles.authors: Franziska Rees; Oliver Wilhelm
articles.abstract:
Fact knowledge accumulates throughout life and its acquisition is determined by fluid 
intelligence, personality traits, domain-specific interests, and education. Research on 
misinformation and cultural cognition suggests that worldviews influence how individuals 
select and evaluate information, but their contribution to individual differences in factual 
knowledge remains unclear. We investigate whether ideological worldviews explain 
individual differences in Planetary Health Knowledge (PHK), beyond formal education and 
broad personality traits. A sample of 878 U.S. adults completed a 14-item PHK test, reported 
educational attainment, and answered a 76-item personality inventory and various measures 
of ideological worldviews, including right-wing-authoritarianism, conspiracy beliefs, and 
climate change skepticism. The strongest worldview correlates of PHK were combined into a 
factor for Exclusionary Authoritarian Ideology (EAI). In latent regression models, education, 
personality, and EAI jointly explained up to 44% of the variance in PHK. EAI was the 
strongest predictor for PHK, incrementally explaining up to 27%. Openness to experience was 
positively associated with PHK, whereas dark personality showed a weak-to-moderate 
negative association. These findings suggest that a general ideological factor captures a 
substantial share of factual knowledge about contemporary global issues. Unlike other 
knowledge areas, PHK is determined by ideological worldviews—which should be 
considered in political controversies and educational interventions.

articles.title: My Personality—Wrapped: Protocol for a Measurement-Burst Design Study to Investigate the Development and Dynamics of Individual Differences Across Time
articles.authors: Amanda Jo Wright; Peter Haehner; Michael Dominik Krämer; Nicholas Poh-Jie Tan; Christopher James Hopwood; Wiebke Bleidorn
articles.abstract: People and their environments continuously shape one another across time. Understanding these person-environment transactions is essential for describing, predicting, and explaining the dynamics and development of individual differences. Yet, progress on this has been constrained by two common limitations: study designs driven by practical rather than theoretical considerations and neglecting how person-environment processes unfold across multiple timescales. To address these limitations, we present the rationale and design of the My Personality—Wrapped (MPW) Study, a 1-year-long measurement-burst study designed to investigate how individual differences in personality, well-being, attitudes, social and interpersonal behaviors, and health develop across multiple timescales and fluctuate alongside environmental influences. Participants complete baseline (T0) and post-study (T6) assessment batteries, five bimonthly surveys (T1–T5), and 15 pseudorandomly scheduled 1-week bursts comprising mobile sensing, experience sampling, daily, and weekly surveys. This intensive, multi-method study provides comprehensive cross-timescale data on psychological constructs and contextual experiences over 1 year. The MPW Study is designed to advance the field’s understanding of temporal dynamics underlying individual differences by disentangling within-person processes from between-person differences, facilitating theory development and testing of multi-timescale person-environment transactions, and informing future theory-driven research on the dynamics of personality and well-being, social and health processes, and life disruptions.

articles.title: ‘For Your Brain’: Neural connectivity tracks perceived personalization success of the TikTok algorithm
articles.authors: Anthony G Vaccaro; Elizabeth Escalante; Kaitlyn Burnell; Mitchell J Prinstein; Eva H. Telzer
articles.abstract: Personalized recommender algorithms are among the most influential design features of modern digital platforms. Yet, most neuroscience research on social media relies on controlled stimuli sets, or associating behaviors with general neuroimaging tasks; these methods cannot capture the dynamic process of how the brain responds to feeds that learn user preferences over time. To address this gap, we used functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) to develop a highly naturalistic paradigm where 72 young adults scrolled on the For You page of a brand new TikTok account for 35 minutes while neural connectivity was measured.Participants reported that content was signifi cantly more personally relevant at the end than at the beginning of scrolling, and durations of felt boredom significantly decreased. Despite all participants encountering unique content and scrolling at their own pace, neural connectivity of prefrontal and temporal regions tracked the emergence of perceived personalization, and these trajectories varied by problematic social media use. These findings suggest that the dynamic neural changes as personalization occur can give insights into problematic social media use tendencies, and highlight the feasibility and value of highly ecologically valid paradigms in understanding digital media use.

articles.title: How Task Demands Shape Reading Behavior: Evidence from Sentence Processing Experiments
articles.authors: Jan Chromý; Markéta Ceháková; Radim Lacina; Jakub Dotlacil
articles.abstract:
Post-reading tasks are a common component of sentence-processing experiments, but their influence on online reading behavior is not fully understood. In the present study, we investigated how different post-sentential tasks affect processing in the word-by-word moving-window self-paced reading paradigm. Three experiments used identical Czech stimuli set but differed in the task administered after each sentence: yes/no comprehension questions, open-ended recall questions, or naturalness judgments. The materials included six item types: garden-path sentences, plausible vs. implausible sentences, grammatical vs. ungrammatical sentences, sentences containing gender interference, sentences comprising generic masculine ambiguity, and sentences with differences in information structure.
