Across all experiments, we analyzed reaction times in theoretically relevant sentence regions as well as responses in the post-reading task.

The results showed clear effects of task type on overall reading behavior. Participants expecting recall questions read more slowly than participants answering yes/no questions, whereas participants making naturalness judgments read fastest. Despite these differences in overall reading speed, several well-established processing effects proved remarkably stable across tasks. Garden-path, plausibility, and grammaticality manipulations produced similar processing costs in critical and spillover regions regardless of the anticipated post-reading task. In contrast, the strongest task-related differences emerged in sentence-final wrap-up regions. For several item types, naturalness judgments produced patterns that differed substantially from those observed in comprehension-based tasks, including reversals of difficulty effects.

These findings suggest that readers adapt their reading strategy to the demands of the expected task. At the same time, established online processing effects appear relatively robust across different post-reading tasks. More generally, the results indicate that post-reading tasks are an important part of the experimental context and can influence reading behavior in systematic ways.

articles.title: Wise Empathy Improves Well-being on Instagram
articles.authors: Gregory John Depow; Christopher Oveis; Emily Zohar; Michael Inzlicht
articles.abstract: Most of the global population spends significant time browsing social media making it critical to understand how to improve experiences online to support well-being. Here, we test whether a brief intervention training individuals to use wise empathy on Instagram can improve users’ well-being. In an ecological momentary intervention, we trained half our sample (N = 260) to wisely regulate empathy for positive and negative posts. Using experience sampling (Nobs. = 5,902), we tracked empathy and well-being in daily life. The intervention increased wise empathy online—boosting appreciative joy, positive emotion sharing, and compassion for negative emotions—while reducing negative emotion sharing, upward social comparisons, and personal distress. When participants had recently browsed Instagram, those in the wise empathy condition reported higher well-being than controls, an effect mediated by changes in wise empathy. These findings position wise empathy as a scalable, trainable skill that can enhance well-being on social media.

articles.title: Organization-level Inclusion Signals: Positive Effects for Both LGBT and non-LGBT Employees
articles.authors: Alexandra Figueroa; Sarah Lian Jensen; Jesse Graham
articles.abstract: This work examines organizational-level inclusion signals and their subsequent effects on employees. Answering the call for more research on concealable stigmatized identities, we consider the effect of such organization-level inclusion signals for sexual and gender minorities (lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender employees) while also considering the effect on non-target employees. In a time-lagged observational study (N = 1,165 ), archival data (N = 229), and a randomized experiment (N = 380), we show that organizational-level inclusion efforts lead to more positive perception of the organization’s psychological climate for sexual and gender minorities, closing the psychological safety gap between non-LGBT and LGBT employees.. Notably, these intentional inclusion efforts also benefit non-LGBT employees, which contradicts recent theoretical assertions that intentional inclusion can harm majority groups, or that organizational inclusion is a zero-sum game.These signals shaped positive behavioral intentions for all employees, leading to non-LGBT employees engaging in more individual ally work, and LGBT employees feeling more free to share their identities. Unexpectedly, inclusion signals even made non-LGBT employees less likely to conceal intimidating parts of their identity (e.g. religion, parental status) as well. In sum, we show that such signaling improves psychological safety for all employees, reducing or eliminating the deficit between target and non-target employees while also encouraging value-aligned positive behaviors.

articles.title: Mood recovery via positive autobiographical recall: The roles of perceived importance and emotional intensity
articles.authors: Jiaqi Zhong; Shu Imaizumi
articles.abstract: This study examined how the perceived importance of positive autobiographical memories (PAMs) is associated with emotion regulation following anger and sadness induction. Utilizing a 2 (high vs. low memory importance) × 2 (anger vs. sadness induction) between-participants design, 282 adults underwent a negative mood induction via video, followed by a PAM recall task. Analysis controlling for depressive symptoms showed significant mood recovery from post-induction to post-recall, but the experimental manipulation of memory importance did not significantly affect the magnitude of recovery. Initial structural equation modeling showed that perceived memory importance was positively associated with self-relevance, reliving, imagery, and emotional intensity, but only emotional intensity uniquely predicted mood recovery. The specific indirect effect of perceived importance on mood recovery through emotional intensity was significant, although the overall model showed poor fit. Exploratory analyses focusing on emotional intensity showed a similar indirect pathway in both the anger and sadness conditions, which remained significant after accounting for emotion-regulation strategies. These findings suggest that perceived memory importance may be indirectly associated with short-term mood recovery through emotional intensity during recall, whereas its direct contribution appears limited.

articles.title: Not Everyone Slows Down After a Mistake: Individual Differences in Post-Error Slowing
articles.authors: Sven Lesche; Carla Michel; Kathrin Sadus; Wiebke Bernhardine Hemming; Dirk Hagemann
articles.abstract:
Does everybody slow down after an error? Across 34 behavioral datasets comprising more than 4,000 participants, we found that some participants reliably do not. While most participants exhibited post-error slowing, a subset reliably showed post-error speeding, often accompanied by reduced accuracy. Bayesian model comparisons consistently favored specifications that allowed for post-error speeding, providing clear evidence for individual differences in the direction of post-error behavior even among participants exposed to the same experimental conditions. 

Additionally, heterogeneity extended beyond response times to post-error accuracy adjustments. Whereas some participants exhibited patterns consistent with adaptive control, characterized by more accurate responding following errors, others showed maladaptive adjustments marked by reduced accuracy. Together, these results suggest that current group-level theories of post-error behavior are incomplete and must be expanded to account not only for posterror speeding, but also for individual differences in the direction of post-error accuracy changes. Rather than reflecting a single underlying mechanism, our findings are more consistent with multiple cognitive, motivational, and affective processes that are jointly engaged following errors. We propose that these processes are present across individuals but vary in their relative contribution, leading to systematic differences in observed behavior, including whether individuals show post-error slowing or speeding.

articles.title: Transdiagnostic factors differentially shape choices and reaction times in social evaluative learning
articles.authors: Aamir Sohail; Aleksandra Magda; Muna Said; Laura Phillips; Yifei Lu; Georgina Reynolds; Alice Comer-Fenn; Jessie Russell; Huafeng Lu; Tally Sims
articles.abstract:
Background
Learning from feedback provided by others is important for navigating complex social environments. Aberrant processing of such social feedback is implicated in the psychopathology of several mental health disorders including social anxiety and depression. Recent psychiatric research increasingly adopts transdiagnostic approaches that examine mechanisms and constructs cutting across traditional diagnostic categories. 

Methods
Here, we applied reinforcement learning models together with transdiagnostic measures of psychopathology to formally assess social evaluation learning. Human participants (n = 193) completed the Social Evaluation Learning Task, learning whether computer personas ‘liked,’ ‘disliked,’ or were ‘neutral’ toward them. Participants also completed six questionnaires assessing socially relevant psychiatric traits. 

Results
Computational modeling revealed that a model with separate learning parameters for positive and negative feedback best accounted for the learning behavior. Exploratory factor analysis identified three transdiagnostic factors. A factor reflecting social avoidance predicted enhanced learning from negative feedback and a reduced positive learning bias. Socially avoidant individuals with heightened negative learning rates additionally showed faster reaction times specifically in positive social contexts. A second factor linking with emotional insensitivity for others predicted a lower choice accuracy in both positively and negatively valanced conditions and was associated with faster reaction times overall. No significant associations emerged for a third factor reflecting depressive and mood-related symptoms. 

Conclusions
These results demonstrate how transdiagnostic trait dimensions shape social learning mechanisms through specific behavioral and computational processes.

articles.title: Elected by the face? Facial impressions of honesty and competence made under suboptimal conditions predict voting intentions
articles.authors: Antonio Olivera-LaRosa; Guido Corradi; Sergio Barbosa; Sissy Delgado-Pacheco; William Jimenez-Leal; Gonzalo Luna-Cortes; Javier Villacampa; Jaume Rosselló
articles.abstract: Rapid judgments based on political candidates' facial features often predict electoral outcomes. Building on this, we explored how facial impressions of honesty and competence—formed under suboptimal processing conditions—predict voting intentions for actual political candidates. In this study, 484 participants (Colombians: 199; Peruvians: 285; male: 30.2%) were exposed to candidate faces from Colombia and Peru under time constraints (33 ms or 100 ms). Participants rated these faces on honesty and competence and subsequently indicated their likelihood of voting for each candidate. Our findings demonstrate that these rapid facial impressions consistently predict voting intentions regardless of candidate familiarity, evaluative dimension, or exposure duration. Specifically, both honesty and competence impressions were formed with as little as 33 ms of exposure and significantly predicted voting preferences. By utilizing real candidate photographs, this study confirms that rapid facial impressions align with electoral preferences in naturalistic settings. These results demonstrate that electoral choices are anchored in early, heuristic-driven processing.

articles.title: Practice elements of effective digital media interventions for youth: A distillation and matching approach
articles.authors: I. Chaplinska; Peter Nikken; Jertberg Robert M; Hilde Brons; Smixioti Efthymia; H.M. Koning Ina; Yvette Edelaar; Carlo Schuengel
articles.abstract: Digital media interventions for youth pursue diverse goals, including media literacy, online safety, cyberbullying prevention, critical information evaluation, and digital participation. They may nonetheless share practice elements – discrete, operationally defined units of action – that recur across interventions effective for particular targets, groups, and contexts. This study applied the Distillation and Matching Model to 91 nominally effective digital media intervention records drawn from a scoping-review database. Intervention content was coded first with predefined elements from youth psychosocial interventions and then inductively to capture digital-media-specific practice elements. Interventions were classified as risk-oriented, opportunity-oriented, or mixed, and element profiles were compared across target-population and implementation characteristics using intraclass correlation coefficients. Seventeen predefined and 15 digital-media-specific elements exceeded the preregistered frequency threshold. Among predefined elements, Psychoeducation (child), Insight Building, Accessibility Promotion, Support Networking, and Talent / Skill Building were most frequent. Among digital-media-specific elements, Content creation and Critical media analysis predominated, followed by Source evaluation, Digital media education, Search training, Cyber safety training, and Regulating digital media use. Participant age group differentiated profiles most strongly: middle childhood and adolescence, the groups with enough records for stable comparison, were organised around content creation and critical media analysis, whereas early childhood (accessibility and support) and young adults (heterogeneous profiles) could be characterised only descriptively. Opportunity-oriented interventions centred on content creation and mixed interventions on critical media analysis, whereas risk-oriented interventions showed more dispersed profiles. These configurations were not fixed but varied with the developmental stage of the audience and with the duration and orientation of the intervention, while delivery mode differentiated profiles least. The study contributes a taxonomy of digital-media-specific practice elements and a transferable vocabulary for designing and comparing interventions, while underscoring that the population and implementation characteristics needed to match elements to contexts remain too often unreported.

articles.title: Broadening the Recipe to Strengthen Democracy
articles.authors: Gijs Schumacher; Jakob Kasper; Mariken Anna Catharina Geertruida van der Velden; Max Zaslove; Matthijs Rooduijn; Bert N. Bakker
articles.abstract: Deep concerns about the ability of democracies to cope with polarization, political violence, and anti-democratic attitudes have motivated social scientists to develop interventions that strengthen democracy. The emerging evidence base has impact on policy globally but is predominantly based on American findings. To strengthen democracies, we need a broader evidence base. To this end, we conducted an intervention tournament (14 interventions, 23,146 participants) in a very different democracy – the Netherlands. Some successful interventions in the US replicate, with others failing to replicate. We identify a newly constructed narrative-based intervention as the most successful in strengthening democracy. By developing a theoretical framework to compare interventions and innovations in our research design we lay the groundwork for a global intervention tournament.

articles.title: Affective Reactivity and Approach-Avoidance Behavior in Daily Life: Insights from Vignettes and Ambulatory Assessment Data
articles.authors: Joana Christine Thiel; Daniel Powell; Andreas B. Neubauer
articles.abstract: The present study examined whether individual differences in affective stress reactivity are associated with stressor avoidance (intentions) in everyday life. We distinguished perceived affective reactivity, defined as participants’ self-estimated tendency to respond affectively to stressors, and experienced affective reactivity, operationalized as the within-person association between momentary stressor occurrence and negative affect. The multimethod preregistered study included 200 healthy participants. At baseline, we applied the novel Perceived Affective Reactivity Scale (PARS) alongside a vignette study capturing stressor avoidance intention in five everyday life scenarios varying in stressor intensity and benefit. In the following two-week ambulatory assessment, we assessed experienced affective reactivity using six momentary assessments per day and stressor avoidance behavior in the evening. Perceived affective reactivity was not associated with avoidance intention assessed with either method. In contrast, experienced affective reactivity was positively associated with both the frequency of stressor avoidance during the same assessment period and avoidance intentions in vignette scenarios involving low-intensity stressors with high potential benefits. Beyond these primary associations, we found (a) a moderate positive association between perceived and experienced reactivity, and (b) everyday avoidance behavior was linked to vignette-derived avoidance intentions only for low-intensity, high-benefit stressors. These findings suggest that (a) – while distinct –experienced and perceived affective reactivity share an underlying core and (b) daily stressors may oftentimes reflect situations of lower stressor intensity and high potential benefits.

articles.title: Sampling Fast and Slow Changes Inferences About Well-Being Dynamics
articles.authors: Michael Aristodemou; Manuel Voelkle; Charles C Driver
articles.abstract: Subjective well-being unfolds over time, but inferences about its dynamics may depend on how often it is measured. We examined whether the same well-being processes yield different conclusions when observed annually versus bimonthly. Using two large German population-based panels, the annual SOEP study and the bimonthly GESIS panel, we fit continuous-time structural equation models to 10 cognitive and affective well-being domains. We used propensity-score matching to reduce observed demographic differences between panels. Our results showed that annual and bimonthly data were not fully exchangeable. Independently fitted models best captured the full predictive distribution. However, pooled models often predicted expected well-being levels as well as, or better than, independent models. Descriptive comparisons showed that baseline levels of subjective well-being were relatively similar across designs, whereas dynamic features differed. Deviations from baseline persisted four to eight times longer in annual than bimonthly data; long-run within-subject correlations were stronger in the bimonthly data for most domain pairs; and long-run within-subject variances were consistently larger in the annual data. Within-sample thinning analyses showed that sparser sampling did not necessarily alter recovered dynamics within the temporal ranges examined. These findings suggest that subjective well-being is a multi-timescale system where different observation schedules reveal different aspects of persistence, fluctuation, covariation, and heterogeneity. Temporal design should therefore be treated as a central determinant of substantive inferences.

articles.title: Fifty Shades of Well-Being: Addressing an Overlooked Source of Confusion in the Science of Well-Being.
articles.authors: Joffrey Fuhrer
articles.abstract: Despite constant progress, the science of well-being remains marked by confusion, with a proliferation of competing conceptual frameworks, theoretical approaches, and measurement tools undermining both scientific progress and real-world applications in areas such as counseling, therapy, and public policy. This paper identifies an overlooked contributor to this confusion: the adoption of Philosophically Dense Concepts (PDC) into empirical science, facilitated by academic practices that favor theoretical novelty and discourage interdisciplinary collaboration. Using a conceptual genealogy of the hedonic-eudaimonic well-being distinction as a paradigmatic example, I show how such PDC, when translated from philosophy into psychology and social and health sciences, became semantically fuzzy and led to inconsistent theoretical frameworks and measurement tools. The paper concludes with recommendations on how to better deal with PDC in well-being research and the emerging science of flourishing.

articles.title: What parents want their children to become: Character strengths as a framework for understanding parental socialization goals
articles.authors: Lisa Wagner; Nina Vaupotič; Johannes Bodo Heekerens; Fabian Gander
articles.abstract:
Objective: Which personality traits do people consider worth fostering? Parents’ aspirations for their children provide a developmental perspective on this question. We examined whether the Values in Action (VIA) classification of character strengths captures these aspirations.
Method: In an online survey, German- and English-speaking parents and expecting parents (N = 1,410; Mage = 31.2 years; 94.3% women) either described the qualities they hoped their children would develop or rated the desirability of the 24 VIA character strengths and ten comparison traits (e.g., intelligence) for their children. Participants also rated their own character strengths.
Results: All 24 character strengths were regarded as desirable, although to varying degrees. Across ratings and open-ended responses, parents consistently prioritized love, honesty, kindness, and social intelligence. Character strengths were generally valued more highly than comparison traits, particularly academic achievement and attractiveness. Parents also placed greater value on strengths they themselves scored higher on. Desirability was also associated with perceived contribution to well-being and, depending on the method, normative levels and societal valuation.
Conclusions: Character strengths capture many of the personality traits parents most want their children to develop, highlighting parental socialization goals as a valuable perspective on desirable personality.

articles.title: Recognition Matters: Exploring Wellbeing for Students with Dyslexic-Type Challenges
articles.authors: Jane Mosco; Megan Frances Lee
articles.abstract: High school students with dyslexia, characterised by reading and spelling struggles, are at greater risk of experiencing poorer wellbeing at school than their peers. Yet there has been limited exploration of wellbeing for students with reading struggles through the lens of recognition theory. We aimed to further understand students’ wellbeing through an exploratory study foregrounding students’ views, alongside those of their educators, to inform school practices. Participants included 22 high school students aged 12-18 years (Years 7-12) from eight regional Australian NSW schools, and 23 of their educators. High school students participated in student focus groups or interviews (Phase 1) and could join student art workshops to elicit insights through images and text (Phase 2). These served as stimuli for subsequent teacher interviews (Phase 3) and intentionally brought students’ views into dialogue with educators', strengthening qualitative data findings. Thematic Analysis generated three overarching factors that potentially influence student wellbeing: 1) Interpersonal interactions and relationships at school; 2) teaching and learning attuned to students’ needs, and 3) relational pedagogy. Further theoretical analysis utilising recognition theory deepened understanding, highlighting how intersubjective and structural recognition can both shape students’ wellbeing. Students and educators highlight significant learning and wellbeing entanglement, describing instances of recognition and misrecognition at school. School psychologists can help improve conditions by reduce instances of misrecognition whilst increasing recognition. Mutual dialogue with students alongside attuned neurodiversity-affirming quality teaching and school practices can simultaneously create the conditions for recognition, enhancing students' learning and wellbeing.

articles.title: Man vs Machine: Electrodermal and Behavioural Responses to Human and AI‑Generated Faces
articles.authors: Giulia Panozzo
articles.abstract:
As technology advances and AI-generated faces increasingly resemble real human faces, it remains unclear whether human autonomic responses differ when viewing human and synthetic faces before explicit judgement. This study investigated whether electrodermal activity (EDA) can reveal pre-conscious physiological differences during the visual presentation of human versus AI-generated faces. Twenty-three adults (25–65 years) viewed static faces from three categories—human, hyper-realistic AI, and less realistic AI-generated faces—while continuous EDA was recorded during an initial passive viewing phase. Participants then completed an active categorisation task in which they classified each face as "human" or "AI", followed by a questionnaire assessing prior exposure to AI-generated content.
Human faces elicited significantly higher skin conductance level (SCL) than both AI-generated categories during passive viewing, indicating stronger autonomic engagement with human faces than synthetic faces prior to explicit categorisation. In the active task, participants correctly classified 89% of human faces and 99% of less realistic AI faces, but only 78% of hyper-realistic AI faces, misclassifying 22% of them as human (60/276 trials across participants). These findings suggest that autonomic sensitivity to human social stimuli persists even when highly realistic AI faces are behaviourally difficult to distinguish from human faces, indicating that pre-conscious physiological responses do not straightforwardly translate into explicit behavioural discrimination. Self-reported familiarity with AI-generated content predicted behavioural performance but was unrelated to autonomic differentiation, further supporting a dissociation between physiological and explicit measures.
Overall, the findings suggest that autonomic responses, explicit behavioural judgements, and prior experience capture complementary aspects of Human–AI face perception. Together, they indicate that increasing visual realism alone is insufficient to eliminate autonomic differentiation. These findings provide a basis for understanding how increasingly realistic AI-generated media are processed and, ultimately, for examining their broader societal implications, with relevance for the ethical development and deployment of synthetic media.

Keywords: electrodermal activity, human-AI perception, Uncanny Valley, autonomic nervous system, artificial intelligence

articles.title: Self-Perceptions on Social Media vs. Offline Contrast With Those Perceived in Generalized  but not Close Others
articles.authors: Cameron James Bunker
articles.abstract:
Self-perception varies across contexts. Do perceptions of others across contexts vary in the same 
way? Here, a multi-study mapping of context-framed person perception addressed this question. 
Participants (N = 1748) reported perceptions of the Big Five personality traits specifying two 
contexts that dominate daily life (offline and social media) regarding three targets: self, the 
typical person (Studies 1-3, 5), and peers (Studies 4 and 5). The perceptions were examined both 
within-person via profile agreements and normatively via mean levels. Profile agreement 
analyses suggested that the similarity between offline and social media contexts was strong in 
self-perceptions (and perceptions of peers) but moderate in perceptions of the typical person. 
Mean level analyses further suggested generally lower trait levels on social media vs. offline in 
self-perceptions (and perceptions of peers). However, perceptions of the typical person showed 
the opposite or attenuated effects in terms of 3/5 traits (openness, extraversion, and neuroticism). 
Perceptions of all three targets showed lower levels of agreeableness on social media than 
offline. Conscientiousness was the only trait to show inconclusive patterns across the studies. 
Together, the findings suggest that self-perceptions on social media vs. offline contexts contrast 
with those perceived in generalized (but not close) others.

articles.title: Errors in social network knowledge predict how ties evolve in the future
articles.authors: Alice Xia; Yi Yang Teoh; Apoorva Bhandari; Oriel FeldmanHall
articles.abstract: A striking feature of people’s social knowledge is that it is riddled with errors. These errors—e.g., making mistakes about who are actually friends in a social network—has typically been attributed to cognitive limitations or heuristics that prioritize knowledge of general social patterns over details about specific ties. Here, we demonstrate that such errors instead reflect an adaptive link prediction process that anticipates how the network will evolve far into the future. By longitudinally following a large, real-world social network (N=196) and tracking the formation and dissolution of social ties over the course of a year, we show that judgments that are wrong in the moment accurately forecast which relationships will emerge or dissolve up to six months later. On average, participants’ errors predicted tie formation nearly 3x, and tie loss more than 1.2x above chance levels. Beyond the use of simple heuristics like triadic closure and homophily, computational modeling reveals that successful link prediction relies on mental representations of the social network that integrates information about both direct and indirect, long-range ties between individuals. Having a social network representation that is future-oriented yields distinct social advantages: those who are better able to predict changes in the network become more centrally positioned over time, contingent on their initial position.

articles.title: Learning with Human Peers and AI Chatbots: Evidence from Two Experimental Studies
articles.authors: Yiliang Jiang; Talia Waltzer; Michelle L Rivers; Gail D. Heyman
articles.abstract: Discussion with peers is a well-established strategy for promoting learning. Because AI chatbots like ChatGPT can respond continuously to students’ questions and explanations, they may serve some of the functions traditionally provided by human discussion partners in learning contexts. Across two pre-registered randomized experiments, we compared learning with human peers and AI chatbots and experimentally manipulated how students interacted with ChatGPT. In Study 1, students learned an unfamiliar physics concept and then discussed the material either with human peers (n = 47) or with ChatGPT (n = 44). Learning outcomes were generally similar across conditions even though many students in the ChatGPT condition just used the chatbot as an answer-generating machine. Study 2 examined whether guidance designed to promote more active engagement with ChatGPT would influence learning with a new set of materials. Participants were assigned to a human-peer condition (n = 43), an AI condition without instruction (n = 43), or an AI condition with instruction (n = 44). The instructional intervention led to more sophisticated prompting and discussion strategies but did not improve learning. Taken together, the findings suggest that learning with ChatGPT can produce outcomes comparable to learning through peer discussion and that even a brief intervention can increase students’ use of recommended interaction strategies. The results also highlight an important distinction between changing how students use AI and changing what they learn from it.

articles.title: Effects of Autism Spectrum Disorder on Discourse: A systematic review
articles.authors: Charalambos Themistocleous; Maria Andreou; Eleni Peristeri
articles.abstract: Language deficits in individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) are manifested in discourse, yet a systematic characterization of these deficits is lacking. To determine deficits in discourse macro-structure and micro-structure in individuals with ASD, we conducted a systematic review of recent studies in Covidence following PRISMA guidelines. This review showed language deficits on both narrative microstructure and macrostructure. The evidence indicates that individuals with ASD produce narratives that are shorter, lexically less diverse, and syntactically less complex than those of neurotypical peers. Morphosyntax is preserved particularly in individuals without comorbid language impairments, though morphosyntactic deficits can emerge under high discourse demands. At the macrostructural level, individuals with ASD include fewer complete story grammar elements, show weaker causal/temporal linking, use sparser mental-state vocabulary, and display greater referential ambiguity. The reviewed evidence suggests that narrative difficulties are primarily associated with deficits in discourse planning and socio-cognitive processing, with structural linguistic forms though being relatively more preserved.

articles.title: Can People Detect an AI Mediator? A Pilot Turing-Test Study of AI-Assisted Conflict Resolution
articles.authors: Paweł Kleka; Anna Szwal
articles.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in social and interpersonal contexts, yet little is known about whether people can identify an AI interlocutor in naturalistic, emotionally salient interactions. We report a pilot experiment in which 20 participants (10 dyads) engaged in a 60-minute text-based mediation of a simulated interpersonal conflict on Discord. Dyads were randomly assigned to a human mediator (control, n = 5 dyads) or to ChatGPT-4 acting as mediator (experimental, n = 5 dyads); the study was single-blind (participants were unaware that AI mediation was possible). After the session, each participant attempted to determine whether their mediator was human or AI. Identification accuracy did not differ from chance ($\chi^2$(1) = 0.20, *p* = .655), and Bayesian analyses indicated a general tendency to attribute mediation to a human agent rather than reliable detection of AI. Self-reported mediation effectiveness did not differ statistically between conditions in a two-sided test. However, equivalence testing did not support practical equivalence, and the observed effect pattern consistently favoured the AI mediator. Taken together, the results provide no evidence for human-mediator superiority and suggest a non-significant numerical trend favouring AI-mediated sessions (Hedges's *g* = −0.77, 90% CI [−1.50, −0.03]). Given the pilot nature and small sample size, these findings should be interpreted as preliminary and require replication in larger, preregistered studies.

articles.title: Chunking improves working memory via compression, not direct retrieval from long-term memory
articles.authors: Juan Manuel Chau Delgado; Joel Shebioba; Anna Pitt; Matias J. Ison; Nicholas E. Myers
articles.abstract: Working memory (WM) capacity is severely limited. Chunking, the process of grouping related items in WM, circumvents this limit and drastically improves performance. Despite decades of research, the mechanism underlying this benefit remains debated. One account proposes that statistical regularities allow multiple items to be compressed into structured WM representations, whereas another argues that structured associations are stored in long‑term memory (LTM) and reinstated at recall, effectively offloading storage demands. These accounts imply fundamentally different interactions between WM and long-term knowledge, yet in most paradigms, they make indistinguishable behavioural predictions. Here, we dissociate them by introducing small, continuous trial‑to‑trial variations in the hues of learned colour pairs, allowing us to test whether chunking benefits arise from compressed memory for the current hue (WM) or retrieval of long‑run feature means (LTM). Across two delayed colour report experiments, chunking reliably improved recall relative to unchunkable arrays. Participants remained sensitive to trial‑specific feature variations, indicating that responses were not driven by retrieval of feature means from LTM templates. At the same time, responses were systematically biased toward each item’s long‑run mean, especially on chunkable trials. To explain this bias, we fit psychophysical models derived from the competing compression and LTM‑retrieval accounts. The compression-based model, in which compression produces graded biases toward learned means within WM, outperformed the LTM-retrieval and baseline models. In a second experiment, we examined whether these biases arise during encoding/maintenance or at the recall stage. Cues in the maintenance period indicating which item would be probed improved recall accuracy but did not reduce bias toward learned structure, indicating that the bias arose during encoding or early maintenance rather than retrieval. These findings show that chunking enhances WM by integrating learned structure into WM representations through compression, rather than by offloading to LTM.

articles_hidden.title: Sport for Flourishing: Challenges, Considerations, and Calls to Action
articles_hidden.authors: Richard Alastair Cameron Simpson; Richard Cowden; Constantine Psimopoulos; Tim Lomas; Matthew J. Moore; Arabella Ashfield; Tyler J. VanderWeele; Todd Barrett Kashdan; Patrick McKnight
articles_hidden.abstract: Sport has often been recognized as a microcosm of broader society. Such acknowledgement demonstrates the potential of sport to shape, and be shaped by, individuals and communities. Indeed, across its many socioecological contexts (e.g., youth, recreational, developmental, educational, organizational, elite), scholars and practitioners from a range of disciplines have shared ways in which sport can contribute to, or undermine, health and well-being. To bridge the chasm between knowledge within sport (e.g., sport psychology, sociology, philosophy) and broader flourishing scholarship, we present a dual conceptual model of sport and flourishing to help align collective efforts and to centralize attention for researchers, practitioners, decision-makers, and sport professionals. First, we discuss the empirical and conceptual challenges that are apparent within sport and why this has limited progress concerning its relations to human flourishing. We also discuss broader contentions about flourishing and how sport could help address these challenges. Second, we discuss the elements of the model pertaining to flourishing within sport (e.g., sport as a sphere for flourishing: comprising embeddedness, purview and scope of well-being, quality of the sport environment) and pertaining to sport for flourishing (e.g., sport as a conduit for flourishing: promoting individual flourishing, communal and relational flourishing, and flourishing of humanity). Third, we conclude with various implications and ‘calls to action’ for methodological (e.g., qualitative and quantitative work), applied (e.g., developing guidelines and interventions for promoting flourishing in sport), and research (e.g., Global Flourishing in Sport Study) advancement to realize a more unified sport and flourishing community.

articles_hidden.title: Perceptual adaptation to human-likeness in voices
articles_hidden.authors: Christine Nussbaum; Sebastian Goerke; Ibrahim Vefa Arslan; Stefan R. Schweinberger
articles_hidden.abstract: With synthetic voices now being a part of everyday life, it is important to understand how the perception of synthetic voices is shaped and modified through exposure. Therefore, we employed an adaptation paradigm to test whether perception of human-likeness is amenable to short-term perceptual encounters. In three experiments, we presented morphed target voices on a human-synthetic-continuum in three conditions: without prior adaptation, and after repeated exposure to adaptor voices that all were either synthetic or human. Experiment 1 (N = 26) was conducted online, Experiment 2 (N = 31) was a full replication in the lab, and Experiment 3 (N = 36) employed an adjusted procedure with blocked and reduced adaptor exposure to test the robustness of effects. In all experiments, we observed consistent contrastive aftereffects: After adaptation to synthetic voices, ambiguous voices were more often classified as human. After adaptation to human voices, the same ambiguous voices were more often classified as synthetic. Intriguingly, in Experiment 1 and 2, contrastive aftereffects were even larger in trials which employed digital caricatures (i.e., 25%-exaggerated human or synthetic voices) as adaptors, even though caricatures themselves were not consistently rated as more human (or synthetic, respectively) compared to original voices. While the adaptation effect survived the adjusted procedure (Experiment 3), substantial modulations by caricatured adaptors were no longer observed. Together, these findings provide robust evidence that impressions of vocal human-likeness are not only determined by the acoustic features but are the result of a complex interplay with listeners and their recent perceptual experiences.

articles_hidden.title: Learners’ beliefs about teachers’ social characteristics influence their pronunciation preferences: A replication and extension of Hayes-Harb, Barrios & Tripp (2022)
articles_hidden.authors: Shannon Barrios; Rachel Hayes-Harb
articles_hidden.abstract: Learners’ beliefs about language and language users impact the inferences they make about linguistic structure as well as their learning outcomes (Ballard & Winke 2017; Falkert 2016; Hayes-Harb, Barrios & Tripp 2022). Hayes-Harb et al. (2022) demonstrated that participants preferred speech samples exhibiting a pronunciation pattern that was associated with a “teacher” over that of a “student” in a simulated language classroom context, indicating that language learners differentially weight their input based on characteristics of the speaker. We first replicated this study with a new pronunciation pattern (Experiment 1), and then extended the work by investigating whether preferences for the teacher’s pronunciation can be modulated by attributing “favorable” versus “unfavorable” social characteristics to the teacher regarding their teaching experience, teaching effectiveness, and linguistic background (Experiment 2). We found that participants still tended to prefer the teacher’s pronunciation, but that the degree of preference was reduced when the teacher had been characterized unfavorably. We thus provide evidence that preferences for speech input from teachers are modulated by beliefs about the social characteristics of the teacher, presenting a challenge for asocial models of pronunciation learning and contributing to our understanding of linguistic stereotyping and its impact on language teaching and learning.

articles_hidden.title: Stimulus selection and sample-size calculation for statistical test of hierarchical cognitive model
articles_hidden.authors: Kazuya Fujita
articles_hidden.abstract: Sample-size calculations are essential for ensuring adequate statistical power. However, these calculations are rarely performed in elaborate models, specifically hierarchical cognitive models in which Bayesian cognitive models for human data are used. We used a population-level Fisher information matrix (PFIM) proposed in the field of pharmacology to develop and demonstrate experimental stimulus selection and sample-size calculations within a hierarchical cognitive model. In Simulation Study 1, we confirmed that PFIM could accurately predict statistical power. Further, a high correlation was observed between the logarithm of the Bayes Factor and the predicted statistical power. In Simulation Study 2, we outlined the process of determining the number of participants and trials after the selection of the optimal experimental stimulus in that the statistical power is maximized. Despite the time-intensive nature of parameter estimation, the sample-size calculation was achievable within a realistic timeframe (e.g., to 2–3 days). The proposed method has low computational load and enables sample-size calculations for elaborate hierarchical cognitive models. Further this method can be applied to a wide range of models.

articles_hidden.title: Failure Feedback: Vehicle for the Transmission of Stereotypes About Intellectual Ability
articles_hidden.authors: Grace Huang Murphy; Uliana Solovieva; Lin Bian
articles_hidden.abstract: Stereotypes linking intellectual ability to particular social groups (e.g., boys) emerge early in childhood, constraining the aspirations of certain groups such as girls. Yet little is known about how children acquire these stereotypes. The present research investigated whether parental responses to children’s failure serve as a pathway through which stereotypes about intellectual ability are communicated. In Experiment 1 (N = 312; 54% women), parents responded to a child, identified as either a boy or a girl, who repeatedly failed a challenging intellectual task. Parents most frequently provided two types of feedback: persistence (which encouraged continued effort) and redirection (which suggested pursuing alternative activities). Following the initial failure, parents were more likely to encourage persistence for the boy but to redirect the girl. Across repeated failures, parents also continued to provide more redirection to the girl than to the boy. In Experiments 2 and 3 (N = 96 and 124 children, respectively), 5- to 10-year-old children watched videos in which unfamiliar individuals or members of novel groups received either persistence or redirection feedback after failure. Across both experiments, children inferred that recipients of redirection feedback were less smart than recipients of persistence feedback. Moreover, children extended these inferences to groups, suggesting that differential failure feedback could contribute to the acquisition of group-based intelligence stereotypes. Together, these findings highlight failure as an important socialization context in which behavioral guidance can carry implicit evaluations of intellectual ability, providing a potential pathway through which intelligence stereotypes are transmitted.

articles_hidden.title: When Mood Turns Attention Inward: Affective and Cognitive Pathways Linking Negative Mind Wandering and Attentional Control
articles_hidden.authors: Nicholaus P. Brosowsky; Emma Dueck; Stephanie Lauren Souliere; Nicholas Daniel Evans; Liam Yeo; Josephine Nicholson
articles_hidden.abstract: Negative mood is associated with both attentional failures and increased mind wandering, but the mechanisms linking mood, thought, and performance remain unclear. In particular, it is unknown whether mood-related performance costs arise primarily from changes in attentional control or from changes in the content of thought. We examined these possibilities in 585 undergraduate participants who completed positive, neutral, or negative mood inductions followed by a sustained attention task with intermittent thought probes. Probes assessed both the intentionality (intentional vs. unintentional) and emotional valence (positive, neutral, or negative) of off-task thought. Structural equation models were used to examine pathways linking mood induction, post-induction affect, mind wandering, task performance, and post-task mood. Negative mood was associated with poorer task performance both directly through post-induction affect and indirectly through increases in negatively valenced mind wandering. These indirect effects were observed for both intentional and unintentional negative mind wandering and generalized across measures of perceptual sensitivity, commission errors, and reaction-time variability. Negative mind wandering also predicted poorer subsequent mood, whereas positive and neutral mind wandering did not. These findings identify negatively valenced thought as a common mechanism linking mood to both sustained-attention performance and subsequent affect.

articles_hidden.title: Negative Urgency, Not Negative Affect, Mediates the Association Between Sleep Problems and Eating Disorder Symptoms
articles_hidden.authors: Victoria Franco; Emily R. Linn; Noa A. Bregmann; Stacey M. Schaefer; Richard Davidson; James I. Hudson; Kristin Javaras
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: There is increasing evidence suggesting that sleep problems may cause alterations in
eating behavior (e.g., poor sleep quality is linked to eating disorders (EDs) and ED symptoms).
However, little is known about the mechanisms by which sleep problems may increase ED
symptoms. Sleep deprivation has been linked to elevated negative urgency (NU; the tendency to
act rashly in response to extreme negative affect [NA]), and NA. Both are consistently linked to
higher ED symptoms and potentially mediate the association between sleep problems and ED
symptoms. This study examined whether NU and NA mediate the relationship between sleep
problems and ED symptoms. Method: Female-identifying introductory psychology students at a
midwestern university (n = 119) completed self-report measures of impulsivity (UPPS-P), ED
symptoms (Eating Disorder Diagnostic Scale), and sleep problems (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality
Index), and a task-based measure of NU (total commission errors for negatively-valenced
distractors in the CANTAB Affective Go/No-go Task). Mediation analyses included bias-
corrected and accelerated confidence intervals estimated via non-parametric bootstrap. Results:
Sleep problems were significantly associated with (Box-Cox-transformed) ED symptoms
(B=0.26, p<0.01). Self-reported NU mediated a significant proportion of the association between
PSQI sleep problems and transformed ED symptoms (Proportion = 61%; p<0.01), but task-based
NU (Proportion = 4%; p=0.73) and NA (Proportion = 23%; p=0.74) did not. Discussion: Poor
sleep may increase ED symptoms partly due to increasing trait-like NU, but not via task-based
NU nor NA. Trait-like NU may be an important mechanism linking sleep problems and eating
disturbances.

articles_hidden.title: Auswirkungen von Künstlicher Intelligenz auf psychische Belastung in der Arbeitswelt – ein Überblick
articles_hidden.authors: Markus Langer; Annette Kluge
articles_hidden.abstract:
Der vorliegende Beitrag arbeitet den Forschungsstand zu den Auswirkungen des KI-Einsatzes auf psychische Belastungen und Ressourcen am Arbeitsplatz auf. Ein Leitgedanke ist die Ambivalenz: KI-Systeme können auf nahezu jeder Dimension gleichzeitig als Ressource und als Belastung wirken – als Produktivitätsgewinn und Überforderung, als Autonomiezuwachs und Kontrollverlust, als Kompetenzerweiterung und Dequalifizierung. Ob im Einzelfall das eine oder das andere überwiegt, hängt maßgeblich davon ab, wie ein KI-System gestaltet ist und genutzt wird und wie es in Arbeitsprozesse eingebettet und organisational begleitet wird.
Im Beitrag bestimmen wir den Neuheitswert aktueller KI-Systeme. Vieles ist eine quantitative Fortschreibung bekannter Automatisierungstechnologien; qualitativ neu sind jedoch Eigenschaften wie die eigenständige Generierung von Inhalten, die Einsetzbarkeit als Allzweck-Werkzeug, nahezu autonome Aufgabenbearbeitung, probabilistisches und lernendes Verhalten, menschenähnliche Interaktion, engmaschige Entscheidungen über Menschen, schnelle Update-Zyklen sowie die verbreitete informelle Nutzung. Für jede dieser Eigenschaften lassen sich konkrete Chancen und Risiken für die psychische Gesundheit ableiten.
Die empirische Synopse (Stand Frühjahr 2026) ordnet die Befunde in einer soziotechnischen Kontext ein: Einflussfaktoren auf organisationaler, arbeits- und technologiegestalterischer sowie personenbezogener Ebene wirken – vermittelt über Moderatoren und Mediatoren auf verschiedene Ergebnisgrößen. Als belastungskritisch erweisen sich beispielsweise unrealistische Erwartungen und fehlendes Change Management, algorithmisches Management mit Autonomie- und Kontrollverlust, Arbeitsverdichtung statt Entlastung, der Verlust sozialer Einbindung sowie Sorgen um Arbeitsplatz und berufliche Identität. Als Gelingensbedingungen werden beispielsweise KI-Kompetenzen und ausreichende Zeit- und Trainingsressourcen beschrieben.
Daraus leiten wir Handlungsempfehlungen auf drei Ebenen ab. Organisational sollte beispielsweise die KI-Einführung konsequent als menschzentrierter Veränderungsprozess verstanden werden;. Auf der Arbeits- und Technologiegestaltungsebene sind Autonomie und Kontrolle zu sichern, Arbeitsverdichtung zu überwachen, Tätigkeitszuschnitte im Sinne der SMART-Kriterien zu prüfen und Technologien so zu gestalten, dass menschliche Aufsicht gelingt. Auf Personenebene rücken KI- und metakognitive Kompetenzen, der Erhalt arbeitsfachlicher Fertigkeiten sowie die neue Kernaufgabe der effektiven menschlichen Aufsicht von KI-Systemen in den Vordergrund.
Dieser Beitrag zeigt, dass eine menschzentrierte, soziotechnisch gedachte Gestaltung und Einführung von KI-Systemen den technischen Fortschritt nicht ausbremst, sondern Arbeit reichhaltiger, gesünder und nachhaltiger macht – und ist die entscheidende Stellschraube dafür, dass KI zur Ressource statt zur Belastung wird.

articles_hidden.title: Evaluating Open-Weight Large Language Models for Structured Depression Assessment from Clinical Interviews
articles_hidden.authors: Jeffrey M. Girard; Gaossou Youssouf Kebe; Louis-Philippe Morency; Fernando De la Torre; Einat Liebenthal; Justin T. Baker
articles_hidden.abstract: The administration of semi-structured clinical interviews for depression assessment is resource-intensive and susceptible to rater drift. While large language models (LLMs) offer potential for automated quality assurance, reliance on proprietary models creates data privacy barriers incompatible with secure clinical workflows. This study evaluates a privacy-preserving pipeline using open-weight LLMs to perform item-level scoring of the Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS) directly from interview transcripts. The sample included 541 video-recorded English-language interviews with 277 psychiatric inpatients diagnosed with diverse affective and psychotic disorders. Benchmarking 25 architectures, we found that an indirect scoring strategy, where models predict individual item scores that are subsequently summed, significantly outperformed direct total score prediction. This suggests that decomposing the assessment into intermediate reasoning steps improves performance. The best-performing models achieved “good” error rates and “excellent” correlations with trusted human labels, approaching established benchmarks for human inter-rater reliability. To determine the active ingredients of effective prompting, we conducted an ablation study. Results revealed that descriptive cues (scoring criteria) were the primary driver of performance, whereas few-shot examples provided negligible additional benefit, suggesting that zero-shot prompting is a viable, efficient strategy. However, error analysis identified a multimodal gap, where text-only models struggled more with items dependent on nonverbal behavior. We conclude that open-weight LLMs demonstrate strong potential to serve as secure “digital second opinions,” representing a promising step toward augmenting clinical decision-making without compromising patient privacy.

articles_hidden.title: Monocular stereopsis, pinholes, and the perils of classroom theorizing:  A response to McIntosh (2025).
articles_hidden.authors: Dhanraj Vishwanath
articles_hidden.abstract: Monocular stereopsis is a compelling perceptual effect wherein viewing a picture of a 3-dimensional scene with one eye through an aperture generates a perceptual impression of depth similar to binocular stereopsis. Here I provide a critique of a recently published report on the topic in the journal i-Perception (McIntosh, 2025).  In the report, the author claims to adjudicate on explanations of the monocular stereopsis effect and the phenomenology of stereopsis more broadly construed.  The author suggests, based on an informal test comparing pinhole and aperture viewing of a picture during a fifteen-minute classroom lecture break, that the monocular-aperture effect is best explained by a 100-year-old description of the phenomenon. I show that McIntosh’s report reveals a lack of understanding of the modern empirical facts and theoretical concepts relevant to this scientific debate and neglects the rudimentary demands of conducting an interpretable perceptual test.

articles_hidden.title: Changing Contributions of Emotion and Reward Information to Learning Through Adolescence
articles_hidden.authors: Camille Phaneuf-Hadd; Elizabeth A. Phelps; Leah Somerville
articles_hidden.abstract: From childhood to adulthood, individuals’ learning and decision-making may be differentially impacted by two salient value signals for adolescents: emotions and rewards. This study superimposed these information sources to assess their independent and joint influences on learning and choice processes. Participants ages 8-22 years completed a reinforcement learning task, in which monetary rewards conveyed information integral to making reward-maximizing choices, while emotional expressions conveyed information incidental to this goal. In some conditions, emotion and reward invoked congruent approach-avoid tendencies; following either information source promoted making reward-maximizing (“correct”) choices. In other conditions, emotion and reward invoked incongruent approach-avoid tendencies; following the emotion cue impeded reward capture. Participants completed several measures indexing the persistence of emotion and reward information on choice and evaluations of these signals. Statistical and computational models revealed that emotion-reward incongruence hampered early learning through an incidental emotion bias on value estimates. The emotion bias decayed as reward learning progressed in adolescents and adults but endured in children. Moreover, reward-based choice increased with age across the additional measures. Although participants of all ages were initially hindered by incidental emotion cues, adults’ shift toward prioritizing integral reward outcomes indicates that goal-relevant information comes to dominate choice with age.

articles_hidden.title: Agency enhances episodic memory across the broader experience
articles_hidden.authors: Tej Bhoga; Zachariah Reagh; Angelique I. Delarazan
articles_hidden.abstract: Agency, the ability to exert control over one’s own experience, enhances memory relative to passive observation. However, it remains unclear whether agency only benefits information that one directly acts on, or if its benefits extend to the fidelity that the broad experience is represented in memory. Across two experiments, participants encoded objects and their locations while exploring a series of rooms, either controlling object placements themselves (Active) or observing the same sequence of events without control (Passive). Memory was assessed using the Mnemonic Similarity Task (MST), along with tests of object-spatial placement and descriptive recall. Critically, mnemonic discrimination required retaining perceptual details beyond what the object-spatial placement task demanded. In Experiment 1, agency enhanced basic object recognition, mnemonic discrimination, and object description recall, but not object-spatial placement. Experiment 2 used a within-subjects design, a recognition-based spatial test with lower retrieval demands, and attention ratings collected throughout encoding. Agency again enhanced mnemonic discrimination, and its benefits extended to object-spatial placement and recall of both object and room descriptions. These effects remained after accounting for self-reported attention during encoding. Together, the findings show that agency enhances mnemonic discrimination on the MST and suggests that its benefits extend beyond information falling within the scope of participants’ direct control, influencing both the detail of individual object representations and memory for the broader context in which they were encountered.

articles_hidden.title: Dyadic Social Dynamics in Separation-Related Anxiety: Multimodal Arousal Synchrony Between 4-Year-Olds and Their Mothers
articles_hidden.authors: Leonard Konstantin Kulisch; Laurin Plank; Anna Exner; Silvia Schneider; Sabine Seehagen; Armin Zlomuzica; Babett Voigt
articles_hidden.abstract: Separation anxiety disorder (SAD) is an early-onset disorder linked to adverse outcomes into adulthood. To advance SAD etiology, this study examined how parental risk factors relate to dyadic social dynamics. Seventy-two four-year-olds (50% girls, 93% primarily German-speaking) and their mothers (74% holding a Bachelor’s degree) participated in a standardized separation paradigm. Parental reports, heart rate, and machine-learning-based measures of facial and vocal arousal were assessed. The announcement of separation increased children’s physiological (ꞵ=.17) and vocal arousal (ꞵ=.13). Within individuals, physiological and vocal arousal were coordinated (r=.18–.20), while across dyads, facial (r=.15) and vocal arousal (r=.09) showed consistent synchrony. Physiological synchrony emerged selectively in dyads with higher maternal anxiety (r=.31) but was unrelated to absolute arousal or SAD symptoms. Anticipatory physiological synchrony was negatively associated with child vocal arousal during separation (r=-.44). Early separation-related anxiety appears embedded in dyadic processes, shaped by vocal arousal transmission and maternal anxiety symptoms.

articles_hidden.title: Attitudinal, Experiential, and Trait-based Correlates of Inceldom
articles_hidden.authors: Robyn Mooney; Millie Hargreaves; Brandon Sparks
articles_hidden.abstract: To prevent radicalisation into the involuntary celibate (‘incel’) community, it is critical to understand individual differences underlying inceldom. This exploratory research aimed to examine relationships between inceldom and attitudinal and trait-based risk factors for extremism. Study 1 explored relationships between misogyny, right-wing authoritarianism (RWA), social dominance orientation (SDO), and incel ideology endorsement in a male community sample (n = 65). Using another male community sample (n = 282), Study 2 examined associations between autistic traits (social-sensory sensitivity and monotropic processing), childhood traumatic experiences (CTEs), misogyny, and incel traits. Results showed that in Study 1, misogyny and RWA positively predicted incel ideology endorsement, while SDO was negatively predictive. In Study 2, CTEs and both aspects of autistic traits were positively associated with incel traits, and these associations were mediated by higher levels of misogyny. Self-identified incels also scored higher than non-incels on incel traits, misogyny, CTEs, and social-sensory sensitivity, but they did not differ on monotropic processing. The findings from these studies can help inform effective, tailored prevention programs and deradicalisation support systems for those wishing to leave the incel community.

articles_hidden.title: Understanding the Impact of Psychological Interventions for Psychosis in Daily Life: Experience Sampling Methodology as an Adjunct Outcome Measure in Clinical Trials
articles_hidden.authors: Clementine Jane Edwards; Ginette Lafit; Joanne R Beames; Morwenna Rickard; Simone Burger; Alyssa Jongeneel; Elise van der Stouwe; Wim Veling; Eric Granholm; Anita Schick
articles_hidden.abstract:
Retrospective outcome measures are widely used in mental health clinical trials. Yet, these gold-standard measures may not capture fully how subjective experiences and behaviours unfold and relate to each other in everyday life context. Experience Sampling Methodology (ESM) offers a complementary approach by collecting repeated assessments in daily life. The ESM allows the measurement of proximal, dynamic and context-dependent outcomes while interventions are being delivered, while classical scales administered in clinics capture retrospective aggregates of experiences over a defined period of time.
In this paper, we draw on learnings from psychological therapy trials in psychosis that applied ESM as an outcome measure to support the wider adoption of this approach in intervention studies. We offer practical suggestions for incorporating ESM into clinical trial design and conduct, including the development of specific momentary research questions, selection and adaptation of questionnaire items, sampling schedules, participant briefing and debriefing, and approaches to maximising compliance and data quality. We also discuss key analytic and conceptual issues, including the interpretation of ESM findings alongside traditional retrospective interviews and self-report measures.
ESM assessments can provide unique insights into mechanisms, variability, context and timing of change in daily life, helping to clarify not only whether an intervention works, but how and when it has an impact. Used to address these research questions through questionnaires and schedules that harness the value of assessments during daily life, ESM can strengthen the evaluation and subsequent development of mental health treatments by capturing meaningful change in the settings in which people live their lives.

articles_hidden.title: Linguistic Affiliation and the Structure of Cultural Values: Evidence from the World Values Survey
articles_hidden.authors: Meriem Boukhris; Farah Benzarti; Peter Wad Sackett; Montassar Ben Messaoud; Gabriel Renaud
articles_hidden.abstract: The values of a society are determined by a plethora of factors, including history, geography and culture. A resource to monitor such values is the World Values Survey, a survey about the predispositions of individuals across 66 societies from various geographic regions. While some analyses have been conducted on this dataset, several questions dealing with circumstances rather than values were not filtered out e.g. ”I feel unsafe at night” and the types of analyses conducted were limited. We removed such situational questions and kept the 199 questions related solely to values, and submitted the resulting data to several supervised and unsupervised numerical analyses. We find that linguistic affiliation provides a strong organizing dimension of cultural-value similarity. We observe a split primarily along morality and religion, accounting for 23.9% of the variance, and in second place along confidence in institutions, accounting for a further 13.5%. We analyzed bilingual countries like Kazakhstan and Canada. We find that English-speaking Canadians are closer to other English-speaking countries than they are to French-speaking Canadians. While the USA initially appeared as an outlier within the English-speaking world, stratifying respondents by Democratic and Republican affiliation revealed deep internal divisions. Strikingly, Americans identifying as Democrats were closer, in terms of values, to other English-speaking nations, especially English-speaking Canadians, than they were to US Republicans.

articles_hidden.title: Parenting sense of competence and dynamic physiological self-regulation before and during parent-child conflict
articles_hidden.authors: Prakash Thambipillai; Salome Vanwoerden; Amy Byrd; J. Richard Jennings; Stephanie Stepp; Vera Vine
articles_hidden.abstract: Parenting sense of competence encompasses both parenting self-efficacy, or parent’s appraisal of their parenting skills, and parenting satisfaction, the affective feelings of gratification from parenting. Parents’ sense of competence may be linked to psychophysiological self-regulation during challenges, which for parents of adolescents with emotion dysregulation difficulties may begin during the anticipation of conflict. 162 clinically-referred, parent-adolescent dyads (adolescents: Mage = 12.59, SD = .59, range 10-14 yrs, 47% girls, 41% African American, 60% minoritized race/ethnicity; caregivers: Mage = 40.35, SD = 7.23, 94% female, 40% African American, 48% minoritized race/ethnicity) completed an ecologically valid, conflict protocol, including a 2-minute conflict anticipation and 8-minute conflict discussion, during which their respiratory sinus arrhythmia (RSA) was recorded. Results of dynamic growth curve models indicated that parenting satisfaction, but not self-efficacy, was associated with parents’ RSA trajectories,  = .33, SE = .12, p = .005, and this effect was robust to respiration adjustment and relevant behavioral confounds. Lower satisfaction was associated with greater anticipatory RSA withdrawal followed by sharp RSA augmentation at conflict onset; higher parenting satisfaction was associated with a more flexible RSA trajectory, beginning with anticipatory augmentation followed by modest, theoretically appropriate withdrawal at conflict onset. Parents’ self-regulation before and during conflict may be especially relevant to the experience of parenting.

articles_hidden.title: How Childhood Adversity Alters Social Information Processing and its Effect on Social Functioning: A Systematic Review
articles_hidden.authors: Hannah Dorsman; Elizabeth E. L. Buimer; Antoinette Haverhals; Pauline Wessels; Peter Bos; Eamon McCrory; Anne-Laura Van Harmelen
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Childhood adversity (CA) affects millions of children worldwide and may change how children perceive and respond to social cues in ways that are adaptive in adverse environments but maladaptive later in life. These maladaptive effects may be particularly pronounced during adolescence, a sensitive period of social reorientation and neurodevelopment. This pre-registered systematic review examined whether CA shapes the way young people process social information, and whether these changes are linked to difficulties in social functioning during adolescence.
Methods: We searched Web of Science, PsycINFO, and PubMed for studies assessing CA before age 18, social information processing across five domains, and social functioning in youth aged 10-24.
Results: Although 6657 studies were identified, only 11 met inclusion criteria. These examined threat-related processing (n=5), emotional reactivity and regulation (n=5), and reward processing and learning (n=3). CA was associated with alterations in social information processing across most domains. If associations between social information processing and social functioning were directly tested, they were generally supported. Evidence spanned different stages of adolescence, but associations with social functioning were tested almost exclusively in early-to-mid adolescent samples.
Conclusions: We find preliminary support for a model where CA is associated with alterations in social information processing which then leads to poorer social functioning. These findings were based mostly on longitudinal samples in early-to-mid adolescent samples, however, prospective examinations of this model were rare. These findings suggest that interventions targeting social information processing may be a promising avenue for supporting adolescents with experiences of CA.

articles_hidden.title: Validation of a German Version of the Barcelona Music  Reward Questionnaire (BMRQ)
articles_hidden.authors: Kim Meyer; Charlotte Jolmes; Madita Jodes; Willi Moxter; Lena Rölz; Maël Roth; Lars Rogenmoser
articles_hidden.abstract:
The Barcelona Music Reward Questionnaire (BMRQ) is a widely used self-report measure of 
individual differences in music reward sensitivity. Although the instrument has been adapted 
into several languages, no validated German version has previously been available. The 
present study translated and psychometrically evaluated a German adaptation of the BMRQ 
in a sample of 471 German-speaking adults. 
A split-sample approach was used to conduct confirmatory and exploratory factor analyses. 
Confirmatory factor analysis supported the original five-factor structure comprising Musical 
Seeking, Emotional Evocation, Mood Regulation, Sensory-Motor, and Social Reward. 
Exploratory analyses broadly reproduced this structure, although overlap emerged between 
Musical Seeking and Social Reward. Internal consistency estimates for the BMRQ dimension 
scores and overall score ranged from acceptable to good. Associations with reward-related 
motivational tendencies provided evidence for convergent validity. 
Scores were distributed across a broad range of the scale and showed moderate negative 
skewness, reflecting a tendency toward higher levels of music reward. 
Overall, the present findings support the German BMRQ as a psychometrically sound 
instrument for assessing individual differences in music reward sensitivity in German
speaking populations.

articles_hidden.title: Navigating Divorce and Partner Bereavement: Personality and Trajectories of Change in Life Satisfaction and Mental Health
articles_hidden.authors: Thao Kieu; Liselotte den Boer; Wiebke Bleidorn; Yu Xie; Jaap J. A. Denissen
articles_hidden.abstract: Dissolutions of romantic relationships can elicit diverse reactions across various aspects of well-being, but they also offer an opportunity to examine which factors promote resilience and identify individuals at risk. In this preregistered multi-sample longitudinal study, we examined the heterogeneity in life satisfaction and mental health changes around and during divorce or partner bereavement, and whether personality (i.e., traits and resilient versus nonresilient personality profiles) may explain individual differences in change trajectories. Data from 1,306 divorcees and 1,150 bereaved partners were drawn from nationally representative panel studies in the Netherlands (N = 12,551), Germany (N = 10,830), and China (N = 28,628), and analyzed using growth mixture modeling. Four life satisfaction trajectories and three mental health trajectories were identified for each event. Recovery and resilience emerged as the most common trajectories across events, outcomes, and samples. Among personality factors, neuroticism was the most consistent predictor of a lower likelihood of belonging to a resilience trajectory. This study advanced the generalizability of findings across diverse loss-based events, populations, and aspects of well-being. The findings further underscore the  influence of neuroticism in shaping, and potentially complicating, psychological adjustment surrounding divorce and partner bereavement.

articles_hidden.title: Dynamic coordination of speech and gesture in the brain
articles_hidden.authors: Jiachen Yao; Cecilia Husta; Linda Drijvers
articles_hidden.abstract: Face-to-face communication relies on the continuous integration of auditory signals, such as speech, and visual signals, such as co-speech gestures. Rather than serving as an add-on to spoken language, gestural information has been shown to actively shape how the brain constructs meaning. A central question is how the brain achieves integrating gestures with speech. This is not a trivial problem, as auditory and visual signals are often noisy, temporally misaligned, variable in length, and ambiguous, yet interlocutors still seem to understand each other effortlessly. This chapter will review evidence from neuroimaging (e.g., fMRI, MEG, (dual-)EEG, fNIRS) and brain stimulation (e.g., TMS, tDCS, tACS) methods, both from a within- and a between-brain perspective. Together, these methods have begun to outline a distributed and flexible brain network that supports the integration of speech and gestures. We will discuss how these brain networks coordinate the integration of speech and gestures, and how speech-gesture integration unfolds over time, in both clear and adverse listening conditions.

articles_hidden.title: Humans learn to distinguish imagination from reality with age
articles_hidden.authors: Andre Sahakian; Stefan van der Stigchel; Nadine Dijkstra; Surya Gayet; Christoph Strauch
articles_hidden.abstract: Telling apart what is the product of one's imagination and what is a true sensory experience (i.e., reality monitoring) might feel trivial to most. Yet it remains unclear whether reality monitoring is an innate ability (like breathing, or aversion to pain) or whether it is a learned skill (like speaking, or walking). Here we extend the age range of participants tested by Dijkstra and Fleming (2023) with young children from the age of 5. In a close replication we tested how likely participants were to report actually seeing a faint left or right tilted grating in dynamic noise, depending on whether they were concurrently imagining the same or an orthogonal grating. We found clear evidence that confusion of imagery and perception steadily declined to none with age - independent of perceptual ability or (subjective) imagery vividness. We empirically show that the ability to tell apart imagination from reality develops over age. These findings provide new insights on how we learn to keep apart imagination from reality, which has important implications for the development of psychopathology.

articles_hidden.title: Displacement, Parenting, and Self-Development in Syrian Refugee Children: A Longitudinal Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Hend Eltanamly; Fiona McEwen; Elie Karam; Sander Thomaes; Michael Pluess
articles_hidden.abstract: Millions of children worldwide endure forced displacement, with profound implications for their psychological well-being. This study examines how forced displacement impacts self-development (i.e., self-esteem and self-efficacy) among Syrian refugee children (N=1576; Mage=11.00; SD=2.30) and their mothers (Mage=38.28; SD=8.97), in Lebanon. Over a one-year follow-up with N=1000 children linear-mixed analyses show that a relatively well-resourced refugee environment is associated with higher self-esteem and self-efficacy cross-sectionally, but does not predict changes in self-development over time. Parenting, however, has distinct effects on self-esteem over time: maternal acceptance buffers against the adverse effects of poor refugee environments on self-esteem, whereas psychological control and abuse at home exacerbate these negative impacts. No such longitudinal effects were found for self-efficacy.

articles_hidden.title: From team rationality to morality:  Implicit joint plans carry moral force
articles_hidden.authors: Arthur Le Pargneux; Fiery Andrews Cushman; Hossam Zeitoun; Nick Chater
articles_hidden.abstract: Collaboration is essential to social life. Sometimes teams, families, companies, and other organizations agree on explicit rules governing such collaboration, and these are backed by moral force: To violate the rule is wrong. Other times, however, we find ways to collaborate on the fly, without rules or norms, or even explicit communication. This often requires inferring a joint plan — imagining “what coordination would we agree to, if we could?” — and playing our surmised role. Is it also considered morally wrong to violate an implicit or inferred joint plan? In five preregistered experiments (n = 1,506), we show that deviating from an inferred joint plan is perceived as morally problematic, even without prior communication or agreement. In other words, just as the agreements we actually make are morally binding, so too are the patterns of conduct that we infer our social partners would agree upon.

articles_hidden.title: Somewhere Over the Rainbow: Introducing the EHPS LGBTQIA+ Research Special Interest Group
articles_hidden.authors: Thomas Gültzow; Udi Davidovich; Chantal den Daas; Siobhan Thomas; Hanne Zimmermann; Anne van Dongen
articles_hidden.abstract: The pursuit of health and well-being remains a fundamental priority for populations with diverse sexual orientations, gender identities, and sex characteristics (LGBTQIA+).
