Despite the unique position of health psychology to address these needs, LGBTQIA+ perspectives have historically been underrepresented within the European Health Psychology Society (EHPS). Following a series of roundtables and a formal launch meeting at the 2025 EHPS conference in Groningen, this article signifies the official launch of the LGBTQIA+ Research Special Interest Group (SIG). We outline the SIG’s foundational mission and strategic agenda, structured around three core pillars: (1) Visibility and Institutional Advocacy, (2) Conference Inclusivity and Best Practice, and (3) Community Building and Knowledge Translation. This article serves as the definitive record of the SIG’s launch and provides a roadmap for advancing inclusive, evidence-based health psychology in Europe and beyond.

articles_hidden.title: Shared research materials in psychology are widely downloaded but often difficult to reuse
articles_hidden.authors: Daniel S Quintana
articles_hidden.abstract: Open science reforms have made posting data and code common, but are shared materials actually used, and easily reused? Treating download counts of Open Science Framework (OSF) supplements as a usage index, I analysed 1,660 articles from four psychology journals (Cognition, Psychological Science, Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, Journal of Memory and Language) across three years (2015, 2020, 2025). OSF sharing rose from 9% in 2015 to 52% in 2025. Among 392 papers with download data, materials were downloaded a median of 152 times; only 1% went undownloaded. Download volume was associated with citation count and altmetric attention. Availability did not ensure easy reuse: only 40% of repositories provided documentation, 34% were flagged for a hard-coded file path, and 42% referenced a missing file — shortcomings that did not improve as sharing grew. Altogether, shared materials are being used, but often not easily reusable.

articles_hidden.title: Substitution, addition, or stepping-stone? Exploring the temporal associations between the consumption of alcoholic and alcohol-free beverages among Dutch university students
articles_hidden.authors: Kirsten van Hooijdonk; Lise Dams; Tirza van Noorden; Jacqueline Vink
articles_hidden.abstract: Background and aim. Stimulating the use of alcohol-free beverages is portrayed as one strategy to reduce excessive alcohol use and alcohol-related harm among students in higher education. This strategy relies on the assumption that students drink alcohol-free to substitute alcohol (i.e. “substitution effect”), while other possibilities like drinking alcohol-free in addition to alcohol (i.e. “addition effect”) or alcohol-free acting as a step-up to consume (more) alcohol (i.e. “stepping-stone” effect) have largely been neglected. Consequently, this preregistered study aimed to examine bi-directional temporal associations between the quantity of alcohol and alcohol-free use among university students (Aim 1). Next, these bi-directional temporal associations were examined in subgroups: females vs. males (Aim 2) and members vs. non-members of student associations (Aim 3). Design. Observational study, utilizing Wave 2, Wave 3, and Wave 4 of Radboud University’s Healthy Student Life study. Data were collected May-July 2022, 2023, and 2024. Setting. The Netherlands. Participants. 9,951 university students of which 6,790 students had only cross-sectional data, while 2,383 and 778 students participated in 2 and 3 surveys, respectively. At Wave 2, participants’ mean age was 23 (SD = 4.0). 70% were female, 17% were members of a student association, 13% were international students, and 57% were enrolled in a bachelor programme. Measurements. At all waves, participants self-reported the frequency and quantity of alcohol and alcohol-free beverage consumption, using two (adapted) items of the Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test – Consumption (AUDIT-C). Additionally, participants self-reported on: gender, student association membership, living situation, relationship status, and other substance use. Last, information on biological sex, age, educational programme, and (inter)national status were received from the university administrative records. Random Intercept Cross-Lagged Panel Models were utilized to study reciprocal effects between the quantity of alcohol and alcohol-free use, by decomposing observed scores in between-person differences and within-person dynamics. Findings. None of the analyses, in the total sample (Aim 1; b between .02 and .03, p between .414 and .779) nor in subgroups (Aims 2-3; b between -.001 and .12, p between .192 and .988), provided support for within-person cross-lagged effects between the quantity of alcohol and alcohol-free use. Conclusions. No evidence was found for substitution or stepping-stone effects, which (indirectly) suggests that students generally drink alcohol-free as an additive to alcohol, rather than as a substitute or stepping-stone. Additional research is needed to strengthen the evidence on the effects of consuming alcohol-free beverages on alcohol use and health in general.

articles_hidden.title: Index-Dependent Detection of Insufficient Effort Responding Under Repeated Administration in a Large-Scale Assessment System
articles_hidden.authors: Victor Vasconcelos de Souza
articles_hidden.abstract: Screening for insufficient effort responding (IER) using response matrix data rests on a small family of indices—longstring, intra-individual response variability, even–odd consistency, and multivariate outlyingness—which are known to identify different respondents and are therefore combined into a composite flag. Whether they also disagree about conditions, rather than about cases, has not been examined. It matters more, because a composite can be robust to disagreement over which respondents are flagged while remaining unable to recover a direction of association on which its components differ. The test case is a burden condition created by assessment design: large-scale assessments may require teachers to complete an identical questionnaire once per sampled class, so that burden is the number of questionnaires rather than the length of one. In the SAEB 2023 teacher file the indices associate with burden in opposite directions, and no aggregation of them—union, intersection, or count—recovers an association: an analyst screening with response variability concludes that quality improves with burden, one screening with multivariate outlyingness concludes that it deteriorates, and one screening with the composite concludes that burden is irrelevant. The divergence is sharper on a homogeneous same-valence block, where the multivariate flag rate roughly doubles across the burden range while run-length flagging falls. Decomposition shows where the divergence lives: the outlyingness gradient is carried by between-school composition and is absorbed or reversed under school fixed effects, so the contradictory verdicts are a property of the file as it would operationally be screened, not of a within-teacher degradation process. A separate consequence of repeated administration is that a teacher's questionnaires are near-duplicates of one another, agreeing on about 98% of responses against roughly 67% for two teachers in the same school, so records in such files are far from independent. The screening verdict therefore depends on the index and the cutoff, and composition alone can manufacture a disagreement that no aggregation rule survives.

articles_hidden.title: Long-Term Outcomes of Childhood ADHD Stimulant Use Trajectories
articles_hidden.authors: N.E. van der Plas; Siri Noordermeer; Catharina Hartman; Pieter Hoekstra; Nanda Rommelse; Emma Sprooten; Jaap Oosterlaan; Marjolein Luman
articles_hidden.abstract: Stimulant medication is the first-line pharmacological treatment option for children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). However, long-term effects remain unclear. Therefore, we explored long-term (>12 years) outcomes of childhood stimulant medication use, using data from the Dutch NeuroIMAGE cohort. Childhood (up to Mage=16.14, SDage=3.48) stimulant treatment trajectories were detected using K-means clustering based on age at initiation, stop age, total and maximum daily dose, and duration and variability of stimulant use in 324 children. The trajectories were compared across seven domains of adult outcomes (controlling for multiple testing) including psychiatric status, behavioral and emotional functioning, academic and professional functioning, adaptive functioning, neurocognitive functioning, physical health, and healthcare service use. At follow-up, 143 adults with childhood ADHD (Mage=28.34, SDage=3.74, 65% males) were part of three stimulant treatment trajectory groups: early-and-intense (n=46), late-and-moderate (n=63), and stimulant-naïve (n=34). The three groups did not differ on any of the 51 adult outcomes and findings did not change after controlling for age and sex, except that a significant group difference emerged for callous and unemotional traits (behavioral and emotional functioning domain). More specifically, the early-and-intense and late-and-moderate groups had more favorable scores compared to stimulant-naïve group, although this may partly reflect pre-existing group differences. The main findings did not change after controlling for ADHD medication use at wave IV. Overall, stimulant medication use in childhood did not predict long-term outcomes in those with childhood ADHD in our sample, suggesting that there may be no lasting effects of stimulants on many long-term functional outcomes.

articles_hidden.title: Embodied Emotions in Natural Language
articles_hidden.authors: Lauri Nummenmaa; Aatu Liimatta; Eleanor Bennett; Birgitta Paranko; Heidi Jauhiainen; Mikko Sams; Saana Svärd; Juha M. Lahnakoski
articles_hidden.abstract: Emotions are often felt in the body, and embodiment is a prominent mechanism supporting language processing. Here we utilized computational linguistics to map embodied representations of emotions in an English text corpus. The data revealed consistent embodied patterns for emotion categories. Comparison between semantics-derived and self-reported bodily maps of emotions revealed similar, discrete bodily representations of different emotions in texts and self-reports. Hierarchical clustering revealed three clusters: positive emotions within the head and chest, negative emotions within the torso and legs, and negative social emotions mostly within the head. Replication in a Finnish corpus yielded consistent results. These findings show that the bodily organization of emotional experience is reflected in the statistical structure of language, linking linguistic meaning to the subjective bodily experience of emotion.

articles_hidden.title: Men report lower perceived social support and a stronger association between childhood adversity and internalising problems than women in young adulthood
articles_hidden.authors: Elizabeth E. L. Buimer; Zenna Liekens; Peter Prinzie
articles_hidden.abstract:
Mental health problems show marked sex/gender differences in young adulthood, with women reporting higher levels of internalising problems and men higher levels of externalising problems. Childhood adversity is one of the strongest predictors of later mental health problems, whereas social support is an important protective factor following childhood adversity. However, it remains unclear whether associations among childhood adversity, perceived social support, and internalising and externalising problems differ between men and women during young adulthood.

Using data from 331 young adults from the Flemish Study on Parenting, Personality and Development (aged 22–27 years; Mage = 24.8, 58% women), we examined whether childhood adversity was associated with internalising and externalising problems, whether these associations were moderated by social support, and whether these patterns differed by sex/gender. Next, we compared perceived social support across different support sources (friends, romantic partners, mother, father, and siblings) while again testing for sex/gender effects.  

Childhood adversity was positively associated with externalising problems and internalising problems. When adjusting for perceived social support, the positive association between childhood adversity and internalising problems was stronger for men compared to women. Social support had a main effect on internalising and externalising problems but did not moderate the association between childhood adversity and mental health outcomes. Perceived social support was highest among romantic partners, followed by friends, mothers, fathers, and siblings. Men reported lower levels of perceived social support than women across all support sources, but no significant sex/gender differences were found on cumulative childhood adversity or internalising/externalising problems. 

Together, these findings suggest lower levels of perceived social support and a stronger association between childhood adversity and internalising problems for men compared to women. Furthermore, we show that social support may function as an independent protective factor for mental health in young adulthood rather than as a buffer against the effects of childhood adversity.

articles_hidden.title: Model Checking for Vector Autoregressive Models
articles_hidden.authors: Jonas M B Haslbeck; Joran Jongerling; Björn S. Siepe; Sacha Epskamp; Lourens Waldorp
articles_hidden.abstract: Time series have become pervasive in psychological science, and Vector Autoregressive (VAR) models are now among the most popular tools for studying within-person dynamics in such data. However, researchers rarely check systematically how well a VAR model fits their data. This is problematic because model misfit can lead both to incorrect interpretations of model parameters and to missed structure in the data that would be theoretically interesting. We provide a tutorial that explains the theory behind model checking, discusses the most common types of VAR model misspecification in psychological time series, and introduces diagnostics for detecting them using plots and simulations. In addition, we provide code to extract predictions and residuals from popular software packages, along with the new R-package VARcheck, which allows researchers to create extensive diagnostic plots with only a few lines of code. We then apply these tools to assess the fit of a multilevel VAR model estimated on a typical empirical dataset of emotion measurements from 179 people over three weeks. We conclude by discussing three complementary ways in which model checking can advance psychological science using time series.

articles_hidden.title: On A Theory of Self-structure II: The Theoretical Dimensions of Self-Structure
articles_hidden.authors: Jie Zhong
articles_hidden.abstract:
This paper, rooted in psychoanalytic traditions including Freud’s libido theory and Kohut’s self psychology and extending the author’s prior work, proposes the Bidimensional Self-Structure Theory. Defining self-structure as an innate, coherent subjective organization shaping psychological experience, the theory identifies two statistically orthogonal core dimensions: self-cathexis (libidinal self-investment, metaphorical "existence-weight") and self-space need (subjective developmental space demand, metaphorical "existence-volume"). Their ratio forms self-structure density, the essence of narcissism, which distinguishes solid narcissism (high density) and void narcissism (low density) and categorizes self-structures into four quadrants. Two clinical cases—Celia (16-year-old with BPD, low self-cathexis + high self-space need) and Zoe (22-year-old with emotional deprivation, low self-cathexis + low self-space need), both typifying void narcissism—validate the model’s efficacy in explaining pathological self-structural heterogeneity. 
The theory bridges the theoretical gap between Freud’s (1914) classical psychoanalytic model of narcissism and Kohut’s (1971, 1977) self psychology model, synthesizes insights from major psychoanalytic schools, and clarifies that pathological diagnoses (symptom clusters) and self-structure (the deep organizational framework of the self) pertain to distinct dimensional systems. It outlines future research directions: identifying falsifiable clinical cases to test theoretical boundaries, conducting quantitative research to operationalize core constructs, and exploring cross-cultural perspectives on selfhood via Chinese philosophical thoughts.

articles_hidden.title: When Real Danger Lowers Anxiety: A Test of Phantom Anxiety Theory
articles_hidden.authors: Marcin Florkowski
articles_hidden.abstract:
One paradox of contemporary anxiety psychopathology is that gains in safety and quality of life do not yield proportional decreases in anxiety-related problems at the population level. This paper introduces Phantom Anxiety Theory (PAT), according to which the human anxiety system includes both a reactive component and an endogenous vigilance component. This yields a counterintuitive prediction: genuine danger may reduce anxiety-related indicators, whereas safer periods may be associated with greater search interest in anxiety-related content.
This prediction was tested by analysing 56 flood and 13 earthquake events across five highly developed countries with a combined population of 289 million. For each event, Google Trends search interest in the Topic “Anxiety” was compared in the most affected region with analogous periods one and two years earlier. 
Consistent with PAT’s differential predictions, “Anxiety” search interest declined after floods but rose after earthquakes. The two disaster types differed significantly in the direction of change, while control topics failed to replicate this pattern. These findings support the hypothesis that the human anxiety system may operate in two complementary modes and remain active without an adequate threat object. They may help explain why reductions in objective stressors do not necessarily reduce anxiety-related phenomena.

articles_hidden.title: Consciousness and emotions in non-human animals: Are laypeople more or less skeptical than experts?
articles_hidden.authors: Bastian Jaeger; Stefan Leach; Matthew Zipple
articles_hidden.abstract: Consciousness and the capacity to experience affective states, such as pain, pleasure, fear, and hunger (i.e., sentience) are seen as key determinants of an individual’s moral status, a view that is shared by scientists, philosophers, and laypeople. Whether (and which) non-human animals are believed to possess these capacities can therefore have important consequences for how they are treated. In this registered report (study design registration: https://doi.org/10.71240/lcyc.238674), we measured people’s attributions of consciousness and emotions to a diverse set of animals, testing whether laypeople overattribute (as suggested by research on anthropomorphizing) or underattribute these mental capacities to animals (as suggested by research on motivated mind denial). Animal consciousness and emotions are famously challenging to study. In the absence of an unambiguous benchmark against which people’s beliefs could be compared, we tested whether laypeople, a nationally representative sample of 600 U.S. participants, are more or less skeptical about animal consciousness and emotions than scientific experts, a sample of 100 behavioral ecologists, evolutionary biologists, and other animal researchers. We find that, compared to scientific experts, laypeople were less likely to attribute consciousness (-8 percentage points), and substantially less likely to attribute emotions (-21 percentage points) to non-human animals. Laypeople were on average more confident in their beliefs than scientific experts.

articles_hidden.title: The partner as reader: recognition, disclosure risk, and the unit of analysis in dyadic reflexive thematic analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Vince Jacques de Blauwe; Alina Gheorghita; Antonio Fidalgo
articles_hidden.abstract:
Thirty widening-participation students in 15 stranger dyads wrote five probe re-sponses after a 14-minute belonging encounter. Reflexive thematic analysis of 150 im-mediate written micro-accounts generated four interpretive themes: calm-as-distance, vocabulary-as-bridge, masking under instruction, and provisional we-ness. A subse-quent dialogue-informed dyad-level configurational reading of paired texts extended, complicated, and bounded selected individual-level interpretations; it was not used as independent corroboration. Participants sometimes described calm or competent partici-pation alongside relational distance, evaluative effort, or uncertainty about mutuality; composure was therefore not treated as evidence of relational arrival.
This methodological case study develops the Partner-Recognition Framework for dyad-ic qualitative research. The framework addresses a risk that conventional de-identification may leave unresolved: a partner who shared an encounter may recognise an account from shared memory even when external identifiers have been removed. The four substantive themes provide the empirical case through which the framework is de-veloped; the disclosure-cost and recursive-risk analyses show what implementation re-quires. Four rules follow: naming partner recognition in consent, prospective specifica-tion of dyadic provenance, default pair separation in public reporting, and screening of derived artefacts. These are prospective design and reporting rules, not a validated risk-assessment instrument, a guarantee of anonymity, or a substitute for case-specific ethi-cal and legal review.

articles_hidden.title: Revisiting Assurance: Theoretical Refinement, Scale Development, and Future Research
articles_hidden.authors: Atsuki Ito; Matthias S Gobel; Kosuke TAKEMURA
articles_hidden.abstract: Expectations that others will cooperate are critical for sustaining intragroup cooperation. Although extensive research has emphasized trust—expectations of cooperation based on others’ traits and intentions—as a strong predictor of cooperation, assurance—expectations grounded in incentive structures—has received little empirical attention. The present research aims to establish a theoretical and methodological foundation for assurance research. First, we propose that assurance can be understood as a process through which perceived incentive structure gives rise to expectations of others’ cooperation and ultimately promotes cooperation. Second, across three studies using American and Japanese samples (total N = 1,589), we developed the Perceived Assurability Scale, a reliable measure of perceived incentive structure underlying assurance and demonstrated that perceived assurability predicts workplace cooperation independently of perceived trustworthiness. Third, we propose future research directions regarding how group contexts are translated into cooperation through psychological processes captured by the concepts of trust and assurance.

articles_hidden.title: State of Social Cognition Research: Challenges, Future Directions, and Efforts Toward Consensus Building
articles_hidden.authors: Niklas Bürgi; Anabela Cantiani; Beatriz Catoira; Mado Gautier; Ilenia Gori; Annika Konrad; Lara Maliske; Annabel Nijhof; Arthur Pabst; Ekaterina Pronizius
articles_hidden.abstract: Social cognition research has become a key area of cognitive science, producing a wealth of theories, methods, and empirical findings. However, the field faces significant challenges that constrain further progress and broader impact. As a group of social cognition researchers from various theoretical and methodological backgrounds, we came together to identify issues we consensually  consider  most  pressing,  highlight  their  negative  consequences,  and  suggest ways forward. We thus offer a synthesis of core issues that are typically treated separately in the literature,and  translate  them  into  a  shared  agenda  for  the  field.  Major  conceptual challenges  include  substantial  variation  in how  social  cognition  is  defined,  subdivided,  and labeled,   alongside   a   limited   understanding   of   its   basic   structure.   Methodologically, shortcomings  include  inadequate  assessment  and  reporting  of  psychometric  properties  of measurement tools. Furthermore, ecologically valid interactive paradigms are still scarce, and the clarification and experimental control over the processes underlying measurement scores remain   insufficient.   We   argue   that   progress   requires   both   humility   and   courage: acknowledging  our  field’s  theoretical  fragmentation  and  methodological  limitations,  and embracing complexity through multimethod, interactive, and computational approaches. We further introduce our community building initiative as a facilitating step toward achieving these objectives through consensus initiatives, open science practices, and large-scale collaborative research.

articles_hidden.title: Cultural Currents of Mindfulness: Tracing Mindfulness’s Use and Influence in Japan
articles_hidden.authors: Takeshi Hamamura; Min Maung; Anuradha Baminiwatta; Jun Chih; Suzanne Gilbey; Monica Gumulya; Masaru Kanetsuki; Trevor Mazzucchelli
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objectives: Mindfulness is now widely studied and applied in psychology, yet its use and adaptation in non-Western contexts remain underexplored. This study examines how mindfulness is discussed and studied within Japanese scholarly literature. 

Methods: A two-pronged approach was employed: a scoping review of English-language publications to identify prevailing research patterns (Study 1), and a topic modelling analysis of Japanese-language literature to explore themes (Study 2). 

Results: Findings from both analyses indicate that mindfulness in Japan is predominantly framed within therapeutic and wellness-oriented contexts in clinical, educational, and occupational settings. At the same time, culturally grounded adaptations were observed, including the incorporation of practices such as Naikan, Zen meditation, and martial arts, alongside thematic emphases on relational and psychosomatic processes. However, explicit engagement with cultural adaptation was relatively limited, raising questions about the extent to which local cultural contexts are informing or being overlooked in the adaptation process. 

Conclusion: As mindfulness continues to circulate globally, findings from this study highlight the need for context-sensitive approaches that engage with both global frameworks and local conceptual traditions.

articles_hidden.title: Mapping United States Federal Funding for Mental Health Difficulties from 2020-2024 to the Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology: A Registered Report
articles_hidden.authors: Nathaniel Luke Phillips; Eli Berman; Courtland Hyatt; Leigha Rose; Thomas M Olino; Donald R Lynam; Josh Miller
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychopathology is a major public health concern, which is why the U.S. government invests billions of dollars annually to investigate its etiology, assessment, course, and treatment. To date, however, there is no empirical mechanism for evaluating how federal research funding is allocated across dimensions of psychopathology. This Registered Report used the Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology (HiTOP) as a framework to classify funded research grants from 2020 through 2024 across four psychopathology-focused institutes within the National Institutes of Health (NIH) according to higher-order dimensions of psychopathology. We first present a pilot study supporting the feasibility of using a large language model (LLM) for this task. In the main study, we quantified the allocation of federal funding across HiTOP spectra, examining differences across funding agencies, grant mechanisms, and time. Results indicated that the Disinhibited Externalizing spectrum received more funding in this time period than all other spectra combined, and this funding was almost entirely driven by substance-use-related research funded by the National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA) and National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA). Internalizing, Autism, Thought Disorder, and Detachment spectra received substantial allocations of federal funding, all of which were predominantly administered by the National Institute on Mental Health (NIMH). Finally, Antagonistic Externalizing and Somatoform spectra received comparatively little federal funding. This work provides the first systematic characterization of U.S. research priorities grounded in a contemporary, dimensional model of psychopathology.

articles_hidden.title: Out-of-Context and In-Context Environmental Effects on Exploratory Reinforcement Learning and Decision-Making
articles_hidden.authors: Mianzhi Hu; Emma Dennin; Ben D. Ulicnik; Darrell A. Worthy
articles_hidden.abstract: Physical environments can shape behavior, yet how they influence the latent cognitive processes underlying experiential, feedback-based learning remains largely unknown. Across two experiments with 486 participants, we examined how visual exposure to natural, urban or control images influenced performance in a non-stationary reinforcement learning task. In Experiment 1, lasting, out-of-context effects of exposure to natural or urban scenes between two task runs increased reward and decision quality while reducing stochastic switching and exploration relative to control images. Urban exposure further promoted exploitation at the cost of poorer exploration quality, whereas natural exposure was associated with higher-quality exploration. In Experiment 2, when the same images were embedded as task backgrounds, in-context exposure produced a different pattern. Natural scenes increased switching, while both natural and urban scenes increased lose-shift behavior. Semantic segmentation combined with computational modeling further suggested that in-context effects were more strongly associated with features that could promote immediate information seeking, whereas out-of-context effects were linked to broader features reflecting the gist of the environment. Together, these findings show that environmental influences on experiential reinforcement learning are dynamic, context-dependent and feature-specific, beyond a general natural-urban contrast.

articles_hidden.title: Developmental Timing of the Reciprocal Prospective Associations Between Cannabis Use and Internalizing and Externalizing Symptoms in Early Adolescence
articles_hidden.authors: Fiona A Ralston; Herry Patel; Isabel R. Aks; Natasha E. Wade; William E. Pelham
articles_hidden.abstract: This paper examines the reciprocal associations between specific internalizing (e.g., depression and anxiety) and externalizing (e.g., Attention Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, Conduct Disorder, and Oppositional Defiant Disorder) disorder symptoms and cannabis use during early adolescence with age differences. We analyzed youth-reported cannabis use, depression, anxiety, Attention Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, Conduct Disorder, and Oppositional Defiant Disorder symptoms in 9- to 15-year-old adolescents enrolled in the longitudinal Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study (N=11,868) using data from the baseline visit through the 4-year follow-up. Multilevel regression models, parsing between- and within-youth effects were fit to examine the association between cannabis use and five different mental health disorders prospectively. Moderation by age was tested. In the main analyses, all between-youth reciprocal associations between internalizing and externalizing disorder symptoms and cannabis use were significant, except anxiety. Anxiety was unidirectionally related to cannabis use, where increased anxiety symptoms predicated greater probability of cannabis use one year later (β = 0.0008, p = .006) but not vice versa. Strongest between- and within-youth reciprocal associations emerged for depression and conduct disorder symptoms with cannabis use prospectively, with age moderating the associations. In a nationwide sample of adolescents ages 9 to 15 years-old, we found depression and conduct disorder symptoms were most strongly and reciprocally associated with greater probability of cannabis use prospectively. Further research is necessary to validate and confirm our findings and extend to greater cannabis use frequency and motives for use in the context of increased acceptance of cannabis use as treatment for mental health issues.

articles_hidden.title: Simple heuristics structure and bias fairness judgements about climate change
articles_hidden.authors: Lucas Woodley; Arthur Le Pargneux; Fiery Andrews Cushman
articles_hidden.abstract: Establishing a fair global carbon budget is crucial for mitigating climate change, yet little is known about what shapes citizens' fairness perceptions. In a pre-registered experiment across five countries (N=3,043), we examine how simple informational cues affect what people propose as fair carbon budgets. We find that people’s judgements are structured around proportionality or nominal equality heuristics, yet they are easily biased and frequently contradict all main climate justice principles.

articles_hidden.title: Validation of the Alcohol Induced Blackout Measure-2 (ABOM-2) among Young Adults Who Experience Blackout
articles_hidden.authors: Cassandra L. Boness; Angelo DiBello; Emily Herberholz; Kara Link; Richard Neil Greene; Jennifer Merrill; Kate Carey; Mary Beth Miller
articles_hidden.abstract: Memory loss from alcohol (“blackout”) is common among young adults who drink and associated with significant alcohol-related harm. Despite longstanding evidence distinguishing fragmentary (transient) and en bloc (permanent) blackouts, a measure distinguishing these two forms of blackout (the Alcohol-Induced Blackout Measure-2 [ABOM-2]) was only recently developed and has not been psychometrically evaluated among young adults with a history of alcohol-induced blackouts. The present study evaluated the psychometric properties of the ABOM-2, particularly its longitudinal measurement invariance and prospective predictive validity, among 169 heavy-drinking young adults (ages 18–30) with a history of blackout. Confirmatory factor analyses at baseline (T1) and one-month follow-up (T2) supported previous research showing the ABOM-2 items are best represented by two correlated factors. Both factors, en bloc and fragmentary, demonstrated convergent validity, showing significant associations with hazardous drinking, alcohol consumption, and alcohol-related consequences. In concurrent convergent and prospective predictive regression models that accounted for relevant covariates and included both types of blackouts, en bloc (but not fragmentary) blackouts significantly predicted hazardous drinking, alcohol consumption, and consequences across time. Longitudinal measurement invariance testing provided evidence for configural, metric, and scalar invariance across T1 and T2, supporting the measurement equivalence of ABOM-2 over time. Findings reinforce the distinction between en bloc and fragmentary blackouts, support the convergent and predictive validity of the ABOM-2, and highlight the clinical and research utility of the ABOM-2 as a reliable tool for assessing blackout across time. En bloc blackouts, in particular, serve as a robust marker of alcohol-related risk among young adults.

articles_hidden.title: Individual differences in visual imagery vividness predict neural responses to language-induced visual expectations
articles_hidden.authors: Ana Chkhaidze; Lera Boroditsky; Sean Trott; Anastasia Kiyonaga; Seana Coulson
articles_hidden.abstract: Grounded accounts of meaning propose that language comprehension recruits sensorimotor systems to represent described content. However, people differ markedly in how vividly they can picture objects and scenes in the mind's eye, raising the question of whether perceptual simulation is recruited similarly across individuals. We addressed this question using the sentence-picture verification task, in which pictures are verified more quickly when their shape matches rather than mismatches the state implied by a preceding sentence, a match effect taken to index perceptual simulation. In preregistered Experiment 1 (N = 110), matching pictures were verified faster and more accurately than mismatching pictures, yet the magnitude of this effect did not vary with imagery vividness. We reasoned that similar behavior might arise from different processes, so in Experiment 2 we recorded picture-locked event-related potentials (ERPs) from 34 participants performing the verification task. Shape mismatch elicited an early right-posterior response at 150-190 ms and a later, broader posterior response at 300-500 ms. Crucially, imagery vividness interacted with the shape match effect in the early window only: stronger imagers showed a pronounced right-posterior negativity, whereas verbal thinking tendency did not, indicating specificity to visual imagery. Together, results suggest that comparable behavioral outcomes may arise through partly different paths to meaning: an early, visually specific route recruited more strongly by vivid imagers, and a later conceptual route shared more broadly across the imagery spectrum. Language comprehension may draw on both perceptual simulation and linguistic associations, with the relative contribution of each depending in part on the comprehender.

articles_hidden.title: Mindscapes of Second Language Acquisition: A New Perspective on the Cognitive Inquiry of Language
articles_hidden.authors: Junya Fukuta
articles_hidden.abstract:
This volume repositions second language acquisition (SLA) not as a peripheral concern, but as a central domain of cognitive science. It establishes the epistemological foundations required for SLA to function as a genuinely cognitive science, and on this basis develops a new Causal-Mechanistic Systems Approach. Through a series of specific models, the book offers fresh resolutions to long-standing theoretical debates in the field.

A distinctive feature of the volume is its attempt to bridge classical cognitivism and complex systems theory while advancing a new form of realist cognitivism. It also brings probabilistic inference, embodiment, and linguistic relativity together within a single integrated explanatory framework.

Departing from approaches that treat pedagogical outcomes in isolation, the book situates SLA within a broader account of cognition and the human mind. In doing so, it connects questions traditionally addressed in second language research with debates across cognitive science, linguistics, and the philosophy of mind. This ambitious and interdisciplinary volume will be essential reading for researchers in SLA, cognitive scientists, linguists, and graduate students seeking a deeper understanding of language, cognition, and the architecture of the human mind.

articles_hidden.title: What is attention for?  A theory of attention as control  over information sampling
articles_hidden.authors: Heleen A Slagter; Thomas Parr
articles_hidden.abstract:
Goal-directed attention shapes what we perceive, learn, and ultimately how we act in the world. Yet, despite its central role in cognition, what attention fundamentally is remains debated, with dominant accounts treating it either as a filter over sensory processing or tightly linked to goal-directed action. Here, we propose a unified account in which goal-directed attention is understood as control over how information is sampled within the framework of active inference. In this perspective, goal-directed attention does not simply modulate sensory processing, nor can it be equated to, or seen as the covert shadow of goal-directed action. Rather, attention governs information seeking, determining what is brought into evidence, and thereby what the organism perceives, learns from, and uses to guide action. Mechanistically, we propose that alternative ways of weighting information are themselves evaluated as candidate courses of action, and selected according to their expected informativeness and usefulness. 
	A conceptualization of goal-directed attention as control over information sampling renders attention inherently inferential, prospective, and agentic, as the organism must evaluate alternative epistemic futures on the basis of what would come to be known if information were sampled in one way rather than another. It also explains attention's sensitivity to salience, prior experience, value, and context, because which way of sampling information is selected is jointly shaped by both what is informative and what matters to the organism. More generally, our review shows that our account can parsimoniously explain a wide range of attentional phenomena, and that influences traditionally attributed to distinct sources of control, such as goals, salience, and selection history, can be understood as different constraints on a single inferential process through which organisms determine how information should be acquired in the service of adaptive behaviour. We discuss this proposal in relation to influential perception- and action-based theories of attention, and explore its implications for understanding the relationship between covert and overt attention, attentional agency, habit formation, and attentional dysfunction. More broadly, we argue that progress in understanding attention requires moving beyond describing the factors that influence attentional selection toward a mechanistic account of how organisms determine what to know next.

articles_hidden.title: UK-Adaptation of the Dutch PET@home Toolkit for Clients Receiving Home Care with Pets (SAFEpet@home): A Participatory Adaptation Study
articles_hidden.authors: Peter Reniers; Ine J.N. Declercq; Marie-Jose Enders-Slegers; Karin Hediger; Elizabeth Ormerod; Ruslan Leontjevas
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Pets can contribute to the wellbeing of people receiving home care but may also present practical challenges for clients, family caregivers, and professional caregivers. The Dutch PET@home Toolkit was developed to support stakeholders in addressing pet-related issues in home care. Differences in care practices and support infrastructure mean that the toolkit cannot simply be transferred to other national contexts.
Objective: To adapt the Dutch PET@home Toolkit for use in the United Kingdom.
Design: Participatory adaptation study using qualitative interviews and focus groups.
Setting(s): Interviews and focus groups were conducted online with participants based in the United Kingdom.
Participants: Twelve participants with backgrounds in social care, veterinary practice, animal welfare, and related fields contributed through individual interviews, focus groups, and/or member checking.
Methods: The Dutch PET@home materials were translated into English and reviewed with UK-based stakeholders. Information relevant to adaptation was identified through a pragmatic and iterative analysis of interviews and focus groups. Suggested adaptations were incorporated into the materials and reviewed within the research team. Revised materials were subsequently returned to participants for member checking and review of UK English.
Results: The adaptation resulted in the SAFEpet@home Toolkit. Key changes included greater emphasis on collaboration with veterinary practices, replacement of the Five Freedoms with the Five Domains Model, increased diversity in visual materials and represented companion animal species, and inclusion of UK-specific organisations and support resources. Other adaptations addressed practical issues such as planning for multiple pets and veterinary decision-making.
Conclusions: The Dutch PET@home Toolkit was adapted to reflect UK care practices, animal welfare guidance, and support infrastructure while retaining the core principles of the original toolkit. The findings suggest that a participatory adaptation process is a feasible approach for adapting toolkits to different national contexts.

articles_hidden.title: The Dutch D70: Psychometric validation of the Dark Factor of Personality
articles_hidden.authors: Ann De Buck; Lieven Pauwels
articles_hidden.abstract: The Dark Factor of Personality (D) represents a common dispositional core underlying socially and morally aversive traits (Moshagen et al., 2018, 2020). This study provides the first psychometric evaluation of the Dutch 70-item D factor scale (Dutch D70) across two independent samples: an online community sample (n = 978) and a student sample (n = 1,806). Using confirmatory factor analysis, we compared a unidimensional model, a hierarchical second-order model, and a bifactor model. In both samples, the bifactor structure demonstrated the best overall fit. It indicated a dominant general Dark Factor accounting for the vast majority of the common variance with high reliability. The specific residual factors contributed minimal unique variance. Multi-group analyses supported full scalar invariance across self-reported sex, showing that the scale functions equivalently for men and women. Construct and nomological validity were supported through consistent associations of D with lower empathic concern and higher levels of low morality and ethnocentrism. Significant relations between D and self-reported out-group aggression further supported criterion-related validity. Overall, the findings show that the Dutch D70 is a reliable and valid instrument for assessing a strong general Dark Factor, with structural and validity evidence replicated across both community and student samples.

articles_hidden.title: Weak language abilities are associated with increased within-individual variability in both response times and rhythm tapping: Support for the intra-individual variability hypothesis from the Steps Study
articles_hidden.authors: Anna Kautto; Mira Karrasch; Viveka Lyberg Åhlander; Annette Nylund
articles_hidden.abstract:
First language acquisition varies substantially between children. A recent hypothesis suggests that intra-individual variability (IIV) in cognitive processing, which is reflected by response time (RT) IIV, underlies individual differences in language acquisition. In this study, we test this hypothesis by investigating associations between different measures of short-time IIV and language abilities in 15-year-old adolescents.

The participants (n=239) were recruited from the Steps cohort study. Our aim was to investigate whether IIV would be associated with language abilities, and whether the possible association is observed in different IIV measures. The participants completed three different tasks measuring IIV: a simple RT task, as well as externally paced metronome tapping and self-paced rhythm tapping. We were interested in whether IIV in tasks that require aligning to temporal patterns of external, sensory information (metronome tapping) or producing temporal patterns without external cues (self-paced tapping) would be differentially associated with language abilities.

In line with the IIV hypothesis of language, we found that pronounced IIV in all task types (metronome and self-paced rhythm tapping, as well as RTs) was related to weak language abilities.  Some differences in the associations between task types and language abilities emerged; RT IIV was a stronger predictor for language abilities than IIV in rhythm tapping tasks. Our sample consisted of adolescents, at which age language abilities are no longer in an active stage of development. If we assume that IIV reflects cognitive instability that underlies individual differences in language acquisition, this instability seems to be a persistent individual trait and could thus potentially be a helpful marker for identifying children at-risk for language learning difficulties.

articles_hidden.title: Stable tendencies in spontaneous working memory usage during flexible behaviour
articles_hidden.authors: Levi Kumle; Amy Xiangjin Li; Joel Kovoor; Amelia G. Rock; Emily Hesselink; Ellen Jones; Meadhbh Brosnan; Anna C Nobre; Dejan Draschkow
articles_hidden.abstract: Unlike standard working memory (WM) tasks, real-world settings allow individuals to spontaneously adapt how much information to use from WM before resampling the environment. Here, we considered whether individuals exhibit distinct, trait-like tendencies in their spontaneous use of WM. Across three studies (N = 220) using an Object Copying Task, we show that some participants consistently exhibited greater WM usage than others. These tendencies were reliable, stable across time, and predicted individuals’ task efficiency and responses to changing task demands. Finally, spontaneous WM usage could only partially be explained by established measures of WM capacity and attentional control – two plausible predictors of natural WM usage. In summary, we find stable tendencies in individuals’ spontaneous WM usage, despite the variable nature of self-structured natural behaviour. Our results position inter-individual variability as an important dimension in understanding natural, memory-guided behaviour, highlighting the need to investigate its broader determinants and behavioural consequences.

articles_hidden.title: Screening for DLD: Reliability and validity of the Screening Tool for Adults with Non-Diagnosed DLD (STAND).
articles_hidden.authors: Michelle St Clair; Jenny Louise Gibson; Suze Leitao; Emily Jackson; Ellie Barker; Mia Travlos; Jiayi Liang; Amy Bennett; Iris Edwards; Nicola Botting
articles_hidden.abstract: Interest in diagnosis of neurodevelopmental disorders (NDD) in adulthood is increasing, but there is no validated screening tool to identify adulthood Developmental Language Disorder (DLD). DLD affects 7% of the population with lifelong impacts on education, employment, and mental-health. This paper evaluates a new screening tool to identify undiagnosed DLD in adulthood: the Screening Tool for Adults with Non-Diagnosed DLD (STAND). Study 1 investigated endorsement rate for STAND items, internal reliability, and test-retest reliability in adults with no NDD and with self-identified DLD. Study 2 (general population sample) and 3 (Student sample) evaluated internal reliability and validity. Study 4 evaluated the STAND’s acceptability by consulting adults with DLD. Internal reliability ranged from excellent to acceptable for current, lifetime, and total scores, and test-retest reliability was good. Adults self-identifying as having DLD endorsed all items more frequently, with significantly higher STAND scores. Studies 2 and 3 demonstrated good construct validity, with family history of language/literacy difficulties and personal NDD history associated with higher scores.  The Language Structure subscale on the Communication Checklist-Self Report (CC-SR) related to more Current and Total Difficulties in Study 2, establishing convergent validity. Study 3 further established convergent validity with the CC-SR Language Structure and Social Engagement subscales predicting STAND scores and the CELF-5 Core Language Score predicting lifetime language difficulties. Study 4 demonstrated broad acceptability of the STAND, leading to minor changes to create a revised STAND. The STAND offers a first step in creating an acceptable, reliable, and valid tool for DLD diagnosis in adults.

articles_hidden.title: How Restorative Justice may Create Social Change: A Contact-to-Change Model
articles_hidden.authors: Kimberley Aspinall; Michael Wenzel; Blake Quinney
articles_hidden.abstract: Restorative justice is a legal philosophy and practice focused on the repair of harm resulting from wrongdoing; as such, it has the transformative potential to facilitate change at individual, interpersonal and societal levels. Yet, restorative justice practices have diverged from their original social justice goals towards an individual-focused model of repair. The question is: how can we return restorative justice processes to their roots of addressing social injustices that underlie crime, and harness their power to mobilise communities for change? How can restorative justice processes speak to the wider community and promote their support for, or engagement in, collective action to address social injustices? To answer these questions, we propose the Restorative Contact-to-Change (RC2C) model, which draws from collective action, allyship and intergroup contact and dialogue literatures. The RC2C model proposes that community involvement in or, at a minimum, observation of restorative justice can be analysed as an instance of indirect intergroup contact, which—through perspective-taking, problem abstraction, and value consensus—can promote collective action and allyship behaviours for social change. The RC2C model may help understand how restorative justice processes can be transformative for individuals and society.

articles_hidden.title: The Neural Bases of Prediction in Music and Speech: An Integrative Theoretical Approach to Understanding Content and Timing Interactions
articles_hidden.authors: Lu Lucuța; Anne Kösem; Peter E. Keller; Anna Fiveash
articles_hidden.abstract: Predictions of content (“what”) and timing (“when”) have been widely investigated in both music and speech research. Considering that music and speech serve distinct communicative functions, predictions of content and timing, as well as their interplay, are likely to exhibit domain-specific characteristics. However, because these domains have largely been studied in isolation, the neural bases of content–timing interactions remain poorly understood. This review sets multiple objectives. The first is to provide an overview of how the neural correlates of content and timing predictions in music and speech have been investigated through the lenses of Predictive Coding and Dynamic Attending Theory. The second is to evaluate the extent to which these frameworks account for the interaction between content and timing predictions, particularly at a neurophysiological level. The third is to highlight points of convergence between the two frameworks that are often difficult to identify due to differences in nomenclature and research design. The fourth is to propose an integrative perspective through which methodological strengths from both research traditions can be complementarily implemented to further our understanding of the neural bases of content and timing predictions in music and speech, by considering different decisions that must be taken when investigating prediction in music and speech (stimulus, analysis, and interpretation decisions). Reconciling key aspects of these theoretical frameworks across multiple levels of description (i.e., computational, algorithmic, implementational) within music and speech processing can provide insights into prediction as a fundamental aspect of cognition.

articles_hidden.title: Understanding and Avoiding Construct Redundancy Fallacies in Environmental Psychology
articles_hidden.authors: Taciano L Milfont; Gordon Hodson
articles_hidden.abstract: Construct proliferation and measurement redundancy can undermine conceptual clarity and cumulative scientific progress. We examine these challenges in environmental psychology, a rapidly growing field characterised by an expanding number of constructs and measures. After reviewing the historical problem of construct redundancy fallacies in psychological science, we illustrate its relevance to environmental psychology with two examples based on re-analysis of published data. We first examine multiple connection-to-nature constructs and measures that may represent alternative operationalisations of the same underlying latent construct. We then consider strong associations among environmentalism-related constructs typically regarded as theoretically distinct. Building on this evidence, we advance consideration of a generalised common factor (g-environmentalism) underlying diverse environmentalism-related measures. We conclude with recommendations for improving conceptual clarity, measurement practices, parsimony, and cumulative progress in environmental psychology.

articles_hidden.title: Out-of-Context and In-Context Environmental Effects on Exploratory Reinforcement Learning and Decision-Making
articles_hidden.authors: Mianzhi Hu; Emma Dennin; Ben D. Ulicnik; Darrell A. Worthy
articles_hidden.abstract: Physical environments can shape behavior, yet how they influence the latent cognitive processes underlying experiential, feedback-based learning remains largely unknown. Across two experiments with 486 participants, we examined how visual exposure to natural, urban or control images influenced performance in a non-stationary reinforcement learning task. In Experiment 1, lasting, out-of-context effects of exposure to natural or urban scenes between two task runs increased reward and decision quality while reducing stochastic switching and exploration relative to control images. Urban exposure further promoted exploitation at the cost of poorer exploration quality, whereas natural exposure was associated with higher-quality exploration. In Experiment 2, when the same images were embedded as task backgrounds, in-context exposure produced a different pattern. Natural scenes increased switching, while both natural and urban scenes increased lose-shift behavior. Semantic segmentation combined with computational modeling further suggested that in-context effects were more strongly associated with features that could promote immediate information seeking, whereas out-of-context effects were linked to broader features reflecting the gist of the environment. Together, these findings show that environmental influences on experiential reinforcement learning are dynamic, context-dependent and feature-specific, beyond a general natural-urban contrast.

articles_hidden.title: “What we found was…” Syntactic prominence cues to information structure affect semantic prediction.
articles_hidden.authors: Eleonora Beier; Adrian Zhou; Fernanda Ferreira
articles_hidden.abstract: While predicting the content of upcoming words facilitates comprehension, it is often what cannot be predicted that conveys the most novel, important information. We address the cognitive mechanisms underlying the interplay between predictions for upcoming content and expectations about its novelty. In Experiment 1, we used eye-tracking to measure reading times to sentences containing a target word that was either predictable or unpredictable (but plausible). Expected novelty was manipulated through syntactic prominence: the target was either narrowly focused through a wh- cleft (“What he made was…”; high prominence), marked as presupposed through a subordinate clause (“After he made…”; low prominence), or presented through a “neutral” structure (“He made…”; intermediate prominence). We found that the facilitatory effect of predictability on reading times was eliminated for words in high prominence, while it was enhanced for words in low prominence. In Experiment 2, we addressed whether this interaction was due to a direct effect of prominence cues on semantic pre-activation, or an indirect effect on ease of integration of unpredictable content, using the visual world paradigm with auditory stimuli. Compared to the neutral baseline condition, we found that while hearing the focusing construction, listeners made fewer fixations towards the predictable item and more towards the unpredictable alternative; while hearing the subordinate clause, they made fewer fixations towards both predictable and unpredictable items. Overall, we show that syntactic prominence affects semantic prediction through multiple cognitive mechanisms: wh- clefts lead listeners to expect the unexpected, while subordinate clauses lead to shallow processing and less prediction.

articles_hidden.title: Environmental Exposures and Brain Health Outcomes in Healthy Ageing: A Systematic Review
articles_hidden.authors: Kelly E Perry; Breanna Watterson; Jenna Louise Merenstein
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Air pollution and built environment features are increasingly associated with negative health outcomes, yet their relation to brain health in older adults without dementia remains unclear.

Methods: To synthesise the extant literature, we conducted a systematic review, searching MEDLINE (PubMed) and Web of Science (Core Collection) from inception to February 23, 2026. Eligible studies assessed a natural or built environmental exposure against brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) measures in cognitively healthy older adults (ages 65+ without dementia). Reviewers screened and extracted summary data from published reports in Covidence; no individual patient data were sought. The main outcome was brain health; findings were synthesised narratively using an effect-direction approach, as heterogeneous exposures, outcomes, and effect metrics precluded pooling.

Findings: Of 2,496 records screened, 26 studies met eligibility, comprising >84,000 older adults across 10 countries: United States, South Korea, United Kingdom, France, Spain, Sweden, Netherlands, Taiwan, Germany, and Japan. Thirteen studies were cross-sectional and 13 were cohort studies (eight observational and five longitudinal). Higher air pollution exposure—particularly PM2·5, NO2, and PM10—was associated with altered brain structure: smaller total, grey matter, and white matter volumes, greater white matter hyperintensities, cortical thinning, and medial temporal and hippocampal atrophy; greenspace was generally protective. 13 studies met criteria for high methodological quality and low risk of bias, though outcome assessment was a recurring source of bias (12 of 26 studies), and four of the five longitudinal studies did not meet criterion for follow-up adequacy.

Interpretation: This novel review synthesises compelling evidence that brain structure is susceptible to air pollution in healthy ageing, supporting the notion that this modifiable environmental exposure may serve as a potential target for physicians and policymakers aiming to protect brain health in the fastest growing segment of the global population.

articles_hidden.title: Executive Function and Affective State Recognition Show Distinct Associations with Empathic Choice Across Socioeconomic Contexts
articles_hidden.authors: Fiorella Macchiavello; Huepe David; Valentina Vallejo-Correa; F. Rojas-Thomas; José Javier Bórquez Henríquez; Consuelo Ruiz; Luis Sebastian Contreras-Huerta
articles_hidden.abstract:
Abstract: Empathy research has traditionally emphasised the capacities and dispositions that enable people to understand and respond to others’ affective states. Motivational accounts, however, have highlighted that empathy also depends on whether individuals choose to engage with those states when engagement is optional. Building on this distinction, we examined how social-specific affective state recognition and domain-general executive function relate to empathic choice, and whether these associations vary with socioeconomic vulnerability (SV). 96 Chilean adults participated (50 High SV; 46 comparison). High SV participants showed lower affective state recognition and executive function, yet the groups did not differ in mean empathic choice. Across participants, better affective state recognition was associated with less frequent empathic choice, whereas dispositional empathy was positively associated with choice. Executive function was associated with more frequent empathic choice in High SV but not comparison participants, and this association differed significantly between groups. In contrast, the association between affective state recognition and empathic choice did not differ by socioeconomic group. Better affective state recognition was also associated with greater relative cognitive effort during empathic engagement. These findings show that distinct cognitive capacities relate differently to empathic motivation and that their behavioural relevance can depend on socioeconomic context.
Keywords: empathy; executive function; motivation; affective state recognition; empathic choice; socioeconomic vulnerability.

articles_hidden.title: Do Large Language Models see the world with rose-colored glasses? Prompting GPT-4o to associate color terms with emotion terms in Spanish and Chinese
articles_hidden.authors: Mingshan Xu; Antonio Benítez-Burraco
articles_hidden.abstract: Color terms and emotion terms frequently intertwine in language. In this paper, we compare the performance of humans and GPT-4o in an association task involving 13 color terms and 20 emotion terms (and 5 intensities of emotion) in two languages, Spanish and Chinese. Overall, we found that GPT-4o associates color terms with emotion terms similarly to humans. This is true for several main dimensions of emotions: valence, arousal, and power. At the same time, in cases where responses by human subjects differ cross-linguistically (such as intensity of emotion in our study with Spanish vs Chinese speakers), GPT-4o tends to reduce the differences between languages. In conclusion, although GPT-4o is a reliable model of human emotional language, it can contribute to eroding its diversity.

articles_hidden.title: The developmental dynamics of bilingual spelling:  Longitudinal and intervention evidence for language-specific orthographic differentiation
articles_hidden.authors: Manon Jones; Catherine Alice Clark; Gwennant Evans; Joseph Benjamin Russell Smith; Carly Deluca; James Hodgetts; Ferrida Ponce; Cadi Sion; Samuel David Jones; Cameron Downing
articles_hidden.abstract: Spelling in bilingual children requires navigating two orthographic systems that may compete as well as cooperate. Although bilingual language research demonstrates extensive cross-language co-activation, far less is known about how such dynamics shape spelling development. We investigated whether cross-linguistic influence in spelling – indexed by the extent to which children’s misspellings conformed to English-consistent versus Welsh-consistent phoneme–grapheme mappings – predicted literacy development in Welsh–English bilingual children. Across three studies involving 524 children aged approximately 7–11 years, we quantified the extent to which misspellings reflected sublexical mappings characteristic of English or Welsh orthography. In Study 1, longitudinal analyses of children in control groups showed that greater phonological plausibility under English-consistent mappings at baseline predicted greater growth in English spelling accuracy, whereas greater plausibility under Welsh-consistent mappings predicted slower growth. In Study 2, a Welsh-medium literacy intervention did not affect English spelling accuracy but strengthened Welsh-consistent mappings and improved English-consistent mappings among children with the weakest baseline skills. In Study 3, an English-medium intervention strengthened English-consistent mappings but did not alter Welsh-consistent mappings. Together, these findings suggest that bilingual spelling development involves increasing differentiation of language-specific sublexical mappings through experience. This differentiation appears to be shaped by instructional context and orthographic depth, such that increasing sensitivity to target-language mappings supports spelling growth, whereas persistent influence of non-target mappings may constrain it.

articles_hidden.title: Assessing Common-Cause Implications of Reflective Models:  A Simulation Study of the Tetrad Fit Index
articles_hidden.authors: Ellie Bastos Degobi; Víthor Rosa Franco; Marcos Jiménez
articles_hidden.abstract:
Conventional factor-analytic fit indices such as the CFI, TLI, RMSEA, and SRMR summarize 
discrepancies between observed and model-implied association structures, but they do not 
directly target the vanishing-tetrad constraints entailed by pure linear common-factor models. We 
evaluated a revised Tetrad Fit Index (TFI), which quantifies discrepancy between tetrads 
computed from the observed correlation matrix and from a purified model-implied correlation 
matrix. Across two simulation scenarios, we manipulated items per factor (8 or 16), 
factor-loading magnitude (low or medium), and sample size (200, 500, or 1,000). In the 
multidimensional scenario, the TFI selected the data-generating model in at least 99.1% of 
replications when compared with underfactored or overfactored alternatives. CFI, TLI, RMSEA, 
and SRMR performed well against the underfactored model but were substantially less accurate 
against the overfactored model. In the bifactor scenario, TFI accuracy ranged from 67.4% to 
99.3%, whereas conventional indices rarely selected the generating correlated-factor model. The 
TFI was only weakly to moderately associated with the other indices, which were highly 
intercorrelated. An empirical illustration with the Antinatalism Scale showed that the TFI 
favored the one-factor solution selected in the original study, whereas conventional indices 
favored a four-factor alternative. These findings support the TFI as a complementary index for 
comparing reflective factor models when researchers wish to evaluate common-cause covariance 
implications in addition to conventional global fit.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond Diagnosis: Shared and Distinct Cognitive Mechanisms Across Developmental Coordination Disorder, Autism, ADHD, and Dyslexia
articles_hidden.authors: Joanna Greer; Lucy H Eddy
articles_hidden.abstract: Background: Developmental Coordination Disorder (DCD) is a neurodevelopmental condition affecting sensorimotor skills in around 5% of the population. Increasingly, research recognises that DCD also impacts cognition and executive functioning (EF). Despite this, cognition in DCD is rarely studied alongside the neurodevelopmental conditions with which it most commonly co-occurs (autism, ADHD, and Dyslexia), despite each also showing cognitive challenges. Much of the literature also relies on binary diagnosed/typically developing comparisons, which cannot capture natural variability within and across these conditions. Methods: This cross-sectional online study used a trait-based approach to explore shared and distinct cognitive profiles across these conditions. Participants (342 adults aged 18–76 years) completed trait questionnaires for autism, ADHD, DCD, and Dyslexia, four cognitive measures (related to executive function and everyday memory), and two mental health and wellbeing questionnaires. Results: K-means cluster analysis and exploratory factor analysis both identified a profile in which DCD traits aligned closely with ADHD and Dyslexia traits, while autism traits remained relatively distinct. Linear regressions showed that DCD traits made small but consistent independent contributions to EF outcomes after accounting for ADHD, autism, and mental health, although ADHD traits typically explained more variance. Critically, difficulties rarely stemmed from a single trait profile - they were more often predicted by a combination of trait profiles. Conclusion: These findings suggest that the cognitive profile of DCD is best understood alongside ADHD and Dyslexia, with executive functioning difficulties frequently mapping onto multiple trait profiles. This has two implications for support: (i) DCD diagnostic criteria do not include cognitive difficulties, thus a diagnosis-led model risks missing additional support needs; and (ii) individuals whose difficulties span multiple trait profiles but do meet diagnostic thresholds, risk being excluded from support altogether.

articles_hidden.title: Adaptation and Validation of the Real Relationship Inventory–Therapist Form into Brazilian Portuguese
articles_hidden.authors: Lucas Remião Sampaio; Eduarda Rossatto de Bona; Manuela Bizzi Schvartzman; Amanda Pacini Teixeira C. Preta; Marcela Alves Sanseverino; Mirian Porciúncula Moreira Cuchiara; Christian Haag Kristensen
articles_hidden.abstract: The real relationship is a relevant component of the therapeutic relationship, yet validated instruments for assessing this construct remain scarce across cultural contexts. This study aimed to translate, culturally adapt, and validate the Real Relationship Inventory–Therapist Form (RRI-T) for use in Brazilian Portuguese, based on data from online psychotherapy. Participants were 142 therapists from different Brazilian states. The study included procedures for cross-cultural adaptation, content validity analysis, confirmatory factor analysis, internal consistency assessment, and convergent validity analysis with the Working Alliance Inventory–Short Revised–Therapist Version (WAI-SR-T). Results indicated satisfactory internal consistency for the total scale and for the realism and genuineness dimensions. Confirmatory factor analysis supported the theoretical two-factor model, with adequate fit indices. Moderate to strong positive correlations were observed between the RRI-T and the WAI-SR-T, suggesting partial convergence between related but distinct constructs. These findings provide satisfactory evidence of validity and reliability for the Brazilian Portuguese version of the RRI-T, particularly in the context of online psychotherapy.

articles_hidden.title: Protective Parenthood Factors in the Context of Sex Chromosome Trisomy: Supporting Social Behavioral Development through Reflective Functioning and Parental Behavior
articles_hidden.authors: Nienke Bouw; Hanna Swaab; Sophie van Rijn
articles_hidden.abstract:
Purpose. Children with Sex Chromosome Trisomies (SCT) are at elevated risk for early social and behavioral difficulties, which can place additional demands on parents. This prospective study examined behavioral development in young children with SCT, alongside parental reflective functioning and observed caregiving, to inform early family-centered support.
Methods. Participants included 107 children with SCT (1-7 years; M = 3.76, SD = 1.92) and 102 population-based controls (58 girls, 44 boys; M = 3.60, SD = 1.62). The SCT group comprised 33 girls with 47,XXX, 50 boys with 47,XXY, and 24 boys with 47,XYY. Most participants were White (83.7%), with others reporting Black/African American, Asian, Latino/Hispanic, Brazilian, or mixed ethnicity. Child social behavioral functioning was assessed via parent-report questionnaires (CBCL, SRS-2) and structured observations (ASIEP-3), while parental reflective functioning and behavior were measured with the Parent Development Interview and an observed Teaching Task.
Results. Children with SCT exhibited persistent social and behavioral vulnerabilities. Parental reflective functioning was comparable to controls, but parents of SCT children showed lower sensitivity and emotional regulation (η² = .06). Better parental regulation and positive affect predicted improved child outcomes (R² = .08 / 07). 
Conclusion. Early interventions should support parents in providing sensitive, well-regulated caregiving to promote resilience.

articles_hidden.title: Consciousness and emotions in non-human animals: Are laypeople more or less skeptical than experts?
articles_hidden.authors: Bastian Jaeger; Stefan Leach; Matthew Zipple
articles_hidden.abstract: Consciousness and the capacity to experience affective states, such as pain, pleasure, fear, and hunger (i.e., sentience) are seen as key determinants of an individual’s moral status, a view that is shared by scientists, philosophers, and laypeople. Whether (and which) non-human animals are believed to possess these capacities can therefore have important consequences for how they are treated. In this registered report (study design registration: https://doi.org/10.71240/lcyc.238674), we measured people’s attributions of consciousness and emotions to a diverse set of animals, testing whether laypeople overattribute (as suggested by research on anthropomorphizing) or underattribute these mental capacities to animals (as suggested by research on motivated mind denial). Animal consciousness and emotions are famously challenging to study. In the absence of an unambiguous benchmark against which people’s beliefs could be compared, we tested whether laypeople, a nationally representative sample of 600 U.S. participants, are more or less skeptical about animal consciousness and emotions than scientific experts, a sample of 100 behavioral ecologists, evolutionary biologists, and other animal researchers. We find that, compared to scientific experts, laypeople were less likely to attribute consciousness (-8 percentage points), and substantially less likely to attribute emotions (-21 percentage points) to non-human animals. Laypeople were on average more confident in their beliefs than scientific experts.

articles_hidden.title: Expectation-management cues modify delayed processing of unexpected words
articles_hidden.authors: Benjamin Adam Menashe; Oren Kadosh; Yoram Bonneh; Michal Ben-Shachar
articles_hidden.abstract: Mirative markers, linguistic elements that encode surprise (e.g., “surprisingly”), are widely used to manage readers’ expectations during sentence processing. In theory, mirative markers should prepare readers for an upcoming expectation violation, mitigating the additional processing costs of unexpected words. However, empirical evidence regarding their real-time efficacy remains limited and contradictory. To test whether these cues modulate real-time processing of subsequent unexpected words, we implemented a simultaneous eye-tracking and EEG paradigm. Thirty native Hebrew speakers read sentences containing an expected or unexpected target word, preceded by a mirative marker or a neutral marker. Processing effort was measured using oculomotor inhibition (OMI) duration and N400 amplitude. OMI is the involuntary suppression of microsaccades and eye blinks following stimulus presentation. Results revealed a clear predictability effect at the target word, with unexpected items eliciting longer OMI duration and greater N400 amplitude than expected items. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first known demonstration that OMI duration is sensitive to word predictability during reading. Additionally, results show that the presence of a mirative marker did not modify the response at the target word, but it did eliminate the “spillover” predictability effect at the subsequent word (T+1). These findings support a delayed modulation account of expectation management, where mirative markers modify delayed, but not immediate, processing costs of unexpected words. The results reconcile previous discrepancies regarding real-time and offline effects of expectation management and support a flexible version of the Uniform Information Density (UID) framework.

articles_hidden.title: Protocol of the CHILL 2.0 Study:  Optimizing, Explaining, and Sustaining Neuroticism Change
articles_hidden.authors: Wiebke Bleidorn; Rosalie Andrae; Peter Haehner; Christopher James Hopwood; Lina Hungerbuehler; Robert Tobias; Amanda Jo Wright
articles_hidden.abstract: This article describes the protocol of the Changing How I Live Life (CHILL) 2.0 project, a large-scale smartphone-based intervention program designed to optimize neuroticism-change interventions, test mechanisms of personality change, and examine the long-term consequences of intervention-induced neuroticism change. Building on findings from CHILL 1.0, CHILL 2.0 employs a fractional factorial randomized design.
