In this design, 1,020 participants are assigned to combinations of six theoretically derived strategy blocks comprising 16 evidence-informed intervention strategies and one attention-matched placebo control group. Participants complete repeated assessments of personality traits, neurotic affects, behaviors, and cognitions (ABCs), consequential life outcomes, peer reports, and mobile sensing before, during, and after a 6-week smartphone intervention, with follow-up extending to 1 year. An independent zero-intervention comparison cohort provides benchmark estimates of natural personality change, while a randomized booster substudy examines whether brief booster sessions enhance the long-term maintenance of intervention effects. By integrating intervention optimization, intensive longitudinal assessment, rigorous comparison groups, and long-term follow-up within a single research program, CHILL 2.0 is designed to identify the active ingredients of neuroticism interventions, test competing theories of personality change, and inform the development of more effective and personalized interventions to promote emotional stability.

articles_hidden.title: Capturing the temporal dynamics of personality in daily life: The Personality and Contextualized Experiences (PACE) Study
articles_hidden.authors: Anabel Büchner; Friedrich Martin Götz; Emorie D Beck; Lisa Shi Yun Li; Andrew Kwok Leung Yeung; Jessie Sun; Benjamin Hardin; Kai Tobias Horstmann
articles_hidden.abstract: Thoughts, feelings, and behaviors constantly change in everyday life. Dynamic personality approaches emphasize that these short-term changes are not only relevant for understanding how enduring personality patterns arise but are themselves central to what personality is. Although the growing use of the experience sampling method (ESM) has made it more feasible to apply such approaches, methodological challenges limit the inferences that can be drawn about temporal personality dynamics. This paper describes the rationale, procedure, and dataset of the Personality and Contextualized Experiences (PACE) Study, a large, multi- site ESM study that comprises 1,908 undergraduates (130,402 observations) across Canada, Germany, and the United States. Of these, 714 participants completed the entire study (baseline survey, ≥ 100 ESM surveys, and follow-up survey). The PACE Study aims to advance the study of personality dynamics by combining a large sample with several methodological features targeting key design and measurement aspects for accurately capturing and interpreting these dynamics. The features encompass an experimental comparison of two sampling designs, retrospective assessments of missed states, and a personalized assessment of situational information. The study further includes a newly developed global self-report questionnaire intended to capture aspects of people’s dynamic patterns of states without requiring ESM data.

articles_hidden.title: Construct Continuity With Limited Cross-Modal Agreement: Attention Networks in Immersive Virtual Reality
articles_hidden.authors: David Levi Tekampe; Anxhela Sulaj; Angelica Mendes; Philip Samuel Santangelo
articles_hidden.abstract:
Immersive virtual reality (VR) is increasingly used in cognitive assessment, yet it remains unclear whether established attention paradigms
retain their interpretability when translated from desktop presentation to head-mounted delivery. The present study examined whether atten-
tional effects measured with the Attention Network Test-Revised (ANT-R) are preserved in immersive VR when task-defining properties are
held constant across modalities. Seventy-nine adults (N = 79) completed a within-subject comparison of a desktop ANT-R and a task-matched
immersive VR implementation (ANT-VR; Meta Quest 3). Across modalities, stimuli, cueing logic, trial timing, conflict manipulations, and
scoring were matched. Trial-level reaction time (RT) and accuracy data were analysed using pre-specified mixed-effects models, and sec-
ondary psychometric analyses examined cross-modal agreement of participant-level effect scores. Canonical ANT-R effects were reproduced
across both modalities, especially in RT, including alerting benefits, orienting and validity effects, flanker conflict, location conflict, and dual-
conflict (flanker-by-location) integration. However, VR was associated with slower responses and slightly lower accuracy than desktop ad-
ministration, and modality moderated selected orienting-related and conflict-related contrasts. Secondary agreement analyses showed selec-
tive participant-level agreement between desktop and VR, with the strongest cross-modal agreement observed for flanker conflict, whereas
equivalence was not supported. These findings indicate that immersive VR preserves the major canonical ANT-R contrast pattern under task-
matched implementation while shifting baseline performance and moderating selected effect magnitudes. Immersive VR therefore supports
construct continuity of ANT-R performance but should be treated as a distinct measurement context rather than as psychometrically inter-
changeable with desktop administration.

articles_hidden.title: On the importance of effort perception in stroke care: From evidence to an ideal care pathway – An opinion paper
articles_hidden.authors: Maëlle Charonitis; Fabienne Collette; Benjamin Pageaux
articles_hidden.abstract:
Post-stroke rehabilitation has traditionally relied on objective assessments of motor and cognitive abilities. However, one crucial factor remains underestimated in current practice: the perception of effort, that is, the conscious experience of task intensity and difficulty. Effort perception is strongly influenced by internal states such as fatigue and pain, two symptoms frequently reported after stroke, even without major neurological deficits. While these symptoms are often treated separately, they converge into a shared experience: heightened perceived effort.
Recent literature suggests that both physical and mental fatigue, along with pain, increase perceived effort by impacting available resources and motivation to engage and persist in cognitive and physical tasks. This modulation can directly affect patient engagement and adherence to rehabilitation. When effort is perceived as disproportionate—even for a simple task—it may lead to reduced participation or withdrawal from the care plan. Conversely, a better understanding of effort perception could pave the way for personalized interventions that consider not only patients’ actual capacities but also their subjective experiences.
It is therefore urgent to consider the perception of effort as a clinical indicator in its own right—one that sits at the intersection of body, brain and lived experience. By integrating this dimension, research could better explain why some patients disengage from post-stroke care, despite good recovery potential and clinical practice could refine motivational strategies and therapeutic adherence models. The stakes are twofold: improving the understanding of the mechanisms underlying effort perception and harnessing it as a lever for optimizing post-stroke care trajectories.

articles_hidden.title: Forecasting next-day urge to drink without craving’s own history: an individualized analysis of responsive EMA in residential alcohol-use-disorder recovery
articles_hidden.authors: Bilal Khan; Dennis McChargue; Kimberly Tyler; Arthur Andrews; Lucy E. Napper; Therese Wang; Tzeyu Michaud; Kaeli Samson
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Just-in-time adaptive interventions (JITAIs) for substance-use recovery need decision inputs that anticipate risk, yet deployed systems rely largely on static rules. A published 30-day responsive ecological momentary assessment (rEMA) study followed adults recovering from severe alcohol use disorder in residential treatment. It collected five daily self-report items: urge to drink, affect intensity, stress, alcohol use, and importance of Alcoholics Anonymous engagement. Adherence and interest in prompt-based support were high. Whether these sparse reports carry a short-horizon forecasting signal was untested.

Methods: We ran a retrospective, individualized forecasting analysis of that cohort (61 enrolled; 53 analytic). Each forecast answers one question: issued daily at 15:30, will the participant’s next 24 hours contain any reported urge to drink (a positive day), or remain urge-free (a negative day)? Rolling-origin ordinary least squares models were fit within each participant, on data available at forecast time, after a burn-in of 10 days. Three pre-specified feature sets decompose the signal: FULL (all five items plus time structure), CONTEXT (urge history withheld), and AR (urge history alone). Forecasts were scored against a per-participant base-rate baseline, with participant-level bootstrap intervals and Wilcoxon tests.

Results: We scored 1,013 participant-days. The cohort summary curves gave mean AUCs of 0.66 (95% CI 0.589 to 0.730) for CONTEXT and 0.62 (0.560 to 0.673) for FULL. Per-participant AUCs exceeded chance in both arms (p = 0.0018 and 0.0077). AR’s cohort summary curve gave 0.56 (0.504 to 0.630); its per-participant AUCs did not exceed chance (p = 0.24). At the operating point, CONTEXT raised recall to 0.619 against the baseline’s 0.366; the false-positive rate did not differ (0.351 versus 0.355). No between-arm difference was significant within participants.

Conclusion: In this cohort, next-day urge to drink was forecastable above chance from sparse rEMA, even with the urge item’s own history withheld. We found no evidence that this history adds signal beyond the other items. These results indicate which items a JITAI trigger model should monitor, groundwork for prospective validation. We do not model drinking or relapse.

articles_hidden.title: An Expressivist Account of Moral Responsibility
articles_hidden.authors: Kiichi INARIMORI; Yugo MAEDA; Shintaro Takahashi; Kengo Miyazono
articles_hidden.abstract: Moral expressivism holds that moral statements fundamentally express non-doxastic attitudes (e.g., emotions or desires) rather than doxastic attitudes (e.g., beliefs) that correspond to objective and descriptive contents. This paper applies expressivism to responsibility statements and proposes Retributive Responsibility Expressivism. According to this account, responsibility statements such as “X deserves to be punished for doing Y” fundamentally express a non-doxastic attitude—specifically, our retributive desire for X to be punished. Across two empirical studies focusing on laypeople’s linguistic intuitions, we adopt the methodology of Moorean absurdities to evaluate this expressivist account. In line with expressivist predictions, participants systematically judged first-person Moorean responsibility sentences (e.g., “X deserves to be punished, but I do not want X to be punished”) as semantically infelicitous, whereas third-person versions were judged as making sense. Furthermore, restricting sentences to an autocentric interpretation markedly strengthened this perceived infelicity. These results provide novel empirical support for an expressivist semantics of moral responsibility. Finally, we argue that accepting an expressivist account of moral responsibility—depending on the specific version (e.g., pure vs. hybrid)—calls for reconsidering the traditional role of responsibility judgments in the free will debate.

articles_hidden.title: Locating Gambling Severity Within Polysubstance Involvement: The Specific Role of Methamphetamine in 9,421 Adults Entering Treatment
articles_hidden.authors: Georgia Murphy; Matthew Browne; Alex M T Russell
articles_hidden.abstract: Gambling problems are common among people entering alcohol and other drug (AOD) treatment, yet they are easily missed and the substance-use patterns that mark them are poorly understood. Population research ties gambling to alcohol, a framing that may not hold in treatment populations where involvement is severe and mixed, and evidence points more consistently to stimulants. Using intake data from 9,421 adults entering Australian AOD treatment who reported past-year gambling, we asked whether gambling severity (PGSI) tracks broader non-alcohol polysubstance involvement, particular substances within it, or alcohol. Confirmatory factor analysis of ten WHO-ASSIST severity indicators identified a single non-alcohol polysubstance dimension, with alcohol loading only weakly and standing apart. Gambling severity was modelled on that dimension, substance-specific severity, and alcohol severity together, using ordinal logistic regression. The clearest and most specific association was with high-severity methamphetamine use (OR ≈ 3.7), which held across gambling-severity thresholds in non-proportional odds models. The polysubstance dimension was independently but more modestly associated; high-severity alcohol was not once other involvement was accounted for. Patterns beyond methamphetamine largely reflected general polysubstance load rather than distinct effects. Gambling severity in this cohort was not primarily alcohol-centred, and was not explained uniformly by polysubstance involvement. It concentrated around high-severity methamphetamine use within a broader non-alcohol context. Routine gambling screening remains warranted, with particular attention to clients presenting with high-severity methamphetamine use and complex polysubstance profiles.

articles_hidden.title: Non-normal Latent Traits and Parameter Estimation in the Bifactor Graded Response Model
articles_hidden.authors: Jujia Li; Chunhua Cao; Nana Kim; Wenchao Ma
articles_hidden.abstract: Item response theory (IRT) models usually assume that latent traits follow normal distributions. Nonetheless, violations of the normality assumption are not uncommon in psychology and psychiatry. While several studies have investigated the impact of non-normality on parameter estimation for some IRT models, bifactor models for polytomous data have been largely excluded despite their increasing popularity in psychology and education. Existing findings on other IRT models may not apply to bifactor models because of their unique characteristics. In this study, we examined the impact of latent trait non-normality on parameter estimation in the bifactor graded response model using a simulation study. The results indicate that (1) general-factor non-normality primarily affected item parameter estimates associated with the general factor but not specific factors, (2) specific-factor non-normality showed smaller and more localized effects, primarily on bias in specific-factor discrimination and intercept estimates; and (3) despite the misspecification of latent trait priors, maximum a posteriori estimates of latent traits tend to be more stable than the maximum likelihood estimates. Implications of the findings are discussed.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond Diagnosis: A Scoping Review of Machine Learning and NLP for Multilevel Mental Health Factors in Population Crises
articles_hidden.authors: Ridwan Monjur; NUR NASUHA BINTI MOHD DAUD; Siti Hafiza Hafiza Abd Hamid
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Natural disasters, pandemics, armed conflict, and economic upheaval inflict lasting harm on mental wellbeing, yet what determines who recovers and who deteriorates remains poorly understood across crisis types.

Objectives: This review maps how crisis exposure shapes wellbeing across four crisis typologies, two surveillance modes (NLP-based and survey/administrative), and three impact directions (favorable, adverse, or mixed).

Eligibility criteria: Peer-reviewed journal articles and conference papers published in English between 2016 and 2026, applying machine learning, NLP, or deep learning methods to a population exposed to one of the four crisis typologies, and reporting at least one measurable mental health outcome.

Sources of evidence: PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, Scopus, and IEEE Xplore, supplemented by forward and backward citation searching and targeted keyword searches.

Charting methods: Factors were charted using the WHO Commission on Social Determinants of Health framework, adapted for the health system where the framework’s coverage is thinnest. They were sorted into tiers, subgroups, and subdimensions with maximum possible fidelity to the original framework.

Results: Across 338 codeable determinants, Intermediary Determinants, particularly psychosocial and behavioral-biological factors, accounted for two-thirds of coded determinants, while NLP-based methods proved most effective at capturing structural and contextual signals (e.g., governance, discourse-based constructs) rather than the clinical burden measures that dominate closer to the individual. Favorable, protective constructs were both rarer and less computationally detected than adverse ones, concentrating almost entirely in mastery, self-concept, coping, and social capital. Forty-five factors were set aside as Outcome Measures because they described prior symptoms, diagnoses, or the study's own outcome construct, with 8 being circular with the study's stated target. Fewer studies examined economic downturns, and conflict studies had almost no NLP presence.

Conclusions: These findings demonstrate this field has matured methodologically in adverse detection but remains structurally limited in reach. This is most evident in armed conflict contexts and in the surveillance of protective, resilience-oriented signals, highlighting the need for digital phenotyping, expanded NLP coverage, and wider adoption of explainable AI methods.

articles_hidden.title: From Concept to Classroom: Teachers Implementing Mindfulness-based Interventions
articles_hidden.authors: Mary L. Phan; Tyler L Renshaw; Melanie M. Domenech Rodríguez; Maggie Chan; Erik J. Reinbergs; Christopher Liang; Stephanie M. Hernandez; Natascha Meyer-Pérez; Amanda Paur; Ginny Watts
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objectives: This study evaluated a collaboratively developed, teacher-implemented mindfulness-based intervention (MBI) targeting teacher stress and coping and students’ prosocial behavior. The study also examined implementation fidelity, social validity, and sustainment.

Methods: Six elementary school teachers in grades 1–3 participated in a single-case multiple-baseline design across participants. Teachers implemented a four-week MBI consisting of daily teacher self-practice and twice-daily classroom mindfulness exercises. Daily measures assessed teacher stress and coping and classroom academic engagement, respectful behavior, and disruptive behavior. Outcomes were evaluated through visual analysis, descriptive statistics, and Non-overlap of All Pairs (NAP) and Improvement Rate Difference (IRD). Fidelity, social validity, and follow-up outcomes through two months post-intervention were also assessed.

Results: Functional relations were not consistently demonstrated across teachers. However, several teachers showed reduced stress and improved coping, while several classrooms showed increased academic engagement and respectful behavior and reduced disruptive behavior. Across outcomes, NAP ranged from .36 to 1.00 and IRD from .28 to 1.00. Teachers reported high social validity, and fidelity was high (self-report: M = 98.33%; observed: M = 93.33%).

Conclusions: Findings support the feasibility and acceptability of brief, teacher-implemented MBIs. Although functional relations were inconsistent, individual patterns suggest potential benefits for teacher coping and classroom behavior. Flexible, context-responsive implementation may support sustained use in schools.

articles_hidden.title: How Many Factors Underlie the WAIS-5? Evidence From the Australian and New Zealand Standardization Sample.
articles_hidden.authors: Paul Skirrow
articles_hidden.abstract:
The latent structure of the Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale-Fifth Edition (WAIS-5) is the subject of recent psychometric debate. Although the publisher's initial confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) supported a theoretically derived five-factor model, a recent independent evaluation of the US standardisation sample found that complementary exploratory and confirmatory analyses favoured a hierarchical four-factor representation. The present study examined whether these findings could be independently replicated using the published WAIS-5 Australasian standardisation sample (N = 677).
Exploratory factor analyses were conducted using principal axis factoring with Promax rotation, followed by Schmid-Leiman transformation and model-based reliability and dimensionality analyses. Confirmatory analyses compared competing oblique, higher-order, and bifactor models evaluated in the US sample.
Factor-retention procedures did not support the proposed five-factor structure. Exploratory analyses consistently recovered four interpretable factors corresponding to Verbal Comprehension, Perceptual Reasoning, Working Memory, and Processing Speed, with Visual Spatial and Fluid Reasoning failing to emerge as distinct latent constructs. Confirmatory analyses identified the same higher-order (4h3) and bifactor (4b3) models as the preferred representations of the data. Model-based reliability analyses indicated a dominant general factor with smaller contributions from the broad cognitive abilities. Despite modest differences in model parameters, the central conclusions closely replicated those of the US sample.

articles_hidden.title: Protocol for a Multi-method Investigation of Moderators of Emotion Regulation in Youth
articles_hidden.authors: Ian Matthew Raugh; Kaitlyn Capano; Diep Nguyen; Gabrielle Reynolds; Allison H. MacNeil; Tovah M Cowan; Jai Shah; Manuela Ferrari
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background
A wide range of psychiatric populations experience difficulties with emotion regulation, including knowing when to regulate, choosing adaptive strategies, and applying selected strategies effectively. To address these challenges, it is important to identify moderators of emotion regulation processes that can be targeted in therapeutic interventions. Although certain moderators, such as mindfulness and cognitive functioning, are relatively well established in the psychiatric literature, cultural background and psychosocial context can be important avenues for investigation.
Aims
This planned project aims to investigate mindfulness, cognitive functioning, cultural background, and context as moderators of emotion regulation processes.
Methods
Data will be collected in two samples, a pilot study (completed April 2026) to validate a novel emotion regulation task and a sample of 100 community members. The full study procedures will include a spontaneous emotion regulation task, ecological momentary assessment, brief mindfulness practices, and a cognitive task across a three-week protocol. The task will assess when people choose to regulate, what strategies they select, and how effectively they implement those strategies. Ecological momentary assessment will be used to assess regulatory processes and relevant moderators in daily life. Optional qualitative interviews will be conducted with a subset of participants.
Results
Results are expected to specify how mindfulness components, cognitive domains, cultural background, and other contextual variables influence specific emotion regulation processes.
Conclusions
The planned research adopts an innovative approach consisting of multiple complementary methods. Through doing so, we aim to offer valuable insights into moderators of emotion regulation that can be targeted in clinical interventions.

articles_hidden.title: Reverse Engineering Depression: Data-Driven Discovery of Causal Dynamical Models
articles_hidden.authors: Sophie Engels; Joshua Curtiss
articles_hidden.abstract: Recent research focusing on formal models of psychiatric disorders has provided a basis for understanding mechanistic relationships between symptoms. Using a complex systems approach, dynamical systems and statistical methods can be used to analyze the interacting parts of the whole psychological framework. Nonlinear differential equations have been of particular interest as they lend themselves well to exploring how symptoms change over time, discovering tipping points, or characterizing attractor states. Thus far, research of this kind has focused primarily on a priori definitions of these disorders using simulated data. While these simulated models have been extremely insightful for discerning the fundamentals of psychological phenomena, much less research has been devoted to aligning these systems with real-world data. We apply a data-driven approach, which allows researchers to deduce systems of differential equations from psychological datasets. We exemplify this method using a theoretically defined model for depression and a dataset measuring passive sensor information, e-communication data, and psychological symptom assessments. In this article, we demonstrate how these variables can be integrated into the differential equation discovery framework and methods for parameterizing nomothetic or idiographic models for the disorder. Overall, we found that empirically determined equations aligned well with our predefined theory of depression, suggesting that a combined empirical and theoretical approach may complement each other in further model development. We also found that personalization offered incremental benefit over global models, suggesting that an idiographic or combined idio-nomo approach may improve further formal model advancement by more explicitly considering individual differences in model parameterization.

articles_hidden.title: Knowing what to look for strengthens memory associations in contextual cuing
articles_hidden.authors: Feifei Zhao; Markus Conci
articles_hidden.abstract: In visual search, attentional guidance towards a target can be improved by learning the association between the target location and its surrounding, repeatedly encountered search context, which in turn expedites target detection (contextual cuing). But can these learned contextual cues also predict specific target identities? The current study explored this question using real-world images of objects as search items. Experiment 1 established a baseline for contextual cuing by specifying one single, to-be-detected target object throughout the entire experiment, which resulted in a small but reliable contextual cuing benefit in search latencies. Experiment 2 then introduced 24 possible target objects that would all appear within a given block on separate trials. The results showed enhanced contextual cuing with multiple, variable targets, and an even larger cuing effect when the repeated contexts were consistently associated with specific target identities. Experiment 3 replicated these findings both in behavioral and oculomotor measures: Contextual cuing was expedited both during early visual search associated with attentional guidance (i.e. before target detection) and at later stages of processing during target identification (i.e. after locating the target). These results suggest that repeated contexts can cue not only where to look but also what to look for – with knowledge about both the target location and its identity enhancing visual search by guiding attention more efficiently while also facilitating the subsequent identification of the target.

articles_hidden.title: Questionable prospective effects between maternal health literacy, psychological empowerment, and health-promoting behaviors among pregnant women: A reanalysis of Chen et al. (2026)
articles_hidden.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen; Bo Melin; Marika Melin
articles_hidden.abstract: Chen et al. examined temporal relations among maternal health literacy, psychological empowerment, and health-promoting behaviors and interpreted their findings as evidence of reciprocal longitudinal influences. However, significant cross-lagged coefficients do not necessarily demonstrate true prospective effects, as such estimates may arise from methodological and statistical artifacts. Using simulated data constructed to match the sample size and correlation matrix reported by Chen et al., we assessed the stability of the reported findings across several analytically plausible models. The results differed markedly depending on the specification employed. Some models suggested positive longitudinal effects, whereas others indicated negative or non-significant associations. After combining all estimates using meta-analytic methods, no overall effect reached statistical significance. These findings indicate that the conclusions drawn by Chen et al. should be interpreted with caution and that the reported cross-lagged associations may not reflect genuine prospective influence. In accordance with multiverse analytic principles, researchers should routinely evaluate multiple reasonable model specifications and synthesize evidence across models before drawing substantive conclusions.

articles_hidden.title: Joint Peer Victimization–Perpetration Trajectories and Cortical Thinning in Early Adolescence
articles_hidden.authors: Hamshitha Sasidhar; Alva Tang; Leehyun Yoon
articles_hidden.abstract:
Importance: Peer victimization and perpetration often co-occur and are associated with adverse psychosocial outcomes, but whether their joint temporal patterns are associated with adolescent brain development is unknown.
Objective: To examine whether joint developmental trajectories of peer victimization and perpetration are associated with cortical thinning in social-affective brain regions during early adolescence.
Design: Longitudinal cohort study using 2 years of follow-up data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study, collected from 2018 to 2022 and analyzed from 2024 to 2026.
Setting: The ABCD Study across 21 US research sites.
Participants: Trajectory analyses included 8792 adolescents with peer experience data from at least 2 assessments; cortical thickness analyses included 2308 adolescents with MRI data at both visits.
Exposures: Joint trajectories of self-reported peer victimization and perpetration assessed at the 2-, 3-, and 4-year follow-ups, spanning ages 11 to 14 years.
Main Outcomes and Measures: Two-year change in MRI-derived cortical thickness across 7 prespecified social-affective brain regions between the 2- and 4-year follow-ups.
Results: Longitudinal clustering (mean [SD] age, 12.08 [0.66] years; 4250 girls [48.3%]) identified 4 joint trajectories: stably low (62%), increasing (24%), decreasing (10%), and persistently high (4%) in both victimization and perpetration. In cortical thickness analyses (mean [SD] age, 11.98 [0.64] years; 1067 girls [46.2%]), no trajectory-group differences survived correction. Exploratory sex-moderation analyses identified persistently high versus stably low differences in the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex and lateral orbitofrontal cortex. Compared with the stably low group, the persistently high group showed little to no dorsal anterior cingulate cortex thinning among boys (β = 0.030; 95% CI, 0.012 to 0.048; P = .001) and greater lateral orbitofrontal cortex thinning among girls (β = −0.029; 95% CI, −0.055 to −0.002; P = .033).
Conclusions and Relevance: Peer victimization and perpetration generally co-occurred and changed together over time in this US adolescent cohort. Exploratory findings suggested that persistently high, co-occurring victimization and perpetration may be neurodevelopmentally relevant, with sex-specific patterns in cortical regions implicated in threat detection, behavioral adaptation, and learning from negative consequences. These findings may inform prevention and early intervention efforts for adolescents persistently embedded in negative peer environments.

articles_hidden.title: Empowering Educators: Designing and Integrating Mindfulness-based Interventions in the Classroom
articles_hidden.authors: Mary L. Phan; Tyler L Renshaw; Melanie M. Domenech Rodríguez; Maggie Chan; Erik J. Reinbergs; Christopher Liang; Amanda Paur; Gretchen Klinger; Kimberly Mills; Kiana Livingston
articles_hidden.abstract: Teacher stress and burnout can affect teacher well-being, classroom functioning, and student outcomes, yet school-based mindfulness interventions (MBIs) may be difficult to sustain without attention to feasibility, social validity, and cultural and contextual fit. Twelve elementary teachers collaborated in the development and adaptation of an MBI for teacher self-practice and classroom implementation. Guided by community-based participatory research principles and the Making Optimal Decisions for Intervention Flexibility during Implementation (MODIFI) framework, the study used a convergent mixed-methods design involving a 2-hour mindfulness training, qualitative interviews, and the Usage Rating Profile–Intervention Revised (URP-IR). Qualitative data were analyzed for implementation barriers, facilitators, and cultural adaptations, while URP-IR subscale scores were summarized descriptively. Teachers reported stress related to workload, limited time, administrative demands, and classroom behavioral needs, but viewed mindfulness as beneficial and feasible when practices were brief, flexible, and integrated into routines. Adaptations addressed language, developmental appropriateness, delivery format, student autonomy, and classroom context. Quantitative findings showed Acceptability (M = 5.5) and Feasibility (M = 5.7), with lower System Support (M = 3.3). Teacher feedback informed audio-guided options, visual practices, developmentally appropriate scripts, and autonomy-supportive language. Findings suggest that engaging teachers as co-designers may strengthen intervention fit, social validity, and implementation readiness.

articles_hidden.title: Where Attention Goes When Rules Change: Eye-Tracking Signatures of Feedback-Driven Rule Reconfiguration and Attentional-Set Stabilisation
articles_hidden.authors: David Levi Tekampe; Angelica Mendes; Katarzyna Bobrowicz; Christine Schiltz; Philip Samuel Santangelo
articles_hidden.abstract:
Cognitive flexibility requires the formation, maintenance, and updating of attentional sets as task contingencies change. Prior Wisconsin-style
eye-tracking studies have primarily examined area-of-interest measures or pupillometry, leaving unclear whether global trial-level gaze in-
dices capture feedback-informed rule reconfiguration and subsequent attentional-set stabilisation. We examined fixation count, total fixation
duration, saccade count, and gaze dispersion in a computerised Wisconsin-style card-sorting task. Eye-tracking analyses included 84 adults
contributing up to 4,711 trials. Participants completed 60 trials organised into deterministic 10-trial blocks defined by colour, shape, or num-
ber, and trial-level gaze and behavioural outcomes were analysed using mixed-effects models. Feedback-driven reconfiguration was examined
by comparing the first trial following change-signalling negative feedback with the immediately preceding pre-feedback objective-change
trial, restricted to transitions in which the objective-change response was incorrect. Following negative feedback, participants showed more
fixations, longer total fixation duration, more saccades, and greater gaze dispersion. Across positions 3–10 of each rule block, later positions
were characterised by fewer fixations, fewer saccades, lower gaze dispersion, and faster correct responses, whereas total fixation duration did
not decrease reliably. Greater whole-decision-period visual sampling was associated with slower correct responses, while higher saccade
count, greater gaze dispersion, and longer total fixation duration were associated with lower accuracy. These findings indicate that global eye-
movement indices distinguish feedback-informed rule reconfiguration from subsequent attentional-set stabilisation while providing process-
level information beyond behavioural performance alone.

articles_hidden.title: Monocular stereopsis, pinholes, and the perils of classroom theorizing:  A response to McIntosh (2025).
articles_hidden.authors: Dhanraj Vishwanath
articles_hidden.abstract: Monocular stereopsis is a compelling perceptual effect wherein viewing a picture of a 3-dimensional scene with one eye through an aperture generates a perceptual impression of depth similar to binocular stereopsis. Here I provide a critique of a recently published report on the topic in the journal i-Perception (McIntosh, 2025).  In the report, the author claims to adjudicate on explanations of the monocular stereopsis effect and the phenomenology of stereopsis more broadly construed.  The author suggests, based on an informal test comparing pinhole and aperture viewing of a picture during a fifteen-minute classroom lecture break, that the monocular-aperture effect is best explained by a 100-year-old description of the phenomenon. I show that McIntosh’s report reveals a lack of understanding of the modern empirical facts and theoretical concepts relevant to this scientific debate and neglects the rudimentary demands of conducting an interpretable perceptual test.

articles_hidden.title: Changes in passion among baseball fans during and between seasons: A closer look at the seasonal attenuation of passion (SAP) hypothesis
articles_hidden.authors: Benjamin J. I. Schellenberg; Jeremie Verner-Filion; Patrick Gaudreau; Nicole Robak
articles_hidden.abstract: People often feel passionate toward meaningful activities in their lives, but this passion can change over time by increasing, decreasing or, in extreme cases, disappearing entirely. Recently, the seasonal attenuation of passion (SAP) hypothesis was proposed to help explain the dynamic nature of passion. The SAP hypothesis predicts that, with seasonal activities, passion tends to decrease within a season but increase between seasons. In this research, we tested this hypothesis and examined several mechanisms that may explain fluctuations in passion over time. Baseball fans (N = 1,254) completed four online surveys throughout the 2023 Major League Baseball season (Times 1-3) and at the start of the 2024 season (Time 4). Each survey assessed indices of passion (harmonious passion, obsessive passion, passion criteria) along with potential mechanisms of change, such as savoring, perceptions of team performance, fan experiences, and team satisfaction. Using piecewise growth modeling, our results showed that (a) average levels of all indices of passion declined throughout the 2023 season, (b) there was very little change in passion between the end of the 2023 MLB season and the start of the 2024 MLB season, and (c) savoring was the most consistent predictor of passion at each time point, such that fans who reported greater savoring also reported greater passion. These results partially support the SAP hypothesis and revealed that people may be able to keep their passion alive by savoring positive experiences in their activity.

articles_hidden.title: Flexible transfer of item-specific cognitive control: From Stroop to visual search
articles_hidden.authors: Xiaojin Ma; Julie Bugg; Richard A. Abrams
articles_hidden.abstract: When repeatedly encountering the same challenge, we learn environmental regularities that predict its reoccurrence and use them to prepare for future encounters. For example, the red color of a stop sign may automatically trigger caution. Past research shows such associative learning flexibly regulates cognitive control and generalizes to similar tasks. A key open question is whether learned control transfers to novel challenges with distinct control demands, and whether such transfer reflects perceptual, feature-based priming or higher-level, goal-based control adaptation. The present study addressed these questions by examining whether cognitive control learned in a Stroop task, that requires information dimension selection, transfers to spatial location selection in visual search. Participants learned item-specific control in a Stroop color-naming task where mostly incongruent colors signaled higher control demands than mostly congruent colors. In a subsequent visual search task, those colors no longer signaled control demands and instead appeared as task-irrelevant distractors while participants searched for a target. This reversal in the roles of the colors enabled a resolution of whether learned control engages feature-based priming or goal-based adaptation. The results support the latter, showing that learned control successfully transferred and adapted to the new goal, such that distractors in the colors previously associated with heightened control demands were more effectively ignored than those associated with relaxed control demands. This cross-task transfer from non-spatial to spatial attentional selection demonstrates a remarkable flexibility of item-specific cognitive control, whereby goal-based adaptation supports generalization across dissimilar contexts, adjustment to reversed stimulus roles, and resolution of novel challenges.

articles_hidden.title: Inclusion Bayes Factors for Conditional Independence in Latent Network Modeling
articles_hidden.authors: Fatih Ozkan
articles_hidden.abstract: The latent network model (LNM) embeds a Gaussian graphical model on the latent variables of a confirmatory factor model, which allows exploratory analysis of conditional independence relations among constructs while accounting for measurement error. Current LNM practice recovers the latent network by penalized estimation or stepwise significance testing, procedures that cannot distinguish absence of evidence from evidence of absence. We develop a Bayesian latent network model (BLNM) that places a prior on the latent network structure and quantifies the evidence for each edge with inclusion Bayes factors. Because latent systems are small, the full structure space (2^(M(M-1)/2) structures for M latent variables) can be enumerated, so posterior structure probabilities and inclusion Bayes factors are computed exactly from per-structure marginal likelihoods, with an analytically marginalized likelihood and a validated Laplace-screening scheme for larger M. Two empirical illustrations recover graded evidence in both directions: in the Holzinger–Swineford data, the textual–speed latent edge receives positive evidence of conditional independence (BF_01=2.5) where the likelihood-ratio test is merely nonsignificant (p=.32); in the Big Five (bfi) data, Openness is conditionally independent of Agreeableness and Neuroticism (BF_01=7.4 and 6.0) given the remaining traits. A simulation study shows that posterior inclusion probabilities are calibrated, evidence for truly absent edges accumulates at the √N rate, and a naive two-step alternative in which a Bayesian graphical model is fitted to factor scores produces decisive false evidence for truly absent edges at rates that fail to diminish with sample size and that approach 50% when measurement is unreliable.

articles_hidden.title: Retained Activity and Psychological Capital in Ukrainian Academic Populations, 2024
articles_hidden.authors: Volodymyr Evheniiovych Momot; Viktoriia Sokolova
articles_hidden.abstract:
Research on Ukrainian higher education under war has documented institutional adaptation in detail, but individual psychological resources remain largely unmeasured, and where activity appears as a coping factor, its content is rarely distinguished from its presence.

This study reports psychological capital (PCQ-24) across three independent Ukrainian academic collections in 2024 (N = 240): faculty at a private university in Dnipro (N = 76), students at the same university (N = 61), and students at two state universities in front-line Zaporizhzhia (N = 103).

Retained activity predicted psychological capital in every sample; geography and demography did not. The employment contrast replicated in two independent student collections under different assignment procedures (g = +0.62, 95% CI [+0.05,+1.23]; g = +1.43). Among faculty, self-rated research activity predicted psychological capital (b = +0.40, p < .0001, R² = 0.31). Location, displacement, gender and age showed no large effects, with Bayes factors weakly supporting the null (BF₀₁ = 2.4–2.9); displacement, available here at individual level, replicated a null reported in earlier work on this population.

Four structural analyses characterise the construct. Profile analysis shows samples differing in elevation rather than shape (variance ratio 58:1). Clustering, blind to all covariates, yields a stable partition (88%) falling along research activity (p = .0006) rather than demography. Network modelling identifies Hope as most central — robustly among students (96–99% of resamples), contested with self-efficacy among faculty (52%). Mokken scaling reveals a reproducible difficulty gradient (ρ = .67–.82) in which Resilience is retained longest and Optimism relinquished first, a possible early depletion marker.

A further claim, more tentative, concerns which activity qualifies. Conservation of Resources holds that investment implies return, predicting that only activity reproducing what was invested generates resource. Two contrasts support this: volunteering dropped out when controlled against research activity (p = .20), and among equally employed students those working in their field scored higher (g = 0.64, p = .023), though this did not survive multivariate control at n = 58. Students holding employment and a merit stipend scored lower than employed non-stipend holders (g = −0.48; BF₀₁ = 0.96), an effect absent among non-working students. These contrasts were formulated after inspecting the data and rest on the weakest links in the chain.

At the institutional level, a single case documents a university resuming teaching eighteen days after suspension in February 2022, enabled by organisational competence built for a different crisis. We propose a refinement to Hobfoll's resource caravan passageways: a passageway defines what is possible but does not itself produce passage through it.

Magnitudes varied across replications (g = 0.62–1.43); the pooled value should not be interpreted.

articles_hidden.title: Construct Continuity With Limited Cross-Modal Agreement: Attention Networks in Immersive Virtual Reality
articles_hidden.authors: David Levi Tekampe; Anxhela Sulaj; Angelica Mendes; Philip Samuel Santangelo
articles_hidden.abstract:
Immersive virtual reality (VR) is increasingly used in cognitive assessment, yet it remains unclear whether established attention paradigms
retain their interpretability when translated from desktop presentation to head-mounted delivery. The present study examined whether atten-
tional effects measured with the Attention Network Test-Revised (ANT-R) are preserved in immersive VR when task-defining properties are
held constant across modalities. Seventy-nine adults (N = 79) completed a within-subject comparison of a desktop ANT-R and a task-matched
immersive VR implementation (ANT-VR; Meta Quest 3). Across modalities, stimuli, cueing logic, trial timing, conflict manipulations, and
scoring were matched. Trial-level reaction time (RT) and accuracy data were analysed using pre-specified mixed-effects models, and sec-
ondary psychometric analyses examined cross-modal agreement of participant-level effect scores. Canonical ANT-R effects were reproduced
across both modalities, especially in RT, including alerting benefits, orienting and validity effects, flanker conflict, location conflict, and dual-
conflict (flanker-by-location) integration. However, VR was associated with slower responses and slightly lower accuracy than desktop ad-
ministration, and modality moderated selected orienting-related and conflict-related contrasts. Secondary agreement analyses showed selec-
tive participant-level agreement between desktop and VR, with the strongest cross-modal agreement observed for flanker conflict, whereas
equivalence was not supported. These findings indicate that immersive VR preserves the major canonical ANT-R contrast pattern under task-
matched implementation while shifting baseline performance and moderating selected effect magnitudes. Immersive VR therefore supports
construct continuity of ANT-R performance but should be treated as a distinct measurement context rather than as psychometrically inter-
changeable with desktop administration.

articles_hidden.title: Effects of Adverse Childhood Experiences on Severe Mental Health Conditions in Early Adulthood: A Twin Study
articles_hidden.authors: Xinyu Meng; Giacomo Bignardi; Jessie Baldwin; Andrea Danese; Thalia Catherine Eley; Chloe Chung Yi Wong; Tom McAdams
articles_hidden.abstract:
Importance Adverse childhood experiences are associated with later severe mental health conditions, but the extent to which these associations reflect a causal effect of adversity rather than confounding remains unclear. 
Objective To test whether within-twin-pair differences in reported adverse childhood experiences predict differences in severe mental health conditions in early adulthood, and to decompose covariation between adverse childhood experiences and severe mental health conditions into genetic and environmental components.
Design Setting and Participants This study used data from the Twins Early Development Study, a population-based cohort of twins born in England and Wales (1994-1996), with assessments at ages 12, 14, 16, 21, and 26. Within-twin-pair regression and bivariate biometric twin models were used to distinguish potential causal effects from familial confounding.
Exposures Childhood maltreatment (abuse and neglect, retrospective, ages 21 and 26) and peer victimization (bullying, prospective, ages 12, 14, 16).
Main Outcomes and Measures Seventeen measures of severe mental health conditions spanning psychosis-spectrum symptoms, (hypo)manic symptoms, self-harm and suicidal behaviour, and reported diagnoses.
Results Outcomes were assessed at ages 21 (13,794 individuals) and 26 (11,436 individuals). After false discovery rate correction, childhood maltreatment was associated with all 17 outcomes at the population level and peer victimization with 16. Monozygotic within-pair models were estimable for 14 outcomes. All 14 maltreatment associations remained significant, with pooled symptom estimates attenuating by 21% (0.30 to 0.24) and pooled odds ratios of 1.85 vs 1.95 at the population level. Only 2 peer victimization associations remained (paranoia and hallucinations at age 21), with attenuation of 53% (0.20 to 0.09) and pooled odds ratios of 1.18 vs 1.59. Bivariate biometric twin models supported the within-pair findings while also demonstrating that all covariances were partially attributable to shared genetic liability.
Conclusions and Relevance Associations between adverse childhood experiences and severe mental health conditions in young adulthood reflected both shared genetic liability and potential causal effects. Childhood maltreatment showed more persistent within-pair associations than peer victimization, consistent with a greater contribution of  non-shared environmental effects. Findings highlight childhood maltreatment as a potentially modifiable pathway to severe psychopathology, supporting the importance of trauma-informed care.

articles_hidden.title: I-ROAR-Word: Validity and reliability of an Italian online screener for single-word reading
articles_hidden.authors: Elisa Bassoli; Giuditta Smith; Yagmur Ozturk; Emily ARTEAGA GARCIA; Wanjing Anya Ma; Jason D. Yeatman; Marilina Mastrogiuseppe; Sendy Caffarra
articles_hidden.abstract:
Large-scale screening of reading abilities is crucial to track learning trajectories and identify learning difficulties early on, but resource constraints and heterogeneity of training make successful implementation challenging. For the present study, we validated an online, self-administered, automated, and open-access screener for Italian single-word reading (I-ROAR-Word).
I-ROAR-Word and standardized measures of Italian reading ability, vocabulary, and non-verbal intelligence were administered to 1045 children aged 6-11 (females = 543, mean age = 8.81) recruited in northern Italy (30% bilinguals, of which 85% born in Italy). The most represented ethnicities were White, Arab, and Black/African. The main I-ROAR-Word outcome measures are Response Time (RT) and accuracy. After selecting the list of stimuli based on item response theory, we found that I-ROAR-Word well approximates standardized reading score DDE-2 word after correcting for age, cognitive measures, and vocabulary measures (concurrent validity), it replicates known lexical effects (theoretical consistency), and it successfully differentiates between struggling readers and typical readers of the same age (construct validity). We conclude that I-ROAR-Word is a valid and reliable screener for Italian single-word reading in elementary school.

articles_hidden.title: Dissociating motion adaptation and action expectation effects when viewing another's gaze
articles_hidden.authors: Christian Renet; Ronja Löfström; Arvid Guterstam
articles_hidden.abstract: Recent publications have reported that brief exposure to static images depicting an agent actively gazing at an object produces a motion adaptation effect congruent with the direction of the gaze, suggesting that encoding of an implied motion in that direction occurs. Three accounts can explain this finding: either the agent’s attentive gaze (attention-motion hypothesis) or an expectation that the agent will perform an action toward the target of gaze (action-expectation hypothesis) is encoded as implied motion, or both. We directly contrasted these hypotheses by replicating the original experiment with one key change: the static image was replaced with one in which the directions of attentive gaze and action expectation were dissociated. A significant motion adaption effect in the agent-to-object direction was detected, which disappeared when the agent was blindfolded. This finding supports the attention-motion hypothesis and rules out action-expectations as an (exclusive) explanation of the previously reported effect.

articles_hidden.title: Traditional plant-based dishes: A gateway to sustainable eating
articles_hidden.authors: Marija Branković; Anastasija Budžak
articles_hidden.abstract: In traditional societies, reducing meat intake can feel threatening to traditional identities, particularly ethnic and/or religious ones. Despite this, a large part of traditional cuisine is plant-based, and fasting is observed as a valued religious tradition. We therefore sought to investigate preferences for a selection of traditional plant-based dishes. We expected them to be evaluated more positively when labeled as Lenten than when they are labeled vegan, as Lenten is a familiar and relatively positively perceived label in the local context. In a preregistered between-subjects experiment (N = 273), we attached the label to the product description, which also included a verbal description and a product photo, for ten traditional plant-based dishes. Results indicated that the mean preference score in the vegan and Lenten conditions did not differ significantly. Our findings suggest a strong overall preference for traditional plant-based dishes, regardless of how they are labeled (i.e., as vegan or Lenten).  The preference for traditional plant-based dishes was positively correlated with less meat consumption, more experience with plant-based products, as well as non-reflexive religiosity and the observance of fasting. The findings thus show no negative effects of the vegan label, and the profile of correlates suggests that these dishes can appeal to both traditionally and non-traditionally inclined individuals. We discuss the traditional plant-based dishes as a nutritional “gateway” between tradition and modern plant-based diets. These implications are encouraging and potentially applicable to promoting plant-based diets.

articles_hidden.title: People remember dot patterns during numerosity estimation tasks
articles_hidden.authors: Declan Devlin; Eivind Kaspersen; Trygve Solstad
articles_hidden.abstract: People are able to rapidly estimate the numerosity of visually presented quantities (e.g., arrays of dots), but precisely how they do so remains debated. One recent proposal is that people may estimate quantities by comparing currently presented arrays with previously presented ones. However, such proposals implicitly assume that people can retain sufficiently detailed information about briefly presented and relatively nondescript arrays. The present study directly investigated this assumption. Specifically, participants completed a quantity estimation task followed by a surprise memory task in which they were asked to identify which of three patterns with identical numerosities but different dot arrangements they had estimated before. Despite each array being presented for only 500 ms, participants recognised previously presented patterns at greater-than-chance levels across two experiments. Moreover, recognition accuracy was associated with participants’ self-reported confidence in their responses across both experiments, suggesting that participants possessed some degree of conscious access to their visual memories. Overall, these findings provide direct evidence that people spontaneously retain visual information about previously presented dot patterns during numerosity estimation tasks. Although these findings do not demonstrate that people actively use such information during estimation, they nevertheless strengthen a foundational assumption underlying visual comparison accounts of numerosity estimation.

articles_hidden.title: Does Outcome Utility Bias the Mental Simulations of Risky Events?
articles_hidden.authors: Yun-Xiao Li; Johanna Falben; Lucas Castillo; Jake Spicer; Jian-Qiao Zhu; Stella Qian; Nick Chater; Adam N Sanborn
articles_hidden.abstract: Does the utility of an outcome influence people's assessment of risk and uncertainty? Prominent theories propose that people rely on mental simulation to evaluate probabilities and risky events, yet prior empirical findings is mixed as to whether and how utility biases this process. Across four experiments (total N=206, with Experiment 4 pre-registered), we tested this question using a random generation paradigm, in which participants mentally simulated gamble outcomes and said them out loud. Then we compared these responses with probability judgments and predictions. While we identified individual differences, the majority of participants exhibited neutrality, with no systematic impact of utility on their sampling distributions. Nevertheless, an optimism subgroup emerged, with a larger proportion of optimistic participants when the monetary context was more salient. Additionally, outcome utilities have similar effects on probability judgments, predictions, and random generation tasks, consistent with the proposal that these tasks are related to each other and may all rely on mental simulation. These findings indicate that utility does not uniformly distort mental simulation, but can do so for a stable subgroup under particular motivational contexts, and they motivate cognitive models that capture both unbiased and optimistic forms of mental sampling.

articles_hidden.title: Maternal Stress and Mother-Child Interaction Dynamics: The Roles of Child Age and Maternal Emotion Regulation
articles_hidden.authors: Julia Folz; Trinh Nguyen; Stefanie Hoehl; Vanessa Anna van Ast; Milica Nikolic
articles_hidden.abstract: Caregivers often face stressful multi-tasking situations in which household- or work-related tasks compete with engaging with their young child. Caregivers’ experiences of stress can affect how they interact with their children and may also be transmitted to the child. This “stress contagion” may be particularly pronounced with caregivers who have difficulties in regulating stress responses. In the current study, we examined how inducing stress in 62 mothers shaped the dyadic interaction (expression of facial affect and cardiovascular activity) with their 6-38 months-old children, and how stress-induced changes varied depending on self-reported maternal emotion regulation difficulties and child age. Mothers’ and children’s positive and negative facial affect, inter-beat intervals (IBIs) and respiratory sinus arrhythmia (RSA), as well as synchrony in each measure, were compared between two-minute face-to-face interactions before and after a stress induction in the mother (pre- and post-stress). Maternal stress impacted the dyad differently depending on the child’s age. In interactions with younger children, both mothers and children showed less positive facial expressions and were less synchronized in their expressions post- versus pre-stress. Older children, in contrast, showed stronger physiological arousal (i.e., decrease in IBIs and RSA), but more positive facial expressions post-stress. In addition, mothers with more emotion regulation difficulties expressed more negative affect, and their heart rates were less synchronized with their children’s post- versus pre-stress. Both child age and mothers’ regulatory abilities are thus shaping the impact of acute maternal stress on mother-child interaction quality and should be considered in interventions on parental stress

articles_hidden.title: Generics and stereotypes: A cognitive account
articles_hidden.authors: Jérémie Lafraire; Adoracion Guzman Garcia
articles_hidden.abstract: Generic statements about social categories (e.g., “Women are nurturing”, “Boys don’t cry”) are a pervasive vehicle for expressing stereotypes. Although descriptively framed, they often generate normative expectations about how members of social groups should think, feel, or behave. Drawing on philosophy of language, developmental psychology, and social cognition, this chapter argues that such normativity does not arise from linguistic meaning alone, but from the interaction between generic language and two cognitive mechanisms: psychological essentialism and the inherence heuristic. By highlighting category-level regularities, generics can encourage socially produced patterns to be interpreted as reflecting deep, stable, and inherent properties of groups, thereby making stereotypes appear natural and normatively appropriate. At the same time, these effects are neither inevitable nor uniform: different linguistic framings and explanatory contexts can substantially alter how social generalizations are interpreted. We conclude by reviewing linguistic and explanatory strategies that can constrain essentialist interpretations and help negotiate or counteract stereotypical norms.

articles_hidden.title: Living in damaged homes: the mental health consequences for parents and children in Ireland’s defective concrete crisis
articles_hidden.authors: Oisin Keenan; Jamie Murphy; Paul Dunlop; Eileen Doherty; Rachel McHugh; Karen Kirby
articles_hidden.abstract: Thousands of families in Ireland are living in unsafe, deteriorating homes due to the defective concrete used in their construction. Although considerable mental health difficulties have been reported in adults, the impact on parents and their children remains unknown. This study estimated probable major depressive disorder (MDD), generalised anxiety disorder (GAD), posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and complex PTSD (CPTSD) among parents, and emotional and behavioural difficulties in their children using the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ). The cross-sectional survey data, collected between March and September 2024, included a convenience sample of 150 parents reporting on 268 children aged 2-17 years. Parental estimates were 33.6% for MDD, 30.7% for GAD, 4.0% for PTSD, and 15.3% for CPTSD. Among children, 26.5% scored in the abnormal range on SDQ Total Difficulties, with the highest difficulties in emotional problems (38.1%). Children scoring in the abnormal range for SDQ total difficulties were almost four times more likely to have a parent who met the clinical threshold for CPTSD, odds ratio (OR) = 3.92, three times more likely to have a parent who reported safety fears, OR = 2.96, and eleven times more likely to have a parent who reported financial stress, OR = 11.18. These findings highlight the mental health consequences for affected families and indicate the need for effective intervention.

articles_hidden.title: Unequal access, comparable benefit: clinical diagnosis, workplace adjustments, and outcomes of digital-human support in autistic and ADHD employees
articles_hidden.authors: Matthew Scott; Abi Jones; Jess Titley; Helen Guyatt
articles_hidden.abstract: Background. Autistic and ADHD employees are entitled to workplace support based on need, yet appropriate and timely support often relies on a clinical diagnosis. Whether a diagnosis tracks experienced challenge, or gates access to support, is unclear. This study examined experienced challenges, access to adjustments, and benefit from a hybrid human-digital support tool among employed autistic and ADHD adults with and without a diagnosis. Methods. 280 employed autistic/ADHD adults (203 diagnosed, 77 without a diagnosis) completed measures of wellbeing, anxiety, stress, and functioning at baseline, three, and six months while using the support tool Brain in Hand. Workplace disclosure and formal adjustments were recorded at baseline. Analyses combined frequentist and Bayesian methods, including equivalence testing. Results. The groups were comparable on measured psychological and functional indicators at baseline, with equivalence supported for wellbeing, anxiety, and stress; functioning was the exception, though inconclusively. Despite broadly comparable measured profiles, diagnosed employees were more likely to have disclosed at work (89.7% vs 62.3%) and to hold formal adjustments (48.8% vs 28.6%) at baseline. Exploratory analyses indicated disclosure likelihood only partially explained this gap. Both groups engaged with support similarly and improved comparably in psychological outcomes over six months. Conclusions. Among employees with comparable measured psychological and functional profiles, access to workplace adjustments tracked clinical diagnosis rather than these indicators. Benefit from support did not differ by baseline diagnostic status. Findings suggest diagnosis functions as an informal gateway to support, and that organising access around need could reach employees more effectively.

articles_hidden.title: The Current State of Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing Therapy in Sport and Exercise Psychology
articles_hidden.authors: Adrian Hase; Michael Hase
articles_hidden.abstract:
Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR) therapy is a tried-andtested treatment for posttraumatic stress disorder but has also established its
efficacy in other fields where psychological problems can be associated with
stressful memories. This article proposes EMDR therapy as a potential tool for
treating the harmful effects of stressful sport-related experiences and their
associated memories on both high-level and recreational athletes. We review the
literature on the efficacy of EMDR therapy interventions for treating such
stressful sport-related memories and propose a foundational conceptual model for
understanding the effects of stressful sport-related memories on psychology,
physiology, sport performance, sport participation, and health outcomes. The
model also identifies targets for, mechanisms of, and focal outcomes of
successful EMDR treatment of stressful sport-related memories. We also discuss
three possible applied use cases focused on the outcomes of sport performance,
sport participation, and emotional responses to sport; and point to avenues for
future EMDR therapy research in sport and exercise science.

articles_hidden.title: Visual hemifield dominance during interocular conflict and why it matters
articles_hidden.authors: Chris Paffen; David Alais; Andre Sahakian
articles_hidden.abstract: Due to the eyes being separated about six centimeters horizontally, the visual system is often confronted with non-overlapping visual input, especially in the visual periphery. Apart from supporting stereovision, non-overlapping – conflicting – visual input can potentially hinder perception of distant, fixated objects of interest. Here we review, on first sight conflicting, studies on interocular conflict in the visual periphery that reported either nasal or temporal visual field preferences during interocular competition. While these studies interpreted hemifield preferences mainly in terms of neuro-anatomical aspects of the visual system, we here argue that they have a functional goal: to suppress information that hinders perception of distant fixated objects of interest. Optimizing hemifield preferences towards this goal leads to a temporal visual field preference at around fixation, a nasal visual field preference in the near periphery, and a temporal visual advantage in the far periphery. Our functional account of hemifield preference during interocular competition thereby reconciles inconsistencies in the literature by analyzing at what eccentricities the interocular conflict in the studies was evoked. Finally, our proposal once more shows that interocular conflict in general, as well as binocular rivalry specifically, are not merely a laboratory curiosity.

articles_hidden.title: What Makes a Representation Current in Working Memory?
articles_hidden.authors: Hyung-Bum Park
articles_hidden.abstract: Working memory (WM) must preserve limited individuated representations while retaining graded information about each. Pointer accounts and theories of item-context binding explain how representations can be individuated and organized, but leave unresolved what makes dynamically expressed content part of the current set. I propose that current WM membership depends on an individuated token remaining appropriately related to its content and present context, enabling selective use. This relation may persist as content expression weakens, be lost while content remains available, or be re-established when content re-enters the current set. Activity-silent states and proactive interference provide complementary tests of these possibilities. The framework therefore identifies item-specific relational organization as a criterion for evaluating current working memory membership.

articles_hidden.title: Discrete Indexing of Graded Sensory Codes in Working Memory
articles_hidden.authors: Hyung-Bum Park
articles_hidden.abstract: Working memory (WM) research has long debated whether storage is limited by discrete slots or distributed resources. Recent neuroscientific findings suggest that neither account alone captures the joint presence of stable item limits and graded variability in representational fidelity. The present study proposes a context-content hierarchical framework that integrates these properties within a two level architecture. A capacity limited “context” system maintains discrete spatiotemporal pointers that individuate and prioritize items, whereas a precision limited “content” system represents detailed sensory information in modality-specific population codes whose fidelity varies with task demands. The framework further posits that pointer states can bias access to content representations and, when needed, support cue-dependent reinstatement of latent sensory traces. This architecture provides a principled interpretation of capacity-like and precision-like measures, accommodates activity-silent storage and retro-cue benefits, and clarifies when contextual retrieval protects performance under proactive interference. The framework also yields falsifiable predictions for neural population geometry, cross domain generalization of load signals, and dissociations between capacity and fidelity under targeted manipulations. By integrating discrete control signals with continuous sensory representations, the context-content framework reconceptualizes WM as a dynamic, generative system that balances sparse indexing with on-demand reconstruction to guide adaptive behavior.

articles_hidden.title: Neural responses to conditioned threat during extinction predict concurrent and future anxiety in late adolescence
articles_hidden.authors: Kubra Ulusoy; Liat Levita
articles_hidden.abstract: Adolescence is a critical developmental period characterised by heightened anxiety and increased risk for anxiety disorders, potentially reflecting developmental differences in threat learning and extinction processes. Although previous research suggests that early adolescents show enhanced visual event-related potential (ERP) responses to conditioned threat cues, it remains unclear whether these neural patterns persist into late adolescence or predict anxiety vulnerability. This study examined neural responses to conditioned threat cues during threat acquisition and extinction in late adolescence and investigated their association with current and future anxiety. Sixty-eight late adolescents (aged 18-19) completed a Pavlovian threat conditioning task in which a conditioned stimulus (CS+) was paired with an aversive sound on 50% of trials, whereas a second cue (CS-) was never reinforced. An immediate extinction phase followed, during which both cues were presented without reinforcement. Behavioural and physiological measures indicated successful threat acquisition and extinction. ERP analyses revealed no evidence of differential conditioning in P1 amplitudes. In contrast, N1 amplitudes were significantly larger to the CS- than the CS+ across both acquisition and extinction. The late positive potential (LPP) showed the opposite pattern, with larger amplitudes to the CS+ than the CS- during both phases. Logistic regression analyses controlling for depressive symptoms and gender indicated that P1 and N1 responses were unrelated to current or future anxiety caseness. Whereas greater LPP differentiation (CS+ > CS-) during extinction was associated with increased odds of belonging to the high-anxiety group both concurrently and six months later. Together, these findings suggest that differences between high- and low-anxiety adolescents are reflected in later neural responses to conditioned threat during extinction, but not in early visual sensory-attentional processing. Extinction-related LPP responses may therefore represent a promising neural marker of current and future anxiety in late adolescence.

articles_hidden.title: A Single Reading of a Self-Help Book Reduces Perceived Problem Burden and State Anxiety and Increases Vitality, With Gains Maintained at Four Weeks: A Preregistered Randomized Controlled Trial in 2,004 Adults
articles_hidden.authors: Nina Verkoeyen
articles_hidden.abstract: Background. Bibliotherapy is among the most scalable psychological interventions, yet randomized trials of self-help books have been small (largest published book-based trial N = 475), and almost none have measured effects on the day the book is read. Method. In a preregistered randomized controlled trial, 2,004 adults (mean age 42.9 years, range 18–73), a self-selected community sample recruited through the author’s digital channels, were randomized 1:1 to read The Meta Self, a book-length intervention targeting self-perceived identity, in a single sitting (n = 1,002), or to a delayed-access waitlist control (n = 1,002). Outcomes — momentary perceived stress, termed perceived problem burden in the preregistration (PSS-EMA-4), state anxiety (STAI-State), positive and negative affect (PANAS), and state subjective vitality (SVS) — were assessed at baseline, immediately after reading (same day), day 7 (both groups), and week 4 (intervention group). Primary analyses were preregistered linear mixed-effects models (Group × Time, intention-to-treat). Results. All ten administered preregistered same-day and day-7 contrasts, corresponding to the eight numbered confirmatory hypotheses, favored the intervention (all p < .001) and remained significant under Bonferroni correction; the ninth registered hypothesis was not tested because the AAQ-2 was not administered. Same-day between-group effects were large: problem burden d = 0.92, state anxiety d = 1.22, negative affect d = 0.80, positive affect d = 1.14, vitality d = 1.31. Day-7 effects were medium to large (d = 0.53–0.85). Within the intervention group, gains were maintained at week 4 (d = 0.89–1.24 vs. baseline). Retention was 92% at week 4. Limitations. Because the study used delayed access rather than an active reading control, it estimates the effect of immediate access to the book relative to waiting but cannot isolate content-specific effects from nonspecific effects of expectancy and intervention engagement. Demographic characteristics other than age were not collected, and one registered outcome (AAQ-2) was not administered. Conclusions. A single reading of a book-length identity-based intervention produced large improvements in self-reported well-being relative to waitlist control, sustained at day 7, in what is, to our knowledge, among the largest randomized trials identified in this literature; within the intervention group, gains persisted at four weeks. Effects of this size from a single-sitting, highly scalable intervention warrant replication with active-control and blinded-assessment designs.

articles_hidden.title: Personality reported:  Attributions, dispositional regularities, and the meaning of trait scores
articles_hidden.authors: Sergei Shchebetenko
articles_hidden.abstract: Personality psychology owes much of its success to self- and informant reports, commonly used to estimate individual differences in personality. This paper argues that reports are also psychological products: task-bounded expressions of how respondents construe themselves or others in personality terms. The attributional model of personality reporting (AMPR) distinguishes contextually anchored behavioural episodes; dispositional regularities, estimated as recurrent person-characteristic patterns across episodes, contexts, and time; personality attributions; and reports. General personality attribution is a dynamically maintained representation assigning personality-descriptive characteristics to a person. Local, time-dependent personality attribution represents how a person or their conduct is construed during a particular episode. General attribution may frame local attribution, whereas salient or consequential local attributions may revise it; most do not. General attribution may also be reorganised through broader changes in self-understanding, comparison standards, personality meanings, or social information. Reports may express general, local, or item-cued attributions; they are indicators of attribution and indirect indicators of dispositional regularities. Semantic and evaluative organisation may make report-derived scores structurally robust and predictively useful without directly recovering dispositional regularities. AMPR conceptualises inventories as item-cued attribution tasks and develops several testable propositions.

articles_hidden.title: Dynamic attribute activation explains gaze biases in choice.
articles_hidden.authors: Xiaozhi Taro Yang; Sudeep Bhatia
articles_hidden.abstract:
People tend to choose the options they look at more. Prior work explains this effect by assuming that visual attention increases preference for the attended option. However, it remains unclear why looking at an option increases its preference and when this relationship is
