The analysis of nine referendums that took place in seven countries between 2015 and 2025 confirm the predictions showing that, after each consulta-tion, a sizeable share of cross-pressured voters who cast a referendum vote against party recom-mendations “follow the issue”, switching to a party that is in line with their issue positions. Ideological proximity with parties, however, moderates vote switching. In highly salient consultations, this pattern persists over time. Further experimental evidence confirms the causal link between issue-based considerations and voting. These findings have relevant implications for how direct democracy impacts a fundamental aspect of democratic representation, namely voting for parties.

articles.title: When the Diagnosis Breaks the Home: Paternal Abandonment and Maternal Endurance in Families of Children with Disabilities in Bangladesh
articles.authors: Syed Jabir Hossain
articles.abstract: In Bangladesh, literature shows that a child with a disability is considered to profoundly reorient family life around the mother, who becomes the primary and often only caregiver. A smaller but growing body of research has also documented the financial hardship, institutional barriers, and religiously-inflected stigma that already accompany this caregiving role. An examination of a dimension that is not closely studied in the context of Bangladesh, a child’s disability in marriage dissolution of the parents, extends that literature. In keeping with the secondary qualitative methodology that Cheong et al. (2023) propose, the study analyses eight past news narratives (2016-2026) in Bangladeshi media, which are publicly available. In these narratives, family members speak for themselves about raising a disabled child. Discourse analysis reveals three themes. First, mothers globally carry the structural weight of caring for the family, regardless of the father’s involvement. Second, some discourse suggests the child’s disability is sometimes ‘responsible’ for the father’s exit, which can occur before and/or after birth. Third, despair for the future collides with maternal agency, best seen through the mother who established her own school after being turned away from every single one. The analysis does not imply a causal link between disability and divorce. It shows how this link is narrated in the Bangladeshi public sphere. The analysis offers the narrated link as a focused question for future primary, interview-based research. As an exploratory secondary analysis, this piece recognises the limitation of the data being drawn from credible journalistic sources rather than high-quality interviews.

articles.title: Position: A Score Should Travel With Its Repair History
articles.authors: Louis Yiven Zhu
articles.abstract: In machine learning a capability claim becomes established when a model outperforms its predecessors on benchmarks the community already accepts, and peer review confines itself to checking that those scores are reported and compared correctly. We argue that benchmarks consequently perform the adjudicating role that peer review performs in other sciences, and that the field has organised no stewardship to match, since a benchmark is reviewed once, when the paper introducing it is accepted, and never again during the years in which it serves as evidence. Our position is that this arrangement, which we call review once and use forever, is the first bottleneck a meta-science of AI research should address. We support the position with the public lifecycle of MMLU, the benchmark its successors describe as the de facto standard for general capability. Between 2024 and 2025 five independent projects repaired four distinct defects in MMLU, none of them by the original authors and none as part of any joint programme. A count across the benchmark paper, model reports, leaderboards and governance syntheses then shows the qualifications attached to an MMLU score falling from 2.4 per reporting event in the repair papers to 1.0 in frontier model reports, three in ten of which carry none. On this basis we propose three norms for venues, funders and governance bodies, and we answer the objection that unstewarded benchmarks have served the field well.

articles.title: Research on Han Nationalism in China in the 2020s (V): Three Frameworks for Interpreting Qing History—Han Nationalism, New Qing History, and Chinese Nationalism
articles.authors: ZY Liu
articles.abstract: This article examines the differences that have arisen among Han nationalism, Chinese nationalism, and international New Qing History in the 2020s concerning the interpretation of Qing history. It argues that the three narratives do not revolve merely around evaluations of the Qing, but respectively focus on questions of ethnic identity, imperial structure, and the historical continuity of the modern state. Han nationalism emphasizes ethnic hierarchy and historical rupture under Qing rule; New Qing History places the Qing within a comparative framework of Eurasian empires and stresses its multi-ethnic imperial character; Chinese nationalism emphasizes the Qing’s important role in the formation of modern China’s territory and national community. The article further points out that controversies surrounding the Qing in fact reflect different understandings within contemporary Chinese society of national identification, ethnic relations, and the allocation of resources.

articles.title: The alchemy linking “gender ideology,” left-wing authoritarianism, and political violence: Comment on Fedida et al.
articles.authors: Alexander C Tsai
articles.abstract: In a report commissioned by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Fedida et al. (2026) analyze data from an opt-in nonprobability sample to describe associations among a newly developed five-item Clinical Gender Affirmation Scale (CGAS), scores on the Brief Left-Wing Authoritarianism Scale, and respondents’ justification of politically charged violent acts. Their interpretation, however, is that “gender ideology,” embedded in clinical guidance, supplies authoritarian psychology with enemies, moral urgency, and rationales for coercion. This commentary argues that the data and analyses do not support this conclusion. First, CGAS measures a narrow cluster of attitudes toward social affirmation and support, not the clinical-institutional ideology attributed to it. Second, Fedida et al. (2026) invoke selection, mediation, and effect-modification theories without specifying or testing them. In particular, an “ideological accelerant” hypothesis requires an interaction between CGAS and authoritarianism, but no such interaction is estimated. Third, the estimated associations are difficult to interpret because the measures contain overlapping ideological and aggression-related content, while the violence items assess reactions to a politically selective set of hypothetical targets rather than a generalized disposition to tolerate political violence. Moreover, modeling CGAS and left-wing authoritarianism in separate regressions adjusted only for political identity does not show that either is associated with justification of violence independently of the other. In summary, Fedida et al. (2026) describe potentially interesting covariances but provide little evidence that “gender ideology” radicalizes people.

articles.title: A Moment or a Movement? The Effects of Spatial Exposure to the 2017 Women’s March on Political Attitudes and Behavior
articles.authors: Colette Marcellin
articles.abstract: How do social movements affect the public in a polarized era? I examine how the 2017 Women’s March—the largest single-day protest in US history—affected Americans who were exposed to the march in their local communities. I theorize that crowd size moved residents’ political attitudes and behavior in a liberal direction, particularly among Republicans. Using an instrumental variables approach, I find that crowd size increased Republican women’s disapproval of Trump and both Republican women and Republican men’s Democratic vote choice in the 2018 midterm elections. This paper has important implications for understanding the effects of protests that reach a range of communities and focus on identity.

articles.title: Discussions of Race in Online Right-Wing Communities: A Cross-platform Computational Analysis of Reddit, Telegram, and Truth Social Using BERT and Structural Topic Modeling
articles.authors: Qin Li; Jack Gabriel Risien Wippell; Jasmine Hunt; Robert Bond; Joseph Tien; Nicole Yadon
articles.abstract: Race has long been a divisive fault line in American public discourse. Yet, political and societal changes have catalyzed the emergence of alternative collective identities, particularly in digital environments where alternative narratives can flourish. We examine right-wing social media spaces as forums in which racial discourse (specifically, that related to Black identities) is produced and contested through conversation, focusing on three platforms—Reddit, Truth Social, and Telegram—during Summer 2022. Structural topic modeling reveals six prominent themes: comparisons of the Black Lives Matter and January 6th protests; persistent discussions of race, crime, and violence; perceived racism within the Democratic party; broad discussion about ``wokeness''; race and health issues (abortion and infectious disease); and racial identity. While their relative prominence and framing vary, these themes appear across all three platforms. This indicates that racial narratives do not vary substantially across platforms. By extending the scope of social media platforms studied and foregrounding everyday conversations about race, this study advances academic understanding of how racial identities are both (re-)constructed and (re-)enforced online. In doing so, this study offers insights for political psychologists concerned with identity and its social underpinnings, as well as for scholars of race, political communication, culture, and collective behavior.

articles.title: Social Cohesion in Iraq: Leveraging Religious, Political, and Tribal Authorities for Conflict Transformation
articles.authors: Mae Anna Chokr; Ali Al-Ahmad; Abbas Aroua
articles.abstract: How can we foster social cohesion by engaging with informal religious and political authorities in conflict contexts, such as present-day Iraq? This report answers this question by outlining a conflict transformation approach developed by Cordoba Peace Institute – Geneva (CPI), and in Samarra, Talafar, and Iraq as a whole, between 2018 and 2023. The methodology used was a combination of: 1) a ‘safe mediation space’ approach and diapraxis, 2) collaboration between insider and outsider mediators, and 3) leveraging formal and informal sources of influence, including religious, political, and tribal. The report aims to learn from the experiences of case studies to guide practitioners applying such methods in other similar contexts.

articles.title: How Much Labelled Data Is Enough? A Simulation Study of Prompting Strategies for Unbiased and Reliable LLM-Based Annotation Workflows in Social Sciences
articles.authors: Qixiang Fang
articles.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in (computational) social science to annotate text at scale. Typically, this approach requires researchers to provide (enough) gold labels, develop and evaluate candidate prompts, and decide on the most promising prompt. Meanwhile, many questions arise and remain unanswered: How much labelled data is enough? How should prompt evaluation be conducted? In particular, how can researchers prevent overfitting, an important consideration many social scientists are unfamiliar with. To address these questions, this paper reports a simulation study of prompt evaluation workflows for LLM-based text annotation. I compare intentionally biased yet often employed all-data reuse and validation-only baseline strategies with two defensible workflows: a two-way development/evaluation split and a three-way Explore--Select--Evaluate (ESE) workflow. Across 360 simulation scenarios and 360,000 workflow-level simulation results, all-data reuse and validation-only workflows produced positive reporting bias, especially under adaptive prompt development. In contrast, both two-way and ESE workflows had near-zero mean reporting bias and close-to-95% coverage. However, ESE did not generally select stronger prompts. In fixed-candidate settings, two-way selection outperformed ESE because ESE retained less data for formal prompt comparison without gaining any benefit from exploration. In adaptive settings, ESE reduced regret only modestly under some split ratios, while two-way workflows usually selected prompts with higher absolute true performance. The results suggest that a held-out evaluation set is essential, but that a separate Select stage should be used selectively rather than treated as universally optimal.

articles.title: Research on Han Nationalism in China in the 2020s (IV): Why Chinese Scholars Rarely Discuss Han Nationalism
articles.authors: ZY Liu
articles.abstract: This article is one of a series of papers examining Han nationalist ideology in China in the 2020s. It seeks to explore the phenomenon whereby discourse related to Han nationalism has increased in Chinese online space in recent years, yet has rarely been treated as an independent object of inquiry within China’s mainstream social-science research system. The article argues that this phenomenon does not simply stem from a lack of scholarly attention, but is related to the operating environment of Chinese social science. Analyzing academic tradition, research frameworks, academic norms, the functions of think tanks, and the situation of scholars, the article points out that Chinese social-science research has long been shaped by existing theoretical systems, modes of resource allocation, and traditions of policy research, making it relatively difficult for certain issues involving ethnic identity, historical memory, and identity competition to form independent research paths. The article further discusses the distance between theoretical systems and public discourse, and how this structure affects the explanatory capacity of Chinese social science with respect to social currents such as Han nationalism. The article does not attempt to provide statistical estimates of the scale or social support for Han nationalism in China; rather, it seeks to pose a question: when a social idea enters the space of public discussion, why does the existing academic system find it difficult to explain the phenomenon adequately?

articles.title: Research on Han Nationalism in China in the 2020s (III): From Banner Affiliation to Ethnicity—The Reconstruction of Modern Manchu Identity and Online Narratives of Manchu–Han Conflict
articles.authors: ZY Liu
articles.abstract: This article examines the formation of modern Manchu identity and its relationship to Manchu–Han tensions within the context of Han nationalist discourse on the Chinese internet in the 2020s. It begins by analyzing the Qing Eight Banner system, arguing that the banners were not a single-ethnicity organization in the modern sense, but a political and social system composed of multiple identity groups including Manchu, Mongol, Han-martial (Hanjun), and bondservant (baoyi) populations. After the fall of the Qing, the former banner affiliation was gradually reorganized within the modern ethnic classification system, producing the Manchu identity of today. The article further discusses the process of reconstituting modern Manchu identity since the 1980s, contending that this process involves both historical continuity and the influence of ethnic policy, local administrative factors, and practical interests. When ethnic identity becomes linked to the allocation of public resources, social policy, and historical narrative, it may shift from cultural identification toward an identity of social interest. The article maintains that contemporary Manchu–Han contradictions are not purely ethnic conflicts, but the product of the combined operation of historical memory, identity recognition, class differences, and material interests. Reducing the binding between ethnic identity and the distribution of public goods, thereby allowing ethnic identity to return more fully to the domain of cultural identification, may be an important direction for alleviating related tensions.

articles.title: Dynamic Democratic Consent: A System Dynamics Framework for Public Trust, Political Communication, and Policy Feedback
articles.authors: Muhammad Sukri Bin Ramli
articles.abstract: Political communication is often analyzed through event-based models that give lim ited attention to feedback, delay, saturation, and changing public trust. This conceptual paper proposes the Dynamic Democratic Consent framework, integrating selected princi ples from Edward Bernays’ account of public relations with the S-E-E-D behavior modes of Snowball growth, Equilibrium seeking, Elastic adjustment, and feedback-loop Dominance. The framework extends the conventional resource categories of manpower, mindpower, and money by treating algorithmic media infrastructure as a conditional fourth dimension. It maps an eight-stage communication-planning process onto reinforcing and balancing feed back structures, perception delays, demographic capacity, and institutional trust. Simulated reference modes illustrate how political-support momentum may encounter electoral satura tion, how delayed perception and corrective response may produce oscillatory adjustment, and how divergence between communication and policy delivery may weaken institutional trust and contract effective support capacity. A four-stage diagnostic process is proposed for describing trajectories, identifying feedback structures, designing policy interventions, and examining potential behavioral shifts. The framework is exploratory rather than predictive. Empirical estimation, comparative case testing, sensitivity analysis, and ethical evaluation are required before it can support applied political analysis.

articles.title: Seizing the Agenda: Polarization and Legislative Autonomy in Brazilian Presidentialism
articles.authors: Jamil Civitarese; Fabiano Guilherme Mendes Santos
articles.abstract: Brazilian coalitional presidentialism has long been read as a system in which the executive sets the agenda and the legislature holds a veto. We argue that, since the mid-2010s, the Congress has been building agenda-setting power. We account for the shift with a formal spatial framework in which a legislature weighs the cost of acquiring agenda power against the costs caused by the executive it expects to face. Two forces drive the investment: the rightward movement of a median legislator dissatisfied with the status quo and the recent polarization of the Executive, a partner that became too radical and costly to legislate with. Reading the record from Lula's first governments through Lula III, we show how the realignment of agenda power came to constrain the president who now has to both manage the coalition and to accommodate increasing policy demands from the legislature.

articles.title: Towards a Typology of Islamic Higher Education in Europe: A Comparative Analysis of Institutional Models
articles.authors: Cemal YILMAZ
articles.abstract: This article examines the emergence and institutional diversity of Islamic higher education in Europe and develops a comparative typology of its principal institutional models. While existing scholarship has focused primarily on individual countries, institutions, or debates concerning imam training, a systematic comparative framework for understanding the broader landscape of Islamic higher education remains underdeveloped. Using a comparative institutional analysis of developments in the Netherlands, Germany, Belgium, Austria, England, France, Spain, and Italy, the study examines historical trajectories, state–religion relations, institutional structures, accreditation systems, leadership formation, and sources of legitimacy. The findings demonstrate that Islamic higher education in Europe has not developed through a single institutional pathway. Instead, five ideal-type models can be identified: the Independent Islamic University Model, the State-Integrated Islamic Theology Model, the Seminary-Based Model, the Hybrid Partnership Model, and the Emerging and Transitional Model. The study contributes to the literature by providing a comparative framework for analyzing institutional diversity and by proposing a typology that facilitates future research on Islamic higher education, Muslim institutionalization, and religious leadership in Europe.

articles.title: Research on Han Nationalism in China in the 2020s (I): Examining the Narrative Contest between Han Nationalism and State Nationalism through the Withdrawal of the Film The Battle of Penghu
articles.authors: ZY Liu
articles.abstract: Taking the withdrawal of the 2026 film The Battle of Penghu as a point of entry, this article explores the rise of Han nationalist ideology within Chinese society in the 2020s, and the increasingly prominent divergences in orientation between it and the officially led “Chinese nationalism (state nationalism).” The article analyzes the institutional roots of Han nationalism during a period of economic zero-sum competition, its contestation of historical narratives in the sphere of popular culture, and its comprehensive deconstruction of the official discursive system on core issues such as the definition of the nation, historical orthodoxy, and territorial legality.

articles.title: Research on Han Nationalism in China in the 2020s (II): Cultural Products, Historical Memory, and the Narrative Conflicts of Zhonghua Nationalism
articles.authors: ZY Liu
articles.abstract: This paper examines how the narrative of Zhonghua nationalism exerts influence over cultural production in contemporary China and analyzes its structural ramifications. Within film and television, specific historical themes are constrained from entering mainstream cultural production; in video games, certain historical factions are minimized or rendered entirely absent from narratives; in online literature, market mechanisms reflect historical preferences distinct from official state narratives through reader subscription behavior; in historical publications, ethnicity-inflected linguistic expressions from the past undergo textual revision; and within the Hanfu movement, Han culture is not directly suppressed but rather subsumed and repackaged within the overarching framework of "Zhonghua culture."

articles.title: Everyday Talk and Child Development: A Conceptual Framework for the Informal Conversation Deficit Hypothesis A Theoretical Paper Proposing an Untested Hypothesis and Research Agenda
articles.authors: Craig Davidon
articles.abstract: Over recent decades, documented shifts in family and community routines — including declining rates of children walking to school, smaller household sizes, and increasingly structured extracurricular scheduling — have measurably reduced the settings in which children once encountered casual, unscripted conversation with a range of adults and peers. This paper proposes the term informal conversation deficit to describe a hypothesized reduction, alongside these routine changes, in children's everyday practice with varied social speech. The framework is motivated by the author's own long-standing personal observations, made over approximately five decades, of apparent declines in children's verbal and nonverbal (for example, body-language-based) social communication. These observations are offered as motivating context only: the paper presents no empirical data of its own, and every causal relationship it proposes is a hypothesis rather than an established finding. Drawing on Vygotsky's (1978) account of private speech, Romeo and colleagues' (2018) finding that conversational turns are associated with language-related brain function, and the ongoing debate over socioeconomic disparities in children's verbal environments, the paper considers how reduced frequency and variety of conversational practice may plausibly be linked to slower pragmatic language development and, in turn, to difficulty articulating internal states such as fear, frustration, or unmet needs. It is hypothesized that resulting frustration may sometimes present as behavior that resembles or compounds features of neurodevelopmental conditions, without being caused by them. The paper closes with explicit limitations and a proposed longitudinal study — using LENA audio-recording metrics — designed to test, for the first time within this framework, the relationship between conversational-turn exposure and children's emotional self-regulation

articles.title: Between Disintermediation and Inertia: Preprints and the Digital Transformation of the Scientific Knowledge Order
articles.authors: Christian Koß; Frank Marcinkowski
articles.abstract: Informed by work on the digital transformation of traditional knowledge orders, this study examines how researchers use preprints relative to journal publication, and how they perceive preprints’ credibility, benefits, and risks. Evidence comes from a cross-disciplinary survey of 1,403 researchers affiliated with German universities who had previously served as corresponding authors on Web of Science-indexed publications. Corresponding authors indexed in Web of Science are not representative of the scientific community as a whole, and participation was low relative to the number invited, so the estimates describe the respondent sample rather than population prevalence. Unlike studies that recruit through preprint servers, however, this frame also reaches researchers who have never posted a preprint. We investigate five dimensions: (1) adoption rates and disciplinary variations, (2) publication practices, (3) audience orientation and reported feedback, (4) motivations for preprint use, and (5) scientific perceptions of preprints’ implications for research integrity and credibility. Our findings reveal disciplinary differences: 48.6% of natural scientists had uploaded a preprint compared with 18.6% of humanities scholars. Among adopters, reported motivations emphasized access, open science, and speed. Respondents also expressed concerns about credibility and premature public reporting. Intended audiences and reported feedback were concentrated within the scientific community, with little frequent feedback reported from journalists, policymakers, industry, or citizens. Most users posted preprints alongside the journal publication process, although 21.6% included having no intention to publish elsewhere among the circumstances in which they usually posted. These findings describe preprints as a widely used but unevenly adopted publication mode that commonly coexists with formal peer review, with implications for scientific policy and research integrity.

articles.title: Cognitive Degradation: The Reconfiguration of the Labor Process and Knowledge Authority in the Era of Generative Artificial Intelligence
articles.authors: 王本杰
articles.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly entering knowledge-intensive work, including programming, writing, design, analysis, and management. Unlike earlier forms of automation that were often concentrated on physical operations or clearly defined executional tasks, generative AI can produce text, code, classifications, and proposals within the workflow itself. Its significance therefore lies not simply in the displacement of particular tasks, but in the possibility that activities once associated with professional judgment become increasingly mediated by corporate technological systems. This paper examines that possibility through the concept of “cognitive degradation.” Drawing on Marx’s analysis of machinery and fixed capital, Braverman’s account of labor-process control and deskilling (Braverman, 1974), and Burawoy’s emphasis on worker agency and consent (Burawoy, 1978; 1979), the paper defines cognitive degradation narrowly. It occurs when AI takes over cognitive tasks previously performed by workers, workers’ effective authority over the criteria and application of judgment declines, and that shift is stabilized through organizational rules, technological systems, or labor institutions. The concept therefore should not be treated as synonymous with deskilling, declining productivity, or algorithmic management. To explore the mechanism, the paper examines three ideal types rather than three directly comparable causal cases: boundary-setting in the Writers Guild of America (WGA), internalization in AI-assisted software development, and institutional mediation through German co-determination. The cases show that AI can increase productivity without necessarily reducing workers’ skills, while still altering how knowledge and judgment are organized. The paper argues that the central issue in AI-mediated labor is therefore not whether machines replace workers, but whether workers retain meaningful authority over the definition, evaluation, and application of knowledge. The paper further proposes that sustained changes in such authority may affect occupational autonomy, skill formation, and bargaining power. Claims about macro-level class restructuring, however, remain propositions for future empirical research rather than conclusions established by the cases examined here.

articles.title: From science to policy: A multilevel framework for measuring institutional policy engagement through Overton
articles.authors: Daniel Torres-Salinas; Wenceslao Arroyo-Machado; Nicolas Robinson-Garcia; Esteban Romero-Frías
articles.abstract: This study presents a multilevel framework to assess the policy attention of academic institutions using Overton as a primary data source. We illustrate this framework through a case study of the University of Granada, combining Overton policy mentions, OpenAlex topics, and bibliometric analysis. Results show policy engagement particularly concentrated in health, physical, and social sciences, with mentions from key governmental and intergovernmental organisations. The study quantifies the university's visibility in policy documents, classifies mentions by scientific domain and issuer type, maps 1,145 research topics to Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), and identifies seven researchers whose work aligns with Spain's Urban Agenda. The findings demonstrate the value of Overton for mapping the presence of institutional research in policy documents and tracing science-policy linkages. However, given the well-documented risks of misuse of bibliometric indicators in research evaluation, users of this framework should be aware of key interpretive boundaries: policy mentions should not be equated with policy impact; raw mention counts cannot establish reliable temporal trends given Overton's continuous expansion; and geographic and linguistic distributions of mentions reflect Overton's structural indexing biases toward OECD countries rather than real-world policy engagement. With these caveats, the framework offers a scalable model for institutional policy engagement assessment.

articles.title: Mapping film commissions in Brazil: Intermediary organizations and institutionalization dynamics in challenging creative ecosystems
articles.authors: Débora Póvoa
articles.abstract: This article presents a panorama of film commissions in Brazil, describing their diverse intermediary roles, tracing their distinct institutionalization paths and reflecting on how trends toward institutional isomorphism or divergence unfold in this emerging field within the Brazilian cultural and creative industries (CCIs). Based on qualitative interviews with 15 film commission representatives, it reveals that these organizations act as strategic intermediaries within local audiovisual ecosystems and follow diverse institutionalization trajectories, with some operating independently with minimal resources and others benefitting from more robust budgets and institutional structures. As relatively new players navigating the uncertainties of Brazil’s cultural and creative landscape, film commissions exhibit a degree of isomorphism in following similar institutional templates, performing analogous logistical functions, and exchanging best practices in consultancies and sector events. Yet, divergence also occurs, particularly due to local and regional inequalities in cultural funding and industry development, which fundamentally shape how each of them operates. Despite their increasing prominence in creative ecosystems worldwide, film commissions remain under-researched, particularly in the Global South. This study fills in this gap by examining the case of Brazil and offering a more nuanced understanding of cultural intermediation and the dynamics of institutional homogeneity and diversity, especially in contexts characterized by significant local and regional variation in the development, size, and funding of the CCIs.

articles.title: Identity as Recognized Rather Than Constructed: Resonant Identity Theory and a Proposed Construct of Field State
articles.authors: James H. Tippins
articles.abstract: Chronic self-referential questioning of identity persists across the interventions designed to resolve it and frequently intensifies with the acquisition of self-knowledge. This paper argues that the persistence is structural, not incidental. Six influential accounts of identity, existentialist, cognitive, achievement-oriented, contemplative, status-based and narrative, differ substantially from one another while sharing the assumption that identity is constructed by the person whose identity it is. A construction that generates its own specification while executing it has no terminating condition, which is what a self-authored identity is. Resonant Identity Theory proposes the alternative: that identity is recognized rather than constructed, and that felt resonance functions as an instrument for self-knowledge rather than merely as an epiphenomenon of it. The ontological claim is acknowledged to be untestable. What is testable is the apparatus it generates. Field state is proposed as a construct describing the current relationship between recognized identity and its expression, distinct from trait profile, self-concept clarity and endorsed values, and operationalized through informant-rated cross-context consistency rather than self-report, on the grounds that the theory itself predicts self-report will fail in precisely the conditions it most needs to detect. Discriminant and falsification conditions are specified, including the finding most likely to refute the theory: if excavated self-relevant content skews toward moral approval, resonance is an approval detector and the epistemological claim fails. No empirical test has been conducted. The author declares a commercial interest in the framework.

articles.title: CHALLENGES AND OPPORTUNITIES FOR DEVELOPING UPCYCLED COSMETIC INGREDIENTS IN BRAZIL: A PERSPECTIVE FOR SMALL AND MEDIUM ENTERPRISES
articles.authors: Murilo Dotti Garcia; Orlando Nastri Neto
articles.abstract: The use of plant by-products to develop cosmetic ingredients has gained considerable momentum globally, driven by growing demand for sustainability and the increasing expectation that ingredients deliver scientifically proven efficacy. Brazil offers particularly favourable conditions for this trend, since the country combines unparalleled biodiversity with a world-scale agribusiness chain that generates vast volumes of largely underused by-products. This article examines the main challenges and opportunities facing Brazilian small and medium cosmetic enterprises (SMEs) as they develop ingredients from these by-products, focusing on regulatory, technical, scientific and market dimensions. Drawing on an integrative review of recent scientific and sectoral literature and on an analysis of the national context, it argues that SMEs, despite capital and infrastructure constraints, hold genuine advantages in agility and proximity to regional production chains. It concludes that conditions are favourable for smaller companies willing to invest in technical capacity, strategic partnerships and differentiation grounded in scientific evidence.

articles.title: Relay cooperation between women and girls during foraging trips among BaYaka hunter-gatherers in the Republic of the Congo
articles.authors: Amandine Erika Stéphanie Visine; Haneul Jang
articles.abstract: Children in small-scale societies contribute to subsistence and infant care from an early age, developing relevant skills through everyday participation. To examine how such participation is organised in practice, we focus on women’s daily foraging among BaYaka hunter-gatherers in the Congolese rainforest, where children frequently accompany adults. Using focal follows, we recorded mothers’ activity states - foraging, travelling, and resting - alongside helping behaviours of group members, including childcare, foraging, and basket carrying. We find that childcare, subsistence, and load-carrying responsibilities are dynamically redistributed through relay cooperation between women and girls, who are not necessarily kin. Infant care is frequently transferred from women to girls, enabling mothers to continue foraging without carrying infants. When mothers pause to rest or breastfeed, girls temporarily take over foraging tasks. These role shifts occur repeatedly within trips, revealing a structured yet flexible system that allows mothers to manage the energetic and mobility constraints of childcare while maintaining productivity.  At the same time, relay cooperation provides girls with repeated opportunities to engage in both caregiving and subsistence, supporting learning through participation with women other than their own mothers. These findings provide insight into how children develop as cooperative actors through active participation in women’s subsistence and caregiving activities.

articles.title: Insufficiently Affordable: Public Opinion About Housing Affordability
articles.authors: Tali Mendelberg; Gustavo Novoa; Adrian C. Pietrzak
articles.abstract: Americans want government to improve housing affordability. Yet proposals for affordable housing often encounter public resistance. We argue for a neglected explanation: concerns that these proposals are insufficiently affordable. Using four original surveys with novel, precise measures of affordability and randomized developer and landlord profiteering, we find wide support for affordable housing when it primarily benefits people of low means and does not favor developer or landlord profiteering. This support holds even when the hypothetical building is proposed in the respondent’s neighborhood, support entails tradeoffs and costly behavior in the survey, and the policy requires tax increases. The tax finding replicates in election outcomes of actual ballot measures. Pro-poor sentiments shape these preferences, above and beyond self-interest, and offset the negative impact of racial attitudes. Buildings and policies that satisfy these sentiments draw much higher public support. However, common policies fail to do so.

articles.title: Spirit Becoming Matter: A Thematic Analysis of Creation Stories
articles.authors: Pamela Venerdrow Lucas; Michelle Fauver
articles.abstract:
Objective
This qualitative study examined the creation stories from a cross-section of cultures and traditions to determine whether there are important similarities. 
Methods
Thematic analysis was conducted with 15 creation stories from 11 traditions. Initial coding was reviewed to develop themes, which were then recursively applied to the stories to find further examples and refine definitions. The resulting 13 themes were then clustered into 4 categories. 
Results
The diverse stories shared significant commonalities in their processes, elements, and implications. The first category is consciousness, which includes the themes of creator being, humans as co-creators, thought/mind, and one source. The second category is the elements, which includes the themes of water, light, and earth. The third category is opposites and similars, with no further subcategories. The fourth category is energy, which includes the themes of energy/vibration, breath, void, and time.
Conclusions
Surprising similarities across cultures point toward a model of reality in which consciousness is primary, preceding, and giving rise to physical form. All matter started as energy, and each part contains elements of the whole. The findings suggest that the divine, or universal consciousness, is contained in all matter, that consciousness may be eternal, and that the continuum of consciousness facilitates communication between humans, the divine, and all manifest forms.

articles.title: Are we nursing the technologies? An ethnographic study of nurses’ tech work and its implications for well-being
articles.authors: Paulien D'Huyvetter; Ellen Algera; Daantje Derks; Pascale Marie Le Blanc; Iris Wallenburg; Rik Wehrens
articles.abstract: Healthcare systems across the world face persistent nursing shortages. Although technological innovations are widely promoted as solutions to rising workloads and staff shortages, they also generate additional, largely invisible forms of work. We examine nurses’ tech work: the unanticipated work nurses perform to keep hospital technologies functioning. Drawing on insights from Science and Technology Studies and Work and Organizational Psychology, we investigate the types of tech work nurses perform and their implications for nurses’ well-being. Based on ethnographically grounded observations, interviews, and focus groups conducted in a Dutch academic hospital, we identify eight types of tech work in nursing. For each type, we show tech work can negatively affect nurses’ well-being through hindrance demands and reduced perceptions of meaningfulness, particularly when combined with other demanding tasks. Our findings suggest that the challenge is not the deployment of more technologies, but their design and implementation in ways that minimize burdensome tech work and better support nurses’ care practices.

articles.title: The Politics of Consolidation: Authoritarian Drift and Economic Ambition in Post-Election Tanzania
articles.authors: Rutashubanyuma Nestory
articles.abstract:
Abstract
Tanzania’s political trajectory in August 2026 is increasingly defined by a striking contradiction: ambitious economic modernization is unfolding alongside a marked contraction of political space. Following the contested October 2025 general election, President Samia Suluhu Hassan’s administration appears increasingly focused on restoring political control while facing unresolved questions concerning electoral legitimacy, accountability and constitutional reform (BBC, 2026; Xinhua, 2026a; Xinhua, 2026b). The resignation of Vice President Emmanuel Nchimbi on 25 August 2026 (BBC, 2026; KBC Digital, 2026), restrictions on opposition political activity (The Citizen, 2026b; Daily News, 2026a), and the prosecution of opposition leader Tundu Lissu (The Citizen, 2026a; Mwananchi, 2026) have intensified concerns about the direction of Tanzania’s political order. At the same time, major infrastructure achievements, particularly the Julius Nyerere Hydropower Project, provide the government with a powerful narrative of developmental competence (Xinhua, 2026c).
This paper situates these developments within the comparative literature on democratic backsliding, electoral authoritarianism, political legitimacy, institutional change and developmental states. Drawing on Bermeo’s (2016) analysis of democratic backsliding, Schedler’s (2013) conception of electoral authoritarianism, Beetham’s (1991) theory of political legitimacy, and Doner, Ritchie, and Slater’s (2005) analysis of developmental states, it argues that Tanzania is exhibiting features of political consolidation in which executive control and developmental performance increasingly operate as mutually reinforcing sources of regime stability. The paper does not suggest that Tanzania has become a fully authoritarian state. Rather, it identifies an authoritarian drift in which restrictions on political competition and civic space coexist with continued electoral institutions and ambitious economic modernization. The central argument is that economic performance may strengthen short-term regime legitimacy, but it cannot permanently substitute for credible elections, accountable institutions, judicial independence and meaningful political inclusion. The widening gap between developmental ambition and political openness consequently represents both a democratic challenge and a long-term governance and investment risk.

articles.title: Does Democratic and Economic Benchmarking Matter for Affective Polarization? A Survey Experiment in Poland
articles.authors: Maciej Sychowiec
articles.abstract: This article examines whether international benchmarking, cross-national comparisons of a country’s democratic or economic performance, intensifies affective polarization among citizens. While prior research has shown that international economic comparisons shape electoral behavior, little is known about how such external evaluations influence emotional hostility between partisan groups. Drawing on a survey experiment conducted as part of the 2023 Polish National Election Study, the study tests whether exposure to negative international assessments increases affective polarization. The results reveal a striking asymmetry. Exposure to democratic benchmarking, information signaling Poland’s decline on democratic indicators relative to regional peers, significantly increases affective polarization, whereas economic benchmarking produces no comparable effect. These effects are conditional. Democratic benchmarking polarizes primarily among citizens with negative evaluations of the outgoing government, while leaving strong government supporters unaffected. The findings suggest that benchmarking is most polarizing when it concerns identity-relevant and normatively charged domains in which responsibility can be credibly attributed to domestic political actors. Overall, the study shows that international reputational cues can deepen partisan divides, reinforcing emotional boundaries between political camps rather than fostering a common ground for evaluating national performance.

articles.title: Institutional Voice Laundering: Multimodal Risks and a Benchmark for Civic Fidelity
articles.authors: Yukai Zeng
articles.abstract: Public institutions are increasingly being designed in forms that Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems can process easily, sometimes before those forms are equally clear to citizens. People increasingly encounter ministries, hospitals, regulators, and courts through AI-mediated summaries, translations, voice interfaces, and visual reformulations, often before seeing the original communication itself. This paper argues that such mediation can weaken important features of institutional communication. Public messages that were originally attributable and open to scrutiny may be recast as apparently neutral assistance, while losing cues about jurisdiction, uncertainty, evidence, and avenues for appeal, even when the output appears fluent and useful. To frame this problem, two linked concepts are introduced here: (1) the machine-readable institution and dual legibility; and (2) a Civic Fidelity Index to assess how much civic meaning is preserved when institutional communication is transformed by AI. This problem is fundamentally multimodal, because many failures arise not from text paraphrase alone but from the way information is reformulated across text, speech, images, and interface elements. We identify research directions around multimodal fidelity, reversible mediation, cross-lingual robustness, and no-laundering standards for accountable AI.

articles.title: NEXUS-HC: A Framework for Technology Foresight in Strategic Communications
articles.authors: Yukai Zeng
articles.abstract:
This conference paper introduces NEXUS-HC (Navigational Examination and Understanding System for Hype Cycle Analysis), a decision-oriented framework for technology foresight in strategic communications. The framework adapts the familiar hype-cycle concept for contested, next-generation information environments shaped by automation, synthetic media, algorithmic information operations, AI avatars, and emerging influence technologies. It standardises technology assessment through a lightweight cross-impact rubric and links assessment outcomes to five portfolio postures: Monitor, Pilot, Adopt, Govern/Harden, or Counter. NEXUS-HC is designed to help strategic communications teams compare emerging technologies, record evidence and confidence levels, set reassessment triggers, and brief leaders using a transparent and auditable decision record.

This is the published conference proceedings paper from the Proceedings of the 25th European Conference on Cyber Warfare & Security (ECCWS 2026). The official version of record is available at https://doi.org/10.34190/eccws.25.1.4709.

articles.title: Transforming Public Sector Corporations in Tanzania: A Capability-Based Framework for Addressing Persistent Governance, Financial, and Organizational Weaknesses
articles.authors: Josephat Lotto
articles.abstract: Public and Statutory Corporations (PSCs) remain important instruments for economic transformation, strategic investment, and public service delivery in developing economies. Governments establish PSCs to address market failures, provide essential services, support industrial development, and advance national economic objectives. However, despite growing interest in PSCs' governance, several gaps remain in existing literature. First, many studies focus primarily on ownership structures, privatization outcomes, and financial performance while paying limited attention to internal institutional capabilities. Second, existing performance assessments frequently identify weaknesses without developing systematic approaches for measuring recurring organizational constraints. Third, limited attention has been given to mechanisms that translate oversight findings into continuous organizational improvement. The study, therefore, addresses these gaps by developing the Public Sector Corporation Performance Weakness Index (PSC-PWI), an analytical framework designed to identify and measure recurring institutional weaknesses affecting PSCs' performance.

articles.title: From Silence to the Archive: The Uneven Institutionalization of Legal-Political Memory Across Displacement Contexts
articles.authors: Ramazan BOZTEPE
articles.abstract: Legal-political memory occupies an ambivalent position in contexts marked by state violence and forced migration: documentation promises evidentiary weight, yet producing it can expose the documenter to risk. Drawing on 80 semi-structured interviews with Kurdish-origin participants across three positional contexts (Bölge, n=25; İç Anadolu, n=25; Diaspora, n=30), coded against a reliability-tested framework (overall κ=0.838), this article examines Documentary Witnessing and Legal Memory (κ=0.818) and Institutional/Archival Memory and Digitization (κ=1.000). Documentary witnessing remains uniformly weak across contexts (8.0–13.3 per cent), while institutional memory diverges sharply, reaching 50.0 per cent among Diaspora participants against 16.0–20.0 per cent within Turkey. Read through Halbwachs, Assmann, Derrida and Trouillot, we read this pattern as consistent with a geography of risk rather than a uniform absence of institutions: within our sample, protective silence is most visible near the site of origin, material erosion under internal displacement, and institutionalization at greater distance. A cross-cutting family-archive practice further complicates the institutional/oral binary.

articles.title: How Organizations Involved in Criminal Activity Sway Public Opinion: An Integrative Framework of Discursive Legitimation Strategies From a Scoping Review
articles.authors: Kristina Sabrina Weißmüller; Tijs van den Broek; Jana S. Krawinkel; Steven James Watson
articles.abstract: This study examines how organizations involved in criminal activities try to publicly legitimize their actions by using discursive legitimation strategies. Often involving moral neutralization and blame deflection techniques, these discursive strategies present organizations involved in criminal activities as virtuous and justified to evade punishment and undermine public support for law enforcement. Although discursive legitimation strategies result in societal harm, little is known about what types of strategies exist for criminal activities, how they differ, and whether they change legitimacy judgments. Based on a framework that integrates the communicative aspects of legitimation and strategic ambiguity, this scoping review identifies, categorizes, and synthesizes the empirical evidence on discursive legitimation strategies used by organizations involved in criminal activities. We identify 10 strategies that are conceptually linked with different legitimacy dimensions and develop testable propositions about how five distinct mechanisms—licensing, contestation, enculturation, neutralization, and cleansing—are used to create strategic ambiguity. This study elevates our understanding of discursive legitimation strategies used to justify illegitimate and criminal practices to sway public opinion and informs practice on how to develop countermeasures and strengthen societal resilience against criminal manipulation.

articles.title: Incarceration and Deservingness: Experimental Evidence on Less Eligibility
articles.authors: Christopher Berk; Lucas Nunez; Brett C Burkhardt
articles.abstract: A substantial literature on welfare politics shows that public support for redistribution depends on markers like need, effort, and reciprocity that sort recipients into deserving and undeserving categories. We test whether incarceration status functions as a particularly powerful deservingness marker, structured by the eighteenth-century principle of "less eligibility": that no one subject to punishment should fare better than the poorest free person. Using a pre-registered conjoint experiment with a representative U.S. sample (N = 1,929), we find that incarcerated applicants to an identical rehabilitative program receive substantially less public support than otherwise-comparable poor or welfare-dependent applicants — a penalty that persists even when the incarcerated applicant is shown to benefit more from the program than the comparison case. Decomposing the moral-cultural mechanisms behind this penalty, we find community-belonging and cost-benefit evidence each narrow it somewhat, while signals of the applicant's hard work and reliability paradoxically widen it. The incarceration penalty, we argue, operates as a durable boundary of moral exclusion rather than a correctable informational gap, with implications for how welfare-state and punishment scholarship jointly understand deservingness.

articles.title: The Q18 Survey: Initial Validation of an Employee-Reported Outcomes
articles.authors: Thibault Bordeaux
articles.abstract: Employee surveys commonly assess individual attitudes and experiences, but fewer instruments integrate these with employees’ perceptions of organisational functioning. This study reports the initial validation of the Q18, a brief employee-reported outcomes instrument designed for employee listening, aggregate-level human resource and managerial monitoring, and perceived organisational assessment. A validation study was conducted with 3,350 employees working in France. Analyses examined score distributions, reliability, confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) structure, discriminant validity, multi-group invariance, multicollinearity, and practical and nomological anchoring with the employee Net Promoter Score (eNPS). CFA model comparisons supported a correlated eight-factor structure comprising four individual outcomes and four perceived organisational outcomes. Reliability estimates were compatible with aggregate-level interpretation for human resource and managerial tracking, and invariance analyses supported measurement stability across the main segmentation variables. Q18 scores increased progressively across eNPS detractors, passives, and promoters. Discriminant validity received partial support: the dimensions were empirically distinguishable, but some remained strongly interdependent.  By bringing together individual outcomes and perceived organisational outcomes, the Q18 provides an integrated interpretation of tensions or alignments between employee experience and perceived collective functioning and helps extend employee listening practices beyond the measurement of individual attitudes alone. Further research is needed to establish its longitudinal, organisational-level, and cross-cultural validity.

articles.title: Strategic behaviour in decision support systems: a conceptual framework for observation in multi-stakeholder decision-making processes
articles.authors: Monique Arkesteijn; Adinda Jongkind; Fatemeh Hedieh Arfa; Haiko van der Voort
articles.abstract:
While DSS are designed to enhance transparency and provide structure in complex, multi-stakeholder settings, they also influence actions of participating stakeholders and thereby their strategic choices. This paper reviews the literature on SB and DSS, identifies diverse forms of strategic action, and proposes a five-step framework for systematically observing SB in DSS-supported processes and environments.
The framework integrates contextual dynamics, stakeholder motivations, strategic approaches, and resource use, offering a structured and comprehensive lens for analysis. By focusing on how stakeholders engage strategically in practice, rather than prescribing how they should behave, the framework enables a nuanced and realistic understanding of stakeholder interaction, behaviour, and power in participatory settings. This conceptual contribution advances both academic and applied discussions by providing a tool that supports empirical investigation as well as the design and use of DSS in real-world decision-making contexts.

articles.title: Capital as a System of Multidimensional Valuations: Transformation, Money Crisis and Contours of New Architecture.
articles.authors: Marat Idrissov; Nazerke Alipbayeva
articles.abstract:
The article is devoted to an analysis of the fundamental transformation of the nature of capital in the 21st century. Despite the growing body of research on intangible assets, debt dynamics, and the concentration of wealth, there is no comprehensive framework linking these trends to the crisis of money’s functions and the formation of a new capital architecture.
Based on a comparison of aggregated data — the share of intangible assets in 92% of the capitalization of the S&P 500 (Ocean Tomo, 2025), global debt of $353 trillion (IIF, 2026), wealth concentration in 0.001% of the population (WIR, 2026) — and illustrative cases (capitalization of Tesla, dynamics of real estate prices in megacities, digital assets) it is shown that the dominant form of capital is shifting from material to a valuation system based on expectations, narratives and trust.
Four key drivers of transformation are identified: technological, institutional, environmental, and socio‑psychological. The crisis of the four functions of money — as a measure of value, a medium of exchange, a store of value, and a means of payment — is interpreted as a symptom of a deeper shift in valuation.
It is substantiated that money will retain its function as a measure of value even as the object of measurement changes — from physical goods and labour to data, algorithms, reputation, and trust. Three scenarios for a new capital architecture are formulated — energy‑based, digital, and institutional — and the need to transition to a multidimensional system of value assessment, which includes energy, data, trust, and natural capital, is substantiated.

articles.title: CLAIM: Calibration of Legitimacy through AI Messaging - A Theory of How Conversational AI Shapes Minority and Majority Voices in Group Deliberation
articles.authors: Hoang Phuong Nhi Do; Suzanne van Gils; Christoph Lutz
articles.abstract: Conversational artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly shapes communicative spaces preceding social interaction, yet its effects are often studied in isolation from subsequent group dynamics. Recognizing this gap, we propose the Calibration of Legitimacy through AI Messaging (CLAIM) theory, which argues that pre-deliberative AI interaction calibrates perceived opinion legitimacy and shapes voice in group deliberation. Drawing on AI sycophancy, the Spiral of Silence, and multi-level legitimacy literature, CLAIM proposes that high AI sycophancy increases validity and propriety beliefs, whereas opposition from AI deflates them. Moreover, structural opinion status moderates these effects: AI sycophancy can generate a compensatory voice effect for opinion-minority participants, while AI challenge can produce compounded silencing. Additionally, a legitimacy shock may emerge when minority-opinion holders encounter group compositions that contradict AI-calibrated legitimacy beliefs. Together, CLAIM extends AI sycophancy research by theorizing conversational AI as a legitimacy-calibrating force that can reshape voice in group deliberation, particularly under structural communicative inequality.

articles.title: Detecting Coordinated Posting Behavior on Social Media. Introducing and Evaluating the Embedding-Based Tool ‘coorsim’
articles.authors: Daniel Thiele; Miriam Milzner
articles.abstract: The detection of coordinated behavior on social media is an effective heuristic for uncovering organized manipulation of online publics. Existing detection tools rely on identifying identical or lexically similar content disseminated rapidly by networks of accounts. However, these tools are ill-suited to detect the coordinated posting of semantically similar content. This is a shortcoming in the age of LLMs that enable the large-scale generation of diverse yet semantically equivalent content. In this paper, we introduce and systematically evaluate coorsim, an open source R package for for detecting semantically similar coordinated posting. The package provides a platform-agnostic end-to-end workflow encompassing embedding retrieval, coordinated community detection, automated community labeling, and visualization. We systematically evaluate its performance against the most comprehensive benchmark dataset of known influence operations to date, covering 15 international campaigns. Across 3,780 evaluated parameter combinations, the best stable configuration achieved an overall F1 of 0.69. Using multilevel Bayesian regression models, we isolated the influence of parameter choices. We also provide a qualitative assessment of automatically generated community labels. Our results demonstrate that coorsim provides a valid, albeit not flawless, contribution to closing a gap in the landscape of computational tools for detecting coordinated online behavior.

articles.title: Five Percent Re-runnable: An Audit of Disclosure in LLM-Based Social Science
articles.authors: Huazhang Shen
articles.abstract: We audited 133 arXiv papers from 2023–2026 (full text obtainable for 129), plus 38 DOAJ-listed open-access journal articles as a comparison group, checking seven disclosure fields in each. We define a study as re-runnable when three conditions hold together: it names a specific model snapshot, its prompt text is obtainable, and it provides code or data. Seven of 129 papers (5%) are re-runnable. Two figures stand out: 29% name a specific model snapshot, and 1 paper in 129 reports a random seed. The structural finding is that of the 21 papers whose prompt text is obtainable at all, about half (11) have it only in a code repository rather than in the paper. The journal group discloses less on six of seven fields, but n=38 is too small to separate that difference from sampling variation — we therefore read this as no evidence that peer review supplies the missing material, not as evidence that it makes disclosure worse.

articles.title: What Drives Legislative Anger? Multimodal Evidence from South Korea's National Assembly
articles.authors: Haejo Kang; Songpo Yang
articles.abstract: Legislative anger is often understood as expressive representation, a signal that legislators passionately defend constituent interests. We argue that partisan blame underpins these displays, especially when parties attack one another over alleged misconduct. Using deep-learning models, we measure vocal and facial anger across 355 hours of plenary debate in South Korea's 20th National Assembly (2016-2020), covering 11,060 speech segments by 247 legislators. We find that anger peaks when legislators discuss scandal, at twice the level of policy debate. Moreover, a quasi-experiment around the impeachment of President Park Geun-hye shows that the same legislators become angrier in opposition and calmer in government. These findings challenge accounts that treat legislative anger primarily as constituency signaling and highlight how partisan blame and institutional position shape emotional expression in legislatures.

articles.title: LINGUISTIC STRATEGIES IN MISINFORMATION: A SEMANTIC-PRAGMATIC FRAMEWORK FOR DETECTING MANIPULATION IN MEDIA DISCOURSE
articles.authors: ANGELICA JEANICE MARTINS ANDERSEN
articles.abstract: This article identifies recurrent patterns of linguistic behaviour characteristic of misinformation and proposes a semantic-pragmatic approach to analysing manipulation in media texts. Through the application of five mechanisms – implicature (GRICE, 1975; HORN, 2011; SPERBER; WILSON, 1995), presupposition (SCHLENKER, 2011; SIMONS, 2005; STALNAKER, 1973), modality (VON FINTEL, 2006), genericity (CARLSON, 2011; MÜLLER, 2003), and deverbal nominalisation (GRIMSHAW, 1990, 2011) – it demonstrates how these resources are exploited to constrain inferential paths and generate interpretive distortions. Although other mechanisms are available, the study focuses on these five because they are most frequently exploited in misinformation discourse. The analysis identifies five main manipulative strategies: (1) the suggestion of misleading meanings through implicatures, which allow the speaker to maintain plausible deniability by keeping manipulative content outside the truth-conditional level of the utterance; (2) the naturalisation of controversial content as established fact; (3) the exploitation of modal asymmetry to obscure the boundary between speculative possibility and normative necessity; (4) the promotion of essentialist universalisations through generic and vague reference; and (5) the suppression of information about agents and responsibilities. These strategies are exemplified by a 2023 news story on inclusive terminology in healthcare, which serves as a paradigmatic case for revealing the linguistic architecture of misinformation. The results contribute to the semantics-pragmatics interface by operationalising the distinction between what is said and what is implicated, and by revealing the recurrent patterns through which ordinary pragmatic mechanisms are strategically exploited to produce manipulative effects in media discourse.

articles.title: A New Approach of Applying the 360-Degree Method for Performance Assessment of Managerial Levels in Mega-Companies
articles.authors: Saber Mirzaei Ahandani
articles.abstract: Questionnaires play the most important role in scientific papers and workplaces. Considering various applications, questionnaires may be designed in different shapes and types. In any case, it is critical to have a questionnaire with appropriate content and a pleasing design. There has been a lot of study done on the validity and reliability of questionnaires used in performance assessments of managerial levels, but users are not sure whether their data is valid or not, yet (Before, it was observed that respondents used steady responses due to boring shapes of the options in questionnaire). This matter has a direct effect on projects or processes you are going to do. This paper considers a questionnaire using in performance assessment of managerial levels in a large company, and presents a new form of questionnaire which combines 5-point Likert scale with competencies definitions. New questionnaire is able to solve some problems in assessment of performance such as invalid data and low return rate. Cronbach's alpha (reliability of this questionnaire) using SPSS software is 0.891.

articles.title: From Division to Action? Mobilizing Women Through Gender Inequality Framing
articles.authors: Colette Marcellin
articles.abstract: Though American women face significant economic, political, and social inequality, it has been far more challenging to mobilize women around this inequality than some other groups. In this paper, I use a multi-method approach to causally examine how women respond to mobilization efforts from women's movements and organizations. First, in a survey experiment, I find that frames that raise awareness of gender inequality and emphasize the need to build on women's progress significantly influence women's participatory intentions and political attitudes. To examine effects among those who are already engaged around issues of inequality, I then conduct a field experiment with a women's political organization. Results from this study suggest more mixed effects of outreach about gender inequality and progress, with null effects on email engagement yet increases in donation behavior. This paper has important implications for academic research on political behavior and applied strategies to engage women in the context of recent social movements and elections.

articles.title: Branding at the Water’s Edge: Perceived Elite Polarization of Ukraine Aid, 2022–2024
articles.authors: Haoran Shi; Wanting Wang; Dario Krpan
articles.abstract: United States assistance to Ukraine began with broad bipartisan support and acquired a durable partisan structure within eighteen months. We treat that transformation as a naturally occurring case for observing party brand formation, which requires parties both to occupy distinct positions and to speak about those positions consistently. Drawing on 37,312 sentences from 11,819 news articles published between March 2022 and December 2024, we annotated each sentence on one general aid dimension and three explanatory dimensions using a large language model, masking party and politician references so that positions were recovered from what a sentence conveys rather than from prior association with a party. Aggregating to articles and then to months produced continuous series of between-party polarization and within-party message coherence as represented in news coverage, which we combined into a Party Brand Index. Polarization on General Ukraine Aid Stance increased, with the fitted gap between the final and initial months widening by 11.71 points, and it did so through three persistent level shifts rather than gradual drift. Both parties moved toward opposition and Republicans moved further. Among the explanatory dimensions, the framing that set foreign commitments against domestic priorities aligned most closely with the aid stance gap, although that ordering did not survive dependence-preserving resampling. Neither party's message coherence tracked polarization from month to month, yet Republican coverage converged substantially across the period while Democratic coverage did not. Brand formation was therefore neither smooth, nor symmetric, nor synchronized, and the two conditions a brand requires advanced within the same party on different schedules.

articles.title: How Segregation Fuels the Far Right: Higher-Educated Social Relationships Buffer the Politically Radicalizing Effect of Economic Insecurity
articles.authors: Jona de Jong; Tarek Jaziri-Arjona
articles.abstract:
In recent decades, economic insecurity has driven some lower-educated voters
to the far right, while others have not moved. We argue that segregation explains
this variation: Higher-educated friends and relatives hold relatively progressive
views and norms against the far right, preventing lower-educated citizens from
politically translating economic insecurity into far-right support. Using existing
panel data from the Netherlands and original data from the U.S. and Germany,
we find that lower-educated individuals in higher-educated networks are much less
likely to respond to economic insecurity by moving to the far right. Differential
access to economic resources does not explain this effect. Rather, novel network
modules and an experimental manipulation of network salience show that network
education levels condition how individuals politicize insecurity. These findings show
that others affect how we make political sense of change, and suggest that societal
resilience against growing far-right appeal depends on the mutual integration of its
citizens.

articles.title: Exploring the relationship between Productivity and Healthcare Systems
articles.authors: Nerhum Sandambi
articles.abstract: The approach explored the relationship between the Productivity and healthcare systems, particularly applied to developing Countries. Main results show that, majority Countries in developing worlds, do not have particularly the strongest affirmation and capacity to create and generate a strong healthcare systems. The majority societies are stunk in developing. These Countries in particular, have for example, a high level of Inefficiency to allocate the public expenditure to the sector in particular. However, the study shows that countries with weak healthcare systems are, naturally, the countries that have a lower labour productivity. Furthermore, this evidence is particularly enough to help understand how for example most developing Countries do not intend the respective expenditure to guarantee high quality healthcare systems and to improve health to society in particular, on the other hand, the existence of a high level of budget in these countries increases the healthcare systems in general. Thus, many of these Countries, the lowest level of healthcare expenditure, show that these Countries are naturally incapable to drive social protection in particular. On the other hand, when this evidence is particularly characterized, the Country does not improve for example the economic performance. Furthermore, high quality institutions, mainly the political institutions for example, help naturally to increase the quality of healthcare systems in general.

articles.title: The Competitiveness and WellFair: An approach of Angola Competitiveness Fail
articles.authors: Nerhum Sandambi
articles.abstract: Competitiveness can, in particular, be a powerful means of improving efficiency and the high quality of products on offer, which significantly drive the market and naturally ensure the greatest possible diversity of products available. On the other hand, some countries, such as Angola, and other developing countries, naturally exhibit a significant lack of a competitive environment; this is further evidenced, for example, by the weak business environment that exists. The weakness of the private sector further helps to explain this situation; for example, in Angola, the two most significant companies are state-owned enterprises, which naturally ensure high and significant sustainability for the Angolan economy as a whole. On the other hand, the strong presence of the informal economy contributes to the creation of a poor competitive environment. Certain fundamental conditions are naturally identified as other key factors contributing to this economic inefficiency, chiefly the lack of adequate economic infrastructure. In many key industries, there is naturally a high degree of concentration; for example, in the telecommunications sector, where Unitel holds the majority share of the market. This concentration, in particular, typically leads to a high level of inefficiency in the services provided. Other services, such as water supply and electricity distribution, naturally exhibit high levels of concentration within the economy; these concentrations are, in particular, reinforced by the nature of the companies involved, the majority of which are public enterprises. Thus, in general, the analysis shows that high levels of industry concentration reduce the diversity of key products on offer and contribute significantly to negative impacts on overall welfare. In Angola in particular, this evidence is strongly consistent with the lack of local production, as the majority of basic needs are met through imported goods. According to the evidence, the absence of a strong competitive environment leads the market towards the emergence of negative externalities.

articles.title: HORMUZ STRAIT GEOPOLITICAL DISRUPTIONS AND PERSONAL FINANCIAL VULNERABILITY: A Case Study of Mid-Career Professionals in India's Private Higher Education Sector (2019-2024)
articles.authors: Jainish Bhagat
articles.abstract: Geopolitical disruptions in critical maritime infrastructure create ripple effects throughout economies, affecting not just international trade but also individual household financial security. This study examines how the Hormuz Strait tensions (2019-2024) impacted personal financial management decisions among mid-career professionals (35-50 years old) employed in India's private university sector. Using mixed-methods research combining survey data (N=847 respondents across 23 private universities in India) and longitudinal financial records, we document that geopolitical uncertainty increased personal financial stress markers by 34-42%, with impacts concentrated among professionals with high exposure to import-dependent sectors, international travel, or savings in foreign currency. We identify three financial vulnerability channels: (1) increased cost-of-living pressures (rising inflation, higher education costs), (2) income volatility (uncertain salary increments, job insecurity), and (3) behavioral shifts (increased precautionary savings, risk-averse investment decisions, delayed major financial commitments). Heterogeneous effects are substantial: professionals in oil-sector-dependent cities experienced 56% higher financial stress; those with daughters in higher education abroad reported 27% greater concern about rupee depreciation. We propose targeted policy interventions including employer-provided geopolitical risk hedging, financial literacy programs emphasizing crisis management, and institutional mechanisms for salary stability during global shocks. This research bridges macroeconomic disruption literature with personal finance vulnerability, contributing to understanding of how global events transmit into household-level financial decision-making in emerging markets.

articles.title: Application of Justice in Nepal: A Case Study of  Rape Criminal Cases
articles.authors: Nirmal Gurung
articles.abstract: Legally Nepal has come a long way in addressing sexual violence, but there is a huge gap between the law in the books and the justice in reality.
