Rape cases in Nepal are showing disturbing trend. There are strict laws in place, but victims often face apathy, delay and systemic roadblocks that deny them the justice they deserve. Studies show that 70 to 90 percent of sexual violence incidents go unreported, due to fear of stigma, retaliation and lack of faith in the justice system. This case study examines the application of justice in rape criminal cases in Nepal by analysing the legal framework, statistical trends, landmark cases, systemic challenges and voices of survivors who continue to fight for justice.

articles.title: Authoritarian Lenses and the Dynamics of Exclusion: The Radical Right in Chile
articles.authors: Lisa Zanotti; Fabian Villalobos-Machuca; Francisco Roldán Duque; Joaquín Valenzuela-Pastén; Sofía Cuadra
articles.abstract: This chapter examines the Chilean radical right through conceptual lenses developed primarily in the European context, using the case to assess the limits of those categories beyond their region of origin. It advances two conceptual claims. First, drawing on Stenner (2005), it argues that authoritarianism is better understood not as an ideology on a par with nativism, but as an individual predisposition activated by perceived normative threat — a lens through which social change is interpreted rather than a fixed doctrine. Second, it argues that nativism, understood as the fusion of nationalism and xenophobia in defence of ethnic homogeneity, is too narrow for a region where migration flows involve culturally proximate populations, and that civic-cultural nationalism captures the Chilean case more accurately. The chapter traces the rise of José Antonio Kast and the Republican Party and the subsequent emergence of the Libertarian Party and Team Patriota, and shows how authoritarian predispositions combine with nationalist, anti-feminist and anti-communist frames to construct migrants, feminists, sexual minorities and leftist actors as outgroups.

articles.title: How Do Voters Respond to Gradual Climate Costs?  Evidence from the Insurance Crisis
articles.authors: Eric Scheuch
articles.abstract: Climate change is transforming the U.S. economy in gradual but increasingly impactful ways. Existing literature on climate shocks and economic transformation is poorly positioned to explain how these gradual costs shape opinions and behavior. I study this through the U.S. home insurance market. Using panel data (2016–2024) and 246 million insurance records, I show voters recognize the insurance crisis and shift away from homeownership in response, but that rate increases do not significantly change climate opinions. With original survey data, I explain why: voters fail to attribute insurance costs to climate change and to connect insurance to climate policy. I trace this gap to the information environment: analysis of posts from 3,000 public officials and 2.9 million news articles shows that neither officials nor media frequently link insurance to climate change. These findings advance understanding of how gradual climate costs are—and are not—reshaping American opinion and behavior.

articles.title: Co-Writing the Self: Conversational AI as a Reflective Partner in Narrative Identity Reconstruction
articles.authors: Reginah Pearl Malebogo Lerubisi
articles.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in writing and reflective practice, yet limited empirical research has examined how sustained interaction with conversational AI may mediate narrative identity. This study explores how ongoing engagement with ChatGPT shaped self-reflection, authorship, authenticity, and the interpretation of lived experience. Guided by an interpretivist paradigm, the study employed analytic autoethnography based on sustained interaction with ChatGPT across a purposively bounded longitudinal conversational corpus on academic, professional, and personal contexts. Conversational transcripts and reflective journal records were analysed using Reflexive Thematic Narrative Analysis, integrating Narrative Identity Theory and Post-Phenomenology. Analysis identified interconnected processes through which ChatGPT shifted from an information tool towards a reflective conversational partner, supported narrative integration, mediated reflection and decision-making, and prompted ongoing negotiation of authenticity and human authorship. ChatGPT contributed linguistic formulation, conceptual organisation, and alternative interpretive possibilities; however, experiential ownership, evaluative authority, and ethical responsibility remained with the researcher. The study develops the Human–AI Narrative Co-Construction Framework (HANCF) to conceptualise narrative reconstruction as a recursive process of AI-mediated reflection governed by human evaluative and narrative authority. The findings suggest that conversational AI may participate in narrative identity reconstruction without possessing narrative identity or displacing human authorship. The study contributes an autoethnographic account of sustained human–AI interaction and offers a framework for understanding how reflective partnership with conversational AI may extend human meaning-making while preserving experiential and ethical authority.

articles.title: Algorithmic Patriarchy: Artificial Intelligence, the Feminisation of Poverty, and the Limits of Governance
articles.authors: Azucena Carrasco-Toronjo
articles.abstract: Nearly fifty years after Diana Pearce named the feminisation of poverty, the systems now deciding who gets hired, credited, or cared for were trained on the same discourse that has kept it in place. Patriarchal capitalist structures have long depended on women's unpaid labour while excluding women from the rewards of the economy they sustain. Neoliberal governance extended that arrangement, swapping a structural vocabulary of poverty for one of resilience, self-improvement, and personal responsibility. The neoliberal discourse brought the shrinking of the welfare state, and with it, a new vocabulary that spread from policy papers to self-help writing, human resources content, and coaching material. It has been produced at internet scale for four decades through the same text now training large language models (LLMs). Currently, this new vocabulary is embedded in the systems that screen résumés, and intertwined with the caseworkers who draft eligibility determinations. To understand algorithmic patriarchy and its relationship with the feminisation of poverty, this paper connects two bodies of scholarship: work on how neoliberal governance produces individualising discourse, and work on how AI systems inherit bias from training data. My contribution is to name and trace the mechanism by which patriarchy, neoliberalism, and unconscious bias combine to produce a vocabulary, reproduced by artificial intelligence systems, that may sustain the feminisation of poverty. Current governance frameworks audit outcomes but not the discourse producing them. This paper argues that language matters, and that identifying the unconscious bias it carries is a precondition for its measurement and correction – the basis on which governance bodies can design policies bypassing their own invisible limitations.

articles.title: The AI Governance Execution Gap: Organizational Readiness as a Condition for Ethical AI Governance
articles.authors: Jessica Jo Montgomery
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence governance frameworks increasingly specify accountability, human oversight, risk management, transparency, and lifecycle monitoring, but formal adoption does not establish that an organization can carry those commitments into consequential operational decisions. This conceptual paper argues that organizational readiness is a necessary condition for ethical AI governance. It defines the Governance Execution Gap as the distance between governance expectations and the institutional capacity to exercise decision authority, route risk, produce evidence, monitor deployed systems, and intervene when conditions change. Drawing on organizational readiness theory, the Technology-Organization-Environment framework, established AI governance standards and policy, and scholarship on translating AI ethics principles into practice, the paper develops an AI Governance Readiness Framework with five interdependent domains and corresponding Governance Execution Gates. It also introduces an Accountability Gap that distinguishes visibility, assigned responsibility, decision authority, and practical capacity to act. The central normative claim is that accountability and human oversight are ethically meaningful only when organizations can make those responsibilities executable under real operating conditions. A practitioner-oriented scorecard and illustrative cybersecurity triage scenario demonstrate how the model may support decisions without claims of empirical validation. The framework is proposed as a testable conceptual model for future empirical evaluation across high-consequence environments.

articles_hidden.title: Natural Hazards Threat and Early Marriage for Women and Girls in Latin America and the Caribbean
articles_hidden.authors: Boyoon Lee; Guilherme Natan Fasolin; Ted Hsuan Yun Chen
articles_hidden.abstract: Natural hazards threat can shift marriage practices in ways that systematically harm young women and girls, as post-disaster conditions incentivize families to marry off daughters as an adaptation response against economic and physical insecurity. We study this link using geolocated representative samples from 15 countries in Latin America and the Caribbean, a region with one of the highest early marriage rates in the world. We show that exposure to natural hazards is associated with higher prevalence of marriage among women under 18 and increased acceptance of these marriage practices among the general population. This relationship is mitigated by strong government institutions, which was previously unobserved in other regions. Our study demonstrates that rational climate adaptation behaviors at the household level can exacerbate within-household distributional inequalities, emphasizing the need for stronger institutional support structures that provide equitable means of adaptation.

articles_hidden.title: Electricity Patronage and the Energy Transition: Indonesia in Comparative Perspective
articles_hidden.authors: Johnathan Guy
articles_hidden.abstract: Governments across the Global South are choosing between clean electricity or fossil fuels. Electricity procurement regimes—the practices governing how governments and utilities allocate generation contracts and associated rents—are a critical and overlooked determinant of this choice. Using Indonesia as a theory-building case, I argue that the programmatic character of electricity procurement shapes whether governments can credibly commit to renewable energy producers, select least-cost projects, and provide the collective goods renewables require to scale. Patronage-based procurement regimes, in contrast, systematically favor fossil fuels. I trace Indonesia’s coal entrenchment to its patronage-based procurement regime, in which clientelist party competition, weak executive constraints, and failed reforms concentrated discretion in the state-owned utility PLN, which operated as a broker for the ruling coalition. Comparative cases in India and South Africa show how programmatic reforms enabled renewable scale-up despite similarly powerful fossil fuel incumbents. The findings advance a meso-level account that bridges the comparative politics literature on patronage and the study of global energy transitions.

articles_hidden.title: ICT, Sustainable Development and Job Polarization: Evidence from ECOWAS
articles_hidden.authors: Dennis Nchor
articles_hidden.abstract: This paper assesses the contribution of information and communication technology (ICT) to sustainable development and job polarization in the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS). Panel pooled mean group models are used to assess the role of ICT in sustainable development whereas changes in employment shares of the International Standard Classification of Occupations (ISCO08) occupations are used to investigate the changing employment distribution in the labor markets in the region. The results show that all measures of ICT had a positive and significant impact on sustainable development. The paper also finds that the West African countries are lagging in terms of ICT adoption and ICT infrastructure. The pace of adoption is slower compared to developed countries thus minimizing the pace of job polarization. The results obtained found no u-shaped employment distribution in the countries to indicate job polarization. Significantly however, there is a decline in the share of employment of the agriculture, forestry and fishery sectors. The decline in the share of employment is however offset by rising employment shares of most middle-skilled occupations in the region.

articles_hidden.title: Radiografía de la Accesibilidad Digital Municipal en Chile 2026
articles_hidden.authors: Jaime Elorrieta
articles_hidden.abstract:
La digitalización de los servicios municipales en Chile promete acercar el Estado a la
ciudadanía, pero revela una barrera crítica: la exclusión por diseño. Hoy, el acceso a la
información pública digital no es universal. Este informe expone los resultados de una
auditoría de accesibilidad web bajo estándares WCAG 2.1, aplicada a veinte plataformas
municipales de las regiones Metropolitana y del Maule. El estudio delimitó su alcance a
versiones de escritorio ya que esto permite establecer una línea base sobre la calidad del
código estructural. El objetivo fue medir empíricamente las barreras que aíslan a personas con
discapacidad visual y motriz, sugiriendo replicar esta metodología en futuros estudios
móviles.Los hallazgos revelan que la exclusión digital es sistémica y no obedece estrictamente a una
falta de presupuesto. Se detectó un severo bloqueo a la navegación motriz: el 50% de la
muestra no puede operarse mediante teclado, impidiendo el acceso a personas con
discapacidad motriz severa o usuarios de lectores de pantalla. Esta exclusión se agudiza en la
Región del Maule, donde el 60% reprueba esta métrica. A esto se suma una profunda brecha de
diseño visual, con 573 errores críticos de contraste lumínico que invisibilizan los textos para
personas con baja visión. Aunque el Maule presenta un 62% más de errores que la
Metropolitana, comunas de altos ingresos como Providencia y Las Condes también
reprobaron, demostrando que se prioriza la estética corporativa por sobre la legibilidad
universal.Finalmente, existen graves deficiencias en la gestión de contenidos. Destaca una invisibilidad
de la información operativa y transversal, al sumar más de 440 imágenes sin textos
alternativos (ALT), censurando el contenido gráfico para usuarios con ceguera. Además, se
advierte un fenómeno de accesibilidad performativa: el 20% de la muestra usa widgets o
botones flotantes que generan una falsa ilusión de inclusión. En la práctica, estas
herramientas institucionales no solucionan el código base excluyente generando nuevos
conflictos de interfaz para quienes dependen de tecnologías de asistencia.

articles_hidden.title: El Encuadre de la Responsabilidad Ciudadana: Comunicación Digital del Servel en la Elección Presidencial y Parlamentaria 2025
articles_hidden.authors: Jaime Elorrieta
articles_hidden.abstract:
Los organismos electorales enfrentan un desafío comunicacional distinto al de los partidos o candidaturas: deben informar y movilizar al electorado sin abandonar su mandato de neutralidad. Este informe examina cómo el Servicio Electoral de Chile (Servel) resolvió ese desafío en su publicidad digital durante la elección presidencial y parlamentaria de 2025, a partir del análisis de 101 anuncios publicados en Google Ads y Meta Ads.
Los resultados muestran que la comunicación del Servel es abrumadoramente práctica: el 85,1% de los anuncios se centra en información procedimental —dónde votar, qué documentos llevar, cómo revisar el rol de vocal de mesa— por sobre la apelación emocional, cívica o sancionatoria. Contra lo esperable, el tono no escala hacia la urgencia a medida que se acerca la elección; en cambio, mensajes puntuales como el llamado al deber cívico o la alerta contra la desinformación aparecen concentrados en momentos específi cos de la campaña, no en un crescendo progresivo. La advertencia sobre multas por no votar, pese a ser un rasgo central del sistema electoral chileno, ocupa un lugar marginal (3% de la muestra) en la comunicación digital del organismo.

articles_hidden.title: Donor Responses to Civil Society Repression
articles_hidden.authors: Andrew Heiss; Suparna Chaudhry
articles_hidden.abstract: This chapter examines donor responses to the global crackdown on civil society, where governments use legal measures to repress NGOs. Donors, including bilateral and multilateral agencies, respond variably; bilateral aid often decreases following anti-NGO laws, while multilateral aid remains stable. Private donors' responses depend on factors like social trust and NGO transparency. NGOs adapt by diversifying funding, forming affiliates, or shifting to community-based support. As the space for civil society continues to shrink, coordinated international efforts are essential to counteract these repressive trends and uphold civil society's role in democratic governance.

articles_hidden.title: Evaluating the Theory of the AnthroShift:  How are Climate Shocks Related to Civic Engagement and Support for Climate Science in the US?
articles_hidden.authors: Dana R Fisher; Arman Azedi
articles_hidden.abstract: Since the theory of the AnthroShift was introduced in 2019, it has been increasingly seen as a theoretical lens through which to analyze social responses to climate change. This paper builds on this small but growing literature to assess the AnthroShift at the individual level.  We analyze a new dataset collected from a national sample of adults in the US to understand how experiencing climate shocks is associated with climate-change supportive attitudes and behaviors.  Specifically, we look at how self-reported experiences with climate shocks are associated with heightened levels of civic engagement and support for the science that documents climate change.  This paper is separated into three sections.  First, we review the theory of the AnthroShift, which explains how risk pivots can drive environmental behaviors, and connect it with the growing research that assesses the social effects of climate shocks.  Next, we describe our data, which were collected from a nationally representative sample of adults in the US in fall 2025 (n=1,068).  Third, we present the results of our analysis that document how individuals’ experience with climate shocks is strongly associated with civic and political engagement and support for climate science.  The paper concludes by discussing the implications of our findings for the relationship between climate shocks, attitudes, and behaviors, as well as for our understanding of the society-environment relationship and the sociological theory of the AnthroShift.

articles_hidden.title: When Belonging Comes Before Belief: Inherited Identity, Social Conformity, and the Difficulty of Looking Outside the Group
articles_hidden.authors: Syed Raheel Shahzad
articles_hidden.abstract:
People normally receive an identity before they are old enough to examine it. A child is born into a family, a language, a religious or non-religious environment, and a set of trusted authorities. By the time the person is able to compare different beliefs, one position already feels familiar and the others often feel foreign. This essay asks a simple social question: how much of what we defend comes from examination, and how much comes from belonging?

The argument is not that inherited beliefs are false, or that following experts is irrational. It is that social identity can make some questions costly to ask. Family ties, community approval, reputation, and fear of exclusion can narrow the range of views people seriously examine. A recent personal example from British Muslim life is used to illustrate the problem: communities with access to the same modern information may still follow different inherited authorities when deciding religious dates.

The wider point applies beyond religion. Political, national, family, and professional identities can work in the same way. The essay argues that genuine conviction is stronger when a person can examine alternatives without having to lose the social world to which he or she belon

articles_hidden.title: Research on Han Nationalism in China in the 2020s (VI): The Social Foundations, Core Demands, and Future Trajectory of Han Nationalism
articles_hidden.authors: ZY Liu
articles_hidden.abstract:
After 2020, discussions related to Han nationalism in Chinese online space have increased markedly and have gradually become an important topic for understanding contemporary Chinese ethnic identification, historical narratives, and social contradictions. As the final article in this series of studies, the present paper attempts, from the angles of demographic change, resource allocation, ethnic policy, and national identification, to analyze the social background of the emergence and development of Han nationalism. The article argues that Han nationalism does not simply originate from historical sentiment, but is a form of identity-political expression formed in the process of change in Chinese social structure. With the decline in birth rates, adjustments in the mode of economic growth, and increases in social competitive pressure, some groups have begun to reopen discussion of the fairness of ethnic policy, the boundaries of the national community, and the relations of responsibility and interest among different groups. The article further organizes the principal demands advanced by some Han nationalists, including the abolition of preferential policies based on ethnic identity, renewed discussion of relations of autonomy and fiscal transfer in ethnic regions, and the improvement of social security for lower- and middle-strata groups. At the same time, the article analyzes the possible positive effects of Han nationalism—for example, pushing long-neglected questions into public discussion, emphasizing the principle of civic equality, and strengthening the sense of social responsibility of the majority group. Yet the article also points out that this body of thought possesses potential risks such as ethnicizing complex social problems, neglecting intra-ethnic class differences, and intensifying logics of group competition.
This article does not attempt simply to affirm or negate Han nationalism; rather, it hopes, by organizing its internal logic and social background, to provide an exploratory analytical framework for understanding changes in Chinese ethnic identification after 2020.

articles_hidden.title: When Full Employment Is No Longer Necessary
articles_hidden.authors: Hong-Ming Chen
articles_hidden.abstract: Artificial intelligence may reduce the economic necessity of some forms of cognitive labour faster than employment and social institutions can reorganize the time, identity and roles that work currently structures. Rather than forecasting mass unemployment, we ask what should be tested if that transition arrives unevenly or abruptly: how people are received after occupational loss, how newly available time becomes genuinely self-directed, whether AI can make heterogeneous, voluntary arrangements administratively feasible without turning personalization into obligation, whether unmet human needs can support voluntary new roles, and what it costs to keep the human last mile human. Employment organizes more than income, so occupational displacement is an institutional problem as well as an economic one. We set out a sequence — receive, stabilize, recover, choose — in which recovery is a legitimate state rather than a delay before activation, and in which voluntary reconnection is one possible exit among many. The central proposition is offered as a hypothesis rather than a finding: full employment may have functioned partly as a technology of standardization, while AI could make heterogeneity administratively affordable. Because the same capacity could also produce a more efficient workfare machine, we propose personalization without compulsory optimization as a governing constraint. AI may make matching cheap without making human contact cheap.

articles_hidden.title: Defaulting to Decarbonization?  Financial Insolvency and the Energy Transition in India’s States
articles_hidden.authors: Johnathan Guy
articles_hidden.abstract:
How do financial constraints shape the energy transition in developing countries? I study this question in India, where electricity procurement is governed at the subnational level. Electoral politics motivates state governments to subsidize electricity consumption, resulting in financial stress for electricity distribution utilities (DISCOMs). Using multiple sources of original data on utility and plant operations, I investigate the relationship between financial distress and decarbonization. I theorize that the effect of utility insolvency depends on the margin considered—dispatch vs. capacity investment—and on institutions. Counterintuitively, but consistent with my theory, I find that financial stress is associated in the short run with greater relative procurement of renewable energy and less procurement of fossil fuels. Mechanism tests suggest that coal dispatch is more sensitive to liquidity constraints, as distressed DISCOMs cut back on coal deliveries while renewable energy remains protected by “must-run” dispatch regulations. In contrast, I find at most weak evidence that insolvency raises challenges for decarbonizing electricity in the long run: insolvency shows no relationship with renewable-energy tendering, only suggestive evidence that it slows renewable capacity investment, and similarly weak evidence that it curtails expansion of transmission lines that renewables need to scale. The results qualify the conventional wisdom that electricity utility
insolvency is a binding constraint on the energy transition.

articles_hidden.title: When Are Asymmetric Fixed-Effects Models Within-Person Tests of Reversibility? Heterogeneous Responses and Bidirectional Support
articles_hidden.authors: Jiwon Lee
articles_hidden.abstract: Asymmetric fixed-effects models are increasingly used in sociological research to test whether an effect reverses when a time-varying predictor changes direction. Because these models rely on within-person change, directional asymmetry is often interpreted as evidence of within-person irreversibility. This study shows that this interpretation requires an additional cross-person homogeneity assumption. I reparameterize Allison’s (2019) cumulative asymmetric fixed-effects model exactly as a model of current state and total movement, revealing that the specification pools current-state responses across individuals. When those responses are heterogeneous and systematically related to who moves upward versus downward, pooled asymmetry can arise even when every individual’s response is perfectly reversible. I derive this mover-composition result and characterize what remains identifiable when individual state responses are unrestricted. A common path response—the additional response associated with accumulated movement conditional on current state—can then be identified only from within-person bidirectional movement, provided that the resulting variation is not absorbed by period effects. Monte Carlo simulations and a reanalysis of Allison’s wage example illustrate the resulting assumption–support–precision trade-off and show that relevant support depends on the structure of observed trajectories, not simply on the number of directional transitions.

articles_hidden.title: Greenhouse Gas Mitigation and Climate Change Adaptation: Some Policy Alternatives for Nepal
articles_hidden.authors: Ambika P. Adhikari
articles_hidden.abstract: Many scientists consider climate change to be the most important environmental issue of this century. Although some controversy lingers about the extent of anthropogenic contribution to global warming, most scientists and experts agree that, due to the increased greenhouse gases (GHG) in the atmosphere, Earth’s average temperature is gradually rising, and the ensuing climate change is causing significant and mostly negative impacts on the environment and human population. Various studies show that average global temperatures have already risen by 0.8 degrees Celsius over pre-industrial levels. Scientists estimate that at this rate, the average temperatures are likely to rise by at least about 2 degrees Celsius by the end of the century. It is widely believed that a rise of more than 2 degrees Celsius in the average global temperature can bring serious adverse impacts to the global ecosystem and human welfare.

articles_hidden.title: Ukrainian Refugees in Switzerland: A research synthesis of what we know
articles_hidden.authors: Didier Ruedin
articles_hidden.abstract: The objective of this research synthesis is to collect and summarize the research literature on Ukrainian refugees in Switzerland. This is done through a systematic review, mostly in the form of a narrative review and with statistical indicators that are synthesized. Graphical summaries and an evidence gap map are provided to better identify the nature of evidence available and highlight areas where comparatively little is known about Ukrainian refugees in Switzerland. There is a wide range of evidence on Ukrainian refugees in Switzerland and their integration, although substantive and systematic gaps remain. The review provides a brief historical background, looks at the demographic composition of Ukrainian refugees in Switzerland, discusses economic integration, housing, education, social integration, crime and safety, health and well-being, and attitudes to Ukrainian refugees. Where feasible, changes over time are discussed. The demographic profile of Ukrainian refugees (many women, many children and elderly people, highly educated) is well documented, as are challenges to economic integration due to an insecure status and limited knowledge of local languages. Much less is known about cultural integration and political participation, for example. Given the size of the population and the ongoing war in Ukraine, more research on Ukrainian refugees is warranted, particularly in the direction of successful integration in a context where return in the near future seems increasingly unlikely, despite so-called dual-intent remaining the official focus. More research is also warranted in areas beyond economic integration that affect well-being and intentions to return.

articles_hidden.title: Vanishing Vanguard:  Decline of Leadership in Revolutionary Mass Mobilization  since the 19th Century
articles_hidden.authors: Vadim Ustyuzhanin; Julia Zinkina; Andrey Korotayev
articles_hidden.abstract: “Leaderlessness” is widely held to be a defining feature of contemporary mass mobilization, yet the claim rests on a handful of recent cases. We offer the first systematic cross-national analysis of this phenomenon from 1791 to 2019. We show that the absence of leadership is real but older and more modest than claimed: the share of campaigns / revolutions lacking discernible leadership has been rising for two centuries, yet in the 21st century only about a half are leaderless. Testing six explanations drawn from the literature, we find that two factors robustly predict the absence of leadership: student participation and democracy & human-rights goals, that is, “thin” ideology in contrast to “thick” ideologies of the past. We detect no significant effect of coalition breadth, nonviolent tactic, and internet use on leadership. Thus, leaderless mobilization is rooted in who mobilizes and what they demand, but not in scale, tactics, or technology.

articles_hidden.title: La deuda que no murió: el convenio de pago que no nova, la fuerza de sentencia del mandamiento y el incidente que no puede matar al juicio ejecutivo (comentario a la sentencia de la Corte Suprema de 2 de junio de 2025, rol N° 38.560-2024)
articles_hidden.authors: Andrés Gabriel Varas Quijón
articles_hidden.abstract:
La Corte Suprema, conociendo de un recurso de casación en el fondo, invalidó de oficio —en
ejercicio de las facultades correctoras del artículo 84 del Código de Procedimiento Civil— la resolución
que, acogiendo un incidente de alzamiento de embargo, había puesto término a un juicio ejecutivo bancario
fundándose en un convenio de pago celebrado tres años después de trabada la ejecución (Primera Sala, 2 de
junio de 2025, rol N° 38.560-2024, redacción de la ministra señora Repetto). La doctrina del fallo es de
manual y de trinchera a la vez: si el ejecutado no opuso excepciones, el mandamiento de ejecución y
embargo adquiere, por el artículo 472, la virtud procesal de una sentencia firme; y el convenio posterior —
que en su propio texto declaraba no producir novación, constituir una mera modalidad o facilidad de pago y
extinguir las obligaciones solo con el pago íntegro— no altera la exigibilidad del título ni autoriza a matar el
procedimiento por vía incidental. El comentario reconstruye el caso —un pagaré de $5,6 millones
convertido, por obra del interés, en un convenio de $27,7 millones—, sistematiza la ratio sobre los artículos
472 y 437 del Código de Procedimiento Civil y 1628, 1634 y 1649 del Código Civil, examina el flanco
olvidado de las cauciones de terceros ante las esperas, destila las cláusulas de blindaje que salvaron el juicio
del banco y cierra con un decálogo del ejecutante prudente. La tesis: el juicio ejecutivo solo muere por pago,
por sentencia o por acto conclusivo expreso — quien calló las excepciones no puede, años después, gritar
convenios.

articles_hidden.title: A cautionary tale of industrial decline, economic grievances, and far-right voting
articles_hidden.authors: Philipp Kerler; Valentina Petrović
articles_hidden.abstract: Economic grievances are central in explaining the rise of right-wing illiberalism. Grievances allow challenger parties to rally around scapegoating outsider groups, such as ethnic minorities, immigrants, or foreigners. Some research argues that continuing decline allows illiberal parties to consolidate power by entrenching and polarizing around such cleavages. However, when illiberal parties are in power and economic decline continues, we argue that, absent cultural cleavages, retrospective economic voting prevails. Zooming in on the case of Trstenik, a Serbian town with a significant industrial legacy, strongly affected by deindustrialization, we leverage data from a novel survey and semi-structured interviews in a mixed-methods approach. We document clear patterns of existing grievances and blame on the government. However, positive, hopeful interpretations also exist among affected individuals. We show that support for the illiberal right-wing incumbent Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) is positively associated with positive interpretations and negatively associated with grievances. Our study contributes an important qualifying account to current debates about the economic roots of right-wing illiberalism by highlighting the importance of scope conditions.

articles_hidden.title: Making the Case for an Experiential Approach to Test Validation
articles_hidden.authors: Sergio Araneda; Stephen Sireci
articles_hidden.abstract: This paper introduces the Experiential Approach to test validation (Araneda, 2023; Araneda & Sireci, 2021), a framework grounded in phenomenology, rhetorical argumentation, and participatory epistemologies. Departing from traditional validation models centered on psychometric inference and technical justification, the Experiential Approach treats the lived experiences of test-takers and stakeholders as primary sources of validity inquiry. Drawing on standpoint theory, situated knowledges, and participatory action research, it reconceptualizes assessment as a system of interrelated devices whose validity depends on how they function in context. The paper contrasts this framework with Kane's argument-based approach, emphasizing its recursive, device-centered structure and its use of normative, functional, comparative, and critical lenses for generating validity claims. It also examines unresolved challenges concerning stakeholder negotiation, face validity, and the political limits of experiential critique. The paper contributes to emerging efforts toward more context-sensitive, pluralistic, and ethically reflexive approaches to validation.

articles_hidden.title: Climate Barriers to Democratic Participation
articles_hidden.authors: Vítor Calafate; Francisco J M Costa; João Paulo Pessoa
articles_hidden.abstract: Climate change can reshape political representation not only by changing voters' preferences, but also by changing who can vote. Using georeferenced polling-station records from eight Brazilian elections (2010-2024) matched to daily river discharge, we show that historically low river discharge on election day increases voter abstention in communities that depend on river transportation. Effects are absent in comparable communities without river transport, consistent with disruption to fluvial access rather than a general drought effect on participation. Losses are larger among married voters and in sections with higher illiteracy rates, thereby shifting the electorate's composition. These shocks reduce votes for parties whose bases overlap with affected populations, redistributing political power along the lines of climate exposure.

articles_hidden.title: Record Linkage Error and Inference in Population Research
articles_hidden.authors: Casey Breen; Won-tak Joo
articles_hidden.abstract: The explosion in digitization of large-scale administrative data and advances in record linkage have opened up new possibilities for studying core topics in population research, including social mobility, early-life determinants of longevity, and shifts in ethnoracial identity. Much attention has been paid to improving record linkage algorithms, but methodological guidance for researchers analyzing linked data is limited. We propose a general framework to explain how different types of linkage errors—false matches and missed matches—impact inference with linked data and introduce a bias-correction method. We then conduct three empirical case studies on canonical topics in population research: social mobility, the education–longevity gradient, and shifts in ethnoracial identification. These case studies demonstrate the settings in which linkage errors do and do not meaningfully impact substantive research findings. We conclude with practical recommendations for researchers performing inference with linked data and provide an accompanying R package implementing the methods introduced in this paper.

articles_hidden.title: Sociotechnical Transition and Uncertainty in the Lithium Mining Industry: Technologies, Politics and Transparency
articles_hidden.authors: Iván Ojeda-Pereira; Sebastián Herrera-León; Marcelo Lufin; Fernando Campos-Medina
articles_hidden.abstract: Technological transitions in extractive industries are commonly assessed through technical and environmental performance, whilst their social and ethical dimensions receive little systematic attention. This article addresses that gap through the adoption of direct lithium extraction (DLE) technologies in Chile, the world’s second largest lithium producer and the leading producer from salt flats. The National Lithium Strategy promotes these technologies as a response to social tensions over the use of water and brine in fragile ecosystems, and the conditions of their implementation remain open. Drawing on interdisciplinary work between the engineering sciences and the social sciences, we ask which technological and social uncertainties experts identify in this transition. Two expert workshops were held with 20 participants from industry, the State and academia, and their contributions were examined through inductive qualitative content analysis. The findings show five uncertainties: (i) there is no consensus on which technologies will be implemented or on the criteria for choosing them; (ii) the effects of brine reinjection lack conclusive evidence; (iii) the role and agency of the State remain undetermined; (iv) no mapping exists of the actors regarded as valid participants in the debate; and (v) there is no agreement on how the social sustainability of this change should be measured. We propose five public information infrastructures as a design response to these uncertainties, whilst acknowledging that transparency is a necessary but not sufficient condition for ethical sociotechnical governance in the extractive industries of the Global South.

articles_hidden.title: Bowling Alone Was Never the Right Diagnosis: On Engineered Isolation and the Mathematics of Community Recovery
articles_hidden.authors: Gavilán Longino
articles_hidden.abstract:
In 2000, Robert Putnam documented a measurable decline in American social capital and named it a crisis. He explained how it happened, but not why. Without that explanation, there could be no real prescription for resolution. This paper argues that what Putnam observed was not cultural drift or technological change but a structural outcome. The systematic extraction of communal infrastructure from American life by market forces that profit from its absence was the mechanism driving the decline. The Social Nest is the term used here for what was lost: the web of informal, reciprocal relationships and shared spaces that historically provided resilience, childcare, elder support, food access, and psychological stability without market mediation. A mathematical framework represented by the Impact Curve is introduced for modeling the conditions under which community infrastructure can be rebuilt. Drawing on Centola et al.'s (2018) experimental confirmation of social tipping dynamics and Rogers' (2003) diffusion research, the framework identifies two critical thresholds (25% and 33% community adoption) that govern the momentum of cooperative formation. The Citadel is introduced as a proposed implementation model: a federated network of community pods designed to reconstitute the Social Nest at scale. This paper is explicitly theoretical. Its purpose is to provide a framework precise enough to test, and to invite the primary research that would validate or falsify its claims.

Keywords: social capital, cooperative economics, community development, tipping points, structural isolation, social nest, impact curve

articles_hidden.title: Exposure to Heat Stress Influences Educational Outcomes in Low- and Middle-Income Countries
articles_hidden.authors: J. Huntley Compton; Brian C. Thiede
articles_hidden.abstract: Environmental stressors have widespread and multi-dimensional impacts on human population dynamics and wellbeing.  A large literature has attempted to measure the effects of environmental shocks on human capital formation, including through studies of child nutrition and development, and there is growing interest in measuring environmental and climatic impacts on educational attainment itself. We advance this literature by linking data from the Multiple Indicator Cluster Surveys with district-level temperature records to measure the effects of heat exposures on educational outcomes across 29 countries. We assess both the medium-term and near-contemporaneous impacts of heat exposures. First, we evaluate how exposures from early life through age 14 are associated with the number of years of completed education among children ages 15-17 (n=307,614). Second, we measure the association between recent heat exposures and current school attendance among 5-17 year-olds (n=1,877,022). Temperature anomalies during the prenatal year through age 4 and between ages 10-14 are both associated with meaningful reductions in education by ages 15-17, with exposures to anomalies of +2 reducing education by 1.5-2.9 years (or approximately 28-53%). Recent temperature exposures were not associated with enrollment among 5-9 and 10-14 year-olds but unexpectedly increased the probability that 15-17 year-olds were enrolled in school. These results suggest that older children’s education may be protected against shocks in the short run but undermined by previous impacts on developmental and economic processes that unfold over multiple years.

articles_hidden.title: Covariate Adjustment in Political Science Experiments: Progress and Recommendations
articles_hidden.authors: Matthew H. Graham; Hai Binh H Hoang
articles_hidden.abstract: Covariate adjustment can reduce the standard error of experimental treatment effect estimates without increasing the sample size but is vulnerable to abuse unless a specific procedure is preregistered. We assess adjustment practices in ten political science journals in 2013, 2018, and 2023-24. Encouragingly, preregistration and covariate adjustment have each been rapidly adopted. Preregistration is also a good predictor of what practices are used in articles. However, just 12% of articles published in 2023-24 preregister a specific covariate adjustment procedure and use adjustment for the main estimate. Although preregistering an adjusted estimator is not always advisable (when covariates are unavailable or preregistration is not possible), there is substantial room for improvement. We recommend that when feasible, researchers preregister a specific covariate adjustment procedure and use it for their preferred estimate regardless of covariate balance. This may require a shift in preregistration culture away from predicting results and toward constraining analysis.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond the Right Answer: Measuring Ethical Logic in Large Language Models
articles_hidden.authors: W. Russell Neuman; Chad Coleman
articles_hidden.abstract:
Research on the ethical capacities of large language models has expanded rapidly, but the field remains conceptually fragmented. Some studies ask whether models agree with human moral judgments. Others examine moral values, developmental schemas, contextual norm recognition, resistance to framing, behavior under incentives, multimodal moral salience, or the perceived quality of model-generated advice. These approaches are often grouped under broad labels such as AI ethics, moral alignment, or moral reasoning, even though they measure substantially different constructs. This field is also distinct from much of the larger domain of LLM benchmarking because ethics does not generally provide ground truths that permit simple calculations of percent correct.

This article reviews an expanded inventory of assessment families designed to evaluate how large language models respond to ethical choices. Building on early reviews such as Snoswell, Kilov, and Lazar (2026), this article treats the assessment family rather than the individual paper as the unit of analysis. It organizes the literature into five ethical measurement (ETHMEAS) dimensions: moral reasoning structure, moral value orientation, alignment with human values, contextual norm understanding, and behavior, harm, and social reception. The review also identifies a separate but increasingly important mechanistic-interpretability literature that attempts to locate moral concepts, values, and ethical-framework pathways inside model activations.

The central claim is that the field is moving from outcome matching toward a more demanding investigation of ethical logic: the reproducible organization of moral attention, value prioritization, principle application, exception handling, justification, and conduct across changes in framing, language, context, modality, incentives, and internal intervention. A key conclusion is that a better understanding of the dynamics of LLM ethical logic informs our understanding of human ethical logic. The review identifies recurring validity challenges, including the transplantation of human psychometrics to language models, benchmark contamination, instability of model values, conflation of majority agreement with moral competence, and uncertainty about the relationship between explanations and underlying decision processes. ETHMEAS is proposed as a multidimensional framework for evaluating model ethical logic without reducing morality to a single score.

articles_hidden.title: Seeds of Change: Structural Transformations and Support for the Radical Right
articles_hidden.authors: Philipp Kerler; David Doyle; Victor Araújo
articles_hidden.abstract: The rise of the radical right is often attributed to economic disappointments rooted in structural transformations. However, these explanations frequently fail to extend beyond advanced democracies, where most structural changes differ. To advance the limited understanding of the political effects of structural transformations in countries of the Global South, we study the shift to high-intensity agricultural production in Brazil in the early 2000s. We argue that -- similar to electoral realignment in advanced democracies -- left majoritarian parties (in this case, the Brazilian Workers' Party, PT) losing the support of those left behind by structural change contributed significantly to Jair Bolsonaro's rise to power. At the same time, Bolsonaro's neoliberal appeals around revoking land protection and reducing trade barriers resonated with workers and farmers embedded in increasingly industrialized, export-oriented agriculture. Therefore, Bolsonaro garnered support from the winners and losers of structural transformation simultaneously. Contrary to the protectionist appeals of the radical right in the Global North, our research highlights the distinct role of neoliberal appeals for the success of the radical right in the Global South.

articles_hidden.title: Elite-Public Gaps on Salient Foreign Policy Issues: Experimental Evidence from the 2022/23 US Sanctions on Russia
articles_hidden.authors: Anton Peez; Felix Bethke; Felix S. Bethke
articles_hidden.abstract: Do citizens and political elites in Western democracies hold different views on foreign policy? ‘Elite-public gaps’ raise questions about whether elites represent public preferences and how much discretion they exercise. Research suggests that although gaps exist, they are significantly driven by ‘mundane’ compositional differences. We examine these gaps during the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine. We ran a paired experiment with US executive staffers (n = 253) and the US public (n = 1,002), asking whether respondents support increasing sanctions on Russia. We randomize information on real public polling highly supportive of sanctions. The public was less supportive than executive staffers at baseline, but more responsive to public opinion. Gaps shrink after accounting for basic sociodemographics. This extends research on elite-public gaps to cover salient real-world events.

articles_hidden.title: Digital Transformation and Strategic Adaptation in Small Businesses: Evidence from Local Interview Case Studies
articles_hidden.authors: Pranay Saripalli; Shaurya Yadav; Ayush Tripathi
articles_hidden.abstract: This qualitative case study examines how small businesses adapt to digital innovation, financial constraints, and external economic pressures. The study draws on structured in-person interviews with owners and representatives of three local businesses—Empxre, Bam Clothing, and American Hide—to examine how business owners assess the costs and benefits of digital adoption and sustain competitiveness amid changing market conditions. Existing research has established that small and medium-sized enterprise (SME) digitalization can improve business performance and customer engagement, but less attention has been given to the strategic reasoning that shapes individual firms’ adaptation decisions. The findings highlight the importance of aligning digital transformation with broader business strategy, customer needs, and available financial resources. Empxre demonstrates how an omnichannel approach incorporating websites and social media can support customer engagement. Bam Clothing illustrates how financial constraints, concerns about debt, and competitive pressures can limit digital adoption even when market conditions favor greater digitalization. American Hide demonstrates how product differentiation can remain an effective competitive strategy when digital expansion is limited. Across the three cases, the COVID-19 pandemic emerged as a common external factor influencing businesses’ approaches to digital transformation and customer engagement. Overall, the study suggests that digital tools do not create value independently; rather, their effectiveness depends on how strategically they are integrated with customer needs, competitive conditions, and a firm’s available capital.

articles_hidden.title: 한국의 복지균열 부상에 관한 연구
articles_hidden.authors: Jihun Yeo
articles_hidden.abstract:
이 연구의 목적은 경제성장담론이 지배적이던 한국정치에서 복지담론 및 전선이 부상한
요인을 규명하는 것이다. 경제 구조의 변화의 기존 규범에의 작용 및 시민사회 내 헤게모니를
둘러싼 담론투쟁 이론을 통해 2009년 무상급식부터 2012년 대선 시기 복지담론의 활성화 및
복지균열의 부상 요인을 추적하였다.
저 발달한 발전주의 복지레짐과 신자유주의 경제정책의 연계된 정책효과는 사회양극화, 빈
곤층 확대 등을 초래하였고, 이것은 ‘경제성장이 민생문제를 해결한다’는 기존의 규범을 약화
시켰다. 경제성장이 민생문제를 해결한다고 주장하고 집권한 이명박 정부의 정당성이 약화되
고, 2009년 경기교육감과 경기의회의 갈등을 계기로 무상급식 논쟁이 촉발하였다. 그리고 시
민사회 내 시민, 사회단체들은 사적이익을 공적이익으로 전환하고, 사회적 정당성을 획득하기
위한 담론투쟁을 전개한다. 이를 통해 국민여론이 무상급식 및 복지에 대한 지지로 변화하였
다. 복지에 대한 국민적 지지를 확인한 정당들은 특정 위기 국면에서 복지를 수용할 정치적
이익이 있는 세력 우선적으로 복지를 수용하게 된다. 그리고 여론, 시민사회단체들의 계속적인
압력 속에서, 선거에서 복지 이슈를 선점하기 위해 양당은 전면적으로 복지를 수용하고, 이후
이것은 경제민주화담론으로 이어지게 된다.

articles_hidden.title: A STUDY OF THE EMERGENCE OF WELFARE CLEAVAGES IN SOUTH KOREA
articles_hidden.authors: Jihun Yeo
articles_hidden.abstract:
This study aims to trace the cause of an emerging welfare cleavage under circumstances where discourses on economic growth have been dominant in Korean politics. On the basis of the theories of interaction between changing social structure and social-norm dynamics, this paper explores the causes of an emerging welfare cleavage in the case of South Korea during the late 2000s. To analyze the change of economic structure and public awareness regarding public welfare, I used the data of macro-economic indicators and public opinion polls and utilized press releases to analyze discourses of political actors.
The linked-policies effects of an immature “developmental welfare regime” and neo-liberal economic policies caused social polarization and expansion of the poverty stratum in the course of a slowdown in economic growth in the 1990s and foreign exchange crisis in 1998. The existing norm (i.e., economic growth could solve problems concerning people's livelihood) that had been maintained in the era of rapid economic growth was weakened. A conflict between an education superintendent and the Gyeonggi-do Provincial Council triggered a debate on free meals and welfare in 2009. Civil society groups were organized on a national scale, and they started a discourse struggle to replace individual interests with public interests and to obtain social legitimacy. Political parties gradually accepted the welfare issue as the primary electoral pledge for their political interests after public preference regarding growth and distribution changed when confronted with political crises.
This study draws an implication that general factors affecting Western welfare states (e.g., power alliance and democratic institutions) influence East Asian welfare states by analyzing the case of South Korean welfare politics. It means that studies of East Asian welfare states can use explanatory building blocks partly from existing welfare theories rather than stressing the exceptionalism of East Asian welfare states. However, owing to the different economic and political structures of East Asian states from those of Western countries during the formative stage of welfare states, studies of East Asian welfare states need to consider path dependency in the historical context of East Asian political economy.

articles_hidden.title: The Divergent Trajectory of Environmental Politics between  the United States and the United Kingdom
articles_hidden.authors: Jihun Yeo
articles_hidden.abstract: This study examines factors affecting the divergent environmental performances between the U.S. and the U.K. from the perspective of social movement. I look into domestic political factors, especially social movements causing different environmental performances in two countries that attain the high level of economic growth and are under the same international factors. Given that previous research dealing with domestic political factors tends to focus on political institutions and that the comparative research on the cases of the U.S. and the U.K. are limited, this research is relevant. I utilize the EPI scores, protest data, public opinion data and party manifestos. I conclude that the strong connection of environmental movement with political parties, less dispersive social movement agendas, favorable conditions from the EU and relatively weak anti-environmental movement led Britain to making a better environmental performance than the U.S.

articles_hidden.title: A study on the influence of social movements on political representation focusing on the minimum wage case in the mid- 2010s American states
articles_hidden.authors: Jihun Yeo
articles_hidden.abstract: This study examines how the social movement can contribute to improving political representation with the case of the minimum wage legislation in American states after 2012. The contribution of this research is that it’s an empirical analysis of how social movement affects the legislative process, especially in the agenda-setting stage and how social discourse takes part in this process, given the lack of research concerning determinants of the state legislation of the higher minimum wage, especially focusing on the influence of the social movement on the legislation. I analyze the impact of the social movement, measured by the media exposure frequency, on public opinion, the proposal of bills and the legislation with the national-level time serial and the state-level data. I investigate the impact of the social discourse on public opinion and the legislative process to illuminate the underlying mechanism where the social movement affects the political outcome. The social movement contributes to the improvement of political representation by spreading the social discourse, setting the agenda in civic and political society and triggering partisan politics for institutional change.

articles_hidden.title: Value-Based Adaptive Reuse: Design and Initial Testing of a Serious-Game Prototype
articles_hidden.authors: Fatemeh Hedieh Arfa
articles_hidden.abstract: Adaptive reuse of heritage buildings requires stakeholders, and more specifically, architects to navigate interdependent questions of heritage significance, contemporary function, environmental performance, community benefit, financial feasibility, and approval of other stakeholders (developers, investors, and regulators). Process models can structure these questions, yet conventional validation methods reveal only part of how practitioners move between them under constraint. This paper presents the design and pilot testing of Architect's Design Challenge, a tabletop serious-game prototype developed to explore professional decision-making in adaptive reuse and to examine the practical legibility of the Effective Adaptive Reuse of Heritage Buildings (EARHB) process model. Players progress through six stations, allocate limited resources, select action cards, respond to stakeholder requirements, and construct a design proposition using four predefined project-value categories represented by coloured components. Two formative test rounds, involving students and architects, were organised around introduction, gameplay, and debriefing. The tests indicated that the prototype could stimulate explicit discussion of priorities, sequencing, resource allocation, and trade-offs. They also revealed a central design tension: abstraction supported strategic play but sometimes weakened correspondence with professional practice, particularly for expert players. The study contributes a transparent mapping between research constructs and game mechanics, identifies requirements for future validation, and shows how serious gaming could make selected moments of value recognition, translation into design choices, negotiation, and revision observable within a simulated decision pathway. The evidence is exploratory. It does not establish learning effects, behavioural validity, or transfer to real projects.

articles_hidden.title: The Cultural Integration of Wellbeing Practices (CIWP) Framework: Conditions of Possibility Through Design
articles_hidden.authors: Carolina Andrea Cárdenas Fernández
articles_hidden.abstract:
The gap between knowing about wellbeing and practicing it constitutes a central challenge for research in design and public health. This article proposes the Cultural Integration of Wellbeing Practices (CIWP) Framework, a conceptual framework developed through Research through Design that articulates five dimensions—connection with meaningful values, situated opportunities, appropriation, everyday sustainability, and social legitimacy—to understand the conditions that support the incorporation of evidence-based wellbeing practices into everyday life and, eventually, into culture. Through a retrospective reading of the Wellbeing Practices in Waiting Spaces (WPWS) Framework, the article shows how these conditions can be translated into concrete design decisions through a situated activation mechanism, operationalized through three interdependent components—spatiotemporal conditions, human capacities, and visual mediation devices—and five design principles. The crosswalk indicates that WPWS provides direct operational expression to three of the five CIWP dimensions—situated opportunities, appropriation, and everyday sustainability—while connection with meaningful values and social legitimacy remain open dimensions that require processes beyond the visual mediation device itself. CIWP is offered as a transferable conceptual architecture—not as a fixed configuration—whose value will be tested through future operationalizations in contexts other than waiting spaces.

Keywords: cultural integration of wellbeing practices; conditions of possibility; salutogenesis; interdisciplinarity for wellbeing; design for wellbeing promotion; Trauma-informed design; Research through Design; situated activation.

articles_hidden.title: Understanding children’s housing in Australia: a data framework
articles_hidden.authors: Amy Clair; Emma Baker; Lynne Giles; Claire Morey; Megan Robinson
articles_hidden.abstract: This project examines the available data on children’s housing and wellbeing and current policy in Australia to highlight how housing affects children’s health and development. It provides policymakers with a guide to the different housing situations children face, identifies significant knowledge gaps and related risks, and proposes priorities for policy-relevant data collection and evidence development. The impacts of Australia’s housing crisis on children have received less attention than for other population groups. Accessible data collections rarely focus on them. Yet households with children are particularly affected by poor quality and insecure housing, and children’s physical vulnerability and dependence on caregivers increases the related risks to their wellbeing. This underscores the need for stronger data insights to support earlier intervention, better targeting and more accountable policy for children.

articles_hidden.title: The lived experience of climate change: a story of one piece of land in Dhaka. Engagement and impact report
articles_hidden.authors: Joanne C. Jordan
articles_hidden.abstract:
This report evaluates the engagement and impact of a research project examining the everyday realities of climate change for low-income communities in Dhaka, Bangladesh. Based on research with more than 600 residents of the Duaripara informal settlement, the project explored how climate change affects daily life, how land tenure shapes vulnerability and adaptation, and the strategies residents use to respond.

To communicate these findings beyond academic audiences, the project partnered with the University of Dhaka’s Department of Theatre and Performance Studies to develop an interactive Pot Gan, a traditional Bengali performance combining music, drama, images and dance. Drawing directly on participants’ testimonies, the performances aimed to make the lived experience of climate change accessible to diverse audiences, including informal-settlement residents, academics, policymakers and practitioners.

Three live performances attracted 634 attendees. Survey findings indicated strong engagement: 100% of respondents considered the Pot Gan useful for raising climate-change awareness, 92% agreed that focusing on everyday experiences was an effective way to communicate climate change, and 83% reported learning something new or changing how they thought about the issue. The project also produced thirteen videos, including a documentary and filmed performance, which reached at least 126,873 viewers. Overall, the findings demonstrate the potential of participatory theatre, storytelling and film to communicate climate research, centre the knowledge of frontline communities, and encourage wider reflection on climate-change policy, practice and communication.

articles_hidden.title: Measuring Christian Nationalism: The Value of Self-Identification
articles_hidden.authors: Amy Grauley; Zachary Lien; Alena Smith; Priscilla Ziegler
articles_hidden.abstract: Scholars typically measure Christian nationalism (CN) using agreement with policy positions or statements linking Christianity to American identity, yet rarely consider whether individuals explicitly self-identify as Christian nationalists. This paper evaluates the analytic value of self-identification by comparing it to scale-based measures of CN. Using data from the Cooperative Election Study (CES), the Public Religion Research Institute (PRRI), and open-ended survey responses, we distinguish between individuals who self-identify as Christian nationalists, those who score high on CN scales but reject the label, and those who reject CN as both an identity and a worldview. We show that CN identity and CN belief are related but distinct, and that self-identification matters most when CN belief is low. Among low-belief respondents, adopting the CN label is associated with markedly different political attitudes, while at high levels of CN belief, identity adds little explanatory power beyond belief. These findings highlight limits of worldview-based measures and demonstrate the value of incorporating identity into the study of Christian nationalism.

articles_hidden.title: Toward an Intersectional Occupational Health Framework: Psychosocial Conditions as Allocated Exposures
articles_hidden.authors: Iara Teixeira
articles_hidden.abstract: Occupational health research treats psychosocial working conditions either as features of a job or as traits that help workers cope. This article proposes the Intersectional Occupational Health (IOH) framework, which instead treats these conditions as exposures that labor regimes allocate to differently positioned workers. Drawing on vulnerability theory and the sociology of work, the framework argues that a worker's psychosocial profile records where that worker has been placed, since who meets high-strain conditions, and for how long, is set by law, immigration rules, and welfare systems. On this reading, the uneven spread of these conditions measures a process that produces vulnerability rather than a tally of how well workers cope. The framework follows the path from social position to health outcome, and it treats a sound intervention as one that redistributes exposure rather than one that raises the average. Two cases, domestic work in Southern Europe and platform delivery in Germany, ground a set of recommendations for governments, ranging from household labor inspection to an enforceable presumption of employment.

articles_hidden.title: From humanitarian design to design for social innovation: a comparative experiment activating reflexivity on coloniality and power dynamics.
articles_hidden.authors: Riccardo Torta; Marco Andrea Finardi; Abigail Turinayo; Victor Muwonge Semaganda; Marco Gobetti
articles_hidden.abstract:
This meta-research originates from two experiences of the first two authors, who respectively worked on a Humanitarian Design (HD) project in Uganda with Design Without Borders and on a Design for Social Innovation (DSI) project in Italy with Polimi DESIS Lab. Similar tensions emerged from both contexts regarding the relationship between the design teams and the communities engaged, highlighting the risk of perpetuating systemic oppression and epistemic injustice. To explore these imbalances, the teams were engaged in two sets of sessions, activating reflexivity on social structures embedded in their practices, to uncover potential dynamics rooted in coloniality and power.

Where the Ugandan HD project served as a testbed for the approach and three reflexive tools, the sessions within the Italian project confirmed the initial proposition, showing the potentially broad impact of the application of reflexivity on oppressive dynamics within DSI projects. This experiment uncovered the risks entailed by engaging with local communities, raised issues about urbanity and rurality, different forms of knowledge and models of development, challenging the conception of modernity and recognising these foundational elements of coloniality even in a European context.

Considering the exploratory nature of this research, the intent is to provide grounding for future critical inquiries within the wider DSI community, demonstrating the need to rethink current design practices from a liberatory and relational perspective.

articles_hidden.title: Occupational AI Exposure and the Reconfiguration of Class Inequalities in Perceived Job Insecurity
articles_hidden.authors: Daniela Bellani; Honorata Bogusz; samuel plach
articles_hidden.abstract: Research on AI and inequality has focused primarily on employment, wages, productivity, and task displacement, while less is known about how occupational AI exposure is associated with workers’ subjective insecurity and how these concerns are distributed across social classes. This study examines perceived job insecurity among employed workers in Europe, distinguishing quantitative insecurity - fear of job loss - from qualitative insecurity - fear of an undesirable change in the work situation. We use the 2024 European Working Conditions Survey, linked to an occupation-level measure of potential AI exposure, to examine whether the class pattern of AI-related insecurity mirrors the conventional class gradient in perceived job insecurity. Manual workers report the highest average fear of job loss, but the positive association between occupational AI exposure and job-loss fear is concentrated among higher- and lower-grade service workers and is weak or absent among manual workers. By contrast, occupational AI exposure shows a positive association with fear of undesirable job change, but this outcome displays no recurrent class pattern. Exploratory analyses show that the service-class association with job-loss fear is especially visible among tertiary-educated and older workers and among those who do not report using AI directly at work, while cross-national estimates indicate that the pattern appears across several institutional contexts.  The findings suggest that occupational AI exposure may reconfigure rather than sim-ply reproduce existing inequalities in insecurity, as the workers reporting the highest baseline insecurity are not those among whom the association with AI exposure is most pronounced

articles_hidden.title: Knowledge to action in alternative crisis response: Examining alignment and misalignment between evidence and practice
articles_hidden.authors: Megan Wheeler Rowe; Claire Ryder; Amanda Mathew; Jenny Angela Hui; Brandon Barksdale; Leyna Lowe; Andrew David Eaton
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Alternative crisis response models have rapidly emerged to reorganize mental health crisis care away from traditional police-led responses. It is important to explore whether the existing evidence base on co-response and civilian-led models aligns with the perspectives of those closest to the field.
Aims: This study examined points of alignment and misalignment between synthesized evidence from two scoping reviews and the lived, practice-based, and systems-level knowledge of key informants in alternative crisis response.
Methods: From August-December 2025, 33 crisis response key informants in Canada and the United States participated in semi-structured interviews prompted by the scoping reviews. Data were analyzed using directed qualitative content analysis, with 13 sensitizing domains regarding key processes of co-response and civilian-led models.
Results. Participants strongly aligned with reducing police involvement and developing distinct crisis response teams. Misalignment most often appeared as contextualization or extension, especially around police involvement, interprofessional collaboration, team composition, local service capacity, and public narratives. Domains related to monitoring, evaluation, and model variation had high counts of no available data.
Conclusions: Findings suggest that evidence on alternative crisis response is broadly resonant but requires contextualization to reflect the realities of practice and the sustainability needs of a rapidly evolving field.
