articles_hidden.title: Older adults without a partner and adult children in Finland
articles_hidden.authors: INVEST Flagship; alyona artamonova; Mirkka Danielsbacka
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Core-kinless older adults, i.e., those lacking a partner and children, represent a potentially vulnerable group. However, the whole population-level research devoted to this group remains scarce.
Objectives: This study estimates the prevalence, sociodemographic characteristics, and geographic distribution of core-kinless adults in Finland, with attention to variation across ethnolinguistic groups of Finnish, Swedish, and other language speakers.
Methods: We used register data covering the entire population aged 65 and over in 2024 (N = 1,328,732) and descriptive analyses. Core-kinlessness was defined as the absence of both a registered co-residing partner and any living children registered in Finland. 
Results: In total, 11.6% of older adults in Finland were core-kinless. Prevalence was 11.3% among Finnish-speaking, 10.3% among Swedish-speaking, and 30.5% among other language-speaking individuals. Migration background in general, being male among Finnish-speaking as well as being female, being older and having lower education among other language-speaking individuals are the characteristics of this group. The positive associations between municipal core-kinlessness and i) demographic dependency ratio, ii) the mortality rate among older adults and iii) the rate of home care clients confirm that municipalities where these older adults are concentrated also face greater demographic and service pressures.
Contribution: This study provides the first register-based national estimates of core-kinlessness in Finland, demonstrating that survey data underestimate this group. The findings offer evidence for targeted care planning at the individual and municipality levels.

articles_hidden.title: Exploitation-based social class, class consciousness and political participation
articles_hidden.authors: Agata Anita Troost; Jaap Nieuwenhuis; Jonathan J.B. Mijs
articles_hidden.abstract:
Departing from recent discussions about social class and relational inequality, we investigate the idea of the power antagonism between the workers and capitalists, and the implications of this antagonism for political participation. While the popular sociological occupation- and income-based schemes can measure social mobility within the existing economic conditions, social class based on exploitation is more relevant for measuring political empowerment. We adopt a quantitative empirical approach to analyse the class structure, class consciousness, and their associations with political behaviour including voting, direct political action and trade union membership.    
We recreate E.O. Wright’s exploitation-based class scheme (1985) with new survey data collected by us in the Netherlands in 2024. We then test whether people’s housing market position, income, wealth and education influence their class consciousness and political actions to a similar degree as their labour market, or production processes, position captured by the class scheme. Exploitation-based social class, more than income, wealth, housing, or occupation, predicts class consciousness and shapes patterns of political participation in the Netherlands, although education remains the strongest predictor of direct political action and voting. High class consciousness only motivates some middle classes to direct political action, but all classes are similarly demotivated by feelings of political resignation and being unable to enact change. While low-skilled workers display relatively high class consciousness, they are unable to translate it into political engagement. Our findings highlight the persistent and complex role of class in contemporary society.

articles_hidden.title: Perceived Benefits of a Cosmetology-Based Self-Care Program for Family Caregivers of Older Adults with Cognitive Decline: An Exploratory Qualitative Study
articles_hidden.authors: Riko Nakayama; Hana Sakurai; Fumiko Miyamae; Mutsuko Okamura; Chiaki Ura; Tsuyoshi Okamura; Tomoko Wakui
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Family caregivers of older adults with cognitive decline often have limited opportunities for self-care. Objective: This study explored the perceived benefits of a cosmetology-based self-care program for family caregivers of community-dwelling older adults with cognitive decline. Methods: A qualitative descriptive study was conducted with family caregivers in a community setting in Tokyo, Japan. Participants attended a cosmetology-based session that included light physical activity, skincare, and makeup. Data were collected using free-response questionnaire and focus group interviews and analyzed using inductive content analysis.
Results: Eight family caregivers were included in the analysis. Inductive qualitative content analysis identified three main categories: (1) emotional relief and enjoyment through shared experience, (2) heightened self-awareness and reorientation toward the self, and (3) emerging motivation for self-care and reframing of caregiving. Participants described relaxation, recognition of accumulated fatigue and neglected personal needs, and reassurance and connection through interactions with other caregivers.

articles_hidden.title: THE HORMUZ STRAIT DISRUPTION AND PAYMENT DELAYS IN INDIAN TRADE FINANCE: A Time-Series Analysis of Banking Sector Vulnerability (2019-2024)
articles_hidden.authors: Jainish Bhagat
articles_hidden.abstract: The Hormuz Strait—through which 21% of global petroleum trade passes—experienced significant geopolitical tensions from 2019-2024, creating disruptions to maritime commerce and financial flows. This paper provides a detailed empirical analysis of how these disruptions affected payment cycles in Indian trade finance and banking. Using Reserve Bank of India (RBI) data, port statistics, and transaction-level banking records (2019-2024, N=18,547 trade credit facilities), we employ time-series analysis, distributed lag models, and shock analysis to quantify the relationship between Hormuz disruptions and payment delays. Key findings: (1) Trade finance payment delays increased by an average of 8.3 days (95% CI: 6.1-10.5) following Hormuz tension announcements; (2) Letter of Credit (LC) issuance costs rose by 42-67 basis points; (3) Banks increased collateral requirements by 12-18%, contracting working capital availability by ₹4,200-6,800 crores; (4) The shock effect persisted for 90-120 days post-incident, with heterogeneous impacts across firm sizes (SMEs experienced 2.1x higher delays than large enterprises). Our analysis reveals that geopolitical shocks in maritime chokepoints generate significant financial friction in emerging market trade finance systems, with particular vulnerability among smaller firms lacking working capital buffers. We propose targeted policy interventions including development of trade credit insurance mechanisms, geographic diversification of banking relationships, and central bank communication frameworks for predictable intervention during crises.

articles_hidden.title: A National Portrait of Life Course Marital and Cohabiting History
articles_hidden.authors: Yiang Li; Kyung Won Choi
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objectives
Partnership histories encompass the duration, timing, and sequence of marital and cohabiting relationships that accumulate across the life course. Taking advantage of detailed cohabitation history data available in The National Social Life and Health and Aging Project (NSHAP), this paper constructs older adults’ partnership histories and describes variation across gender, race and ethnicity, and social class. It also examines the associations between partnership histories and health outcomes.  
Methods
Using NSHAP Rounds 1 through 4, we harmonized retrospective marriage and cohabitation records for 6,618 respondents and constructed measures of union counts, timing, duration, sequence, and dissolution, with 7-, 11-, and 14-category classifications. We evaluated missingness and consistency, summarized sociodemographic differences, and illustrated associations with three health outcomes.
Results
Older adults married to their first spouse (37.7%) and widowed (14.9%) comprise over half of the sample. Yet divorce and cohabitation are also common in older adults’ partnership histories, with over one third of the sample reporting having ever divorced (38.5%) and having ever cohabited before a marriage (36.7%). Partnership histories involving union disruption, never marrying, and cohabitation are associated with differences in self-rated health, depressive symptoms, and functional limitations relative to continuous first marriage. 
Discussion
The partnership history data available in NSHAP provides a novel opportunity for researchers to examine the significance of intimate relationships accumulated across the life course for health and aging beyond marital histories alone or current relationship status.

articles_hidden.title: El contrato que cambia de manos: la cesión de la posición contractual en el derecho comparado y su silencio en el derecho chileno (revisión de un estudio de 2023 a la luz del Code civil reformado y del Código Civil y Comercial argentino)
articles_hidden.authors: Andrés Gabriel Varas Quijón
articles_hidden.abstract:
Este trabajo revisa y pone al día, desde la perspectiva chilena, un estudio del propio autor de
2023 sobre la cesión de contrato: la transferencia de la calidad de parte —créditos, deudas, potestades y
cargas— que uno de los contratantes hace a un tercero. El paisaje comparado cambió de raíz: Francia
codificó la figura en los artículos 1216 a 1216-3 del Code (reforma de 2016), zanjando por ley el duelo entre
monismo y dualismo; Argentina la reguló en los artículos 1636 a 1640 del Código Civil y Comercial (2015);
Italia la consagra desde 1942 y Alemania la practica como construcción jurisprudencial; los Principios
UNIDROIT y los PECL la reciben como derecho uniforme. Chile, en cambio, mantiene el silencio: islas de
cesión legal sin archipiélago, una doctrina clásica que la negó por la incesibilidad de la deuda y una práctica
—promesas inmobiliarias, suministro, concesiones, carteras de contratos— que la celebra a diario sin
régimen. El artículo demuestra la admisibilidad de la figura en el derecho chileno sobre el artículo 1545,
propone su régimen supletorio (consentimiento del cedido como condición de eficacia liberatoria, cesión
perfecta e imperfecta, oponibilidad por las reglas de la cesión de créditos, excepciones y suerte de las
garantías) y constata una vindicación: la regla de las garantías de terceros que aquel estudio de 2023
defendía es hoy texto expreso en el artículo 1640 argentino y en el 1216-3 francés. Cierra con un decálogo
del cedente prudente. La tesis: lo que el consentimiento ató, el consentimiento puede hacer circular — y el
derecho chileno merece un texto que lo diga.
Palabras clave: cesión de contrato — posición contractual — cesión de créditos — asunción de deudas —
artículos 1216 a 1216-3 del Código Civil francés — artículos 1636 a 1640 del Código Civil y Comercial
argentino — consentimiento del cedido — cesión perfecta e imperfecta — garantías de terceros — libertad
contractual — artículo 1545 — derecho comparado.

articles_hidden.title: Psychological Readiness, Innovation Management, and the Adoption of Sustainable Agriculture: An Extended Theory of Planned Behaviour Model of Food Security among Smallholder Farmers in Climate-Vulnerable Bangladesh
articles_hidden.authors: Enamul Haque; M. Nasim Reza; Nurul Islam Nepo; Syed M. Ali Reza; Solaiman Chowdhury; Atikur Rahman
articles_hidden.abstract: This study examines the psychological and managerial factors that influence the adoption of sustainable agricultural practices (SA) and household food security (FS) in climate-vulnerable regions of Bangladesh. Drawing on an integrated framework that combines the Extended Theory of Planned Behaviour (ETPB) with Innovation Diffusion Theory (IDT), the study analyses a refined sample of 380 smallholder farmers using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM). Unlike earlier models that confounded institutional and individual respondents, this study isolates the psychological readiness of primary producers by restricting the quantitative sample to active smallholders. The results show that climate change beliefs exert a significant positive effect on attitude, subjective norms, and perceived behavioural control, and that these socio-cognitive constructs in turn positively predict sustainable behavioural intention. Both behavioural intention and perceived behavioural control significantly influence the adoption of sustainable agriculture, which subsequently enhances food security. Individual innovation management further contributes to both the adoption of sustainable agriculture and food security outcomes. The findings underscore the importance of aligning the psychological readiness of individual farmers with the institutional readiness of the wider innovation system, offering a holistic basis for designing rural development strategies in climate-stressed agrarian economies.

articles_hidden.title: Legitimacy Without Exit: Why Voluntary Alternatives to the State Lose to Involuntary Ones
articles_hidden.authors: Tymur Kisielov
articles_hidden.abstract:
Discourse on the future of the state usually treats voluntary alternatives (network states, micronations, charter cities) and involuntary reconfigurations of political identity (civilizational-state rhetoric, corporate infrastructural control) as one phenomenon — "the state losing its monopoly." This paper argues the frame conflates two structurally different processes and proposes a testable thesis: a new political container's durable legitimacy — from an offshore platform to a state itself — depends not on the voluntariness of its formation, but on whether it inherits an existing power's legitimating apparatus, secures that power's patronage, or independently builds comparable governance competence.

The thesis is tested on controlled comparisons rather than mismatched object types: unpatronized claimants (Sealand, Republic of Minerva, Liberland, Próspera, Ciudad Morazán) against patronized de facto states of the same type (Abkhazia, Transnistria, Northern Cyprus), backed by a systematic dataset of all 34 de facto states, 1945–2011, including the author's own reanalysis of its raw data, and re-tested on an independent second dataset (Kursani, 2023) where patronage showed no statistical link to legitimacy. A further check replacing a blunt democracy proxy with a variable matching the paper's own institutional argument (party-ban severity, V-Dem data) found the regime-type confound more robust, not less — reported honestly rather than as a convenient result. Negotiated decolonization is compared with unilateral declarations of independence across three post-communist federations (Bunce, 1999) and illustratively via Rhodesia and the 2023–2024 collapse of Nagorno-Karabakh, where patron withdrawal itself proved to be a product of internal delegitimation inside the patron state. For micronations, lacking any peer-reviewed dataset, the paper builds its own coding of all 81 documented cases (0/81 with a patron, 0/81 with confirmed recognition). Two cases the mechanism explains only partially are addressed directly: the USSR's collapse despite one of history's highest documented exit costs, and the breakdown of Sweden's neo-corporatist model. The causal mechanism (Weberian legitimacy via Hirschmanian exit/voice/loyalty) is marked as interpretation, not fact, and is empirically hard to distinguish from simple patronized power; open survey data on four de facto states offers a first partial, substantive test of this distinction.

The thesis is probabilistic, not universal: no single future case falsifies it — a pattern across independent cases is required. The paper addresses three potential counterexamples (neo-corporatism, EU constitutional patriotism, universal basic income) and twelve explicitly unresolved debates, presenting none as settled consensus.

articles_hidden.title: Exclusion by inclusion: How diverse sex/gender measures can inadvertently contribute to the exclusion of beyond-binary respondents from survey-based research
articles_hidden.authors: Leonie C Steckermeier; Alba María Kugelmeier López; Stephanie Hess
articles_hidden.abstract:
This paper illustrates how the inclusion of beyond-binary gender measures in large-scale population surveys can inadvertently contribute to the exclusion of the very populations they aim to represent. Recent international and EU efforts to integrate more inclusive sex and gender measures in surveys aim to improve data collection for evidence-based policymaking. While best practices in operationalization, reporting, and data protection have received substantial attention, the potential challenges of making sex/gender minorities identifiable in survey data remain largely overlooked. 
Based on examples from three established surveys in political and social science research—the European Social Survey, the International Social Survey Programme, and the Eurobarometer—we illustrate how more inclusive gender measures can render beyond-binary respondents vulnerable to exclusion, due to questionnaire design, data protection practices, and methodological challenges arising from their small numbers. We conclude with recommendations for questionnaire design and routing, data collection and documentation, and the analytical treatment of beyond-binary respondents.

articles_hidden.title: EDUCAÇÃO SEXUAL NO ENSINO MÉDIO: IMPACTOS DA AUSÊNCIA DE CONHECIMENTO SEXUAL
articles_hidden.authors: Ruan Vinícius Lopes Da Silva
articles_hidden.abstract: A educação sexual constitui um pilar fundamental no desenvolvimento integral de adolescentes, abordando não apenas aspectos biológicos da sexualidade, mas também dimensões psicossociais, relacionais e éticas. No contexto do ensino médio, a ausência ou precariedade de um ensino sexual abrangente e de qualidade gera lacunas de conhecimento que tornam os estudantes mais vulneráveis a riscos e desafios relacionados à saúde sexual e reprodutiva, como a gravidez não planejada, as infecções sexualmente transmissíveis (ISTs), além de comprometer a percepção sobre consentimento, limites corporais e relacionamentos saudáveis. Este trabalho tem como objetivo investigar os impactos decorrentes da carência de uma educação sexual introdutória adequada, identificando as principais dúvidas, fontes de informação e necessidades de orientação entre os jovens. A justificativa fundamenta-se na urgência de tratar a saúde sexual como uma pauta de saúde pública e desenvolvimento humano, ressaltando o papel mediador da escola e a importância de abordagens pedagógicas interdisciplinares, estruturadas e contextualizadas na promoção do bem-estar e da cidadania no ambiente escolar.

articles_hidden.title: Sociotechnical Transition and Uncertainty in the Lithium Mining Industry: Technologies, Politics and Transparency
articles_hidden.authors: Iván Ojeda-Pereira; Sebastián Herrera-León; Marcelo Lufin; Fernando Campos-Medina
articles_hidden.abstract: Technological transitions in extractive industries are commonly assessed through technical and environmental performance, whilst their social and ethical dimensions receive little systematic attention. This article addresses that gap through the adoption of direct lithium extraction (DLE) technologies in Chile, the world’s second largest lithium producer and the leading producer from salt flats. The National Lithium Strategy promotes these technologies as a response to social tensions over the use of water and brine in fragile ecosystems, and the conditions of their implementation remain open. Drawing on interdisciplinary work between the engineering sciences and the social sciences, we ask which technological and social uncertainties experts identify in this transition. Two expert workshops were held with 20 participants from industry, the State and academia, and their contributions were examined through inductive qualitative content analysis. The findings show five uncertainties: (i) there is no consensus on which technologies will be implemented or on the criteria for choosing them; (ii) the effects of brine reinjection lack conclusive evidence; (iii) the role and agency of the State remain undetermined; (iv) no mapping exists of the actors regarded as valid participants in the debate; and (v) there is no agreement on how the social sustainability of this change should be measured. We propose five public information infrastructures as a design response to these uncertainties, whilst acknowledging that transparency is a necessary but not sufficient condition for ethical sociotechnical governance in the extractive industries of the Global South.

articles_hidden.title: Using Geospatial modeling to Understand Spatial Job Access for TANF Recipients
articles_hidden.authors: Gabriel Appiah; Arthi Rao; Latrice Rollins; Andrew Cooper; Alex Camardelle
articles_hidden.abstract: Access to employment is central to the effectiveness of the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) program, yet job opportunities are unevenly distributed across space. This study examines county-level patterns in job accessibility for TANF recipients, with a particular focus on African American (AA) populations and urban–rural differences in commuting behavior. Using data from Alabama, Louisiana, Georgia, Virginia, and the District of Columbia, we construct gravity-based job accessibility indices for high-, median-, and low-paying employment. Distance-decay parameters are empirically estimated from Longitudinal Employer–Household Dynamics (LEHD) commuting flows, allowing travel sensitivity to vary between urban and rural areas. Accessibility measures are computed for total employment and compared across AA TANF - majority and minority counties. We then apply hierarchical clustering to county-level indicators of accessibility, socioeconomic vulnerability, housing and mobility constraints, and TANF caseload composition. The resulting seven-cluster typology reveals distinct TANF opportunity contexts, including counties characterized by severe spatial isolation and others where high accessibility coexists with persistent disadvantage. These findings highlight the limitations of uniform TANF work requirements and support the need for place-sensitive, equity-oriented welfare policy design.

articles_hidden.authors: Amt für Statistik und Wahlen Stadt Leipzig
articles_hidden.abstract: Regelmäßige vierteljährliche Veröffentlichung: Textbeiträge zu ausgewählten Themen (Teil 1) und statistische Daten (Teil 2)

articles_hidden.title: Cost of Safe Abortion Care in Kigali, Rwanda: A Retrospective Analysis of Hospital Billing Data
articles_hidden.authors: Melina Gaju Uwamwezi; Stephanie Küng; Ritah Mukashyaka; Allan Higiro; Lawrence Rugema; Alain Favina; Aflodis Kagaba; Margaret Giorgio
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Rwanda has progressively liberalized its abortion law over the past decade, most recently through a 2024 order decentralizing safe abortion care (SAC) to health centres and clinics. However, the financial accessibility of legally provided SAC remains poorly understood; existing cost evidence in Rwanda focuses on post-abortion care, which has a different clinical and cost profile. This study assessed the direct facility-based costs of legally provided SAC in Kigali, Rwanda.
Methods: We conducted a retrospective analysis of itemized hospital billing data from the Health Development Initiative (HDI) Rwanda for 236 SAC patients treated at 4 public and 1 private facility in Kigali from June 2022 to December 2024, including total costs and costs across 9 categories. Total and category-specific costs were compared by visit type using the Mann-Whitney U test; associations between characteristics and visit type were assessed using chi-square or Fisher's exact tests.
Results: The median total cost of a SAC visit was 62,353 RWF (range: 282-256,100 RWF). Consultation fees (94.9%) and commodities (92.8%) were incurred by nearly all patients, while medical acts (76.3%), imaging (75.4%), and laboratory tests (70.8%) were also common. Two-thirds of patients (66.1%) were treated as inpatients, with a mean length of stay of 3.1 days. Inpatients incurred more than twice the mean total cost of outpatients (96,572 RWF vs. 47,167 RWF; p<0.001), driven by significantly higher costs across most categories except examinations. Visit type varied by age group (p=0.014); adolescents (15-18 years) were least likely to be inpatients.
Conclusions: Legally provided SAC in Kigali carries a non-trivial financial burden relative to household income, and heavy reliance on inpatient care, inconsistent with WHO guidance, inflates costs. These findings point to the need for a standardized SAC tariff, alignment of admission practices with evidence-based guidelines, and further research into drivers of cost variation in abortion care access.

articles_hidden.title: the em—dash fails to em–erge: a registered null result for U+2014 in Polish and an exploratory function-word shift in 60,275 Sejm interpellations, 2015–2025
articles_hidden.authors: PRZEMYSŁAW CZUMA
articles_hidden.abstract:
Since the release of ChatGPT (30 November 2022) a belief has spread that the em-dash "—" reveals text written with the help of a language model. This preregistered study tested that claim on 60,275 single-author written parliamentary questions (interpelacje) submitted to the Polish Sejm between 2015 and 2025. The decision rule was registered on OSF before the data were seen.

The cue does not work in Polish. The registered hypothesis was not confirmed: in the decisive cell the share of documents containing an em-dash rose by 1.73 percentage points, but the confidence interval of that difference includes zero (−4.44 to +8.07 pp), so the second condition of the two-part decision rule was not satisfied, and three registered disconfirmation conditions fired. Follow-up tests point to the cause: models writing in Polish, and machine-translation flows, put a shorter dash there – the en-dash "–". The marker is anglocentric and is not suitable for Polish.

An exploratory analysis measured something else: the frequency of Polish closed-class words (conjunctions, prepositions, particles) that a writer does not choose consciously. The reference point was an independently published corpus of Polish human-written and model-written texts, frozen together with its reading rule before measurement. From 2024 the distribution of these words moves toward the profile of the models (rank correlation rho = +0.368; 95% CI +0.228 to +0.461), while at a placebo date – the 2019 change of parliamentary term, where no such effect is expected – it does not move at all (−0.070; difference +0.438, +0.221 to +0.611). The shift survives four term-change controls.

The change is small but widespread, and that is the correct description of its strength. Inside a single parliamentary office it is barely visible (median rho +0.125), yet it points the same way in 61 of 84 offices that could be measured separately (72.6%, one-sided p = 2·10⁻⁵), against 53.8% at the control date, which is what chance produces.

There is no sudden jump at the date of the ChatGPT release. The change becomes visible in 2024 and unambiguous in 2025, and the shape of the transition (ramp versus late step) is not identified. The result describes a shift across a whole population of documents and allows no statement about the authorship of any single document or about any individual member of parliament. It does not establish a cause: changes in office staff, in subject matter and in editing practice remain possible explanations alongside tools. An independent reimplementation, with no access to the author's code, reproduced the corpus, the deduplication, the author panel and the headline analyses from raw HTML down.

articles_hidden.title: Locating the evidence: a Minimal Geography scale for the geographic locatability of research, demonstrated on LGBTQ+ fertility studies
articles_hidden.authors: Boyana Buyuklieva; Hanxi Wang; Martin Gozzi
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Reporting checklists require a setting to be stated, but are satisfied at any granularity: "conducted in the United States" complies while remaining placeless. Access to fertility care and assisted reproduction depends heavily on where people live, and evidence-appraisal frameworks (GRADE indirectness, CERQual relevance) presuppose that a study's setting can be ascertained. Yet how practically locatable a study's evidence is (i.e., whether a reader can tell where it was produced) has rarely been treated as a measurable property. 

Methods: We introduce Minimal Geography (MG), a five-point ordinal scale rating how precisely a study's evidence can be resolved to a real place, from placeless (MG 1) to a named local site whose own population was sampled (MG 5), with a self-contained codebook. We applied it to 116 primary studies of LGBTQ+ fertility intentions identified through a scoping review, recording the verbatim source excerpt behind every rating. A second coder blind-rated a 10% sample.

Results: Geographic locatability is strongly bimodal: 91 of 116 studies (78.4%) are vague (MG 1-2), two sit at the anonymised midpoint, and 23 (19.8%) are clearly locatable (MG 4-5). We observe the locatable minority to be concentrated in named specialist clinics, predominantly in the US. Quantitative studies were far more often locatable than qualitative ones, reflecting how each design recruits. Blind double-coding showed 75% band agreement and a linearly weighted kappa of 0.68. The instrument, codebook, and dataset are openly deposited (doi:10.5281/zenodo.21496412) to invite comparator corpora test of whether our observed bimodal distribution is distinctive or typical.

Conclusions: Reporting compliance is not locatability and we discuss the coarsest-safe-level reporting (CSLR). We conclude that CSLR must state the most specific geography compatible with participant safety, and importantly, flag deliberate masking.

articles_hidden.title: Local Governance and Maternal Health Outcomes: A Case Study of Nepal’s Decentralized Health Reforms
articles_hidden.authors: Nirmal Gurung
articles_hidden.abstract: Nepal has made impressive gains in reducing maternal deaths in the last 25 years. The maternal mortality ratio dropped from 539 to 151 deaths per 100,000 live births between 1996 and 2022. During the same period, skilled birth attendance rose from 9% to 77% and institutional delivery from 8% to 79%. Alongside these improvements have been major reforms in the health system, especially decentralization. The Local Self-Governance Act of 1999 assigned local bodies responsibility of health facilities. In 2015, the Constitution of Nepal established a federal system with 753 local governments responsible for basic health services. This case study explores the role of decentralization in improving maternal health outcomes in Nepal. It draws on data from national demographic and health surveys, policy documents and global health estimates. The study finds that decentralization was helpful as it increased local resources, improved community participation, strengthened accountability and supported national programs such as the Aama Program. However, the challenges remain and include inadequate local capacity, lack of clarity of roles, quality gaps and disparities between rich and poor, urban and rural and between provinces. Nepal’s experience provides important lessons for other countries looking to reduce maternal mortality rates through devolved health systems.

articles_hidden.title: Housing and the False Promise of Abundance
articles_hidden.authors: Sophie Bandarkar; Tahir de Noronha; Maximilian Buchholz
articles_hidden.abstract: Following the publication of Klein and Thompson’s (2025) remarkably popular book, Abundance has emerged as the key diagnosis and remedy for America’s housing affordability challenges. The book’s central argument, along with allied academic work, is that deregulation will substantially increase housing supply and in turn meaningfully improve housing affordability. We argue this framework rests on inconclusive and contested empirical ground. First, a thorough literature review of relevant research demonstrates the links between deregulation, supply, and prices are much weaker and more complex than abundance advocates suggest. Second, returning to descriptive evidence shows that the basic facts which motivate the abundance argument are also contested. There is no incontrovertible evidence of a major supply shortage in the U.S. The abundance movement’s hyper fixation on housing supply and deregulation risks foreclosing possibilities for other targeted interventions that have a greater potential for remedying the affordability crisis.

articles_hidden.title: A Replication Framework for Observational Research: From Specification Restriction to Specification Expansion
articles_hidden.authors: Jonathan Ben-Menachem; Ari Galper; Nic Fishman
articles_hidden.abstract: Sociology has remained relatively insulated from debates about the "replication crisis." Heeding calls to consider replication more deeply, we introduce a distinction between two types of research reforms that have emerged in the wake of the crisis: specification-restricting and specification-expanding reforms. Specification restriction is often promoted as a way to increase the repeatability of research findings by controlling false positives. We argue that this statistical justification is less compelling in observational contexts---where the assumptions licensing false-positive control are harder to sustain and rigid ex ante analytical commitments can instead enshrine fragile specifications---than in experimental contexts. We further argue that apparently low replication rates do not necessarily imply a high prevalence of false positive findings. Instead, we propose a replication framework centered on specification-expanding reforms, stronger incentives for confirmatory research, and meta-analysis. This approach equips sociologists to assess the repeatability of findings and build a more cumulative discipline.

articles_hidden.title: No drain, no gain? The problems with unequal exchange
articles_hidden.authors: Niall Reddy; Virgilio Urbina Lazardi
articles_hidden.abstract: Recent empirical work (Hickel et al. 2021, 2022) appears to show that the Global South is being ``drained" of resources and value on a vast scale through unequal exchange (UE) and/or ecologically unequal exchange (EUE). Headline estimates of the aggregate value of this extraction have been widely taken to substantiate two politico-normative issues: that the South is systematically exploited through international price formation, and that this drain constitutes a binding constraint on Southern development and a precondition for Northern prosperity. This paper argues that neither claim is supported by the new measurement agenda. It shows that new drain estimates rely on untenable premises -- in particular, claims of North-South parity in productivity and export composition. Stipped of these assumptions, Hickel et al's method can't yield a counterfactual ``fair price" vector, meaning that their estimates are ungrounded and indeterminate. Moreover, even granting the estimates, they do not sustain an underdevelopment thesis. In standard growth regressions and long-run club-convergence tests, higher measured drain is non-negative and often positively associated with Southern growth once conventional fundamentals are controlled for. The paper suggests ways that research in ecological economics can be placed on a firmer conceptual footing.

articles_hidden.title: Examining reasoning in process recording: An exploration of instructions in guiding students towards social work competencies
articles_hidden.authors: Jemel P. Aguilar; Debra Crist; Huangshu Xu; Maria Mangiameli; Shirin Sultana
articles_hidden.abstract: This article describes an exploratory study of a sample of process recording instructions from field manuals used by social work programs. Process recording in this study is conceptualized as a mechanism for assessing competency-based education, in which students, supervisors, and faculty members gain insight into students’ professional reasoning procedures, strengths, and weaknesses. Ideally, instructions should lead students to demonstrate reasoning aligned with social work competencies; supervisors would examine students’ reasoning, and field faculty members can assess field-seminar-level professional reasoning. Using logic models to analyze how the instructions work, we found considerable gaps in the logic of process recording instructions that do not align with the goals of competency-based education or social work’s emphasis on evidence-based practice. We found that undefined learning mechanisms, assumed integration, unstructured evaluation, and vague learning goals hampered the connection between process recording and competency-based education. We discuss the implications of these findings for social work’s emphasis on competency-based education, evidence-based practice, and professional reasoning, and we call for further research on process recording in social work education.

articles_hidden.title: Using Theories of Social Exchange and Status Construction in Mixed-Group Cooperative Learning Practices
articles_hidden.authors: Joseph M Quinn; Valerie K. Barron
articles_hidden.abstract: Classroom group work can reproduce broader social inequalities when status-based expectations shape whose contributions are valued or ignored. Intergroup Contact Theory (IGCT) proposes conditions of contact that can reduce prejudice but provides limited explanation of the interactional processes through which these conditions generate cooperation or alter status expectations. We integrate IGCT with the Theory of Social Commitments and Status Construction Theory to identify micro-level structural mechanisms that instructors can leverage to create more equitable intergroup interactions that can also enable social learning and bias reduction toward underrepresented groups. Drawing on these theories, we propose a three-part strategy: forming strategically mixed-status groups, designing highly joint tasks that create mutual dependence and shared responsibility, and providing process-centered feedback that rewards cooperation while making diverse forms of competence visible. Together, these practices can foster positive relational experiences, disrupt status-based performance expectations, and reduce inequities in participation and evaluation. We argue that incorporating these interactional mechanisms into the IGCT framework strengthens contact-based approaches to cooperative learning and offers instructors a theoretically grounded strategy for making diverse classrooms sites of prosocial intergroup contact and positive meaning-making about categorically dissimilar peers.

articles_hidden.title: Deleting the call does not delete the evidence: a within-recording validity test for passive-acoustic whale-call detection benchmarks
articles_hidden.authors: Dharit Shah
articles_hidden.abstract:
Problem. Detection benchmarks in passive acoustic monitoring are built from temporally
clustered events, so a period that contained an annotated call may differ from a period that
never did in more than the call itself.

Diagnostic. We delete the annotated call from a positive window, replace that interval
with background from the same window, leave every other sample intact, and measure ablation
AUC — P(call-removed positive scores above true negative). Null 0.5; higher means more
shortcut. A splice control applies the identical operator to windows that never held a call.

Findings. On the DCLDE 2013 right whale upcall benchmark the trained detector scores a
same-recording ablation AUC of 0.635 [0.552, 0.710] — both arms from the same 15-minute
source recording, 887-window negative pool — against the 0.5 no-shortcut null. The splice
control sits at the null (0.483 [0.455, 0.510], 889-window frozen stimulus), so the cut is not
the effect. Pooled values are larger and partly a between-recording contrast; they are
reported beside the headline and never instead of it. Two spectrogram representations never
trained on the task reproduce the within-recording separability under a fitted logistic
readout (raw tile 0.688 [0.606, 0.772]; random projection 0.687 [0.598, 0.770]), so
detectors inherit it rather than create it. It replicates across 30 SanctSound day-sites
(same-day-site 0.566 [0.528, 0.604]). Five preregistered mechanisms — hard negatives,
receptive field, context access, capacity, temporally matched negatives — were tested and all
five failed: we report a measurement, not a mechanism. A preregistered second benchmark in
a killer whale regime, its clustering precondition verified in advance, did not detect the
effect: zero of four evaluable provider × species cells survive multiplicity correction on the
same-recording-day estimand.

Recommendation. Report ablation AUC beside average precision, and name its estimand.

---

articles_hidden.title: Population Development In The Roman Empire
articles_hidden.authors: Ulrik Vachet Rasmussen
articles_hidden.abstract:
This paper addresses the problem of reconstructing the population development of 
the Roman Republic and the Roman Empire despite the scarcity, inconsistency, and indirect 
nature of the available evidence. Its primary objective is to produce a continuous population 
curve spanning from 508 BC to AD 395, which is internally consistent in the assumptions of 
underlying growth and other factors over time. To achieve this, the study critically integrates 
multiple methodological approaches, including Beloch’s area-and-density estimates, Lo 
Cascio’s revisions, and Scheidel’s demographic critiques, alongside archaeological, 
economic, and comparative demographic evidence.  
By combining these methods and cross-validating their results, a coherent framework 
is established for estimating both population levels and growth rates. It adopts moderate 
empire-wide growth assumptions, 2-3‰ annually, while allowing for significant variation 
between core and newly incorporated territories. This enables the interpolation between key 
chronological benchmarks and the extension of estimates across periods lacking direct 
evidence.  
The resulting reconstruction yields a continuous demographic trajectory showing the 
full consequences of the growth assumptions.

articles_hidden.title: AGIR: a theory-based framework to evaluate impacts of game-based interventions for sustainability transitions
articles_hidden.authors: Sylvain Dernat; Clara Fiorio; Myriam Grillot; Gilles Martel; Médulline Terrier-Gesbert
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Game-based interventions (GBI) increasingly embed simulation games within broader transformation processes targeting sustainability challenges. However, evaluation frameworks remain predominantly session-centred and learning-oriented, offering limited insight into how in-game dynamics translate into real-world practice change. This gap is particularly critical for GBI seeking to influence behaviours, coordination mechanisms, and institutional trajectories over extended time horizons.
Method: This article proposes a framework for Assessing Game-based Interventions in Real-world contexts (AGIR), a theory-based tool designed to assess multi-level change processes in GBI. Drawing on program evaluation theory, behavioural sciences, and simulation and gaming research, AGIR structures evaluation across six levels (L0–L5): from game design and in-session dynamics (L0–L1), through learning (L2) and behavioural change (L3), to practice change (L4) and transformative systemic impacts (L5). The framework explicitly models mechanisms, contextual factors, and temporal pathways linking intervention design to sustainability outcomes.
Contribution: AGIR’s contribution is threefold: it reinforces theoretical foundations by explicitly connecting design choices with evaluation concepts; it provides a comprehensive reference point enabling comparison across contexts through standardised levels and hypothesised mechanisms; and it functions as a formative accompaniment tool supporting ex ante hypothesis formulation, in itinere adjustments, and ex post impact analysis. By shifting evaluation from end-point outcome measurement toward process-oriented understanding of contribution, AGIR addresses longstanding calls for rigorous yet practical frameworks adapted to complex, action-oriented interventions.
Conclusion: The framework is designed for adaptability across intervention contexts while preserving theoretical coherence. Though resource-intensive, AGIR offers practitioners and researchers a structured approach to assess whether and how GBI contribute to sustainable change, fostering an evaluation culture essential for demonstrating the impact potential of simulation games.

articles_hidden.title: Exposure to Homeless Shelters and Support for Policy Remedies
articles_hidden.authors: Jacob Brown; Adrian C. Pietrzak; Alexander Sahn
articles_hidden.abstract: American cities have rapidly built new homeless service facilities - shelters and supportive housing - over the last decade in response to rising homelessness. We study how voters react to these facilities once they are built and operational, leveraging a pair of statewide ballot propositions to fund new homeless services in California. We find that voters living closest to newly opened facilities became more supportive of spending on homelessness services compared to those living further away. We argue and show using survey data that new shelters increase the salience of homelessness in the minds of voters, driving positive policy feedback. We rule out the effects of positive changes in street conditions, improvements over existing land-uses, and financial self-interest as alternative mechanisms. Our findings suggest that voters can reward policy action and that NIMBY opposition may be more prospective than retrospective.

articles_hidden.title: Stakeholders’ perceptions of AI-assisted obstetric ultrasound in rural and urban Kenya: a qualitative study
articles_hidden.authors: Emmah Ng'ang'a
articles_hidden.abstract:
Introduction: As artificial intelligence (AI) tools gain popularity in maternal healthcare, understanding community and health system perspectives is essential for inclusive and ethical implementation. This study explores stakeholder views on AI-supported ultrasound for pregnancy care in Kenya, that emphasized trust, equity, system readiness, and the importance of community engagement.
Methods: A qualitative study was conducted in two Kenyan settings: Nairobi (urban) and Kilifi County (rural). Fifty-five semi-structured interviews and three focus group discussions were conducted with pregnant women, partners, healthcare providers, Sub-County Health Management Teams (SCHMTs), Community Health Promoters (CHPs), and community and religious leaders. Data were analyzed inductively using grounded theory principles.
Results: The participants viewed AI with cautious optimism. While many welcomed its potential to enhance diagnostic accuracy and access, concerns emerged around data privacy, informed consent, quality of care, and over-automation. Reliability or trust was linked to transparency, human oversight, and the use of local data. Participants highlighted structural challenges, including weak referral systems and staffing gaps, raising questions about the health system’s readiness to integrate AI. Fears of equity and “pilotitis”, short-lived projects without sustainability, were also expressed.
Conclusion: Findings from this study suggest that AI implementation in maternal health may need to go beyond technology development and deployment.  Developers and relevant stakeholders may need to consider co-designing with communities, alignment with health system realities, and the integration of ethical principles such as equity, accountability, and transparency.

articles_hidden.title: Sovereign ESG and the Hydrological Constraint: Rethinking the Determinants of Water Stress
articles_hidden.authors: Aneta Kargol-Wasiluk; Katarzyna Lewkowicz-Grzegorczyk; Carlo Drago; Alberto Costantiello; Angelo Leogrande
articles_hidden.abstract: Water stress is read in the sustainability literature as either a physical or an institutional outcome, but the two readings have never been tested jointly within the sovereign ESG framework. This paper estimates the environmental, social and governance determinants of the freshwater withdrawal-to-availability ratio across up to 170 economies observed between 2002 and 2022, drawing on the World Bank Sovereign ESG Data Portal. Three equations share the same dependent variable and differ only in the pillar supplying the regressors. Each is developed along three tracks: panel econometrics, comprising pooled OLS, fixed and random effects, between and weighted least squares estimators and two-step difference and system GMM; a competition among six clustering algorithms assessed on eleven internal validity indices; and a competition among six supervised learners used to validate the specification rather than to forecast. Water stress proves overwhelmingly structural, with 99.1 per cent of its log variance lying between countries. The governance block explains 38 per cent of cross-sectional and 4 per cent of within-country variation. The level of institutional quality, measured as the first principal component of four Worldwide Governance Indicators and absorbing 91.9 per cent of their variance, is unrelated to water stress in every estimator; its composition is not, with accountability relative to state capacity carrying a coefficient of −1.10 between countries. The dominant predictor across all three tracks is the female-to-male labour force participation ratio, whose partial dependence reveals a discontinuity concentrated in a five-point interval. Under cross-validation with countries held out, no flexible learner outperforms ordinary least squares.

articles_hidden.title: Designing Biodiversity Credit Schemes: Combining Implementation Scale and Certification Metrics for Farmers' Participation
articles_hidden.authors: Kota Mameno; Masayuki Sato; Yasushi Shoji; Takahiro KUBO
articles_hidden.abstract: Biodiversity credit schemes have gained attention as a mechanism for mobilizing private finance for biodiversity conservation. As primary suppliers of biodiversity outcomes in agricultural landscapes, farmers’ willingness to participate is critical to the success of these schemes. However, little is known about farmers' preferences for biodiversity credit designs, particularly regarding metrics used to certify biodiversity outcomes and the spatial scales at which biodiversity credits are implemented. To our knowledge, this is the first study to provide empirical evidence on how certification metrics and implementation scales influence farmers' preferences for voluntary biodiversity credit schemes. A discrete choice experiment with a latent class model were applied to examine Japanese farmers' preferences for alternative biodiversity credit schemes. The results showed substantial heterogeneity in farmers' willingness to participate in biodiversity credit schemes, with approximately half of the farmers belonging to a participation-averse group. In both groups, implementation scale was the primary determinant of participation decisions. Farmers preferred individual farmland scale implementation over coordinated participation. Certification metric exerted limited influence on participation decisions, suggesting that ecosystem-based credits can be implemented without substantially reducing farmers' willingness to participate. Additional bonuses increased participation among farmers already willing to participate, but had little effect on initially reluctant farmers . Membership analysis indicated that willingness to participate was positively associated with biodiversity policy awareness, biodiversity-friendly farming practices, pro-biodiversity attitudes, and expectations of branding-related benefits. Expanding voluntary biodiversity credit markets, therefore, requires not only financial compensation but also information provision, demonstration projects, and communication of potential market benefits.

articles_hidden.title: Statistischer Quartalsbericht 3/2022
articles_hidden.authors: Amt für Statistik und Wahlen Stadt Leipzig
articles_hidden.abstract: Regelmäßige vierteljährliche Veröffentlichung: Textbeiträge zu ausgewählten Themen (Teil 1) und statistische Daten (Teil 2)

articles_hidden.title: The empirically inscrutable climate-economy relationship
articles_hidden.authors: Finbar Curtin; Matthew G. Burgess
articles_hidden.abstract: Empirical models of the macro-level climate-economy relationship project climate change impacts ranging from trivial to catastrophic. This wide range suggests identification challenges. Here, we show that such models indeed face identification challenges that are axiomatic and irreducible. The climate-economy relationship has qualitatively important variation across space and time, due to complex regional heterogeneity and affluence-driven adaptation, among other factors. Empirical models must assume away some of this variation to preserve degrees of freedom. Influential observations caused by economic disasters and miracles, along with low signal-to-noise ratios, create additional challenges. We illustrate these challenges theoretically and then empirically by replicating and sensitivity testing prominent climate-econometric studies. The estimation challenges create economically meaningful sensitivities and fragilities. We recommend a cautious and uncertainty-emphasizing approach to applying climate econometrics to public and private decision-making. Importantly, however, our analysis does not dismiss the existence of a negative carbon externality nor economically beneficial efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions.

articles_hidden.title: Recycling fabricated narratives about an early-career researcher is not a valid defence: a reply to Caruso et al.
articles_hidden.authors: Saul Newman
articles_hidden.abstract: Here, I respond to Caruso et al. regarding their recent paper defending the Sardinian blue zone. Despite the brevity of the work, the paper relies on an extensive set of straw-man arguments, falsehoods, and libels. These appear deployed as little more than a coping mechanism in the absence of arguments, and the errors and misrepresentations are tallied below. However, rather than restrict the reply to raising these issues, it seems appropriate to use this venue to highlight some of the far deeper problems with the blue zones concept as a scientific, social, and financial enterprise. That is, it seems worthwhile to address this paper on a few scientific failings first, and its many logical and ethical failures second.

articles_hidden.title: Antidemocratic Policing in America: The Institutionalization of Historical Trauma
articles_hidden.authors: Angelina Inesia-Forde
articles_hidden.abstract: Countries have begun reforms to align their police forces with a democratic policing culture. Despite significant progress, the United States has failed to fulfill a key aspect of democratic governance: democratic policing. Consequently, the gap between law and departmental policy, and policing culture continues to widen. This study aims to contribute to Forde’s theory by applying the antidemocratic framework at the institutional level to describe policing practices that have received widespread attention by exploring police misconduct through a power lens of regressive strategies. The sample includes extant literature and data from exonerees. This study uses an innovative methodology grounded in the GQI and integrated with grounded theory analysis to answer the research question: How does Forde’s antidemocratic framework, rooted in historical trauma and political demoralization, manifest in contemporary police-civilian interactions? Forde’s antidemocratic concepts—nativism, social distinctions, misinformation, fear, dehumanization, and subjugation—frame this study. The framework underpins the understanding of antidemocratic policing and how micro-level disempowerment and macro-historical trauma (colonialism) converge in modern institutions. The primary finding is that antidemocratic practices are institutionalized. Future studies on democratic policing could inform the field and policymakers on whether misconduct, particularly excessive use of force, is a symptom of police demoralization.

articles_hidden.title: Classification testing: A new framework for drawing qualitative conclusions from quantitative estimates
articles_hidden.authors: Andrew C. Eggers; Zikai Li
articles_hidden.abstract: Social scientists rely on hypothesis testing to support their research conclusions, but the standard tests are designed for testing one hypothesis rather than adjudicating between rival possibilities.  We develop a new framework, "classification testing", as an alternative. Instead of selecting one hypothesis to test, a researcher conducting a classification test decides what qualitative distinctions ("classes") are most substantively relevant; the test either assigns the estimand to a class  with error control similar to that of a conventional hypothesis test,  or declares the result inconclusive. We argue that classification testing is superior to current practice not just when the objective is to adjudicate between rival possibilities but also when there is one research hypothesis to be tested, because classification testing exposes that hypothesis to refutation.  We illustrate the framework by applying it to a well-known media experiment and offer an R package to aid in implementation.

articles_hidden.title: Energy Transitions and Political Transformation: Evidence from the Shale Oil Revolution
articles_hidden.authors: Christian J. Baehr
articles_hidden.abstract: An outstanding question in climate politics is how oil-exporting governments will respond to a global clean energy transition. I argue that persistent oil revenue shortfalls strain social contracts in oil-exporting states, compelling governments to enact targeted governance reforms under tightening fiscal constraints. I exploit the sudden emergence of the U.S. shale oil industry as an exogenous supply shock to examine how oil exporters adjust to sustained revenue declines. Using a difference-in-differences design, I find governments exposed to the shale revolution did not respond through broad political liberalization or public goods retrenchment and instead adopted targeted reforms. Systematic evidence on specific reform uptake and a case study indicate these reforms protected public goods provision and curtailed private capture, consistent with a political survival motive driven by rising mass public threats. The findings point to an asymmetric resource curse, in which oil shortfalls generate political responses distinct from those produced by windfalls.

articles_hidden.title: Infrastructural Mothering under Ukrainian Displacement
articles_hidden.authors: Tamara Fedotiuk; Lisa Marzano; Emma Victoria Ward; Valentyna Voloshyna; Antonia Bifulco
articles_hidden.abstract: This article examines how displaced Ukrainian mothers with children organise adaptation under ongoing war, institutional fragmentation and temporal uncertainty. Drawing on 30 semi-structured interviews with internally displaced mothers in Ukraine and Ukrainian mothers displaced to the United Kingdom, alongside four focus groups with service providers, the study compares how two displacement regimes shape care work, service access and future planning. The findings show that mothers’ care-centred aspirations motivate infrastructural mothering: unpaid emotional, administrative, educational and relational labour through which they create conditions for children’s stabilisation. As mothers direct time, skills and resources towards children, their employment, language learning, psychosocial recovery, belonging and future-planning capabilities may become suspended. By conceptualising adaptation as relational  and care-mediated, the study advances refugee integration scholarship, feminist care theory, and comparative forced migration research by demonstrating how distinct displacement regimes reorganise maternal labour and unevenly distribute adaptation opportunities within displaced families.

articles_hidden.title: Black Feminist Social Work: Centering Black Women's Knowledge in Social Work Theory, Education, Research, Policy, and Practice
articles_hidden.authors: Vanessa M. Talley
articles_hidden.abstract: Social work acknowledges Black Feminist Thought as a framework and praxis, yet the profession has not established a social work framework that explicitly centers Black women’s epistemologies as foundational to education, theory, research, policy, and practice. Although social work maintains a historical commitment to social justice, person-in-environment, and human rights perspectives, dominant theories and knowledge systems continue to reflect Eurocentric assumptions regarding knowledge production and professional expertise. This article introduces Black Feminist Social Work (BFSW) as a conceptual framework that centers Black women’s individual and collective lived experiences, intellectual traditions, historical resistance, and knowledge to inform social work theory, education, research, policy, and practice. Drawing upon Black feminism, Black Feminist Thought, Womanism, Intersectionality, and the profession’s ethical commitments, the BFSW framework proposes a necessary shift from positioning Black women primarily as a population to be studied to recognizing them as producers of transformative knowledge. This article introduces four organizing principles, the Four C’s: Centering, Contextualizing, Co-Creating, and Changing, as foundational processes for Black Feminist Social Work and discusses the implications for curriculum development, clinical practice, research methodologies, policy advocacy, and future scholarship. Rather than positioning Black Feminist Social Work as an alternative specialization, this framework argues that centering Black women’s knowledge expands the social work profession’s capacity to pursue equity, liberation, and social transformation.

articles_hidden.title: Social Stressors and Gender Inequalities in Post-COVID-19 Syndrome: Evidence from a Population-Based Cohort in Germany
articles_hidden.authors: Nicolai Gröpler; Meike Dirks; Andrea Hildebrandt; Thomas Keil; Ann-Kathrin Knak; Sina M. Pütz; Mandy Roheger; Antje Wulff; Gundula Zoch
articles_hidden.abstract: Women report post-COVID-19 symptoms more often and more severely than men, but the contribu-tion of socially structured stress exposure to this difference is largely unexamined. Social stressors are particularly relevant in the context of infectious diseases such as COVID-19, as they may influ-ence health outcomes through hormonal processes and their impact on immune function. This study examines whether stressors and coping resources in work and family life are associated with post-COVID-19 symptoms and whether they account for sex/gender differences in it. Integrating psycho-logical and sociological perspectives with contemporary medical knowledge, we hypothesized that social stressors influence the development of post-COVID-19 symptoms and, in part, explain sex and other socio-economic disparities. We utilized data from population-based COVIDOM study within the German National Pandemic Cohort Network (NAPKON-POP, 2020-23, N=2,941), recruited by local health authorities on the basis of a positive PCR test irrespective of symptom burden. 86 per-cent of women vs 76 of men reported at least one persistent symptom complex, with women report-ing a 4point higher Post-COVID Syndrome Score on the 0-59 scale. Results from stepwise linear regression models confirm statistically significant sex differences in symptom burden that mostly withstood adjustment for medical composition and social stressors. Accounting for perceived stress and resilience attenuated them by roughly one third, leaving a substantial and statistically significant residual gap between women and men. Overall, these findings suggest that sex differences in post-COVID-19 symptoms are bound up with differences in stress exposure and coping resources, and, thus, complement biological explanations.

articles_hidden.title: Guarantee Fulfillment, Asymmetry, and Desire Shutdown: Exploratory Multi-Level Evidence and Measurement Development for an Existential Guarantee System Theory
articles_hidden.authors: Yong Yue
articles_hidden.abstract:
Terror Management Theory (TMT) holds that cultural worldviews buffer death anxiety by offering symbolic immortality and literal safety. But what happens when the worldview's promises fail to deliver? This paper introduces the Existential Guarantee System (EGS) theory, which proposes that societies function as guarantee systems: they promise rewards (stable income, status, family, housing) in exchange for participation, and threaten punishments (poverty, shame, exclusion) for exit. The Guarantee Fulfillment Rate (GFR) is the perceived rate at which these promises actually deliver. EGS predicts that when GFR declines, positive promise expectations decay first while negative sanction expectations persist — producing a Guarantee Asymmetry Index (GAI) that tracks the divergence, and downstream consequences including desire shutdown and post-goal disappointment.

We present multi-level exploratory evidence for EGS across three measurement levels: (1) a preregistered pilot study (N = 68 after exclusion) developing a GFR/GAI scale with good internal consistency (GFR α = .94; desire-shutdown α = .84; sanction α = .88) and exploratory signals consistent with all five preregistered hypotheses, including a mechanical-overlap decomposition showing the asymmetry signal is direct (|r(GFR–S)| = .37 < |r(GFR–P)| = .78; composite GFR–GAI r = −.69); (2) an individual-level proxy test in a national probability sample (CGSS 2023, N = 11,326): opportunity-fairness beliefs predict ideal children count (β = .209, p < .0001) with the steepest slope in the youngest cohort (18–35: β = .306) — an age-gradient double confirmation (youngest cohorts hold the lowest fulfillment expectations and respond most strongly); (3) macro-level panel evidence (38 countries, 35 years): youth unemployment (an absolute-fulfillment proxy) predicts fertility decline (β = −.0099, p = .0012, two-way fixed effects), with relative-inequality proxies (Gini) showing the opposite direction — fulfillment failure is about absolute attainability, not relative distribution.

All results are honestly graded: directional predictions matched expectations across all tests, but construct-level inference is limited to exploratory signals pending a fully powered preregistered study (N ≥ 300). The paper is positioned as the first empirical proof-of-concept and measurement-development wave for EGS — not as confirmatory validation. We discuss the Korea paradox (world-lowest fertility with low youth unemployment) as explained by housing costs (price-to-income ratio 24.4, top 12% globally), and the theoretical and practical implications for AI companionship as a novel guarantee system.

articles_hidden.title: Sociotechnical Transition and Uncertainty in the Lithium Mining Industry: Technologies, Politics and Transparency
articles_hidden.authors: Iván Ojeda-Pereira; Sebastián Herrera-León; Marcelo Lufin; Fernando Campos-Medina
articles_hidden.abstract: Technological transitions in extractive industries are commonly assessed through technical and environmental performance, whilst their social and ethical dimensions receive little systematic attention. This article addresses that gap through the adoption of direct lithium extraction (DLE) technologies in Chile, the world’s second largest lithium producer and the leading producer from salt flats. The National Lithium Strategy promotes these technologies as a response to social tensions over the use of water and brine in fragile ecosystems, and the conditions of their implementation remain open. Drawing on interdisciplinary work between the engineering sciences and the social sciences, we ask which technological and social uncertainties experts identify in this transition. Two expert workshops were held with 20 participants from industry, the State and academia, and their contributions were examined through inductive qualitative content analysis. The findings show five uncertainties: (i) there is no consensus on which technologies will be implemented or on the criteria for choosing them; (ii) the effects of brine reinjection lack conclusive evidence; (iii) the role and agency of the State remain undetermined; (iv) no mapping exists of the actors regarded as valid participants in the debate; and (v) there is no agreement on how the social sustainability of this change should be measured. We propose five public information infrastructures as a design response to these uncertainties, whilst acknowledging that transparency is a necessary but not sufficient condition for ethical sociotechnical governance in the extractive industries of the Global South.
